nodes.description: Because real-world inversion is imperfect and under-determined, rather than learning decoders that map neural representations directly to stimuli, the approach takes a meta-learning view and learns a model to perform in-context functional inversion across a variable number of voxels.

nodes.name: Decoding is structured as a two-stage hierarchical in-context process
nodes.description: Following the meta-learning reformulation, the decoding process first estimates per-voxel encoder weights in-context, then builds a decoder that performs contextual integration across multiple voxels/brain regions for subject-specific functional inversion.

nodes.name: This two-stage process enables fine-tuning-free generalization with small new-subject data
nodes.description: The two-stage in-context learning process enables generalization to novel subjects without any fine-tuning and with relatively small amounts of new subject data.

components.name: Two-stage hierarchical in-context mechanism

nodes.name: Stage 1: per-voxel encoder parameter estimation via in-context learning
nodes.description: In Stage 1, a pretrained BrainCoRL-based transformer infers per-voxel response function weights from a context of stimulus-activation pairs for a single voxel, repeated independently across all voxels of interest, without any fine-tuning.

nodes.name: Stage 2: context tokens combine encoder parameters with activations
nodes.description: In Stage 2, each voxel is represented by a context token formed by concatenating its Stage-1 predicted response parameters with the measured activation for the novel stimulus.

nodes.name: Stage 2 transformer performs aggregated functional inversion across voxels
nodes.description: A learned transformer takes the voxel context (tokens across a variable number of voxels, up to the subject's total voxel count) as input and approximates the aggregated inverse mapping to estimate the image embedding.

nodes.name: No anatomical alignment or stimulus overlap required
nodes.description: Because the approach constructs context per-subject over voxels rather than aligning voxels anatomically across subjects, it requires neither anatomical alignment nor stimulus overlap across subjects, and flexibly adapts to novel subjects with different voxel counts.

nodes.name: Variable context length requires order- and length-invariant model design
nodes.description: Because the number and identity of available voxels varies across subjects, the model must be invariant to both the number and order of voxel tokens, unlike typical sequential language-model transformers.

nodes.name: Logit scaling and omitted positional embeddings achieve length/order invariance
nodes.description: To accommodate variable-length contexts and remain length/order invariant, the model adopts logit scaling (scaling attention logits by log of context length) and omits positional embeddings, using a [CLS] token for output.

nodes.name: Hybrid cosine-contrastive loss balances alignment and discriminability
nodes.description: A hybrid loss combining a cosine embedding loss with an InfoNCE contrastive loss is used to jointly achieve fine-grained embedding alignment and instance-level discriminability.

components.name: Three-stage training strategy

nodes.name: Training strategy inspired by LLM pipelines
nodes.description: The training strategy is inspired by LLM pipelines and consists of three stages: pretraining, contextual extension, and supervised fine-tuning.

nodes.name: Pretraining uses synthetic analysis-by-synthesis data, not real fMRI
nodes.description: The pretraining stage adopts an analysis-by-synthesis scheme using no real fMRI data, simulating a large population of voxels via sampled synthetic weights and Gaussian-noise beta responses, with a fixed voxel-context size of 200.

nodes.name: Contextual extension introduces variable-length context robustness
nodes.description: The second stage introduces variable-length contexts by randomly drawing the number of voxels from Uniform(200, 4000), enabling the model to become robust to changes in context length.

nodes.name: Final fine-tuning stage uses real fMRI measurements for fast, effective adaptation
nodes.description: In the final stage, the model is optimized on real fMRI measurements using subject-specific beta values and voxel response parameters from the pretrained BrainCoRL across different image-context sizes, leading to fast convergence and effective adaptation to biologically realistic neural signals.

components.name: Results: unseen-subject decoding, contextual scaling, and ablations

nodes.name: BrainCoDec-200 outperforms MindEye2 and TGBD on unseen subjects
nodes.description: Across all four leave-one-subject-out conditions on NSD, BrainCoDec (using only 200 of 9,000 support images) delivers consistently stronger Top-1/Top-5 retrieval performance than both MindEye2 (with anatomical alignment) and TGBD, without any subject-specific fine-tuning or retraining.

nodes.name: Decoding performance scales positively with image and voxel context size
nodes.description: Increasing either the image context size (Stage 1) or the voxel context size (Stage 2) consistently improves decoding performance across all subjects and visual backbones (CLIP, DINO, SigLIP).

nodes.name: A small context (200 images, 4000 voxels) achieves near-full-context accuracy
nodes.description: With only 200 images and 4,000 voxels, BrainCoDec achieves similar accuracy to inference using the full context (all ~9,000 images and all higher-visual-cortex voxels), showing the framework needs only a fraction of subject-specific data for comparable performance.

nodes.name: Real-data fine-tuned variants greatly outperform synthetic-only or direct-inversion baselines
nodes.description: Ablation comparing four configurations shows both fine-tuned variants (with and without subject holdout) significantly outperform pretrained-only (synthetic data) and gradient-based direct-inversion baselines in cosine similarity.

nodes.name: Subject-holdout performance gap is marginal
nodes.description: The performance gap between training with subject holdout (novel-subject generalization scenario) versus training on seen subjects is marginal, underscoring that contextual fine-tuning -- not subject-specific training -- is what drives accurate cross-subject decoding.

components.name: Robustness to functional-region dropout

nodes.name: Category-selective ROIs are systematically masked and evaluated
nodes.description: For each semantic category (faces, places, food, words), test images eliciting the strongest activation in the corresponding functional voxels are identified, and the corresponding category-selective regions are masked out to evaluate resulting decoding performance.

nodes.name: Masking category-related ROIs causes minimal degradation for most categories
nodes.description: The model exhibits remarkable robustness to targeted regional dropout, with masking category-related ROIs leading to minimal performance degradation for most categories.

nodes.name: This indicates the model does not rely on any single functional region
nodes.description: Because masking a specific category's selective region has minimal impact, this indicates BrainCoDec does not rely on any single functional region to perform aggregated decoding, consistent with distributed representation learning.

components.name: Interpretability via attention analysis

nodes.name: Attention weights are extracted during decoding of category-specific stimuli
nodes.description: Attention weights from the last layer are extracted while decoding test images from distinct semantic categories, using the same activation-based selection criterion as the ROI-dropout analysis.

nodes.name: Learned attention maps align with known functional regions
nodes.description: Face-related stimuli elicit elevated attention in face- (FFA) and body-selective (EBA) voxels, while place-related stimuli elicit elevated attention in place-related regions (PPA, OPA, RSC), matching independent functional-localizer t-value maps.

nodes.name: This confirms the model allocates selective focus consistent with cortical semantics
nodes.description: The correspondence between learned attention patterns and known functional-localizer maps confirms that BrainCoDec learns to allocate selective focus consistent with established cortical semantics.

nodes.name: UMAP projection of attention weights shows semantic clustering across cortex
nodes.description: Projecting voxelwise attention weights across the full test set via UMAP produces clear semantic clustering (body/face-selective regions vs. scene-selective regions), mirroring known representational gradients in visual areas.

nodes.name: The model internalizes both how and where to find semantically relevant representations
nodes.description: The emergent semantic clustering in the UMAP embedding demonstrates that the model internalizes not merely how to perform functional inversion, but where to find semantically relevant neural representations.

components.name: Cross-scanner generalization on BOLD5000

nodes.name: BOLD5000 differs substantially from NSD along several axes
nodes.description: BOLD5000 was acquired on a 3T scanner (vs. NSD's 7T) with different stimulus timing, a substantially different image set, different voxel size, and a different subject pool, providing a stringent test of new-scanner adaptation.

nodes.name: The model trained on NSD is evaluated directly on BOLD5000 without additional training
nodes.description: A model trained on the four NSD subjects (no subject held out) is evaluated directly on BOLD5000 subjects using 5-fold cross-validation, without any additional training on BOLD5000 data.

nodes.name: BrainCoDec achieves strong retrieval performance despite these shifts
nodes.description: Despite the substantial scanner, timing, image-set, voxel-size, and subject-pool shifts, BrainCoDec achieves strong retrieval performance on BOLD5000, consistent across held-out subjects and image-encoder backbones.

nodes.name: A similar contextual scaling trend holds on BOLD5000
nodes.description: BrainCoDec exhibits a similar contextual scaling trend on BOLD5000 as on NSD, with retrieval performance improving as the number of in-context image-brain pairs increases.

nodes.name: This demonstrates practical value for avoiding costly per-subject/scanner retraining
nodes.description: Because the model transfers pretrained knowledge to new scanners without retraining, this is valuable in practical applications where retraining new models for new subjects or scanners is resource-intensive and time-consuming.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior generalization methods implicitly or explicitly require anatomical alignment
isolated_nodes.description: Recent approaches seeking generalization via flatmaps, 1D pooling, or surface learning implicitly (flatmaps, pooling) or explicitly (surface) require anatomical alignment, unlike this paper's approach.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior encoder-inversion decoding methods use direct solving/identification
isolated_nodes.description: Prior work reconstructing viewed images by inverting a forward model has used approaches like ordinary least squares (for simple stimuli) and similar techniques for motion direction, orientation, faces, natural images, and movies, generally matching predicted to observed brain activity and solving or identifying the solution directly, rather than learning the inversion via meta-learning.

isolated_nodes.name: ICL in LLMs may be an implicit meta-learning mechanism
isolated_nodes.description: Large language models' in-context learning capability -- adjusting behavior at inference time from prompted demonstrations without parameter updates -- may serve as an implicit meta-learning mechanism, whereby transformers develop internal adaptation procedures during pretraining.

isolated_nodes.name: NSD and BOLD5000 dataset characteristics
isolated_nodes.description: NSD is the largest available 7T neural dataset (each subject viewing ~10,000 images up to three times, four subjects S1/S2/S5/S7 completing the full scan used mainly in experiments); BOLD5000 is a 3T dataset with ~5,000 images per subject, only a subset viewed four times.

isolated_nodes.name: Data preprocessing and quality-control procedures
isolated_nodes.description: Voxelwise betas are z-scored within session and averaged across stimulus repeats; ROI definitions use a t>2 threshold from independent functional localizer data; quantitative evaluation uses an ncsnr>0.2 voxel-quality cutoff for NSD and ncsnr>0.3 for BOLD5000.

isolated_nodes.name: Evaluation uses nearest-neighbor image retrieval as the primary task
isolated_nodes.description: Cross-subject decoding is evaluated on the nearest-neighbor image retrieval task using top-1 accuracy, top-5 accuracy, mean rank, and cosine similarity, following prior evaluation protocols; the approach can be extended to full image reconstruction via pretrained generators like IP-Adapter and Stable Diffusion.

structural_reasoning: The graph closely follows BrainCoDec's own argumentative structure. C1 establishes the cross-subject variability problem as the paper's central motivating bottleneck. C2 traces the paper's key conceptual move: reframing decoding as functional inversion, identifying why naive inversion fails in practice, and using that failure to motivate the meta-learning reformulation, which is directly implemented by the two-stage hierarchical process detailed in C3 (mirroring the paper's own Stage 1 / Stage 2 structure, including the technical necessities of order/length invariance that follow directly from allowing variable voxel counts). C4 mirrors the three-stage training curriculum as an explicit, sequentially dependent pipeline. C5-C8 mirror the paper's own four-part experimental structure (SOTA comparison and scaling/ablation; ROI-dropout robustness; attention-based interpretability; cross-scanner generalization), with each results claim connected to the interpretive claim the paper draws from it (e.g., minimal ROI-dropout degradation -> distributed representation learning; attention-functional-localizer correspondence -> the model captures where as well as how). Isolated nodes are appropriately limited to related-work context, dataset/preprocessing specifications, and evaluation-metric definitions that support but are not premises within the paper's central argument chain.

nodes.name: Stationary point ambiguity
nodes.description: A stationary point can be a global minimizer, a poor local minimizer, or a saddle point; first-order information alone does not distinguish among these possibilities.

nodes.name: Near-zero gradient regions far from global solutions
nodes.description: In highly non-convex landscapes, large regions of near-zero gradient may exist far from any global solution.

nodes.name: Gradient-based methods can stagnate misleadingly
nodes.description: Algorithms following gradient-based dynamics can stagnate in near-zero-gradient regions, producing iterates certified as theoretically successful while being arbitrarily suboptimal in objective value.

nodes.name: Stationarity is a weak proxy for optimization progress
nodes.description: Because stationary points can be far from global solutions and gradient-based methods can get stuck there, stationarity-based guarantees are a weak proxy for actual optimization success.

nodes.name: Empirical gradient norm stagnation observed
nodes.description: In long training runs of modern ML models, the gradient norm has been observed not to decrease, and in some cases to increase, toward the end of training.

nodes.name: Central motivating question
nodes.description: This state of affairs motivates the central question of the paper: how to obtain global convergence guarantees for non-convex problems without relying on gradient-based dynamics and gradient-norm metrics.

nodes.name: Perturbation/noise methods remain fundamentally local
nodes.description: Escaping stationary points via explicit perturbed-gradient methods or implicit mini-batch noise typically yields guarantees that remain fundamentally local, at best ensuring convergence to approximate second-order stationary points.

nodes.name: BPM as trust-region-style ball oracle method
nodes.description: The Ball Proximal Point Method (BPM) is a trust-region-type method where each iterate is obtained by minimizing the objective over a ball of radius t centered at the current point, via the set-valued broximal operator.

nodes.name: BPM converges linearly without strong convexity
nodes.description: BPM was found to converge linearly without the strong convexity assumptions required by methods like the classical Proximal Point Method (PPM).

nodes.name: BPM can attain exact global minimum in finite steps
nodes.description: Unlike PPM with finite steps, which can only produce approximate solutions, BPM can attain the exact global minimum in a finite number of iterations using finite radii.

nodes.name: Existing BPM analyses focus on convex objectives
nodes.description: Despite BPM's strong convergence guarantees and evidence that it can handle non-convexity, existing analyses focus almost exclusively on convex objectives, with only limited non-convex treatment.

nodes.name: Paper revisits BPM to study non-convex global convergence
nodes.description: Motivated by the gap between BPM's demonstrated non-convex potential and its convex-focused existing analysis, this paper revisits BPM to identify structural conditions enabling global convergence in the non-convex setting.

nodes.name: Broximal oracle is generally intractable
nodes.description: The broximal oracle is very powerful and generally intractable: if the radius is sufficiently large, a global solution can be found in one step, meaning solving the subproblem can be as hard as solving the original problem.

nodes.name: BPM treated as conceptual tool, not practical algorithm
nodes.description: Because the broximal oracle is generally intractable, the paper treats BPM as a conceptual tool for isolating a novel class of non-convex functions for which global convergence can be established, rather than as a practical algorithm.

nodes.name: Second Brox Theorem exploits convexity
nodes.description: The original convex analysis of BPM relies on the Second Brox Theorem, which shows that for convex f there exists a coefficient such that a specific inner-product inequality holds between the current point, the broximal update, and any reference point.

nodes.name: Specializing to global minimizer yields nonnegative inner product
nodes.description: Specializing the Second Brox Theorem's inequality to the reference point being a global minimizer yields a nonnegative inner-product relation between the step direction and the direction to that minimizer.

nodes.name: Observation motivates dropping convexity, positing inequality directly
nodes.description: This observation motivates dropping convexity altogether and instead directly postulating the geometric alignment inequality as an assumption (Assumption 3.1), independent of any convexity assumption.

nodes.name: Assumption 3.1: geometric alignment condition
nodes.description: Assumption 3.1 posits that outside a t-neighborhood of the global minimizer set, the inner product between the step direction (x minus broximal update u) and the direction toward a fixed global minimizer is non-positive, i.e., the broximal step is aligned toward the global minimizer.

nodes.name: Relaxation dist(x,Xf) > t is essential for non-uniqueness
nodes.description: The relaxation restricting Assumption 3.1 to points outside the t-neighborhood of the minimizer set is essential; imposing the condition for all x would force uniqueness of the global minimizer.

nodes.name: Assumption 3.1 alone does not rule out broxtf(x)={x} away from Xf
nodes.description: Under Assumption 3.1 alone, having broxtf(x) equal to the singleton {x} does not necessarily imply that x is a global minimizer, leaving a gap that must be addressed by an additional assumption.

nodes.name: Assumption 3.2: no isolated local minima
nodes.description: Assumption 3.2 states that if the broximal operator at x is the singleton {x} (x is a strict minimizer within its own ball), then x must already be a global minimizer, ruling out 'bad' local minima detectable at scale t.

nodes.name: Definition of Broximal Aligned Functions
nodes.description: A proper, closed function belongs to the class of Broximal Aligned Functions if it satisfies both Assumption 3.1 and Assumption 3.2 for a given radius t and geometry X.

nodes.name: Non-decreasing step must be followed by strict decrease
nodes.description: Under Assumption 3.1, as long as the algorithm makes progress (x_k not equal x_{k+1}), a non-decreasing function-value step must be followed by a strict decrease at the next step.

nodes.name: Consequent separation distance bound (Lemma A.4)
nodes.description: The non-decrease-then-strict-decrease pattern implies that the distance between iterates two steps apart exceeds the radius t, formalized in Lemma A.4.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1: every second iterate separated by distance >= t
nodes.description: Building on Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, the main convergence theorem (4.1) relies on the fact that every second BPM iterate is separated by a distance of at least t, unless a global minimizer has already been reached.

nodes.name: Distances to minimizer are non-increasing
nodes.description: Theorem 4.1 shows the distances from the iterates to the global minimizer are non-increasing, with a quantified decrease of at least t^2/3 every third iterate when the current ball does not yet contain a global minimizer.

nodes.name: Finite-iteration exact global convergence
nodes.description: Theorem 4.1 concludes that after a sufficient finite number of iterations K (of order the squared initial distance over t^2), the BPM iterate is exactly a global minimizer.

nodes.name: Example 1: |x|+10sin(x) has infinitely many local minima
nodes.description: The one-dimensional function f(x) = |x| + 10*sin(x) has infinitely many local minima spaced every 2*pi, yet satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 for any radius t >= 2*pi.

nodes.name: Example 1 shows multiple local minima permitted
nodes.description: Example 1 demonstrates that the Broximal Aligned function class does not preclude the existence of multiple local minima, in contrast to classical conditions where all stationary points are globally optimal.

nodes.name: Example 2: disconnected minimizer set
nodes.description: A function with minimizer set Xf = {0, a} for a nonzero vector a is shown to belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any t > 0, despite having a disconnected minimizer set.

nodes.name: Examples 1 and 2 fail all classical conditions
nodes.description: Both Example 1 and Example 2 belong to the Broximal Aligned class for suitable t, yet fail to satisfy any of the classical generalized-convexity conditions listed in the paper's comparison table.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.1: strict quasiconvexity implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Strictly quasiconvex functions belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.2: pseudoconvexity implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Pseudoconvex functions belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.3: quasar convexity implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Functions that are zeta-quasar convex with respect to a global minimizer belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.4: aiming condition with unique minimizer implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Functions satisfying the aiming condition with a unique global minimizer belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Broximal Aligned class strictly subsumes classical non-convex frameworks
nodes.description: Because quasiconvexity, pseudoconvexity, quasar convexity, and aiming (with unique minimizer) all imply Broximal Alignment, while Examples 1 and 2 show functions in the Broximal Aligned class satisfying none of these conditions, the Broximal Aligned framework strictly generalizes these classical non-convex function classes.

nodes.name: Broximal oracle intractable for practical objectives
nodes.description: For many objectives of practical interest, particularly in modern ML, exactly minimizing f over balls B_X(x,t) is computationally intractable.

nodes.name: Approximate broximal subproblem solving
nodes.description: One practical approximation strategy is to approximately solve the broximal subproblem itself, e.g., via sampling-based approaches or an iterative method run up to prescribed accuracy.

nodes.name: Local model substitution (e.g., linearization)
nodes.description: A second practical approximation strategy replaces the original objective with a simpler local model, such as a linearized or quadratic trust-region subproblem, which is often tractable and sometimes has closed-form solutions.

nodes.name: Muon optimizer as approximate broximal step in non-Euclidean geometry
nodes.description: The Muon optimizer can be interpreted as performing approximate broximal steps by minimizing linearized local models over non-Euclidean balls induced by the spectral norm, illustrating that local-model approximations extend beyond the Euclidean setting.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-convex optimization central to ML
isolated_nodes.description: Matrix factorization, phase retrieval, representation learning, and deep neural networks all lead to objective functions with highly non-convex landscapes.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-convex problems can be NP-hard
isolated_nodes.description: Many non-convex optimization tasks are NP-hard to solve, and a number of them are NP-hard even to approximate.

isolated_nodes.name: Convex optimization has efficient global toolkit
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike non-convex optimization, convex optimization has an established toolkit for efficiently finding global minimizers.

isolated_nodes.name: Intermediate convexity relaxations
isolated_nodes.description: A number of intermediate frameworks (star convexity, quasar convexity, pseudoconvexity, quasiconvexity, invexity, variational coherence, the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, and the aiming condition) retain meaningful convergence properties for broader problem classes than convexity, each with its own limitations.

isolated_nodes.name: Special-structure tractability examples
isolated_nodes.description: Certain non-convex problems become tractable when the objective has special structure, e.g., one-layer neural networks having no spurious local minima, or SGD finding global minima in sufficiently wide over-parameterized networks.

isolated_nodes.name: Particle-based PDE methods for global non-convex solutions
isolated_nodes.description: Particle-based approaches reformulate non-convex problems as PDE-governed dynamics over measures, now admitting provable global solutions, though typically requiring an exponentially large or infinite number of particles.

isolated_nodes.name: Contribution: novel non-convex function class
isolated_nodes.description: The paper introduces a novel class of non-convex functions, Broximal Aligned Functions, defined by Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, enabling global optimization guarantees beyond gradient-based reasoning.

isolated_nodes.name: Lemma 5.1: monotone transformation preserves assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: If h satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 for radius t, then composing h with a strictly increasing scalar function g also satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 with the same t.

isolated_nodes.name: Lemma 5.2: X-orthogonal affine transformations preserve assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 are invariant under affine changes of coordinates that preserve the geometry induced by X.

isolated_nodes.name: Lemma 5.3: affine transformations of function value preserve assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: Scaling and shifting the function value (af(x)+b for a>0) preserves Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 with the same radius and minimizer set.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework intentionally conceptual, not efficient algorithm
isolated_nodes.description: The framework is intentionally conceptual since the broximal oracle is generally intractable, so the results do not directly yield efficient algorithms, motivating future work on practical approximations.

structural_reasoning: The graph is highly coherent, mirroring the paper's tightly argued theoretical structure: the motivation chain critiquing stationarity-based theory (C1) directly motivates revisiting BPM and identifying its underexplored non-convex potential (C2); the intractability of the general broximal oracle and the convex-case Second Brox Theorem motivate dropping convexity in favor of a direct geometric postulate (C3); this postulate is formalized into the two core assumptions defining the Broximal Aligned function class (C4); the main convergence theorem is derived through a clear proof chain building on these assumptions (C5); concrete examples demonstrate the class's generality beyond classical conditions (C6); formal theorems establish that classical generalized-convexity conditions are special cases (C7); and practical approximation strategies are discussed as a natural coda (C8). Edge confidence is high throughout given the paper's explicit deductive theorem-proof style and clearly stated motivational transitions between sections. The isolated-node set reflects broader contextual and background material (application domains, related relaxations, closure-property lemmas, and general framing statements) that support but are not part of the core technical dependency chain. No cycles or ambiguous directions were identified.

components.description: Motivation: legal mandate for fairness, causal fairness's advantages, and the unrealistic no-unobserved-confounding assumption.

nodes.name: Fairness legally mandated
nodes.description: Fairness of machine learning predictions is widely required by legal frameworks, notably in credit lending and law enforcement.

nodes.name: Causal fairness relates directly to legal terminology
nodes.description: Causal fairness leverages causal theory to ensure a sensitive attribute does not affect prediction outcomes, directly relating to legal terminology requiring outcome independence from sensitive attributes.

nodes.name: Existing causal fairness methods assume no unobserved confounding
nodes.description: Existing works on causally fair predictions commonly focus on settings with no unobserved confounding, assuming the causal structure is fully known.

nodes.name: No-confounding assumption is unrealistic
nodes.description: The assumption of no unobserved confounding is fairly strong and unrealistic in practice.

nodes.name: Unobserved confounding can violate causal fairness
nodes.description: Due to unobserved confounding, causal fairness may be violated, and predictions can cause harm as they may actually be unfair.

nodes.name: Prison sentence example illustrates the problem
nodes.description: In predicting prison sentences, unobserved confounders such as housing situation, family background, and birthplace can bias predictions if not accounted for, even when race is excluded and offense/crime history are controlled.

components.description: Research gap and positioning relative to related literature streams.

nodes.name: Sensitivity models exist for interventional effects only
nodes.description: Sensitivity models are common tools for partial identification under unobserved confounding, but they perform partial identification on interventional effects (level 2 of Pearl's ladder).

nodes.name: Causal fairness involves nested counterfactuals
nodes.description: Causal fairness involves nested counterfactual effects (level 3 of Pearl's ladder), which differ from the interventional effects that sensitivity models directly handle.

nodes.name: Sensitivity models not directly applicable
nodes.description: Because of the level mismatch between interventional effects and nested counterfactuals, it is not possible to directly apply existing sensitivity models to the causal fairness setting.

nodes.name: Kilbertus et al. only prior sensitivity-fairness work, but limited
nodes.description: The only prior work analyzing sensitivity of fairness to unobserved confounding (Kilbertus et al. 2019) focuses on counterfactual fairness, allows confounding only between covariates, and relies on restrictive non-linear additive noise model assumptions.

nodes.name: No work on causal fairness sensitivity to unobserved confounding
nodes.description: To the authors' knowledge, no work has analyzed the sensitivity of causal fairness specifically (as opposed to counterfactual fairness) to unobserved confounding.

nodes.name: Research gap established
nodes.description: The combination of the level mismatch, the narrow scope of prior sensitivity-fairness work, and the absence of causal-fairness-specific sensitivity analysis establishes the paper's research gap.

components.description: Standard Fairness Model setup with three sources of unobserved confounding and path-specific fairness effects.

nodes.name: Standard Fairness Model adopted
nodes.description: The paper adopts the Standard Fairness Model with data V = {A, Z, M, Y}: sensitive attribute A, observed confounders Z, mediators M, and outcome Y.

nodes.name: Three types of unobserved confounding modeled
nodes.description: The setup uniquely allows three types of unobserved confounding: direct (U_DE, between A and Y), indirect (U_IE, between A and M), and spurious (U_SE, between A and Z).

nodes.name: Path-specific effects defined
nodes.description: Path-specific causal fairness is defined via three effects: counterfactual direct effect (Ctf-DE) for A→Y, indirect effect (Ctf-IE) for A→M→Y, and spurious effect (Ctf-SE) for Z→A.

nodes.name: DE measures direct discrimination
nodes.description: Ctf-DE measures direct discrimination based on the sensitive attribute.

nodes.name: IE and SE measure indirect discrimination
nodes.description: Ctf-IE and Ctf-SE together measure indirect discrimination through factors related to the sensitive attribute, potentially acting as proxies.

nodes.name: Causal fairness achieved when effects near zero
nodes.description: Causal fairness is achieved when DE, IE, and SE are zero or close to zero, operationalized via user-defined thresholds.

components.description: From non-identifiability under confounding to the two-step bound-derivation workflow.

nodes.name: CF effects unidentifiable under unobserved confounding
nodes.description: Under unobserved confounding, the path-specific causal fairness effects (DE, IE, SE) are not identifiable from observational data, so naive estimates are biased.

nodes.name: Move from point to partial identification
nodes.description: As a remedy, the paper moves from point identification to partial identification, deriving upper and lower bounds for DE, IE, SE under a sensitivity model.

nodes.name: Step 1: counterfactual unnesting
nodes.description: Each CF is decomposed into identifiable parts and unnested (single-intervention) interventional effects, since sensitivity analysis operates on interventional (level-2) effects while CF involves nested (level-3) counterfactuals.

nodes.name: Step 2: sensitivity-model bounding
nodes.description: The unnested interventional effects are then bounded using the GMSM sensitivity model, yielding upper and lower bounds for each CF.

nodes.name: GMSM chosen for generality
nodes.description: The generalized marginal sensitivity model (GMSM) is adopted because it handles discrete mediators and both discrete/continuous outcomes, and subsumes many existing sensitivity models (e.g., MSM) as special cases.

edges.note: cross-component link from C2: level mismatch necessitates unnesting

components.description: Lemma 1 (unnesting) and the resulting sharp, general bounds of Theorem 1.

nodes.name: Lemma 1: CF as function of unidentifiable effects plus identifiable term
nodes.description: Lemma 1 shows each CF can be written as a monotonically increasing function of a sum of unidentifiable single-intervention effects plus an identifiable term q.

nodes.name: Unidentifiable effects can be bounded by sensitivity analysis
nodes.description: The unidentifiable single-intervention effects in Lemma 1's decomposition are exactly the type of effect that causal sensitivity analysis can bound.

nodes.name: Identifiable term estimable from data
nodes.description: The identifiable term q in the decomposition can be directly estimated from observational data.

nodes.name: Theorem 1: explicit bounds derived
nodes.description: Using the unnested expressions, Theorem 1 derives explicit closed-form upper and lower bounds on DE, IE, and SE under the GMSM for binary sensitive attribute A and discrete Z.

nodes.name: Bounds are distribution/SCM agnostic
nodes.description: Theorem 1's bounds are independent of the distribution and dimensionality of unobserved confounders and specific SCM formulations, applying to discrete, categorical, and continuous outcomes.

nodes.name: Bounds are sharp (Remark 2)
nodes.description: The derived bounds are sharp/optimal, meaning the supremum/infimum equality in the bound definition holds exactly.

nodes.name: Wider intervals indicate greater sensitivity
nodes.description: The wider the interval between CF+ and CF-, the more sensitive the path-specific effect is to unobserved confounding, giving less confidence in unconfounded estimates.

components.description: From bounds to a robust fair-prediction training objective.

nodes.name: CF bounds used to limit worst-case unfairness
nodes.description: Since path-specific causal fairness is unidentifiable under confounding, the derived bounds CF+ and CF- are used to limit the worst-case (maximum deviation from zero) unfairness of the prediction model.

nodes.name: Predicted outcome substituted into bound formulas
nodes.description: To train the model, P±(y|z,m,a) in the bounds is replaced by the non-random predicted outcome f_θ(a,z,m), requiring only estimation of P±(m|z,a) via pre-trained density estimators.

nodes.name: Constrained optimization objective formulated
nodes.description: The training objective is formulated as minimizing prediction loss subject to worst-case fairness bound constraints |CF+_E|,|CF-_E| ≤ γ_CF for each CF in {DE, IE, SE}.

nodes.name: Augmented Lagrangian used to solve constrained problem
nodes.description: To solve the constrained optimization with gradient-based solvers, augmented Lagrangian optimization is used to convert it into a single loss function with an estimated Lagrange multiplier.

nodes.name: Algorithm 1 trains the robust fair predictor
nodes.description: Algorithm 1 iteratively computes upper/lower CF bounds via Theorem 1, updates the Lagrangian loss, and updates the predictor parameters, checking convergence on both prediction loss and fairness constraints.

components.description: Experimental design: absence of baselines and the three-model comparison used instead.

nodes.name: No existing baselines for this setting
nodes.description: Baselines for causal fairness under unobserved confounding are absent in prior literature.

nodes.name: Three comparison models defined instead
nodes.description: Because no baselines exist, the paper compares three models with identical network architecture: Standard (no fairness constraint), Fair naive (fairness assuming no unobserved confounding), and Fair robust (the proposed framework).

nodes.name: Fair naive expected to be miscalibrated under confounding
nodes.description: Fair naive considers causal fairness only under the assumption of no unobserved confounding, so it is expected to underestimate true unfairness when confounding is present.

nodes.name: Identical architecture isolates the learning objective
nodes.description: Because the three models share identical network architecture, any fairness improvement can be attributed specifically to the tailored learning objective rather than model capacity.

edges.note: cross-component link from C6: Fair robust is Algorithm 1

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: bounds for CF under unobserved confounding
nodes.description: Bounds are derived for causal fairness metrics under different sources of unobserved confounding, serving as a refutation strategy for practitioners.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: robust neural fair-prediction framework
nodes.description: A novel neural framework is developed for learning fair predictions with worst-case guarantees on the extent of causal fairness violation due to unobserved confounding.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: empirical demonstration including real-world case study
nodes.description: The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated in experiments on synthetic and real-world data, including a real-world case study predicting prison sentences.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework generalizes to other fairness notions
isolated_nodes.description: Although the paper focuses on DE, IE, SE, the bound-derivation framework can also be employed for other fairness notions.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework valid for known and unknown Gamma_W
isolated_nodes.description: The framework applies not only when the sensitivity parameter is known but is also of practical value when it is unknown, via data-driven heuristics.
