components.description: Motivation: static-fairness dominance, statistical-fairness limitations in TTE, and the resulting research gap.

nodes.name: Fair ML largely static
nodes.description: Existing works in fair ML cover bias detection, fair prediction, and fair decision-making, but largely focus on static settings.

nodes.name: TTE fairness underexplored
nodes.description: Fairness in temporal contexts, particularly survival/time-to-event (TTE) analysis, remains relatively underexplored.

nodes.name: Existing TTE fairness uses statistical definitions
nodes.description: Current approaches to fair survival analysis adopt statistical fairness definitions rather than causal ones.

nodes.name: Statistical definitions can't disentangle causal mechanisms
nodes.description: Statistical fairness definitions, even with unlimited data, cannot disentangle the causal mechanisms that generate disparities.

nodes.name: Causal fairness literature mostly static
nodes.description: Causal fairness literature introduces important causal fairness notions but is concerned with the static setting only, with few dynamic-setting exceptions.

nodes.name: Gap: causal reasoning for TTE fairness
nodes.description: There remains a need for a deeper understanding of how causal reasoning can be applied to fairness in temporal/TTE data, which this paper aims to fill.

components.description: Standard Fairness Model (SFM) adapted to survival analysis, and the resulting two independence assumptions it encodes.

nodes.name: SFM adapted to survival setting
nodes.description: The Standard Fairness Model (SFM) cluster causal diagram is adapted to survival analysis, with protected attribute X, confounders Z, mediators W, survival time T, and censoring time C.

nodes.name: T, C unobserved; (M, δ) observed instead
nodes.description: T and C are assumed unobserved; instead the pair (M, δ) is observed, where M = min(T,C) and δ indicates whether the observed event is death.

nodes.name: No bidirected T–C edge implies conditional independence
nodes.description: Absence of a bidirected arrow between T and C in the SFM implies T ⊥ C | X, Z, W, i.e., the censoring mechanism is conditionally independent of the survival mechanism.

nodes.name: Conditional independence enables standard survival tools
nodes.description: The T ⊥ C | X,Z,W assumption allows application of standard survival-analysis tools such as conditional Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen estimators.

nodes.name: No further bidirected edges among {T,C,M,δ} and {X,Z,W}
nodes.description: The SFM further encodes lack-of-confounding assumptions: no bidirected edges between {T,C,M,δ} and {X,Z,W}, and none between X,W or Z,W.

nodes.name: Lack-of-confounding enables effect identification
nodes.description: These lack-of-confounding assumptions are important for identifying the different causal effects of X on the survival curve.

components.description: Two-step decomposition strategy for the TV disparity measure, motivated directly by the two SFM assumption groups.

nodes.name: TV disparity measure defined
nodes.description: The total variation measure TV_{x0,x1}(t) = P(T>t|X=x1) - P(T>t|X=x0) is used to quantify survival differences across demographic groups at time t.

nodes.name: Goal: decompose TV into pathway contributions
nodes.description: The goal is to decompose the TV disparity into contributions from the direct (X→T), indirect (X→W→T), and spurious (X⇢Z→T) pathways.

nodes.name: Two-step process mirrors the two SFM assumption groups
nodes.description: The decomposition proceeds in two steps closely related to the two types of assumptions encoded in the SFM: Step 1 (inference of P(T|X,Z,W)) and Step 2 (inference of causal effects of X on functionals of P(T|X,Z,W)).

nodes.name: Step 1: infer P(T|X,Z,W) via conditional independence
nodes.description: Under T⊥C|X,Z,W, the likelihood for T depends only on (M,δ), so conditional Kaplan-Meier/Nelson-Aalen estimators validly recover P(T|X,Z,W).

nodes.name: Step 2 setup: define Φ as a functional of P(T|X,Z,W)
nodes.description: Given P(T|X,Z,W), a mapping Φ = ϕ(P(T|X,Z,W)) is defined so the TV measure can be rewritten as E[Φ|X=x1] - E[Φ|X=x0].

components.description: The Causal Reduction Theorem (Thm 1) and the resulting decomposition/identification results.

nodes.name: Φ is a deterministic function of X,Z,W
nodes.description: Theorem 1 (Causal Reduction) shows that Φ's structural mechanism f_Φ(x,z,w)=ϕ(P(T|X=x,Z=z,W=w)) makes Φ a deterministic function of X,Z,W, not depending on noise variables.

nodes.name: Φ can be added to the causal diagram
nodes.description: Because Φ is a deterministic function of X,Z,W, it can be added as a new node to the causal diagram, yielding a reduced causal model.

nodes.name: Direct/indirect/spurious Φ-effects defined
nodes.description: Using the reduced model, x-specific direct (x-DE), indirect (x-IE), and spurious (x-SE) effects of X on Φ are defined analogously to standard causal fairness effects.

nodes.name: TV(Φ) decomposes into DE, IE, SE
nodes.description: The TV_{x0,x1}(Φ) disparity measure decomposes as TV = x-DE - x-IE - x-SE, following prior causal-fairness decomposition results.

nodes.name: Decomposition holds at each time point
nodes.description: Because Theorem 1 applies to Φ(t) for any t, the pathway decomposition of disparity can be performed at each individual time point, yielding a time-resolved explanation of disparity evolution.

nodes.name: Effects identifiable under the SFM (Prop. 1)
nodes.description: Proposition 1 shows that, under the SFM, the potential outcome E[Φ_{xy,W_xw}(t)|X=xz] is identifiable as a weighted sum over Z,W of conditional expectations of Φ, using estimable propensities.

components.description: Estimation strategies for the identified causal effects: model-based (RSF) and doubly-robust.

nodes.name: RSF used for model-based estimation
nodes.description: Random survival forests (RSF) are used to non-parametrically estimate P(T|X,Z,W) via the conditional cumulative hazard function, from which the survival function is obtained.

nodes.name: Model-based estimator of causal effects (Prop. 2)
nodes.description: Proposition 2 gives a plug-in model-based estimator for the potential outcome E[Φ_{xy,W_xw}(t)|X=xz] using the fitted f(x,z,w) and estimated propensities.

nodes.name: Time-invariant covariates make time-decomposition cheap
nodes.description: Because X,Z,W are time-invariant in this setting, the estimated propensities do not depend on time, making the temporal causal decomposition computationally inexpensive.

nodes.name: Doubly-robust estimator derived (Thm 2)
nodes.description: Theorem 2 derives a novel influence function for the potential outcome ψ under censored data, enabling doubly-robust debiasing of the model-based estimator.

nodes.name: Cross-fitting used for debiased estimation
nodes.description: The influence function is used with cross-fitting: nuisance functions are fit on one fold via xgboost while the influence function is evaluated on the remaining fold, with folds swapped to obtain a one-step debiased estimate.

components.description: Extension to competing risks: why joint event-time distributions are infeasible and CIFs are used instead.

nodes.name: Multiple event types motivate competing risks setting
nodes.description: Individuals may be simultaneously at risk of multiple distinct event types, motivating the competing risks (CR) extension beyond the basic non-informative-censoring case.

nodes.name: Only minimum event time observed
nodes.description: In the CR setting only M = min(T1,...,TK,C) and the event-type indicator δ are observed, not the individual event times.

nodes.name: Competing events may have unobserved common causes
nodes.description: Competing events may have unobserved common causes, represented as bidirected edges among T1,...,TK.

nodes.name: Full joint distribution generally infeasible to identify
nodes.description: Because only the minimum event time is observed and competing events may share unobserved causes, identifying the full joint distribution P(T1,...,TK|X,Z,W) is generally infeasible without strong assumptions like independence of failure times, which rarely hold.

nodes.name: CIFs used as the observable functional instead
nodes.description: As a result, most competing-risks approaches, including this work, focus on cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) rather than the full joint distribution.

nodes.name: CIFs account for competition between event types
nodes.description: CIFs explicitly account for competition: increasing one event type's rate necessarily reduces the CIFs of the remaining events, and CIFs sum with all-cause survival to 1.

nodes.name: Thm 1 applies to CIFs as Φ_k(t)
nodes.description: By the Causal Reduction Theorem, each Φ_k(t) := CIF_k(t) is a deterministic functional of P(T1,...,TK|X,Z,W) and hence a deterministic function of (X,Z,W), enabling the same direct/indirect/spurious decomposition for each cause k.

components.description: Extension to informative censoring via copula-based sensitivity analysis and the copula-graphic bounds theorem.

nodes.name: Informative censoring breaks T⊥C assumption
nodes.description: In the informative censoring (IC) setting, T ⊥ C | X,Z,W no longer holds (a bidirected T⇢C arrow exists), so standard survival-analysis tools are not directly applicable.

nodes.name: Inference requires additional assumptions
nodes.description: Because T⊥C|X,Z,W fails, inference of S(t|X,Z,W) is not possible without additional assumptions, motivating a sensitivity analysis approach.

nodes.name: Archimedean copula assumption adopted
nodes.description: The joint survival function H(t,c)=P(T>t,C>c) is assumed to follow an Archimedean copula parameterized by Kendall's τ, the sensitivity parameter.

nodes.name: Classical CGE assumes disjoint jumps
nodes.description: The classical copula-graphic estimator (CGE) assumes that at each grid point only one of S(t) or G(t) jumps, recursively identifying S(t) and G(t) from CIFs.

nodes.name: Fixed-grid CIF estimation violates disjoint-jump assumption
nodes.description: In this setting, estimation proceeds on a fixed grid of estimated CIFs where both Ŝ and Ĝ may jump at the same grid point, violating the classical CGE's disjoint-increment assumption.

nodes.name: Classical CGE must be adapted
nodes.description: Because the disjoint-jump assumption is violated, the classical CGE must be adapted: τ no longer uniquely identifies S(t_{i+1}), G(t_{i+1}).

nodes.name: Thm 3: sharp bounds under non-disjoint increments
nodes.description: Theorem 3 derives sharp, closed-form bounds on S(t_{i+1}) and G(t_{i+1}) given prior values and CIF increments, which collapse to point estimates as the grid is refined.

nodes.name: Midpoint interpolation yields point estimates
nodes.description: Point estimates of S(t) and G(t) are obtained via midpoint interpolation of the derived bounds, yielding a point-identified estimator as the grid becomes refined.

nodes.name: Recovered Ŝ(t) enables Thm 1 decomposition under IC
nodes.description: After recovering Ŝ(t), the Causal Reduction Theorem is invoked again to compute direct/indirect/spurious effects of X on S(t), quantifying causal fairness under informative censoring via sensitivity analysis on τ.

components.description: Case study setup: ICU race-differential analysis and its causal-structure justification.

nodes.name: ANZICS APD cohort constructed
nodes.description: The case study uses the ANZICS Adult Patient Database, covering 181 hospitals across Australia (Jan 2023-Jul 2024), yielding 249,958 patients, 10,436 (~4.2%) Indigenous.

nodes.name: Indigenous status modeled as X, no reverse causation with Z
nodes.description: Indigenous status and sociodemographic variables may share common causes but neither causes the other, motivating the X⇢Z spurious relationship as in prior literature.

nodes.name: Clinical variables modeled as mediators W
nodes.description: Clinical variables are temporally downstream of X and Z (e.g., indigenous status may influence illness severity via healthcare-access disparities), justifying their role as mediators W.

nodes.name: Censoring is administrative, justifying NIC for death analysis
nodes.description: The censoring mechanism is related to the data extraction process (an administrative reason), justifying the non-informative censoring assumption for the death-outcome analysis.

nodes.name: Death censoring is informative for readmission
nodes.description: Death censoring has unobserved common causes with readmission (latent illness severity, unmeasured frailty, care quality), so the readmission analysis falls under informative censoring.

nodes.name: Two potential unmeasured confounders acknowledged
nodes.description: The causal structure has two acknowledged limitations: genetic variation may confound X→W, and geographic remoteness may confound X, W, and T jointly.

components.description: Case study findings: death disparities (NIC) reveal masked opposing pathway effects.

nodes.name: TV measure near zero after T=80 days
nodes.description: The raw TV disparity measure for death rises then falls, with confidence intervals including 0 after T=80 days, appearing to suggest little disparity.

nodes.name: Direct effect favors minority patients
nodes.description: The direct effect decreases up to T=50 days then stabilizes, with its sign implying minority patients experience improved survival along the direct path.

nodes.name: Indirect effect harms minority patients, growing over time
nodes.description: The indirect effect decreases over time, implying reduced minority survival along this pathway (due to higher chronic/acute illness burden), reaching ~3% difference by T=50 days and continuing to amplify to T=180 days.

nodes.name: Spurious effect favors minority patients, growing over time
nodes.description: The spurious effect increases up to T=180 days, implying improved minority survival along the spurious pathway, related to lower average age at admission.

nodes.name: Decomposition reveals masked opposing effects
nodes.description: Together, the near-zero TV measure masks substantial, opposing pathway-specific effects — a pattern that would be missed by standard statistical fairness analysis.

edges.note: cross-component link from C4: time-resolved decomposition enables detecting the masked pattern

components.description: Case study findings: readmission disparities (IC) via sensitivity analysis.

nodes.name: TV measure for readmission increases over time
nodes.description: The readmission TV measure increases over time, indicating higher readmission burden for minority patients.

nodes.name: Route II sensitivity analysis applied with τ>0
nodes.description: Sensitivity analysis is performed via Route II (population-level copula) with τ ∈ {0.1,0.5,0.8}, assuming T1,T2 are positively correlated due to shared causes.

nodes.name: Direct/indirect effects show higher minority readmission burden
nodes.description: Along both the direct and indirect pathways, minority patients show increased readmission burden, with the indirect effect attributed to more complicated admission diagnoses and worse chronic health.

nodes.name: Spurious effect favors minority patients again
nodes.description: Along the spurious pathway, minority patients again show lower readmission burden, likely due to lower average age at ICU admission.

nodes.name: Confidence bounds limit definitive conclusions on direct effect
nodes.description: Despite the directional findings, the confidence bounds for the direct effect do not allow definitive conclusions about effect sizes.

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: formalize causal fairness for TTE + Causal Reduction Theorem
nodes.description: Causal fairness is formalized for survival analysis, proving the Causal Reduction Theorem that enables identification and decomposition of group disparities in TTE settings.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: three regimes instantiated with identification results
nodes.description: The framework is instantiated in three regimes (non-informative censoring, competing risks, informative censoring), with identification results derived for each (Prop. 1).

nodes.name: Contribution 3: two new technical results (Thm 2, Thm 3)
nodes.description: Two new technical results are proven: a doubly robust estimator for censored data, and sharp bounds for copula-graphic estimation under non-disjoint increments.

nodes.name: Contribution 4: real-world ICU case study
nodes.description: Race differentials in post-ICU mortality are analyzed, demonstrating that causal fairness for TTE yields scientific insights missed by standard statistical fairness analyses.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-parametric focus distinguishes from prior mediation-survival work
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike most causal mediation literature for survival analysis, which adopts parametric models, this work focuses on non-parametric inference, avoiding strong distributional assumptions.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in mediation
isolated_nodes.description: Developing sensitivity analyses for causal decompositions in the presence of unmeasured confounding (e.g., genetic variation, geographic remoteness) is left as an important future direction.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: relax copula family assumption
isolated_nodes.description: The choice of Archimedean copula family in the informative censoring setting is itself an additional modeling assumption that future work could relax.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: time-varying covariates and isolating competing-risk effects
isolated_nodes.description: The current formulation assumes time-invariant covariates and does not isolate primary from competing hazard effects in the competing-risks analysis; both are left for future extensions.

title_ref: Causal Machine Learning Is Not a Panacea: A Roadmap for Observational Causal Inference in Health
notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the DecomposeRL example graph. This source document (a JAMIA-style perspective/roadmap article, not a preprint with an arXiv ID) was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Motivation: why causal ML on observational data is attractive, and why that attractiveness creates risk.

nodes.name: RCTs not always feasible
nodes.description: Randomized controlled trials remain the gold standard for establishing causal relationships, but are not always feasible due to ethical or logistical constraints.

nodes.name: Observational data seen as a bridge
nodes.description: Researchers may consider causal inference on large-scale observational, retrospective data as a bridge between gold-standard RCTs and ubiquitous real-world data.

nodes.name: Curated observational data can emulate an RCT
nodes.description: When observational data are curated to follow a set of assumptions, causal inference can be applied to emulate an RCT, yielding valid treatment effect estimates.

nodes.name: Causal ML promising for complex confounders
nodes.description: Causal ML shows promise because ML excels at extracting signals from multi-modal data (images, notes, time-series), allowing adjustment on complex confounders that traditional statistical methods struggle to incorporate.

nodes.name: ML flexibility increases risk of erroneous findings
nodes.description: Drawing valid causal inferences requires justifying assumptions in the data and modeling choices; the flexibility of ML increases the risk of erroneous findings.

nodes.name: Erroneous causal conclusions risk patient safety
nodes.description: Inappropriately drawing causal conclusions from ML carries risks to medical science and potentially patient safety.

nodes.name: Limitations of causal ML under-appreciated
nodes.description: Despite advances in causal ML, its limitations remain largely under-appreciated across disciplines, and this gap in shared knowledge may impact the validity of findings.

components.description: Causal DAG as the foundation for identifiability, and how ML's optimization for prediction creates new verification challenges.

nodes.name: Non-random treatment assignment causes confounding
nodes.description: When estimating causal effects from observational data, treatments are often non-randomly assigned, confounding direct comparisons of outcomes.

nodes.name: Causal DAG models treatment-outcome relationships
nodes.description: The causal relationships between treatment, outcome, and other relevant variables can be modeled using a causal directed acyclic graph (DAG).

nodes.name: DAG structure implies identifiability assumptions
nodes.description: The structure of a causal DAG implies a set of independence conditions between variables that generate identifiability assumptions, determining when a causal interpretation of treatment effects is tenable.

nodes.name: Accurate DAG construction is a crucial first step
nodes.description: Constructing an accurate DAG with input from domain experts is a crucial first step in ensuring meaningful causal conclusions.

nodes.name: ML models optimized for prediction, not causal validity
nodes.description: By default, most ML approaches are optimized for predictive performance.

nodes.name: ML may exploit spurious associations
nodes.description: Because ML is optimized for predictive performance, ML models may leverage spurious associations to make predictions even when an underlying causal relationship exists.

nodes.name: This obscures identifiability-assumption violations
nodes.description: This tendency to exploit spurious associations means ML introduces new challenges in verifying (and can obscure violations of) the causal identifiability assumptions.

components.description: The Overlap assumption: how to assess it, and the diagnostic ambiguity of propensity-model performance.

nodes.name: Overlap assumption defined
nodes.description: The overlap assumption requires every patient to have a non-zero probability of receiving the treatment.

nodes.name: Propensity model used to assess overlap
nodes.description: Overlap can be partly assessed by fitting a propensity score model to predict treatment assignment from variables that could influence it, per the causal DAG.

nodes.name: High discrimination + well-specified model implies low overlap
nodes.description: If the propensity model is well-specified, high discriminative performance implies low overlap, while poor discriminative performance indicates more randomness in treatment assignment.

nodes.name: Poor performance can also indicate underfitting
nodes.description: If the model is poorly specified, near-random discriminative performance could simply indicate underfitting rather than true overlap.

nodes.name: Standard ML techniques mitigate specification issues
nodes.description: Issues with model specification can be mitigated in part using standard supervised ML techniques such as cross-validation for model selection.

nodes.name: Domain experts needed for thorough overlap evaluation
nodes.description: To more thoroughly evaluate overlap, one should consult domain experts, ideally those responsible for assigning the treatments, who can help identify settings where overlap is impossible.

components.description: Conditional exchangeability (no unobserved confounding): unverifiability and mitigation strategies.

nodes.name: No-unobserved-confounding is unverifiable
nodes.description: The assumption of no unobserved confounding is unverifiable in observational data.

nodes.name: Identifying confounders requires domain expertise
nodes.description: Identifying confounders generally requires domain expertise.

nodes.name: Missing confounders can make interpretation untenable
nodes.description: If potential confounders (e.g., social determinants of health, patient preferences) are unavailable in the data, a causal interpretation may be untenable if their influence could flip the conclusions.

nodes.name: Small unmeasured confounders should still be disclosed
nodes.description: Even if unmeasured confounders are believed small in magnitude, they should be acknowledged as a limitation when communicating findings.

nodes.name: Sensitivity analyses provide further assurance
nodes.description: As further assurance, one can employ sensitivity analyses that quantify the magnitude of an unobserved confounder necessary to change the conclusions.

components.description: SUTVA: consistency and non-interference violations, and how ML practitioners without clinical expertise can mishandle them.

nodes.name: SUTVA requires consistency and non-interference
nodes.description: SUTVA requires that all patients receive the same version of treatment (consistency) and that no patient's outcome is affected by others' treatment assignments (non-interference).

nodes.name: Hidden treatment variation causes consistency violations
nodes.description: Consistency violations may arise from hidden variation in the treatment variable, e.g., dose strength.

nodes.name: Treating variation source as a confounder washes out effect
nodes.description: When sources of treatment variation are inadvertently treated as confounders (e.g., dose strength), subsequent adjustment can wash out the treatment effect.

nodes.name: Interference example: nosocomial infection transmission
nodes.description: Interference may occur when treating one patient affects outcomes for others, as in nosocomial infection management, where an ML model might use room ID (predictive of transmission) as a feature.

nodes.name: Non-expert ML practitioners may misclassify these variables
nodes.description: ML practitioners with limited clinical expertise may overlook the causal significance of variables like dose strength or room ID and include them in model development purely because they boost predictive performance.

nodes.name: Correct handling requires distinguishing treatment-definition vs. interference variables
nodes.description: The predictive utility of dose strength suggests it should be incorporated into the treatment definition, whereas the utility of room ID reflects interference rather than treatment, requiring different handling.

nodes.name: Without expertise, predictive associations get mistaken for causal factors
nodes.description: Without domain expertise, researchers risk mistaking predictive associations for sources of treatment effect heterogeneity or genuine causal factors.

components.description: Synthesis of identification-challenges section into a single takeaway.

nodes.name: DAG-first, domain-expert-checked workflow required
nodes.description: It is essential to first define a causal DAG, then examine the data for potential assumption violations using domain expertise and empirical checks.

nodes.name: ML flexibility raises overfitting-to-spurious-signal risk across all three assumptions
nodes.description: The flexibility of ML models increases the risk of overfitting to spurious signals that may obscure violations of overlap, exchangeability, and SUTVA.

nodes.name: Careful collaborative variable/model selection mitigates risk
nodes.description: Careful selection of confounders, treatment/outcome definitions, and associated models in collaboration with domain experts can mitigate assumption-violation risks or quantify their potential impact.

components.description: Covariate selection for modeling: avoiding irrelevant variables and mediators.

nodes.name: Temptation to include all covariates
nodes.description: For ML practitioners it is tempting to incorporate all observed covariates as predictors to adjust for confounding.

nodes.name: Irrelevant variables risk spurious correlation
nodes.description: Irrelevant variables may be spuriously correlated with the outcome.

nodes.name: Mediators lie on the treatment-outcome path
nodes.description: Some variables may be causal mediators — intermediate variables caused by the treatment that influence the outcome, occurring along the DAG path from treatment to outcome.

nodes.name: Adjusting for mediators dilutes treatment effect estimates
nodes.description: Adjusting for mediators dilutes estimates of treatment effects, since the treatment may not get credit for changes in outcomes it caused via the mediator.

nodes.name: Consulting the DAG avoids mediator inclusion
nodes.description: One can avoid including mediators by consulting the DAG and ensuring all predictors are measured before treatment and follow-up.

components.description: Metalearner modeling choices: indirect vs. direct estimators and their robustness trade-offs.

nodes.name: Metalearners plug in arbitrary base models
nodes.description: Metalearners allow users to plug in base models of arbitrary complexity and estimate treatment effects from combinations of the base models' outputs.

nodes.name: Indirect estimators predict outcomes per arm then difference
nodes.description: Indirect estimators (S-learner, T-learner) estimate the outcome under each treatment assignment separately given covariates, then take the difference.

nodes.name: Indirect estimators are fragile to base-model error
nodes.description: Because the treatment effect is the difference between two separate predictions, errors in either prediction can be magnified and distort the final estimate.

nodes.name: Regularization can flatten outcome estimates and conceal heterogeneity
nodes.description: In high-dimensional data, model-simplifying techniques like regularization can shrink away treatment heterogeneity, flattening outcome estimates and potentially causing a premature conclusion of no treatment effect.

nodes.name: Direct estimators model treatment effect explicitly
nodes.description: Direct estimators (X-learner, DR-learner, R-learner, double ML, orthogonal statistical learning) use base-model outputs to model the treatment effect directly in a second step, via pseudo-outcomes or residual-based isolation, since the true effect is never directly observed per individual.

nodes.name: Direct methods more robust to base-model error
nodes.description: Although base-model errors can still bias direct methods' estimates, direct methods are often more robust to these errors than indirect methods.

components.description: Synthesis of modeling-choices section into a single takeaway.

nodes.name: DAG consultation reduces irrelevant/mediator inclusion risk
nodes.description: Consulting the causal DAG when choosing covariates reduces the risk of including irrelevant variables and mediators.

nodes.name: Choice of combination method affects estimate quality
nodes.description: The method of combining base model outputs (indirect vs. direct) impacts the quality of treatment effect estimates.

nodes.name: Direct methods preferable when base-model accuracy is a central concern
nodes.description: Indirect methods are attractive for their simplicity, but if the accuracy of base models is a central concern, direct methods may be preferable.

components.description: Evaluation problem: no ground-truth treatment effect, and the surrogate strategies proposed instead.

nodes.name: No true treatment effect for validation
nodes.description: In causal inference only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed, so there is no 'true' treatment effect available for held-out validation as in standard supervised ML.

nodes.name: Standard ML test-set paradigm does not apply
nodes.description: Because there is no ground-truth treatment effect, the standard ML paradigm of comparing predicted to observed outcomes on a held-out test set does not apply to causal effect evaluation.

nodes.name: Global null analysis proposed
nodes.description: One strategy is a global null analysis using a synthetic treatment with no true effect, allowing estimated effects to be directly evaluated similarly to supervised ML since the expected effect is zero.

nodes.name: Negative control / plasmode simulation as complements
nodes.description: To complement a global null analysis, one can perform a negative control analysis (a treatment with no effect per expert knowledge) or plasmode simulation when feasible.

nodes.name: Cross-modeling-approach stability as a second strategy
nodes.description: Another strategy is comparing estimates across different modeling approaches and assessing whether sign and magnitude are stable, since each approach encodes different assumptions.

nodes.name: Stability builds confidence but doesn't replace RCTs
nodes.description: Stability across modeling approaches builds confidence in results but these analyses do not supersede evaluation through RCTs or grounding in real-world causal mechanisms.

components.description: Synthesis of evaluation section: treat causal ML outputs as hypotheses, not findings.

nodes.name: Gold-standard validation generally infeasible
nodes.description: Gold-standard validation is generally infeasible in observational causal inference.

nodes.name: Results should be treated as hypotheses, not definitive findings
nodes.description: Causal ML results from observational data should be treated as causal hypotheses rather than definitive findings.

nodes.name: Hypotheses can guide RCT prioritization or mechanistic evaluation
nodes.description: These hypotheses can then be prioritized for testing in RCTs or evaluated against plausible physiological or biological mechanisms.

components.description: Overall conclusion: toward responsible use, and the proposed roadmap.

nodes.name: Unjustified assumptions/choices risk misleading conclusions
nodes.description: Without well-justified causal assumptions and ML modeling choices, analyses may yield conclusions that are misleading.

nodes.name: Roadmap proposed organizing recommendations
nodes.description: A roadmap is proposed that organizes recommendations for using causal ML in observational data into questions addressing causal assumptions, modeling, and evaluation.

nodes.name: Roadmap is a non-exhaustive foundation for interdisciplinary teams
nodes.description: Although not exhaustive, the roadmap offers a foundation for interdisciplinary teams to ground their causal ML analyses.

isolated_nodes.name: Causal ML adapts standard ML techniques for causal inference
isolated_nodes.description: Regardless of the use case (population-level trends or personalized treatment-effect prediction), the field of causal ML adapts standard ML techniques for causal inference.

isolated_nodes.name: Paper scopes to binary treatment/outcome
isolated_nodes.description: The paper considers the setting of a binary treatment and outcome to lay the foundation for more complex analyses (e.g., multiple treatments), as a deliberate scoping choice.

notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the DecomposeRL example graph. This is a long survey/position paper; the graph covers its main structural arguments rather than every citation-level claim. This source document was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Motivation: ML's generalization gap relative to animals, and the argument that this stems from ignoring interventions/structure.

nodes.name: ML lags animals at strong generalization
nodes.description: Compared to animals, ML is limited at transfer to new problems and forms of generalization beyond sampling from the same distribution (horizontal/strong/OOD generalization).

nodes.name: ML disregards interventions, domain shifts, temporal structure
nodes.description: This shortcoming is unsurprising given that ML often disregards information animals use heavily: interventions, domain shifts, temporal structure, treating these as nuisance to be engineered away.

nodes.name: Current ML successes reduce to i.i.d. pattern recognition
nodes.description: The majority of current ML successes boil down to large-scale pattern recognition on suitably collected i.i.d. data.

nodes.name: Robustness research reveals i.i.d. models are fragile
nodes.description: A substantial literature on robustness (Issue 1) documents that deep networks are sensitive to distribution shifts like blur, noise, rotation, viewpoint, with no definitive consensus on solving this via augmentation/pretraining alone.

nodes.name: Argument: generalizing OOD requires an underlying causal model
nodes.description: It has been argued that fixes like augmentation may not be sufficient, and generalizing well outside the i.i.d. setting requires learning not mere statistical associations but an underlying causal model, which models distribution shifts via interventions.

nodes.name: Reusable mechanisms enable efficient adaptation (Issue 2)
nodes.description: Modular representations where modules correspond to physical causal mechanisms allow an agent facing a new environment to adapt only a few modules, requiring fewer examples since most knowledge/modules can be re-used without further training.

components.description: Levels of causal modeling: from differential equations to statistical models, with causal models occupying a middle ground.

nodes.name: Differential equations are the most detailed physical model
nodes.description: A set of coupled differential equations describing physical mechanisms allows predicting future behavior, reasoning about interventions, and reading off causal structure — the gold standard, most detailed model.

nodes.name: Statistical models are superficial, only valid under fixed conditions
nodes.description: A statistical model tells us how some variables predict others as long as experimental conditions don't change; it does not refer to dynamic processes and cannot predict intervention effects.

nodes.name: Causal models lie in between: predict interventions, learned from data
nodes.description: Causal modeling lies between differential equations and statistical models: like physics, it predicts intervention effects, but causal discovery arrives at such models in a data-driven way with weak generic assumptions rather than requiring expert-derived differential equations.

nodes.name: Taxonomy of models by capability (Table I)
nodes.description: A taxonomy ranks models by capability: mechanistic/structural-causal/causal-graphical models can predict under distribution shift and (for the first two) answer counterfactuals, while statistical models can only predict in the i.i.d. setting.

components.description: Predicting under i.i.d. vs. distribution shift vs. counterfactuals: three tiers of questions with increasing difficulty and requirements.

nodes.name: i.i.d. prediction answerable from sufficient observational data
nodes.description: Questions like P(Y|X) can, subject to suitable assumptions, be provably answered by observing sufficient i.i.d. data from P(X,Y).

nodes.name: Accurate prediction is not sufficient for decision-making
nodes.description: The stork/birth-rate example shows a statistical model may predict well even with no causal link, so accurate predictions may not suffice to inform decisions like interventions.

nodes.name: Interventional questions take us out of the i.i.d. setting
nodes.description: Interventional questions involve actions taking us out of the usual i.i.d. setting; interventions change the joint distribution, so classical statistical learning guarantees no longer apply.

nodes.name: Learning about interventions can yield distribution-shift-robust models
nodes.description: On the other hand, learning about interventions may allow training predictive models robust against the naturally occurring distribution changes in the real world.

nodes.name: Counterfactual questions are harder than interventional ones
nodes.description: Counterfactual problems (reasoning about why things happened, imagining consequences of different actions in hindsight) can be more difficult to answer than interventional questions.

nodes.name: Counterfactuals may be key for AI, especially RL
nodes.description: This may be a key challenge for AI since an intelligent agent may benefit from imagining action consequences and understanding retrospectively what led to outcomes; counterfactuals are especially critical in reinforcement learning.

components.description: SCM formalism: structural assignments, causal factorization, and why it differs from arbitrary factorizations.

nodes.name: SCM defines each variable via a structural assignment
nodes.description: In the SCM viewpoint, each observable Xi is the result of a deterministic assignment Xi := fi(PAi, Ui) depending on its graph parents and an independent noise term Ui.

nodes.name: Jointly independent noises required for causal sufficiency
nodes.description: The noises U1,...,Un are assumed jointly independent; if they were not, by the Common Cause Principle there should be another variable causing their dependence, meaning the model would not be causally sufficient.

nodes.name: SCM entails the causal (disentangled) factorization
nodes.description: The graph structure plus joint noise independence implies a canonical causal factorization P(X1,...,Xn) = Π P(Xi|PAi), distinct from other valid but entangled factorizations like the reverse-chain one.

nodes.name: Only the causal factorization corresponds to structural assignments
nodes.description: While many entangled factorizations are mathematically valid, only the causal factorization (4) is the one that decomposes the joint distribution into conditionals corresponding to the actual structural assignments — the causal mechanisms responsible for the statistical dependencies.

nodes.name: SCMs uniquely support counterfactuals; graphs support interventions
nodes.description: Both causal graphical models and SCMs allow computing interventional distributions, but only SCMs (via fixing noise-variable values) allow computing counterfactuals.

components.description: The Reichenbach Common Cause Principle and why more than two variables makes causal discovery from observational data tractable.

nodes.name: Common Cause Principle: dependence implies a common-cause explanation
nodes.description: Reichenbach's Common Cause Principle: if X and Y are statistically dependent, there exists a variable Z that causally influences both and renders them independent when conditioned on Z.

nodes.name: Two-variable case is underdetermined without extra assumptions
nodes.description: Without additional assumptions, the three causal explanations (X→Y, X←Y, or a common confounder) cannot be distinguished using only observational data over X,Y, since they realize the same class of observational distributions.

nodes.name: More observables yield nontrivial conditional independencies
nodes.description: With more than two observables, nontrivial conditional independence properties implied by causal structure become available, generalizing the Reichenbach Principle and making causal discovery surprisingly easier than the two-variable case.

components.description: The Independent Causal Mechanisms (ICM) Principle and its two components.

nodes.name: ICM Principle stated
nodes.description: The causal generative process is composed of autonomous modules that do not inform or influence each other; the conditional distribution of each variable given its causes does not inform or influence the other mechanisms.

nodes.name: ICM has an influence component
nodes.description: Applied to the causal factorization, ICM implies changing/intervening on one mechanism P(Xi|PAi) does not change any other mechanism P(Xj|PAj) for i≠j.

nodes.name: ICM has an information component
nodes.description: ICM also implies knowing some other mechanisms P(Xi|PAi) (i≠j) does not give information about mechanism P(Xj|PAj).

nodes.name: In non-causal factorizations, changes affect many terms simultaneously
nodes.description: In contrast, under a non-causal (entangled) factorization, changing a physical mechanism will typically affect many or all terms simultaneously, since the entangled factorization does not isolate mechanisms.

components.description: From ICM to the Sparse Mechanism Shift (SMS) hypothesis, and its role in learning causal models.

nodes.name: Any real-world distribution viewed as a product of causal mechanisms
nodes.description: Any real-world distribution is viewed as a product of causal mechanisms; a change in the distribution when moving to a related domain will always be due to changes in at least one of those mechanisms.

nodes.name: SMS hypothesis stated
nodes.description: Sparse Mechanism Shift: small distribution changes tend to manifest in a sparse or local way in the causal/disentangled factorization, usually not affecting all factors simultaneously.

nodes.name: SMS contrasts with entangled factorizations under change
nodes.description: Under a non-causal (entangled) factorization, many or all terms will be affected simultaneously as a physical mechanism changes, unlike the sparse effect seen in the causal factorization — motivating the 'disentangled' terminology.

components.description: Causal discovery from observational data: why finite-sample conditional independence testing and the two-variable case require function-class assumptions.

nodes.name: CI testing is hard for finite data, especially with continuous conditioning sets
nodes.description: Although conditional independencies implied by the Markov condition hold irrespective of function complexity in principle, conditional independence testing is a notoriously difficult problem for finite datasets, especially with continuous multi-dimensional conditioning sets.

nodes.name: Two-variable case has no nontrivial CI implications
nodes.description: In the two-variable case, the ternary concept of conditional independence collapses, so the Markov condition has no nontrivial implications, echoing the earlier two-variable underdetermination result.

nodes.name: Both problems addressed by restricting function classes
nodes.description: Both the finite-sample CI-testing problem and the two-variable underdetermination problem can be addressed by making assumptions on function classes, analogous to how finite-sample generalization in ML requires assumptions on function classes.

nodes.name: Additive noise models break cause-effect symmetry
nodes.description: Restricting to an additive noise model Y=f(X)+V (rather than allowing f to depend arbitrarily on noise) both reduces the effective function class size and, under genericity assumptions, breaks the symmetry between cause and effect: one cannot generally fit an additive noise model in the reversed direction.

components.description: Using environments/contexts and function-class restrictions to identify causal structure beyond the classical two-variable setting.

nodes.name: SMS implies invariance across environments/contexts
nodes.description: By the SMS hypothesis, much causal structure is assumed to remain invariant across changing environments, so distribution shifts (from interventions, non-stationary time series, or multiple views) can significantly help identify causal structure.

nodes.name: Environments connect to meta-learning
nodes.description: Contexts/environments can likewise be interpreted as different tasks, providing a connection to meta-learning.

nodes.name: Causal invariance tied to faster meta-learning adaptation
nodes.description: Prior work ties generalization in meta-learning to invariance properties of causal models, using the idea that a causal model should adapt faster to interventions than purely predictive models, later extended to multiple variables and unknown interventions via continuous-optimization causal discovery.

components.description: Motivating causal representation learning: real-world data isn't pre-structured into causal units.

nodes.name: Traditional causal discovery assumes units are already given
nodes.description: Traditional causal discovery and reasoning assume the units are random variables already connected by a causal graph.

nodes.name: Real-world observations aren't structured into such units
nodes.description: Real-world observations (e.g., objects in images) are usually not structured into those causal units to begin with.

nodes.name: Causal representation learning aims to learn the variables themselves
nodes.description: This gap motivates causal representation learning: learning the causal variables S1,...,Sn connecting to observations X=G(S1,...,Sn) from data, rather than assuming them given, paralleling how ML moved beyond requiring symbols be given a priori.

nodes.name: Defining causally-interventionable coarse-grained variables is hard
nodes.description: It is challenging to state general conditions under which coarse-grained variables admit causal models with well-defined interventions; defining suitable units amounts to coarse-graining more detailed models (SCMs, differential equations, time series).

components.description: Embedding SCMs into representation-learning architectures: the encoder-mechanism-decoder pipeline and its use of SMS.

nodes.name: Goal: embed SCM into larger ML models
nodes.description: To combine SCM and representation learning, one should embed an SCM into larger ML models whose inputs/outputs may be high-dimensional and unstructured but whose inner workings are partly governed by an SCM, parameterized with a neural network.

nodes.name: Result is a modular, re-purposable architecture
nodes.description: The result may be a modular architecture where different modules can be individually fine-tuned and re-purposed for new tasks, with the SMS hypothesis used to enforce the appropriate sparse-change structure.

nodes.name: Encoder-mechanism-decoder pipeline proposed
nodes.description: An encoder q maps observations to a noise-variable bottleneck U; a mapping f(U) determined by structural assignments produces causal variables; a decoder p reconstructs the observation, trained via reconstruction error to satisfy p∘f∘q≈id.

nodes.name: If causal graph unknown, decoder absorbs it as an unspecified component
nodes.description: If the causal graph is known, the network topology implementing f can be fixed accordingly; if not, the decoder learns the composition p∘f as a single unspecified part, i.e., one only learns an autoencoder p̃∘q.

components.description: Problem 1: Learning disentangled representations, its relation to independent factors of variation and object-centric learning, and identifiability challenges.

nodes.name: Standard disentanglement work assumes trivial causal graph
nodes.description: Much existing work on disentanglement focuses on independent factors of variation, which is the special case where the causal graph is trivial (all parent sets empty), a special case of the more general ICM Principle.

nodes.name: Object-centric learning is a special case of disentangled factorization
nodes.description: Object-centric representation learning can also be viewed as a special case of disentangled factorization: objects should be building blocks of an overall causal factorization, complemented by mechanisms like orientation and lighting.

nodes.name: Recovering exogenous noise variables is ill-defined without further assumptions
nodes.description: The problem of recovering exogenous noise variables is ill-defined in the i.i.d. case since there are infinitely many equivalent solutions yielding the same observational distribution; additional assumptions or biases are needed to favor certain solutions.

nodes.name: ICM/SMS can be used to make (12) causal
nodes.description: To make the representation causal, one can apply the ICM Principle (statistically independent Ui, independent mechanisms via invariance across problems, sparse changes to actions, or independent intervenability); SMS is theoretically sufficient given suitable training data and can be used as a supervision signal even with nontrivial parent sets.

nodes.name: Which factors are disentangleable depends on available interventions/supervision
nodes.description: Which factors of variation can be disentangled depends on which interventions can be observed, and different supervision signals can be used to identify different subsets of factors and their granularity.

components.description: Problem 2 and Problem 3: learning transferable mechanisms and interventional world models/reasoning.

nodes.name: Limited resources motivate re-usable modular structure
nodes.description: Agents face limited training data and computational resources, motivating modular structures that mirror modularity in the world so components/mechanisms can be re-used across environments, tasks, and settings.

nodes.name: ICM is a sensible inductive bias for such modularity
nodes.description: A sensible inductive bias for learning such transferable modular models is to look for independent causal mechanisms, which may help transfer modules across substantially different domains.

nodes.name: Deep learning preserves statistical but not causal/interventional properties
nodes.description: Deep learning excels at learning representations preserving statistical properties, but does so without regard to interventional properties of the variables it analyzes.

nodes.name: Causal representation learning should support intervention, planning, reasoning
nodes.description: Causal representation learning should move beyond statistical dependence structures towards models supporting intervention, planning, and reasoning, realizing 'thinking as acting in an imagined space.'

components.description: Implications for ML: semi-supervised learning as a case study in the ICM Principle's predictive consequences.

nodes.name: Causal-direction SSL: ICM implies P(X) uninformative about P(Y|X)
nodes.description: If the causal graph is X→Y, ICM implies P(X) contains no information about the mechanism P(Y|X), implying SSL using unlabeled data to improve estimation of P(Y|X) should be futile in the causal direction.

nodes.name: Anticausal-direction SSL can be effective
nodes.description: In the anticausal direction (prediction target opposite the causal generative process), a measure of dependence between P(X) and P(Y|X) is strictly positive, implying the input distribution can be informative about the conditional, so SSL may be possible.

nodes.name: Empirical study corroborates the causal/anticausal SSL asymmetry
nodes.description: This prediction was empirically corroborated, establishing a bridge between the structure of learning problems and the causal direction of real-world data-generating processes, inspiring follow-up work in ML and statistics.

components.description: Adversarial vulnerability reframed through the causal-vs-anticausal lens, and a resulting defense strategy.

nodes.name: Adversarial attacks violate the i.i.d. assumption
nodes.description: Adversarial attacks constitute minute, human-imperceptible changes to inputs that alter a classifier's output; test examples in this setting are not drawn from the training distribution.

nodes.name: Causal setting: predictor approximating the causal mechanism should be more transferable/robust
nodes.description: In the causal setting, if a predictor approximates the causal mechanism (which is by definition valid under every allowed intervention), one may expect adversarial examples to be harder to find.

nodes.name: Anticausal defense via analysis-by-synthesis / reconstruction
nodes.description: Recent work supports this view: a defense against adversarial attacks solves the anticausal classification problem by modeling the causal generative direction (analysis by synthesis), or reconstructs the input via an autoencoder before classification.

components.description: Robustness and strong OOD generalization formalized via worst-case risk over a causally-defined distribution class.

nodes.name: Autonomous-module structures should be robust to component swaps
nodes.description: Structures composed of autonomous modules, as given by a causal factorization, should be relatively robust to swapping out or modifying individual components.

nodes.name: Causal features give strategic-behavior robustness
nodes.description: A scoring system using only causal features (e.g., debt paid off, which causally affects repayment) rather than non-causal correlates (e.g., address) can be more robust to strategic behavior by agents gaming the score.

nodes.name: OOD risk formalized as worst case over an interventional distribution class
nodes.description: Restricting the test distribution P† to lie in a set PG of interventional distributions over a causal graph, worst-case OOD risk is the max expected loss over P†∈PG, and a robust predictor solves the corresponding minimax problem using a subset of environment distributions E⊂PG.

nodes.name: Estimation error remains if observed environments don't cover the true set
nodes.description: If the observed environment set E does not coincide with the full possible set PG, there is an additional estimation error that may be arbitrarily large in the worst case.

components.description: Pre-training, data augmentation, and self-supervision reinterpreted as approximations to the causal minimax objective.

nodes.name: Enriching training distribution as one approximation strategy
nodes.description: Enriching the training distribution (e.g., pre-training on huge diverse corpora) is one way to approximate the minimax OOD objective, but only helps if the new distribution is diverse enough to contain information about other distributions in PG.

nodes.name: Data augmentation specifies a set of interventions the model should be robust to
nodes.description: Data augmentation increases data diversity via artificially generated interventions (rotation, translation, flipping); one can view this as specifying a set of interventions E the model should be robust to.

nodes.name: Self-supervision learns about P(X) via pretext tasks
nodes.description: Self-supervision learns useful representations of P(X) via pretext tasks with artificially generated labels, converting an unsupervised problem into a supervised one, aiming to extract features informative about the data-generating distribution.

components.description: Reinforcement learning as a domain especially amenable to and requiring causal reasoning.

nodes.name: On-policy RL directly estimates do-probabilities
nodes.description: RL is closer to causality than mainstream ML in that on-policy learning effectively directly estimates do-probabilities for interventions specified by the policy.

nodes.name: Off-policy/batch RL raises subtle causal issues
nodes.description: As soon as off-policy learning is considered, especially in the batch/observational setting, issues of causality become subtle.

nodes.name: Partial world models risk unobserved confounding from the environment
nodes.description: Many current model-based RL approaches only build partial models of the environment; since they don't observe every time step, the environment may become an unobserved confounder affecting both actions and reward, addressable via a backdoor-criterion conditioning on the policy.

nodes.name: Causal invariances could enable generalization/fast transfer in RL
nodes.description: Learning invariances in a causal graph structure is proposed as a path to RL generalization; causal models may allow modeling the environment as independent mechanisms so not all mechanisms need re-learning under distribution shift.

nodes.name: Offline RL is fundamentally a counterfactual inference problem
nodes.description: Offline RL learns a policy from a fixed trajectory dataset without environment interaction; succeeding requires inferring consequences of actions not seen during training, essentially a counterfactual inference problem, made harder by distribution mismatch between current and data-collection policies.

components.description: Scientific applications: why lack of systematic experimental control makes causal understanding valuable in healthcare and astronomy.

nodes.name: Physics simulators may not need strong OOD generalization if conditions are controlled
nodes.description: Significant OOD generalization of learned physical simulators may not be necessary if experimental conditions are carefully controlled, though the simulator must be retrained if conditions change.

nodes.name: Uncontrolled clinical settings risk models that merely mimic doctors
nodes.description: In healthcare, if a clinical system is trained on doctors' actions in controlled settings, it will likely provide little additional insight compared to doctors' own knowledge and may fail unexpectedly when deployed.

nodes.name: Causal understanding needed for reliable personalized treatment recommendations
nodes.description: An understanding of causality may be necessary to recommend treatment options that are personalized and reliable, beyond merely automating existing decisions.

nodes.name: Causal mediation analysis disentangles confounded effects (Covid-19 example)
nodes.description: Causal mediation analysis helped disentangle effects contributing to Covid-19 case fatality rates when a textbook Simpson's paradox was observed.

nodes.name: Causal instrument-confounding removal enabled exoplanet discovery
nodes.description: In astronomy, causal models identifying and removing shared instrument-noise patterns across confounded stars led to the discovery of 36 planet candidates (21 later validated), including one later found to show water vapor in its atmosphere.

components.description: Rebuttal to 'just train a huge model' objection, closing the case for integrating causality with deep learning.

nodes.name: Objection: why not just train a huge model over all interventions?
nodes.description: A critical question is why not just train a huge model that learns environment dynamics including all possible interventions, expecting a big network to generalize across them given enough diverse data.

nodes.name: Rebuttal: undiverse data still yields arbitrarily high worst-case error
nodes.description: If data is not sufficiently diverse (an a priori untestable assumption), the worst-case error to unseen shifts may still be arbitrarily high, per the earlier OOD risk analysis.

nodes.name: Causal assumptions make generalization capability explicit and aligned with cognition/physics
nodes.description: The causal approach makes a model's generalization-relevant assumptions more explicit and aligned with our understanding of physics and human cognition (e.g., via the ICM Principle); when these assumptions are valid, a learner using them should fare better than one that does not.

nodes.name: ICM motivates decomposing knowledge into recomposable pieces
nodes.description: If a model succeeds across an environment's interventions, one may want to transfer it to different but related environments; the ICM principle points to decomposing knowledge into independent, recomposable pieces, motivating modular ML architectures.

components.description: Future research areas identified in the conclusion.

nodes.name: Future area 1: learning non-linear causal relations at scale
nodes.description: Future work should understand under which conditions non-linear causal relations can be learned at scale, which training frameworks best exploit ML scalability for this, and provide evidence of advantages over non-causal representations on real-world tasks.

nodes.name: Future area 2: learning causal variables (beyond fixed-format disentanglement)
nodes.description: Future work should address that current disentangled representations are still distributed in a fixed-format vector, unable to dynamically change representation size (e.g., number of objects), and should investigate task-dependent extraction of high-level variables.

nodes.name: Future area 3: understanding biases of existing deep learning approaches
nodes.description: Future work should disentangle the benefits of individual robustness-improving components (scaling, augmentation, self-supervision) and build a taxonomy of inductive biases, understanding how pre-training design choices causally impact transfer and robustness.

nodes.name: Future area 4: learning causally correct models of the world and the agent
nodes.description: Future work should address deriving abstract causal variables from high-dimensional pixel representations and recovering causal graphs in RL settings, essential for robust and versatile model-based RL.

isolated_nodes.name: Causal explanations can be viewed as reasoning-chain components
isolated_nodes.description: Causal relations can be viewed as components of reasoning chains providing predictions far from the observed distribution, possibly hypothetical or requiring conscious deliberation.

isolated_nodes.name: Manipulative definition of causation
isolated_nodes.description: The manipulative definition of causation focuses on the fact that conditional probabilities cannot reliably predict the outcome of an active intervention (e.g., open umbrellas predict rain, but closing umbrellas does not stop it).

isolated_nodes.name: Algorithmic-independence formalization of mechanism independence
isolated_nodes.description: Independence of mechanisms can alternatively be formalized via vanishing mutual algorithmic (Kolmogorov) information between their bit-string encodings, showing causality is not intrinsically bound to statistics.

isolated_nodes.name: Multi-task/continual learning connects to shared causal generative structure
isolated_nodes.description: Multi-task learning can exploit a shared underlying data-generating process modeled as a causal generative model whose components satisfy SMS, with causal models sometimes adapting faster to sparse distributional interventions.

components.description: Motivation: sensitive attributes warp manifold geometry, not just distributions, and existing fairness alignment is insufficient.

nodes.name: Standard fairness treats data as static points
nodes.description: Standard fairness approaches often treat data as static points in high-dimensional space, ignoring the underlying generative structure.

nodes.name: Sensitive attributes causally warp geometry
nodes.description: Sensitive attributes do not merely shift data distributions but causally warp the geometry of the data manifold itself.

nodes.name: Distributional alignment insufficient
nodes.description: Distributional alignment (matching P(Z|do(A=a)) across a) is often insufficient for complex data manifolds where A also affects correlation structure and variance.

nodes.name: Warped Swiss Roll illustration
nodes.description: In the Warped Swiss Roll problem, one group resides on a tightly coiled manifold and another on a loose one, illustrating structural warping beyond mean shift.

nodes.name: Naive latent alignment fails geometrically
nodes.description: A model that aligns points in latent space can map distinct geometries to the same region without correcting the underlying structural warping, yielding representations that are statistically indistinguishable but geometrically unfaithful.

components.description: CMF's proposed reframing of fairness as geometric invariance.

nodes.name: Fairness as geometric invariance
nodes.description: A representation is truly fair only if the geometry of the mapping from latent space to data space is invariant to the sensitive attribute.

nodes.name: Penalize metric tensor differences
nodes.description: CMF enforces geometric invariance by penalizing differences in the Pullback Metric Tensor (first-order geometry) of the decoder between factual and counterfactual pairs.

nodes.name: Penalize Hessian differences
nodes.description: CMF enforces geometric invariance by penalizing differences in the Hessian (second-order geometry) of the decoder between factual and counterfactual pairs.

nodes.name: Rules of latent space preserved
nodes.description: By enforcing constraints on the Jacobian and Hessian of the decoder, CMF ensures that distances and shapes in the latent space are preserved across demographic groups.

components.description: Gap in related work that CMF fills.

nodes.name: Counterfactual fairness assumes fixed geometry
nodes.description: Counterfactual fairness and related SCM-based extensions encode fairness constraints at the level of predictions or representations, assuming a fixed geometry of the latent space.

nodes.name: Fairness enforced via statistical dependencies only
nodes.description: These approaches ensure fairness primarily by controlling statistical dependencies rather than geometric or structural ones.

nodes.name: Fair representation learning uses flat Euclidean embeddings
nodes.description: Fair representation learning methods typically treat embeddings as flat Euclidean spaces and evaluate fairness via prediction invariance or statistical independence, not geometric structure.

nodes.name: Geometric deep learning studies geometry, not fairness
nodes.description: Work on Riemannian VAEs and geometry-aware generative models studies latent geometry as an inherent property of generative models, not as an object regularized for fairness under sensitive-attribute interventions.

nodes.name: No prior work enforces geometric invariance under intervention
nodes.description: To the authors' knowledge, no prior work examines how interventions on sensitive variables should preserve local geometric properties such as curvature, metric tensors, or geodesic flows.

nodes.name: CMF fills this gap
nodes.description: CMF introduces a fairness criterion assessed at the level of geometric invariance rather than statistical independence or causal effects alone, unifying SCMs, differential geometry, and fair representation learning.

components.description: Causal setup: SCM formalization and the representation-recovery goal.

nodes.name: SCM with invertible mechanism
nodes.description: An SCM is assumed where observed features X are generated by an invertible mechanism from exogenous noise U and sensitive attribute A: X = f(U, A).

nodes.name: A warps manifestation of intrinsic U
nodes.description: U represents intrinsic individual properties (e.g., talent, health), while A acts as a parameter that warps the manifestation of U into X.

nodes.name: Goal: recover A-invariant representation
nodes.description: The representation-learning goal is to recover a representation z approximately equal to U that is invariant to A.

components.description: Geometric definitions: metric tensor and Hessian as first- and second-order invariance constraints.

nodes.name: Decoder defines a smooth manifold
nodes.description: An encoder-decoder (autoencoder) framework is used where the decoder D: Z -> X defines a smooth manifold M embedded in X.

nodes.name: Pullback metric tensor defined via Jacobian
nodes.description: The geometry of the latent space is characterized by the Pullback Metric Tensor G(z) = J_D(z)^T J_D(z), measuring how infinitesimal distances scale under the decoder map.

nodes.name: Fair representation implies matched metric tensors
nodes.description: If the representation is fair, local manifold scaling should not depend on A, i.e., G(z_factual) ≈ G(z_counterfactual).

nodes.name: Metric tensor only captures first-order stretching
nodes.description: The metric tensor only captures first-order local linearities (stretching), motivating a second-order extension to capture bending and twisting.

nodes.name: Hessian defined dimension-wise
nodes.description: Since the decoder is vector-valued, the curvature constraint is defined dimension-wise via the Hessian H_k(z) = ∇²D_k(z) for each output dimension k.

components.description: Loss function construction combining task, alignment, and geometric terms.

nodes.name: Combined training loss
nodes.description: The model is trained to minimize L = L_task + L_align + λ_geo · L_geo, combining reconstruction/prediction loss, counterfactual alignment, and geometric regularization.

nodes.name: L_align is standard counterfactual alignment
nodes.description: L_align = ||E(x) - E(xcf)||^2 enforces standard counterfactual alignment of encoder outputs.

nodes.name: L_geo penalizes metric and curvature differences
nodes.description: L_geo is the novel contribution, combining the Frobenius-norm difference of metric tensors and a weighted sum of Frobenius-norm differences of per-dimension Hessians between factual and counterfactual latents.

nodes.name: do(A) enforced as isometry
nodes.description: Minimizing L_geo forces the model to learn a representation where the causal intervention do(A) acts as an isometry (preserving distances and shapes), not merely a translation.

components.description: Experimental setup: synthetic Warped Swiss Roll SCM used to validate CMF.

nodes.name: Warped Swiss Roll SCM constructed
nodes.description: A synthetic SCM is constructed with A in {0,1} and U ~ Uniform(0,4π), where observed features X in R^3 are generated via a frequency/radius parameter w = 1.0 + 0.5A.

nodes.name: A controls tightness/twist of manifold
nodes.description: The construction creates a manifold that is tighter and more twisted when A = 1, directly instantiating causal geometric warping by the sensitive attribute.

nodes.name: Ground-truth geometry known
nodes.description: The synthetic dataset is used because the ground-truth geometry is known, enabling direct evaluation of geometric invariance.

nodes.name: ELU chosen for C² continuity
nodes.description: ELU activations are used instead of ReLU because they are twice-differentiable (C² continuous), which is required for stable Hessian computation.

components.description: Quantitative results: geometric invariance and fairness-utility trade-off.

nodes.name: Baseline exhibits high geometric error
nodes.description: The Baseline autoencoder exhibits extremely high geometric errors (Metric Error 16.39, Curvature Error 4.32).

nodes.name: Baseline relies on A to reconstruct warped manifold
nodes.description: The high baseline geometric error confirms that the standard autoencoder learns to rely on the sensitive attribute A to reconstruct the warped manifold.

nodes.name: CMF reduces metric error ~1000x
nodes.description: CMF reduces the Metric Error to 0.018, an approximately 1000x reduction relative to baseline.

nodes.name: CMF reduces curvature error ~100x
nodes.description: CMF reduces the Curvature Error to 0.046, an approximately 100x reduction relative to baseline.

nodes.name: CMF achieves geometric invariance
nodes.description: The large reductions in metric and curvature error demonstrate that CMF successfully creates a representation geometrically invariant to A.

nodes.name: Accuracy drops negligibly
nodes.description: Despite heavy geometric regularization, classification accuracy drops only negligibly from 1.000 (Baseline) to 0.995 (CMF).

nodes.name: Intrinsic variable U preserved
nodes.description: The negligible accuracy drop proves that the intrinsic variable U, which predicts Y, was preserved by CMF's representation.

nodes.name: Reconstruction MSE increases
nodes.description: Reconstruction MSE increases from 0.070 (Baseline) to 0.754 (CMF), reflecting the cost of not using A as a reconstruction shortcut.

nodes.name: MSE increase reflects necessary compromise
nodes.description: The MSE increase is expected: the Baseline 'cheats' by using A to perfectly reconstruct the warped data, while CMF must find a compromise manifold fitting both demographic groups without encoding the warping factor.

nodes.name: Fairness-utility trade-off quantified
nodes.description: Together, the near-perfect fairness metrics with only a negligible accuracy drop and a moderate MSE increase quantify CMF's fairness-utility trade-off.

components.description: Qualitative results: latent space visualization.

nodes.name: Baseline latent space separated by A
nodes.description: The Baseline latent space visualization is sharply divided by the sensitive attribute A (shown as Red/Blue clusters).

nodes.name: CMF latent space aligns distributions
nodes.description: The CMF latent space visualization shows distributions overlapping across A while preserving intrinsic structure U.

nodes.name: Alignment does not destroy causal information
nodes.description: The high accuracy score alongside distributional overlap confirms that CMF's alignment did not destroy the causal information required for prediction.

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: geometric invariance formalization
nodes.description: Fairness is formalized as a geometric invariance problem requiring stability of the Riemannian metric and curvature under causal intervention.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: differentiable Jacobian/Hessian alignment loss
nodes.description: A differentiable loss function is proposed that aligns the Jacobian and Hessian of the generator across counterfactual worlds.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: GIE validation on nonlinear SCM
nodes.description: CMF is experimentally validated on a non-linear SCM, introducing Geometric Invariance Error (GIE) metrics to quantify disentanglement of structural bias.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: approximate Hessian-vector products
isolated_nodes.description: Future work will scale CMF to high-dimensional image data using approximate Hessian-vector products to bypass the computational cost of full Hessian calculation.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: graph-structured data
isolated_nodes.description: Future work will extend the CMF framework to graph-structured data.
