components.name: Motivation: adversarial training's real-world value for deepfake detection is underexplored

nodes.name: Adversarial examples transfer across models, enabling black-box attacks
nodes.description: Adversarial examples are inputs perturbed by small, carefully crafted noise, and their transferability across models enables black-box attacks, making defenses challenging in practice.

nodes.name: Adversarial training is widely adopted but mostly studied under white-box assumptions
nodes.description: While adversarial training is widely adopted to improve robustness, it is studied under white-box assumptions that ignore realistic conditions where attackers operate with different architectures or datasets.

nodes.name: This leaves a gap in understanding AT's practical, real-world value
nodes.description: Because AT is predominantly evaluated under unrealistic white-box, matched-distribution assumptions, this gap limits understanding of AT's practical value in deployment conditions where attacker and defender differ.

nodes.name: Deepfake detection is especially vulnerable, relying on subtle spatial/frequency artifacts that perturbations disrupt
nodes.description: Deepfake detection is particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbation because it relies on subtle spatial and frequency artifacts, which adversarial perturbations can easily disrupt.

nodes.name: This combination motivates systematically evaluating AT for deepfake detectors under realistic mismatch
nodes.description: The general gap in understanding AT's real-world value, combined with deepfake detection's specific reliance on fragile spatial/frequency artifacts, motivates a systematic evaluation of adversarial training for deepfake detectors under realistic attacker-defender mismatch scenarios.

components.name: Positioning: extending DUMB/DUMBer to an unexplored domain

nodes.name: DUMB formalized attacker-defender mismatch scenarios along dataset, model, and balance axes
nodes.description: The DUMB framework formalized attacker-defender mismatch scenarios along dataset source, model architecture, and class balance axes.

nodes.name: DUMBer extended DUMB to adversarially trained models, revealing robustness gaps under transfer attacks
nodes.description: DUMBer extended the DUMB framework to adversarially trained models, revealing significant gaps in robustness under transfer-based attacks.

nodes.name: DUMB/DUMBer have not yet been applied to deepfake detection
nodes.description: The DUMB and DUMBer frameworks offer systematic evaluation protocols for transferability but have not yet been applied to deepfake detection.

nodes.name: Limited research has assessed AT for deepfake detectors under transfer attacks and dataset shift
nodes.description: Beyond the DUMB/DUMBer gap specifically, limited research more broadly has assessed adversarial training for deepfake detectors under transfer-based attacks and dataset shifts.

nodes.name: This motivates extending DUMB/DUMBer methodology specifically to deepfake detection
nodes.description: Because DUMB/DUMBer's systematic mismatch-evaluation methodology exists but is unapplied to deepfakes, and because deepfake-specific AT robustness under transfer/shift is otherwise underexplored, this work extends the DUMB/DUMBer methodology to the deepfake detection domain.

components.name: Method: adapting the DUMB taxonomy into four mismatch cases and an evaluation protocol

nodes.name: The full DUMB taxonomy varies dataset, model, and class balance jointly
nodes.description: The DUMB taxonomy formalizes attacker-defender mismatch scenarios along three axes: Dataset soUrce, Model architecture, and class Balance.

nodes.name: This work fixes class balance to focus on the most interpretable dataset/model mismatch subset
nodes.description: The paper adopts a balanced class configuration throughout, simplifying the DUMB notation to the most practically relevant and interpretable four cases varying only dataset and model architecture: C1 (white-box), C3 (cross-model), C5 (cross-dataset), C7 (cross-dataset & cross-model).

nodes.name: Transfer-based attacks are chosen as the focus since they best reflect realistic no-access threat scenarios
nodes.description: Transfer-based attacks require no access to target parameters and only a single application, closely reflecting realistic threat scenarios, unlike query-heavy decision-based or score-based black-box attacks; this is the focus of the study's attack setting.

nodes.name: ASR and AMR are defined to quantify attack success and the robustness gain from adversarial training
nodes.description: Attack Success Rate (ASR) measures the fraction of attacked samples misclassified after attack, and Attack Mitigation Rate (AMR, Eq. 1) measures the relative reduction in ASR after adversarial training, together quantifying both raw attack effectiveness and AT's protective benefit.

nodes.name: Together these choices define a 1920-evaluation protocol spanning models, attacks, datasets, and AT strategies
nodes.description: Combining the four mismatch cases, transfer-based attack focus, and the ASR/AMR metrics yields the full evaluation protocol: 5 detectors × 3 attacks × 2 datasets × 12 training strategies × multiple surrogate/test-set combinations, totaling 1920 evaluations (Section 3.5).

components.name: Motivating diverse adversarial training strategies from AT's known limitations

nodes.name: AT's main challenge is balancing robustness against clean accuracy
nodes.description: The main challenge of adversarial training lies in enhancing robustness to adversarial examples without significantly compromising accuracy on clean data, a trade-off highlighted in prior work and addressed by regularization approaches like TRADES.

nodes.name: Standard AT relies on a single attack and is evaluated mainly in white-box settings
nodes.description: Standard adversarial training typically relies on a single attack such as FGSM, PGD, or a variant, with evaluations usually restricted to white-box settings.

nodes.name: Single-attack AT is susceptible to catastrophic overfitting, reducing resilience to unseen attacks
nodes.description: Relying on a single attack during AT provides robustness against that specific attack but is susceptible to catastrophic overfitting, which reduces the resilience of retrained models to unseen attacks.

nodes.name: Prior work proposed adaptive, curriculum, and ensemble strategies to counter single-attack overfitting
nodes.description: To address single-attack overfitting, prior methods vary the perturbation budget adaptively or via curriculum, or use ensemble strategies combining multiple attacks such as PGD and FGSM in training.

nodes.name: This motivates testing eleven AT strategies varying attack and surrogate diversity under the DUMB mismatch cases
nodes.description: Building on the known limitation of single-attack AT and prior diversity-based mitigations, this paper defines and tests eleven adversarial training strategies (single, dual, triple/ensemble, and surrogate-diversified) to assess whether increased diversity improves robustness specifically under the DUMB mismatch scenarios.

components.name: Results: transfer-based attacks remain a credible threat even under severe mismatch

nodes.name: PGD achieves the highest ASR across all DUMB cases, including strong cross-dataset transfer
nodes.description: PGD consistently achieved the highest ASR in all settings, with near-perfect success in white-box (C1: 99.6%) and substantial transferability in cross-model (C3: 89.8%) and cross-dataset (C5: 65.1%; C7: 66.7%) cases (Table 1).

nodes.name: FGSM and FPBA also show significant transferability despite lower overall potency than PGD
nodes.description: FGSM, while less effective than PGD, still showed significant transferability especially in white-box and cross-model settings, and FPBA, though especially effective against frequency-based detectors, had lower overall transferability than PGD (Table 1).

nodes.name: ASR remains non-negligible (~50%) even under severe cross-dataset and cross-model mismatch
nodes.description: The ASR remains non-negligible, around 50%, in cross-dataset scenarios (C5, C7), indicating attackers do not require access to the defender's data distribution to significantly degrade detection performance.

nodes.name: This confirms transfer-based attacks are a credible real-world threat, exposing limits of white-box-only defenses
nodes.description: Because attack success persists substantially even under severe architecture and dataset mismatch, transfer-based adversarial attacks are confirmed as a credible threat under realistic conditions, and PGD's especially high transferability highlights the limitations of defenses that focus solely on white-box robustness.

components.name: Results: adversarial training preserves nominal (clean) performance

nodes.name: All eleven AT strategies maintain high clean AUC on both FF++ and Celeb-DF-V2
nodes.description: All AT strategies maintained high clean performance, with AUC exceeding 94% on FF++ and robust performance on Celeb-DF-V2, ranging from 81.9% to 82.9% (Table 2).

nodes.name: No catastrophic overfitting was observed even with multi-attack or multi-surrogate training
nodes.description: No catastrophic overfitting was observed in nominal performance, even when employing multi-attack or multi-surrogate training strategies, unlike the failure mode associated with single-attack AT described in Section 2.3.

nodes.name: Ensemble and surrogate-based strategies preserve nominal performance with only limited fluctuation from baseline
nodes.description: The ensemble and surrogate-based AT strategies preserved nominal performance, with limited fluctuations compared to the Base (no-AT) baseline.

nodes.name: This supports the practical deployability of AT, since it does not trade away clean accuracy
nodes.description: Because high AUC is preserved across all AT strategies and both datasets, this supports the practical deployment of adversarial training in real-world systems, satisfying the basic requirement that a defense not sacrifice nominal performance.

components.name: Results: AT diversity helps in-distribution robustness but degrades under cross-dataset mismatch

nodes.name: Single-attack AT (e.g. PGD) already yields substantial in-distribution ASR reduction
nodes.description: AT with a single strong attack such as PGD yields substantial ASR reductions in-distribution, e.g. reducing C1 ASR from 99.6% to 20.2% (Table 3).

nodes.name: Ensemble and surrogate-diversified AT achieve further, larger ASR reductions in-distribution
nodes.description: Increasing diversity of adversarial examples brings further gains: Ensemble AT achieves the lowest C1 ASR (1.1%) and strong C3 reduction, and surrogate-based AT (PGD_surr, Ens_surr) generally outperforms single-attack counterparts, with an exception for FPBA in C1/C5.

nodes.name: This confirms diversity in AT improves in-distribution and cross-model generalization to unseen attacks
nodes.description: Because broader exposure to adversarial perturbations during training reduces ASR further than single-attack AT, particularly and most pronouncedly in cross-model configuration C3, this confirms that diversity in AT enhances the model's ability to generalize to unseen attacks and transfer scenarios in-distribution.

nodes.name: Under cross-dataset conditions (C5, C7), diversity's benefits diminish and ASR often stays above 50%
nodes.description: The benefits of AT diversity diminish under cross-dataset (C5) and cross-dataset & cross-model (C7) conditions; even Ens_Surr, the most diverse strategy, yields only modest ASR reductions and remains above 50% ASR in some cases.

nodes.name: Some AT strategies show negative AMR under high mismatch, meaning AT increases vulnerability
nodes.description: In certain cross-dataset configurations such as FGSM, FPBA, Ens, and Surr, negative AMR values are observed, indicating that adversarial training can inadvertently increase vulnerability rather than reduce it.

nodes.name: Negative AMR is hypothesized to stem from overfitting to the adversarial artifact distribution seen in training
nodes.description: The authors hypothesize the observed negative AMR values can be attributed to models overfitting on the adversarial artifacts distribution seen during training, leading them to be less accurate on perturbations from other (unseen dataset) distributions.

nodes.name: Together this shows AT robustness is highly sensitive to alignment between training and evaluation distributions
nodes.description: The combination of diminished gains, near-50%+ residual ASR, and outright negative AMR under cross-dataset mismatch shows that the robustness conferred by adversarial training is highly sensitive to the alignment between training and evaluation distributions, revealing a critical limitation of AT alone.

nodes.name: Leave-one-out analysis confirms full attack coverage matters, with FPBA omission especially costly cross-dataset
nodes.description: Leave-one-out ensemble AT shows that omitting any single attack consistently increases ASR across all DUMB cases, with omitting FPBA (leaving PGD_FGSM) causing especially higher cross-dataset ASR (C5: 64.1%, C7: 66.2%), highlighting the unique value of frequency-domain-specific attacks in training coverage.

nodes.name: Surrogate diversity helps mitigate single-model overfitting but cannot fully compensate for distribution shift
nodes.description: Surrogate-based AT strategies demonstrate that leveraging adversarial examples from multiple model architectures further enhances robustness versus single-surrogate counterparts, particularly cross-model and cross-dataset, but surrogate diversity alone cannot fully compensate for distributional shift between training and evaluation data.

isolated_nodes.name: DeepfakeBench's three-way detector taxonomy: naive, spatial, frequential
isolated_nodes.description: DeepfakeBench introduced a classification of deepfake detectors into three categories according to the information leveraged: naive, spatial, and frequential.

isolated_nodes.name: Deepfake generation categories: face swapping, editing, synthesis, reenactment
isolated_nodes.description: Deepfakes are commonly classified into four generation categories: face swapping, face editing, entire face synthesis, and face reenactment, using GAN- and diffusion-based generative techniques.

isolated_nodes.name: Black-box attack taxonomy: decision-based, score-based, transfer-based
isolated_nodes.description: Black-box attacks assuming limited/no target-model knowledge are typically divided into decision-based and score-based (both requiring extensive queries) and transfer-based attacks (crafted on surrogates, applied without queries).

isolated_nodes.name: Five detector architectures selected for the study
isolated_nodes.description: Five state-of-the-art detectors are used: Xception (baseline CNN), UCF (feature disentanglement), RECCE (reconstruction+classification dual-task), SPSL (phase-spectrum analysis), and SRM (learnable high-frequency noise filters), chosen for benchmark performance, code availability, and coverage of spatial/frequency methods.

isolated_nodes.name: Three attacks selected: FGSM, PGD, FPBA
isolated_nodes.description: FGSM (single-step gradient-sign), PGD (iterative FGSM variant), and FPBA (a deepfake-specific attack combining spatial and frequency artifacts) are used to cover both gradient-based literature-standard attacks and a domain-specific attack.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal ASR definitions for white-box (C1) and cross-model (C3) cases
isolated_nodes.description: ASR for the white-box case (C1) is defined as the average fraction of successful attacks per model/attack pair (Eq. 2), and for the cross-model case (C3) as the average over all surrogate/target model pairs with differing architecture (Eq. 3); cross-dataset analogues (C5, C7) follow the same form on Celeb-DF-V2 and are given in the Appendix.

isolated_nodes.name: Dataset and preprocessing details: FF++ and Celeb-DF-V2
isolated_nodes.description: FaceForensics++ (four forgery methods, 70/10/20 video-level split to avoid identity leakage) is used for training and in-distribution evaluation, while Celeb-DF-V2 (a single distinct face-swapping method, DeepfakeBench's preprocessed version) is used for out-of-distribution evaluation.

isolated_nodes.name: Attack implementation and perturbation budget details
isolated_nodes.description: All attacks are constrained to an ℓ∞ perturbation budget of 9/255 determined via a qualitative imperceptibility study; PGD uses alpha=4/255 with 4 steps and random start via TorchAttacks, and FPBA uses K=3 appended models, learning rate 0.001, N=5 spectrum transformations per step, and 4 iterations.

isolated_nodes.name: Adversarial training data composition: 80% clean / 20% adversarial
isolated_nodes.description: Following the DUMB/DUMBer configuration, all AT strategies are trained from scratch (not fine-tuned) using training sets composed of 80% clean and 20% adversarial samples, with the adversarial subset split equally among attacks/surrogates when multiple are used.

structural_reasoning: The graph mirrors the paper's applied-benchmark structure: motivate an underexplored gap, adapt an existing framework (DUMB/DUMBer) to fill it, then report layered empirical findings that answer the three stated research questions. C1 and C2 separate the general AT-realism gap from the specific DUMB/DUMBer-to-deepfake extension gap, since the Introduction and Related Work advance these as two linked but distinct motivating claims. C3 reconstructs the Method section's taxonomy adaptation and evaluation-protocol construction (the four DUMB cases, ASR/AMR metrics, 1920-evaluation design). C4 isolates the AT-diversity rationale (single-attack overfitting, prior mitigations) as its own chain, since it specifically motivates the eleven-strategy ablation studied in C7, distinct from the taxonomy-adaptation reasoning in C3. C5-C7 mirror the paper's three experimental subsections (attack effectiveness, defense validation, diversity ablation) and are explicitly aligned with the paper's own three stated research questions from the Introduction/Conclusion, each culminating in the paper's own interpretive claim (transferability persists; AT preserves clean accuracy; diversity helps in-distribution but can backfire cross-dataset). Isolated nodes are limited to background taxonomies (detector types, deepfake generation categories, black-box attack taxonomy), model/attack/dataset selection descriptions, formal ASR equations, and implementation details that support but are not premises within the central argument chains.

note_on_evidence: Evidence fields cite paper sections/subsections (e.g. 'S2.2', 'S4.1.1') rather than sentence indices, since a sentence-indexed source was not available for this document.

components.name: Pre-training corpus construction and quality

nodes.name: Iterative fastText recall pipeline
nodes.description: DeepSeekMath uses an iterative pipeline: train a fastText classifier on a seed corpus (OpenWebMath), recall math web pages from deduplicated Common Crawl, discover math-related domains, manually annotate math URL paths, and add newly found pages back to the seed corpus.

nodes.name: Iteration yields 120B token corpus
nodes.description: After four iterations of data collection, the pipeline yields 35.5M mathematical web pages totaling 120B tokens, at which point collection is stopped because ~98% of data was already collected in the prior iteration.

nodes.name: Benchmark decontamination
nodes.description: Web pages containing 10-gram (or 3-gram for short texts) overlaps with English/Chinese evaluation benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, AGIEval) are filtered out of the training corpus.

nodes.name: DeepSeekMath Corpus outperforms other math corpora
nodes.description: DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B trained on the DeepSeekMath Corpus outperforms models trained on MathPile, OpenWebMath, and Proof-Pile-2 across GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, and BBH.

nodes.name: Corpus is multilingual and large-scale
nodes.description: The DeepSeekMath Corpus is several times larger than prior math corpora and contains substantial English and Chinese content, improving performance in both languages, whereas prior English-centric corpora show limited or negative Chinese performance.

nodes.name: DeepSeekMath-Base 7B strong benchmark results
nodes.description: DeepSeekMath-Base 7B (initialized from DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B and trained on the corpus) achieves 64.2% on GSM8K and 36.2% on MATH, leading all open-source base models on 8 English/Chinese benchmarks.

nodes.name: Base model rivals Minerva 540B
nodes.description: DeepSeekMath-Base 7B is competitive with the much larger closed-source Minerva 540B model on mathematical benchmarks.

nodes.name: Parameter count is not the sole factor
nodes.description: The comparable performance of a 7B model against a 540B model indicates that model scale alone does not determine mathematical reasoning capability; high-quality pre-training data is also a key factor.

components.name: Effect of code and arXiv training on math reasoning

nodes.name: Code training benefits tool-based math reasoning
nodes.description: Two-stage training with code tokens before math tokens significantly enhances the ability to solve GSM8K/MATH problems using Python compared to general-token pretraining.

nodes.name: Code training benefits non-tool math reasoning
nodes.description: Code training also moderately improves chain-of-thought (non-tool) mathematical reasoning and boosts the efficiency of subsequent math training.

nodes.name: One-stage mixed training trade-off
nodes.description: Mixing code and math tokens in one-stage training mitigates catastrophic forgetting of coding ability but compromises non-tool mathematical reasoning, plausibly due to limited model capacity at 1.3B scale.

nodes.name: ArXiv-only training tested
nodes.description: DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B and DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B were separately trained on MathPile and ArXiv-RedPajama arXiv corpora.

nodes.name: ArXiv papers show no benefit
nodes.description: Training on arXiv-only corpora shows no notable improvement, and sometimes deterioration, across quantitative reasoning, multiple-choice, and formal math benchmarks.

components.name: GRPO algorithm design

nodes.name: PPO value-function burden
nodes.description: PPO requires training a value function typically as large as the policy model, creating substantial memory and computational burden, complicated further because usually only the last token receives a reward score.

nodes.name: GRPO removes the value function
nodes.description: GRPO obviates the need for a separate value function by using the average reward of a group of sampled outputs for the same question as the baseline.

nodes.name: GRPO reduces training resources
nodes.description: By removing the value model, GRPO significantly reduces the training resources required compared to PPO.

nodes.name: GRPO group-relative advantage aligns with reward model training
nodes.description: The group-relative way GRPO computes advantages aligns with the comparative nature of reward models, which are typically trained on pairwise/group comparisons of outputs to the same question.

nodes.name: GRPO regularizes via direct KL term in loss
nodes.description: Instead of folding a KL penalty into the per-token reward as PPO does, GRPO adds the KL divergence between policy and reference model directly to the loss, avoiding complications in advantage estimation.

nodes.name: Outcome supervision variant
nodes.description: Outcome-supervised GRPO normalizes the group's rewards and assigns the same normalized reward as the advantage to every token in an output.

nodes.name: Process supervision variant
nodes.description: Process-supervised GRPO scores each reasoning step and assigns a token's advantage as the sum of normalized rewards from subsequent steps, providing finer-grained supervision.

nodes.name: Iterative GRPO with reward model replay
nodes.description: In iterative GRPO, the reward model is continually retrained on new samples from the policy (with a replay mechanism retaining historical data), and the reference model is periodically reset to the current policy.

components.name: RL (GRPO) results on DeepSeekMath-Instruct

nodes.name: GRPO training setup
nodes.description: GRPO is applied to DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B using ~144K chain-of-thought GSM8K/MATH questions, excluding other SFT data to isolate the effect of RL on out-of-domain benchmarks.

nodes.name: In-domain gains: GSM8K and MATH
nodes.description: GRPO improves DeepSeekMath-Instruct from 82.9% to 88.2% on GSM8K and from 46.8% to 51.7% on MATH.

nodes.name: Out-of-domain gains: CMATH
nodes.description: GRPO also improves out-of-domain performance, e.g. CMATH improves from 84.6% to 88.8%, despite RL training data being restricted to GSM8K/MATH.

nodes.name: DeepSeekMath-RL 7B beats larger open-source models
nodes.description: DeepSeekMath-RL 7B surpasses all open-source models from 7B to 70B and the majority of closed-source models on the evaluated benchmarks.

components.name: Unified RL paradigm and comparative training-method analysis

nodes.name: Unified paradigm: data source, reward function, algorithm
nodes.description: SFT, RFT, DPO, Online RFT, PPO, and GRPO can all be described within a single gradient formulation composed of a data source, a reward function, and an algorithm producing a gradient coefficient.

nodes.name: Online sampling outperforms offline sampling
nodes.description: Online RFT significantly outperforms offline RFT on GSM8K and MATH, with the advantage growing in later training stages as the policy diverges further from the original SFT model.

nodes.name: GRPO surpasses Online RFT
nodes.description: GRPO outperforms Online RFT because it adjusts its gradient coefficient based on the reward model's magnitude (differential reinforcement/penalization), whereas Online RFT uniformly reinforces all correct responses.

nodes.name: Process supervision outperforms outcome supervision
nodes.description: GRPO with process supervision (GRPO+PS) shows superior performance to GRPO with outcome supervision (GRPO+OS), indicating the benefit of fine-grained, step-aware gradient coefficients.

nodes.name: Iterative RL further improves performance
nodes.description: Across two rounds of iterative RL, performance improves further, with the largest gain observed at the first iteration.

components.name: Why RL works

nodes.name: RL improves Maj@K but not Pass@K
nodes.description: Evaluating Maj@K and Pass@K for Instruct vs RL models shows RL improves Maj@K accuracy but not Pass@K accuracy on GSM8K and MATH.

nodes.name: RL reshapes output distribution rather than adding capability
nodes.description: Because RL boosts Maj@K but not Pass@K, the improvement is attributed to making correct responses more likely to surface from the TopK candidates (a more robust output distribution), rather than to an enhancement of the model's fundamental reasoning capability.

isolated_nodes.name: GRPO removes KL penalty from reward
isolated_nodes.description: GRPO uses an unbiased KL divergence estimator added directly to the loss, guaranteed to be positive, rather than an approximate per-token penalty folded into the reward.

isolated_nodes.name: Reward model over-optimization risk
isolated_nodes.description: A per-token KL penalty (in PPO) or loss-level KL term (in GRPO) is used to prevent the policy from over-optimizing against the reward model and drifting too far from the reference model.

isolated_nodes.name: SFT instruction data scale
isolated_nodes.description: The mathematical instruction-tuning dataset used for DeepSeekMath-Instruct totals 776K examples spanning CoT, PoT, and tool-integrated formats in English and Chinese.

isolated_nodes.name: Reward signal noise
isolated_nodes.description: Even carefully human-annotated reward datasets like PRM800K contain roughly 20% incorrect annotations, motivating research into RL algorithms robust to noisy reward signals.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: advanced sampling
isolated_nodes.description: The paper suggests exploring RL with out-of-distribution prompts and advanced/tree-search-based sampling strategies as a future direction for more effective RL.

isolated_nodes.name: Geometry and theorem-proving weakness
isolated_nodes.description: DeepSeekMath's capability on geometry and theorem-proving is relatively weaker than closed models, e.g. it struggles with problems involving triangles and ellipses.

isolated_nodes.name: Weaker few-shot gains than GPT-4
isolated_nodes.description: Restricted by model scale, DeepSeekMath shows similar performance in zero-shot and few-shot settings, unlike GPT-4 which improves substantially with few-shot prompting.

structural_reasoning: The graph is coherent within each thematic component: corpus construction cleanly leads to corpus quality and base-model results (C1); the code/arXiv ablation findings form a clear chain (C2); the GRPO design rationale (removing the value function, enabling group-relative advantages, and its supervision variants) is logically sequenced (C3); the RL results and unified-paradigm comparison sections (C4, C5) follow the paper's own narrative of increasingly refined methods (RFT -> Online RFT -> GRPO -> GRPO+PS -> iterative GRPO); and the Maj@K/Pass@K analysis (C6) is a tight two-node causal claim. Cross-component links (e.g., between GRPO's design in C3 and its measured results in C4, or between C1's corpus-quality claims and downstream RL in C4) are implicit in the paper but were not asserted as edges here since they involve different sections/experiments joined only by general narrative flow rather than direct evidentiary sentences, so the graph is intentionally left as separate components rather than force-connected.

title_ref: Differentially Private Federated Learning: A Systematic Review
notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the DecomposeRL example graph. This is a long systematic-review/survey paper (no arXiv ID given; ACM manuscript format), so the graph covers its main taxonomic and argumentative structure rather than every one of the 70+ cited algorithms. This source document was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Motivation: why centralized data governance is impractical, motivating FL, and why FL alone is still vulnerable.

nodes.name: Traditional DL assumes centralized trustworthy data governance
nodes.description: Traditional deep learning frameworks assume all pertinent training data is centralized under the governance of a singular, trustworthy entity.

nodes.name: Real-world data is distributed and central trust is impractical
nodes.description: In real-world industrial contexts, data is often distributed across multiple independent parties where a central trusted authority is impractical, and legal restrictions (CCPA, GDPR) plus business competition further limit data sharing.

nodes.name: FL emerges as a collaborative alternative keeping raw data local
nodes.description: Federated learning emerged as a promising collaborative learning infrastructure where participants retain data locally, training models locally and sharing only model parameters with a central server that aggregates and redistributes updates.

nodes.name: Shared model parameters still leak private information
nodes.description: Even though raw data stays local, adversaries may still infer sensitive data from shared model parameters — raw data content can be inverted from parameters, or membership information can be inferred.

nodes.name: Encryption/MPC defenses are costly and don't protect the final output
nodes.description: Methods based on homomorphic encryption or secure multiparty computation (MPC) require significant computational overhead and do not protect the final output of the computation, leaving them vulnerable to inference attacks.

nodes.name: DP emerges as a SOTA mitigation for FL privacy risk
nodes.description: Differential privacy (DP) is one state-of-the-art paradigm to mitigate privacy risks in FL; adding proper DP noise during local training or to uploaded parameters can prevent unintentional leakage (e.g., via membership inference attacks).

components.description: Research gap: existing DP-FL surveys are inadequate, motivating a new taxonomy.

nodes.name: Publication volume makes synthesis urgent
nodes.description: As the volume of publications on differentially private federated learning continues to grow, summarizing and organizing this research has become both urgent and challenging.

nodes.name: Existing surveys lack comprehensive technical/systematic analysis
nodes.description: Despite existing surveys on DP-FL, they do not provide a comprehensive, technical, and systematic analysis of differential privacy within the federated learning context.

nodes.name: Existing taxonomies inadequately consider protection object/level
nodes.description: Existing taxonomies have not adequately considered the objects and level of privacy protection provided by various DP models in federated learning.

nodes.name: Prior classifications based on presence of a trusted server are imprecise
nodes.description: Prior classification approaches based on the presence of a centralized trusted server lack precision, because FL is inherently a composite framework (e.g., cross-silo clients may also maintain local servers), so characterizing scenarios lacking a trusted central aggregator solely as LDP is overly simplistic.

nodes.name: This motivates a new definition/guarantee-based taxonomy
nodes.description: This gap motivates a new taxonomy of DP-FL based on the definition and guarantee of various DP models (DP, LDP, shuffle model) and federated scenarios, rather than server-trust assumptions alone.

components.description: The two-axis taxonomy: FL scenarios (Horizontal/Vertical/Transfer) crossed with DP models (DP/LDP/Shuffle), further split by neighborhood level.

nodes.name: Three FL scenarios classified by data partitioning
nodes.description: The survey classifies works into Horizontal FL, Vertical FL, and Transfer FL based on how data is partitioned among participants, encompassing all federated learning scenarios.

nodes.name: Most prior DP-FL work is Horizontal; Vertical/Transfer growing in importance
nodes.description: Although most prior work on DP for FL has been conducted in Horizontal FL, as more privacy issues are exposed in vertical and transfer FL, research on DP models in those settings is becoming increasingly important.

nodes.name: DP models further split by neighborhood level (sample vs. client)
nodes.description: For DP and the shuffle model, works are further categorized into sample-level and client-level based on the definition of neighboring datasets, corresponding to the protected objects (LDP lacks this neighboring-dataset concept).

nodes.name: Rigorous DP-model differentiation clarifies protection subjects and methods
nodes.description: Rigorous differentiation of DP models based on definitions and privacy guarantees clarifies the protection subjects of different DP models and enhances understanding of their associated implementation methods.

components.description: Formal relationships among DP, LDP, and the shuffle model.

nodes.name: DP relies on neighboring datasets; LDP does not
nodes.description: The main difference between DP and LDP lies in their definitions: DP relies on neighboring datasets as input, while LDP has no concept of neighboring datasets.

nodes.name: LDP is derivable from DP as a single-record special case
nodes.description: LDP can be derived from DP when the input datasets are taken to be single-record datasets, since any two single-record datasets are trivially neighbors; this makes LDP a stronger condition requiring the mechanism to satisfy DP for any two domain values.

nodes.name: LDP implies DP-compliance but not vice versa
nodes.description: LDP can comply with (imply) DP, but the reverse does not hold true.

nodes.name: Shuffle model builds on LDP and adds anonymization to reach DP
nodes.description: The shuffle model adds a trusted shuffler between server and clients; each client satisfies LDP facing the shuffler, and the shuffled data (now forming a dataset with a neighboring-dataset concept) satisfies DP facing the server.

nodes.name: Shuffling yields a tighter centralized privacy budget (privacy amplification)
nodes.description: Thanks to anonymity from shuffling, each user's privacy benefits from both local randomization and randomness from other clients, yielding a smaller centralized privacy loss ε_c than the local budget ε_l — a phenomenon called privacy amplification, roughly O(√n) smaller.

components.description: Neighboring-dataset levels within HFL: sample-level (SL-DP) vs. client-level (CL-DP), and their distinct protection goals/server-trust assumptions.

nodes.name: SL-DP protects presence of a single sample under a semi-honest server
nodes.description: Sample-level DP (SL-DP): two datasets are neighboring if they differ in a single sample; the goal is to bound the influence of any single sample/record on the learning outcome distribution, generally assuming a semi-honest (honest-but-curious) server, with independent per-client privacy budgets.

nodes.name: DPSGD is the mainstream SL-DP implementation
nodes.description: The most mainstream approach to implementing SL-DP is executing Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD) on each client: per-sample gradient clipping bounds sensitivity, then Gaussian noise scaled to the clipping bound is added to the batch-averaged gradient before the descent step.

nodes.name: CL-DP protects presence of a single client under an honest server
nodes.description: Client-level DP (CL-DP): two datasets are neighboring if they differ in a single client/device; the goal is to limit the impact of any single client on the aggregation result distribution, generally assuming a fully honest server acting as data owner.

nodes.name: SL-DP vs LDP are often conflated but differ structurally
nodes.description: SL-DP and LDP are often confused because both assume a semi-honest server, but they differ: SL-DP has a neighboring-dataset concept requiring per-sample clipping across local iterations, whereas LDP's neighboring datasets degenerate to any two inputs, with sensitivity from directly clipping model parameters and privacy loss occurring only at upload time; LDP mechanisms generally achieve SL-DP protection but not vice versa (except the rare single-data-point case).

nodes.name: LDP and CL-DP-with-Secure-Aggregation differ in local noise scale
nodes.description: LDP and CL-DP-with-Secure-Aggregation both add local noise but at different scales (e.g., Lap(0, ε/Δf) for LDP vs. Lap(0, ε/(KΔf)) for CL-DP with K clients), so CL-DP-with-SA's local noise, though nonzero, provides far weaker local protection than true ε-LDP.

components.description: CL-DP with Secure Aggregation: motivation for eliminating trusted-server reliance and the resulting discrete-noise research thread.

nodes.name: CL-DP typically requires a secure/trusted aggregation server
nodes.description: CL-DP as described requires the server to be trusted to correctly aggregate client updates, which is itself a strong assumption.

nodes.name: Secure aggregation combined with DP removes trusted-authority reliance
nodes.description: To eliminate reliance on a trusted central authority, recent studies combine DP techniques with secure aggregation: each client adds noise locally, encrypts, and sends to the server, which aggregates, so the aggregate noise level across clients ensures the encrypted model satisfies CL-DP.

nodes.name: Secure aggregation's modular arithmetic is incompatible with continuous noise
nodes.description: Secure aggregation relies on modular arithmetic and cannot be directly compatible with continuous noise mechanisms (Laplace, Gaussian) traditionally used for DP.

nodes.name: This incompatibility drove development of discrete noise mechanisms
nodes.description: This incompatibility motivated researchers to design discrete noise-addition mechanisms (binomial, discrete Gaussian, Skellam, Poisson Binomial) integrable with secure aggregation, each addressing limitations of the prior mechanism (e.g., binomial noise only achieves approximate DP; discrete Gaussian isn't closed under addition; Skellam's noise is unbounded requiring modular clipping bias; Poisson Binomial is unbiased and bounded).

components.description: LDP-HFL's core obstacle: the curse of dimensionality, and the two families of solutions (shuffling and dimension selection).

nodes.name: LDP-HFL is essentially high-dimensional mean estimation
nodes.description: LDP-HFL can be viewed as a mean estimation problem based on LDP, since each model parameter represents a high-dimensional continuous data point that each client perturbs locally before the server aggregates.

nodes.name: High model dimensionality causes exponential variance growth
nodes.description: Directly applying LDP mean estimation to FL faces obstacles because model-parameter dimensionality is extremely high, and as dimension increases, the privacy budget allocated per dimension decreases, leading to exponential increase in statistical variance.

nodes.name: Parameter shuffling mitigates the dimensionality curse
nodes.description: One family of solutions uses parameter shuffling (splitting parameters by layer and shuffling within each layer) to break cross-dimension associations, avoiding privacy-budget division across dimensions under the independence assumption — though this does not itself constitute the formal shuffle model's privacy amplification.

nodes.name: Dimension selection/sampling is an alternative mitigation family
nodes.description: A second family selects or samples a subset of important dimensions (e.g., top-k by update magnitude) to perturb, rather than perturbing all dimensions, trading off convergence speed for reduced noise.

components.description: Applying the shuffle model within HFL, split again by CL-DP vs SL-DP neighborhood level.

nodes.name: Shuffle model in HFL split into CL-DP and SL-DP classes
nodes.description: Referring to the HFL taxonomy, the shuffle model within HFL is divided into two classes: client-level (shuffle CL-DP) and sample-level (shuffle SL-DP).

nodes.name: Shuffle CL-DP: per-user LDP randomization aggregated into DP via shuffling
nodes.description: In shuffle CL-DP, each user randomizes local updates with LDP, and the aggregated updates through shuffling satisfy DP; researchers typically set δ_l=0 for the local LDP budget.

nodes.name: Shuffle SL-DP redefines neighboring datasets at the sample rather than client level
nodes.description: In shuffle SL-DP, the neighboring-dataset definition for the resulting DP analysis is based on samples rather than clients; a straightforward approach perturbs each sample's update separately before aggregating and shuffling.

components.description: Why VFL and TFL require distinct DP treatment from HFL, and their characteristic threat models.

nodes.name: VFL/TFL research volume lags far behind HFL
nodes.description: The amount of work on DP models in VFL and TFL is far less than in HFL, though as more privacy issues are exposed in VFL and TFL, research there is becoming increasingly important.

nodes.name: VFL joint training risks leaking both features and labels
nodes.description: In VFL, parties share sample IDs but hold different feature spaces (one party typically holding labels); joint training poses privacy threats because both extracted features and gradient-derived label information can potentially be inferred by the respective other party.

nodes.name: VFL DP work splits into feature-protection and label-protection strands
nodes.description: Consequently, DP-VFL research splits into work protecting features (perturbing the feature extractor's output before transmission to the server) and work protecting labels (perturbing gradients or labels themselves, since the server/label-holder needs label access to compute gradients), with some work protecting both sides simultaneously.

nodes.name: TFL involves little/no feature or sample overlap, motivating knowledge distillation
nodes.description: TFL applies when clients (source domains) and a server (target domain) have limited or no overlap in features or samples; knowledge distillation is commonly used to transfer knowledge from local 'teacher' models to an unlabeled public/target dataset via aggregated predictions.

nodes.name: Teacher-prediction outputs themselves leak information, motivating DP-PATE lineage
nodes.description: Because attackers can exploit teacher models' output predictions to attack original data, DP is incorporated into the aggregation of teacher predictions, originating with the PATE algorithm and its subsequent refinements (Gaussian-mechanism/RDP tightening, multi-client extensions, LDP variants without a trusted aggregator).

components.description: Extension of DP-FL to modality- and domain-specific application challenges (graph data as an illustrative case).

nodes.name: GNN message passing creates node interdependence, complicating sensitivity
nodes.description: In graph-data FL, GNN message passing makes a node's embedding depend on both itself and neighboring nodes, so accurately measuring this dependency is crucial for determining sensitivity (which drives DP noise scale), but doing so is hard.

nodes.name: Two solution families: noise outside GNN training vs. dependency-aware gradient perturbation
nodes.description: Methods addressing this either avoid direct dependency measurement by perturbing the graph structure/embeddings outside standard GNN training (at the cost of usability, since perturbation isn't tailored to GNNs), or explicitly measure node dependency level (e.g., bounding in-degree via sampling) and apply gradient perturbation via DP-SGD, at the cost of high sensitivity that grows with GNN depth.

components.description: Open challenge: convergence analysis for DP-HFL is fundamentally harder than for standard HFL.

nodes.name: Tight convergence bounds guide theory and hyperparameter tuning
nodes.description: A tight upper bound on convergence provides theoretical assurance of rapid convergence and enables analyzing how hyperparameters affect convergence speed, guiding tuning or new optimization algorithm design.

nodes.name: DP-HFL convergence analysis must additionally model clipping and noise
nodes.description: Compared to standard HFL, DP-HFL convergence analysis must consider the effects of clipping and noise addition, making it more challenging to obtain a relatively tight upper bound.

nodes.name: Existing analyses rely on strong assumptions and loose bounds
nodes.description: Existing convergence analyses for DP-HFL algorithms either make strong assumptions about the objective function/gradients (e.g., Bounded Gradient, Bounded Variance) or remain at a loose O(1/ε) bound, leaving tighter, assumption-light convergence analysis as an open future direction.

edges.note: cross-component link from C5: DPSGD's clipping+noise is exactly what complicates convergence analysis

components.description: Open challenge: User-level DP as a needed generalization beyond sample-level and client-level.

nodes.name: Real clients often contain multiple users with multiple records each
nodes.description: In many scenarios a client (e.g., a hospital) contains many users, and an individual user may contribute multiple samples/records (e.g., a patient with multiple medical records), which neither SL-DP nor CL-DP directly captures.

nodes.name: User-level DP (UL-DP) defined to hide a single user's full record set
nodes.description: User-level DP is defined so that two datasets are neighboring if they differ in all samples from a single user, aiming to bound the influence of any single user's entire contribution on the learning outcome distribution.

nodes.name: UL-DP faces a fundamental noise-vs-bias trade-off
nodes.description: Allowing users to contribute many samples (to protect minority high-contribution outliers) may introduce excessive noise, while restricting user contribution keeps noise lower but discards surplus data and introduces bias; this field remains underexplored in FL specifically.

edges.note: cross-component link from C5: motivated as a gap relative to SL-DP/CL-DP

components.description: Open challenge: absence of comprehensive empirical privacy auditing across DP models/levels, despite shared theoretical budget notation.

nodes.name: Different DP models/levels protect different objects despite shared ε notation
nodes.description: The objects directly protected by DP-FL vary based on the DP model and neighborhood level used, yet privacy protection is commonly characterized by a single privacy budget ε across all of them.

nodes.name: No article provides comprehensive empirical comparison across models/levels
nodes.description: Although many articles design algorithms for different DP models and levels, no article yet provides a comprehensive comparison among them, and definitions with the same nominal ε may have different real-world privacy effects due to their different protection objects.

nodes.name: Practical attack-based/audit-based quantification proposed as the fix
nodes.description: Conducting practical attacks (membership inference, attribute inference, data reconstruction) or applying DP auditing technology to approach worst-case guarantees is proposed as a way to empirically quantify and compare privacy effects across DP models and levels.

nodes.name: Prior SL-DP vs CL-DP comparisons are insufficiently rigorous
nodes.description: While some prior work (Naseri et al.) compared SL-DP and CL-DP under a trusted server, the survey argues this comparison is not comprehensive enough since the two definitions have different security assumptions and protection objects and cannot be directly compared without accounting for that.

edges.note: cross-component link from C3: the taxonomy's protection-object distinctions are exactly what motivates this open challenge

components.description: Open challenge: DP-FL for LLM fine-tuning faces communication overhead and the dimensionality-driven utility/privacy trade-off.

nodes.name: LLM fine-tuning via FL has significant promise but high communication cost
nodes.description: Federated fine-tuning of LLMs with DP has significant promise for privacy-preserving personalization, but faces substantial communication overhead from the iterative aggregation of model updates for a complex, large model.

nodes.name: Existing communication-mitigation strategies don't guarantee privacy
nodes.description: Some strategies mitigate communication bottlenecks but cannot provide concrete guarantees for protecting training data privacy, motivating approaches (like DP-LoRA) that reduce communication cost while retaining formal DP guarantees by fine-tuning only a small set of low-rank parameters.

nodes.name: Embedding-layer dimensionality causes a severe utility/privacy trade-off
nodes.description: DPSGD's added noise, applied to the immense parameter count of language-model embedding layers, severely impacts learning ability — the curse of dimensionality — requiring solutions like public-data pre-training plus private fine-tuning, or knowledge distillation, to bypass adding heavy noise directly to high-dimensional private data.

edges.note: cross-component link from C7: same dimensionality-curse mechanism recurs for LLM embeddings

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: reviewed and summarized DP model definitions/properties
nodes.description: The survey reviewed the definitions and guarantees of DP, LDP, and shuffle model, summarizing their relaxations/differentiation, plus commonly used properties, composition mechanisms, and perturbation methods.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: novel rigorous taxonomy based on DP definitions/guarantees
nodes.description: The survey broke from the traditional server-trust-based classification and explored a new taxonomy grounded in DP definitions and guarantees.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: discussed 70+ articles across all three FL scenarios
nodes.description: Over 70 recent articles on DP-FL are discussed and clarified by protection target, covering not just Horizontal FL but also Vertical and Transfer FL.

nodes.name: Contribution 4: summarized applications by data type and real-world domain
nodes.description: Applications of DP-FL are summarized by data modality (graph, bipartite/recommendation, time series) and real-world scenario (healthcare, IoT, finance).

nodes.name: Contribution 5: proposed 6 future research directions
nodes.description: Based on the preceding discussion, 6 promising future research directions are proposed (convergence analysis, user-level DP, privacy auditing, LLM fine-tuning, cross-domain TFL, multimodal FL).

isolated_nodes.name: Cross-silo suits SL-DP; cross-device suits CL-DP/LDP
isolated_nodes.description: Cross-silo settings (fewer clients, more samples each) better leverage SL-DP's strengths, while cross-device settings (many clients, e.g. mobile devices) better realize the advantages of CL-DP and LDP.

isolated_nodes.name: Time series DP-FL commonly uses hierarchical granularity with truncation
isolated_nodes.description: Publishing time-series data with DP in FL typically partitions the series into multiple granularities and adds noise at each, using truncation-based methods since real data often concentrates well below the theoretical upper bound used to size DP noise.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: cross-domain differentially private TFL
isolated_nodes.description: Current DP-TFL work mostly assumes intra-domain (similar-feature) source/target datasets; real-world cross-domain scenarios require balancing privacy and utility while transferring features from decentralized multi-source domains via unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: multimodal federated learning with DP
isolated_nodes.description: Multimodal FL (multi-sensor, vision-language) combined with DP is underexplored; cross-modal complementary information can enable inference attacks, and varying modality dimensions complicate DP noise calibration, with DPSGD often failing to converge on high-dimensional multimodal models.
