components.name: Motivation: robustness alone is insufficient without reliable uncertainty for selective classification

nodes.name: Safety-critical deployment requires models that are both robust and uncertainty-aware
nodes.description: Recent trustworthy machine learning efforts emphasize that reliable systems in safety-critical deployments must be both robust to perturbations and uncertainty-aware.

nodes.name: Adversarial training is the dominant paradigm for improving robustness
nodes.description: Adversarial training has emerged as the dominant paradigm to improve robustness against imperceptible, often transferable adversarial perturbations.

nodes.name: Robustness alone is insufficient for risk-sensitive decisions; a system must know when not to predict
nodes.description: When errors are costly, robustness alone is insufficient for risk-sensitive decision making; a system must also know when not to predict, a requirement naturally captured by selective classification, where the model can abstain on inputs it considers unreliable.

nodes.name: Selective behavior depends on the integrity of uncertainty under perturbation, not just accuracy under attack
nodes.description: Selective behavior depends not only on accuracy under attack but on the integrity of uncertainty under perturbations: errors, especially adversarial ones, must be assigned high uncertainty so they can be rejected.

nodes.name: Standard robustness evaluations reporting only robust accuracy can hide degraded uncertainty ranking
nodes.description: Robustness evaluations that primarily report robust accuracy can hide a damaging failure mode: a method may become harder to fool while simultaneously degrading uncertainty ranking, producing confident adversarial mistakes that bypass rejection and manifest as silent failures at practically relevant operating points.

nodes.name: This motivates systematically studying the effect of adversarial training on uncertainty reliability via selective classification
nodes.description: Because robust accuracy alone can mask degraded uncertainty ranking, and selective classification has rarely been systematically analyzed alongside adversarial robustness, this motivates investigating adversarial training's effect on predictive uncertainty through the lens of selective classification.

components.name: A second gap: confounded, non-standardized robustness-uncertainty evaluation

nodes.name: Robustness and uncertainty are both highly sensitive to experimental confounders
nodes.description: Both robustness and uncertainty are highly sensitive to experimental confounders (architecture, augmentation, threat model, etc.), making it difficult to draw controlled conclusions about their trade-off.

nodes.name: This methodological gap motivates a unified, standardized benchmark
nodes.description: The sensitivity of both robustness and uncertainty to uncontrolled confounders motivates introducing a unified benchmark that standardizes these factors and evaluates models as selective systems across clean, adversarial, and common-corruption regimes.

nodes.name: The benchmark reveals that robustness gains do not reliably translate to robust uncertainty across SOTA AT methods
nodes.description: Across a broad set of state-of-the-art adversarial training methods evaluated under this standardized benchmark, robustness gains do not reliably translate to robust uncertainty, and several strong defenses improve adversarial accuracy while worsening risk-coverage behavior due to degraded uncertainty ranking.

nodes.name: This empirical pattern motivates a new training objective that explicitly targets uncertainty under attack
nodes.description: Because the standardized benchmark reveals that existing SOTA adversarial training methods do not reliably preserve uncertainty quality under attack, this motivates developing a training objective that explicitly targets predictive uncertainty and regularizes the posterior under attack.

components.name: Positioning against prior AT, EDL, and robustness-uncertainty literature

nodes.name: Adversarial training induces a clean-vs-robust accuracy trade-off, which prior work (TRADES etc.) addresses on the accuracy side only
nodes.description: AT often induces a trade-off between clean and robust accuracy; TRADES addresses this by balancing clean classification performance with clean-adversarial prediction consistency, while MART, AWP, SEAT, and Generalist improve robust generalization through other example-aware or ensembling mechanisms, but none explicitly targets uncertainty quality.

nodes.name: Evidential Deep Learning models a Dirichlet posterior over class probabilities to represent evidence
nodes.description: Evidential Deep Learning parameterizes a higher-order distribution (e.g., a Dirichlet) to represent evidence over class probabilities, and despite known theoretical limitations (e.g., absence of strictly proper scoring rules for second-order distributions), EDL uncertainties are often well-ranked in practice for selective prediction and OOD detection.

nodes.name: Robustness and uncertainty have largely been studied separately despite being closely related
nodes.description: Robustness and uncertainty are often studied separately despite being closely related; under adversarial perturbations even conformal and representation-distance uncertainty methods may become unreliable, and both conventional and EDL classifiers can produce overconfident adversarial errors.

nodes.name: The effect of adversarial training on uncertainty ranking and selective performance remains comparatively underexplored
nodes.description: Despite growing recognition that robustness and uncertainty interact, the specific effect of adversarial training on uncertainty ranking and selective performance remains comparatively underexplored in the literature.

nodes.name: This motivates combining EDL's well-ranked uncertainty with an adversarial training objective specifically targeting posterior robustness
nodes.description: Because prior AT variants target only accuracy-level consistency, EDL provides well-ranked but not adversarially-tested uncertainty, and the AT-uncertainty interaction is underexplored, this motivates a method that combines evidential (Dirichlet) uncertainty modeling with an adversarial training objective explicitly enforcing posterior-level robustness.

components.name: The evidential classifier: Dirichlet parameterization and entropy-based selection

nodes.name: The network outputs non-negative evidence that parameterizes a Dirichlet distribution
nodes.description: For input x, the network outputs a non-negative evidence vector eθ(x), parameterizing a Dirichlet distribution over categorical probabilities via concentration parameters α = eθ(x) + 1.

nodes.name: The Dirichlet mean gives the predictive distribution; the total concentration (strength) gives a confidence proxy
nodes.description: This induces a posterior predictive distribution Cat(π̄) with predictive mean π̄ = α/S used for classification, while the total concentration S = Σαc inversely quantifies model uncertainty, so the Dirichlet parameterization structurally separates the classification signal from the confidence signal.

nodes.name: Total predictive uncertainty is defined as the entropy of the posterior predictive distribution
nodes.description: Total predictive uncertainty is quantified as u(x) = H[Cat(π̄)] = -Σc (αc/S)log(αc/S) (Eq. 1), enabling a threshold-based selective rule that rejects predictions whose entropy exceeds τ.

nodes.name: This structured decomposition gives a principled foundation for selective classification via uncertainty thresholding
nodes.description: Because the Dirichlet parameterization cleanly separates predictive mean (label) from strength (confidence), and total uncertainty is defined directly from the resulting posterior predictive entropy, this provides a principled basis for the selective rule gτ(x;u) = 1[u(x) ≤ τ] used throughout the paper.

components.name: EV-AT objective: evidence-targeted adversary and robust evidence alignment

nodes.name: Standard AT minimizes worst-case classification loss but does not explicitly enforce uncertainty integrity
nodes.description: Adversarial training addresses clean accuracy and robustness of the predicted label by minimizing worst-case classification loss over the ℓp-ball, but it does not explicitly enforce integrity of uncertainty; robust-accuracy gains can therefore coincide with degraded uncertainty ranking.

nodes.name: EV-AT instead regularizes uncertainty via posterior-level robustness in log-Dirichlet space
nodes.description: EV-AT regularizes uncertainty under adversarial perturbation via posterior-level robustness, aligning clean and adversarial evidential representations in log-parameter space (η = log α) to jointly stabilize the predictive mean and the evidence strength/concentration.

nodes.name: Clean evidential learning uses a Type-II maximum likelihood loss plus a KL regularizer toward the uniform prior
nodes.description: The evidential classification loss LEV combines the negative log marginal likelihood over the Dirichlet-Categorical model (Eq. 2) with a KL regularizer toward the uniform Dirichlet prior on non-ground-truth evidence, encouraging vacuity when evidence is weak (Eq. 3).

nodes.name: The adversary is evidence-targeted: it maximizes drift in log-Dirichlet parameters rather than just cross-entropy
nodes.description: Unlike standard AT, which constructs adversarial examples by maximizing classification loss, EV-AT's adversary explicitly maximizes a discrepancy D between clean and adversarial log-Dirichlet parameters η via K-step PGD, directly stress-testing uncertainty integrity rather than only flipping the predicted label.

nodes.name: The robust evidence alignment term penalizes this worst-case evidence drift during training
nodes.description: The robust evidence alignment loss LREA = D(η, η_adv) is minimized alongside LEV in the overall EV-AT objective L = LEV + β·LREA (Eq. 4), where β trades off clean evidential fitting against robust posterior alignment.

nodes.name: IKL divergence is used to instantiate D, chosen for stable gradients in log-parameter space
nodes.description: EV-AT instantiates the discrepancy D as the Improved Kullback-Leibler (IKL) Divergence, which measures drift directly in log-parameter space and yields stable gradients for both the evidence-targeted attack and the alignment objective.

nodes.name: This objective enforces posterior-level rather than logit-level consistency, directly discouraging confident adversarial errors
nodes.description: Because LREA penalizes worst-case discrepancy in the full log-Dirichlet posterior rather than only logits, the EV-AT objective directly discourages confident adversarial errors by jointly limiting attack-induced changes in both the predictive mean and the evidence strength.

components.name: Theoretical motivation: why align in log-Dirichlet (η) space rather than logits or α

nodes.name: Logit alignment only indirectly constrains the quantities selection actually depends on
nodes.description: Logits alignment is a common robustness heuristic, but logits are not identifiable (e.g. additive shifts leave softmax unchanged) and standard alignment targets only a single classification vector, not the confidence structure needed for abstention.

nodes.name: The Dirichlet posterior separates label (mean) and confidence (strength) into distinct roles
nodes.description: In an evidential model, the Dirichlet posterior separates these roles: the mean π̄ determines the predicted class, while the strength S controls uncertainty, so aligning the (log-)posterior directly stabilizes both the predictive distribution and its confidence.

nodes.name: Log-parameters induce the predictive mean via softmax, so constraining η-drift constrains mean-drift
nodes.description: With η = log α, the predictive mean equals softmax(η) (Eq. 5), so constraining drift in η directly constrains drift in the predictive mean π̄.

nodes.name: Lemma 1 shows η-drift bounds give multiplicative stability of concentrations, strength, and mean simultaneously
nodes.description: Lemma 1 shows that if the ℓ∞ drift in η is bounded by ρ, then the ratios of perturbed to original αc, S, and π̄c are all bounded within multiplicative factors of e^ρ or e^(2ρ) (Eq. 6), formalizing that log-Dirichlet alignment jointly limits changes in class probabilities and evidence scale.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 shows strength upper-bounds posterior variance, so controlling strength stabilizes confidence
nodes.description: Lemma 2 shows that for any Dirichlet distribution, the maximum per-class posterior variance is upper-bounded by 1/(4(S+1)) (Eq. 7), so higher, stabilized strength directly limits posterior variance/precision.

nodes.name: Since the selector thresholds entropy of the mean, stabilizing the mean and strength together stabilizes the selection decision
nodes.description: Because the selective rule thresholds predictive entropy u(x) = H[Cat(π̄)], and η-alignment (via Lemmas 1-2) jointly stabilizes both the mean π̄ (which determines entropy) and the strength S (which governs precision), aligning in η-space is theoretically the appropriate target for robust selective behavior.

nodes.name: Entropy continuity (Lemma 3) and a selection-stability result show bounded mean-drift implies bounded, often unchanged selection decisions
nodes.description: Lemma 3 (a Fannes-type entropy continuity bound, Eqs. 8-10) shows that if π̄_adv stays close to π̄ in total variation, the resulting uncertainty score changes by a bounded amount, and consequently the accept/reject decision gτ is provably unchanged whenever this uncertainty change is smaller than the margin to the threshold τ.

components.name: Benchmark findings: SOTA AT methods show weak/inconsistent robustness-uncertainty correlation

nodes.name: No SOTA baseline dominates as a selective system across metrics
nodes.description: Across the standardized benchmark, no SOTA baseline dominates as a selective system: higher AutoAttack accuracy does not reliably imply lower adversarial AUGRC (Table 1).

nodes.name: Some methods with the strongest AA accuracy show comparatively weak adversarial uncertainty ranking
nodes.description: Under Basic augmentation, IKL-AT and TRADES-AWP achieve the strongest AA accuracies among baselines yet remain comparatively weak in AUGRC under AA, indicating degraded uncertainty ranking under attack despite strong robust accuracy.

nodes.name: Conversely, some methods with weaker accuracy show the best uncertainty, revealing an internal trade-off
nodes.description: AT-AWP attains the best Clean/AA AUGRC among baselines under Basic augmentation despite lower AA accuracy than other baselines, revealing an internal robustness-uncertainty trade-off within existing methods.

nodes.name: The robustness-uncertainty correlation across baselines is weak overall
nodes.description: Plotting average accuracy versus average AUGRC across methods shows a weak correlation: e.g. IKL-AT increases robustness over AT (69.90 vs 68.05) but yields worse uncertainty (8.00 vs 7.85), and AT-AWP matches AT's robustness while degrading uncertainty.

nodes.name: TRADES-AWP offers the best trade-off among baselines but the Pareto structure is non-trivial
nodes.description: Among SOTA baselines on CIFAR-10/WRN-34-10, TRADES-AWP offers the strongest trade-off (Acc.avg=70.29, AUGRCavg=7.68), illustrating that no single baseline is uniformly best across the robustness-uncertainty space.

nodes.name: Under adversarial attack, failures concentrate as accepted (confident) errors at moderate-to-high coverage
nodes.description: Under AA perturbations, retention and generalized-risk curves degrade more severely than under common corruptions, with failures concentrating at moderate-to-high coverage where many adversarial errors remain accepted, i.e. overconfident mistakes reflected in low coverage at fixed risk for baselines.

nodes.name: This confirms the paper's central diagnosis: uncertainty no longer separates correct from incorrect predictions under attack for SOTA baselines
nodes.description: The weak accuracy-uncertainty correlation, internal trade-offs among baselines, and concentrated confident-error failures together confirm that under attack, uncertainty no longer reliably separates correct from incorrect predictions for existing SOTA adversarial training methods, leading to silent failures at practical operating points.

components.name: EV-AT results: shifting the Pareto frontier and generalizing across attacks/architectures

nodes.name: EV-AT improves both robustness and uncertainty simultaneously over the best baseline
nodes.description: Averaged over augmentations, EV-AT improves Acc.avg from 70.29 (TRADES-AWP) to 71.84, and reduces AUGRCavg from 7.68 to 6.52, moving beyond the Pareto frontier formed by prior objectives (Figure 1a).

nodes.name: This improvement is consistent across all four augmentation regimes and extends to corruption shift
nodes.description: The Clean/AA improvement is consistent across all four augmentation regimes in Table 1, and extends to corruption shift, where EV-AT also achieves the best corruption accuracy and corruption AUGRC.

nodes.name: EV-AT reduces the clean-to-adversarial retention gap and increases coverage at fixed risk
nodes.description: In selective operating point analysis, EV-AT reduces the clean-AA retention-gap and substantially increases coverage at fixed risk relative to strong baselines (Figure 5), directly addressing the confident-error failure mode identified in C7.

nodes.name: Gains generalize across stronger attacks (PGD-20/100, AutoAttack) and both ℓ∞ and ℓ2 threat models
nodes.description: Compared with the strongest baseline IKL-AT, EV-AT consistently achieves higher accuracy and lower AUGRC under PGD-20, PGD-100, and AutoAttack, for both ℓ∞ and ℓ2 threat models (Table 2), indicating gains are not an artifact of weak attack evaluation.

nodes.name: Gains persist across a swept range of perturbation budgets, not just the standard ε=8/255
nodes.description: Sweeping the ℓ∞ radius from 0 to 8/255, EV-AT remains consistently best across the full range, with gains persisting at both small and large budgets (Figure 6), indicating improvement beyond a single evaluation radius rather than overfitting to it.

nodes.name: Gains generalize across architectures (WRN-34-10, PreActResNet-18) and datasets (CIFAR-10/100)
nodes.description: Across architectures and datasets, EV-AT remains on or beyond the Pareto frontier in the Acc.avg-AUGRCavg plane (Figure 4), indicating the advantage is stable across model capacity and dataset choice rather than an artifact of a specific pipeline.

nodes.name: Together this establishes that EV-AT's Pareto improvement is robust and not a narrow evaluation artifact
nodes.description: Because the robustness-uncertainty improvement holds across augmentations, attack strength/type, perturbation budget, architecture, and dataset, the paper concludes that EV-AT genuinely shifts the robustness-uncertainty Pareto frontier rather than exploiting a narrow or confounded evaluation setting.

components.name: Ablations: validating REA, the evidential loss, alignment space, and divergence choice

nodes.name: Removing REA (β=0) collapses performance, showing the clean evidential loss alone is not robust
nodes.description: Removing the robust evidence alignment term (β=0) collapses performance (Acc. 71.51→20.11, AUGRC 6.67→37.67), indicating the clean evidential loss alone is not robust and that posterior alignment prevents pathological evidence mismatch under attack (Table 3).

nodes.name: AWP provides an additional, non-substitutable gain on top of the evidential+REA objective
nodes.description: Removing AWP degrades performance (Acc. 68.46, AUGRC 8.21) relative to the full EV-AT, showing AWP contributes an additional gain that is not substitutable by the evidential/REA components alone.

nodes.name: Replacing the evidential clean loss with cross-entropy also degrades the trade-off
nodes.description: Replacing the evidential clean loss with standard cross-entropy degrades the robustness-uncertainty trade-off (Acc. 69.56, AUGRC 7.88 vs. the full EV-AT's Acc. 71.51, AUGRC 6.67), confirming the evidential formulation itself contributes to the gains.

nodes.name: Aligning in log-Dirichlet space (η) substantially outperforms aligning in α or the mean π̄
nodes.description: Aligning in α or in the Dirichlet mean π̄ substantially degrades the trade-off (Acc. 67.32/64.64, AUGRC 10.26/10.43) compared to aligning in η=log α (Acc. 71.51, AUGRC 6.67), empirically confirming the theoretical motivation in C6 for log-parameter alignment.

nodes.name: IKL divergence for REA outperforms ℓ2 or KL alternatives
nodes.description: Using IKL as the REA divergence outperforms ℓ2 or KL divergence alternatives (Acc. 69.81/70.61, AUGRC 7.64/7.60 vs. IKL's Acc. 71.51, AUGRC 6.67), confirming the choice of discrepancy measure matters for alignment quality.

nodes.name: The REA weight β has an intermediate optimum balancing clean structure and adversarial alignment
nodes.description: Sweeping β shows small values under-emphasize alignment (weaker robustness/selective performance) while overly large values cause over-regularization that harms both AA accuracy and AUGRC, with an intermediate value giving the best joint operating point (Figure 7).

nodes.name: Together the ablations confirm each EV-AT component (evidential loss, REA, η-alignment, IKL, tuned β) is necessary for the full gain
nodes.description: Because removing or substituting any individual component (REA, AWP, evidential loss, alignment space, divergence choice) degrades the robustness-uncertainty trade-off relative to the full configuration, the ablations confirm that EV-AT's gains arise from the combination of its evidential objective, evidence-targeted adversary, and η-space alignment via IKL, rather than any single component in isolation.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal problem setup: predictor, uncertainty estimator, and selective rule
isolated_nodes.description: The paper formalizes a C-class predictor fθ:X→ΔC-1, an uncertainty estimator u:X→R, and a selective rule gτ(x;u)=1[u(x)≤τ] that accepts/rejects predictions based on a threshold τ, under ℓp-bounded adversarial perturbations Bp(x;ε).

isolated_nodes.name: Adversarial selective risk minimization objective at target coverage
isolated_nodes.description: The stated overall objective is to minimize adversarial selective risk riskadv(θ;τ) subject to adversarial coverage covadv(τ;θ) ≥ γcov at a target coverage level γcov.

isolated_nodes.name: AutoAttack as a strong, reliable adversarial evaluation standard
isolated_nodes.description: Because robustness can be overestimated due to weak attack settings or gradient masking, AutoAttack (AA), a strong parameter-free ensemble evaluation framework, is used alongside benchmarks like RobustBench and AttackBench to provide reliable, standardized assessment.

isolated_nodes.name: Sampling-based vs. sampling-free uncertainty estimation paradigms
isolated_nodes.description: Uncertainty estimation methods broadly fall into sampling-based approaches (approximating a posterior via multiple evaluations) and sampling-free alternatives (conformal prediction, representation-distance OOD detection, or directly learned predictive distributions like EDL).

isolated_nodes.name: Benchmark design layers: data, method, evaluation, and reporting
isolated_nodes.description: The benchmark comprises four layers: a data layer (CIFAR-10/100 and their corruption variants under four augmentation strategies), a method layer (fixed architecture/optimizer/budget/threat model across compared objectives), an evaluation layer (ℓ∞/ℓ2 threat models, AA/PGD attacks, AURC/AUGRC/AUROC metrics), and a reporting layer (per-regime and clean/AA aggregate statistics).

isolated_nodes.name: Selective classification metrics: AURC, AUGRC, and AUROC
isolated_nodes.description: The benchmark reports retention and risk-coverage curves summarized by scalar metrics AURC, AUGRC (used as the primary metric), and AUROC for error detection, computed consistently across clean, adversarial, and corruption settings.

isolated_nodes.name: Baseline method coverage: AT, TRADES, AWP variants, IKL-AT, TRADES-EMFF
isolated_nodes.description: EV-AT is compared against AT, TRADES, AT-AWP, TRADES-AWP, IKL-AT, and TRADES-EMFF, evaluated on WideResNet-34-10 and PreActResNet-18, covering standard adversarial optimization, consistency regularization, adversarial weight perturbation, and recent uncertainty-aware objectives.

structural_reasoning: The graph closely mirrors EV-AT's own two-part structure: diagnose a robustness-uncertainty gap via a standardized benchmark, then propose and validate a method that closes it. C1 and C2 separate the substantive motivating claim (robustness without reliable uncertainty is unsafe for selective classification) from the methodological motivating claim (confounded evaluation obscures this), since the Introduction advances both as distinct but jointly necessary justifications for building a standardized benchmark. C3 captures the Related Work's positioning across three separate literatures (AT variants, EDL, and robustness-uncertainty interaction) that jointly motivate combining evidential modeling with adversarially-robust posterior alignment. C4-C6 reconstruct Section 3's derivation in the paper's own order: the evidential classifier's structural setup, the EV-AT objective built on top of it (evidence-targeted adversary, REA loss, IKL instantiation), and the theoretical justification (Lemmas 1-3) for the paper's specific design choice of η-space alignment, kept as a separate component since it is a self-contained mathematical argument that the ablations later validate empirically. C7 and C8 mirror the two main empirical claims of Section 4.2 (the diagnostic benchmark finding, then EV-AT's resolution of it) plus Section 4.3's generalization stress tests, and C9 mirrors Section 4.4's ablations, each ablation explicitly tied back to the specific design component it validates from C5/C6. Isolated nodes are limited to formal setup definitions, evaluation-protocol/metric descriptions, and baseline/background coverage that support but are not premises within the central argument chains.

components.description: Motivation: why variable-level causal-graph methods for fairness are impractical, motivating cluster CPDAGs.

nodes.name: Full causal graph assumption
nodes.description: Most existing causality-based fairness methods assume access to the ground-truth causal graph over an individual's features.

nodes.name: Structure learning is hard
nodes.description: Lacking perfect domain knowledge forces solving the notoriously difficult problem of learning the entire causal graph structure from observational data.

nodes.name: Restrictive functional assumptions
nodes.description: Learning the full graph relies on restrictive functional assumptions about the data-generating process, whose violations can undermine fairness guarantees.

nodes.name: CPDAG relaxation
nodes.description: Recent methods leverage a CPDAG, identifiable from conditional independence relations, to relax the full-graph assumption.

nodes.name: CPDAG estimation still hard in high dimensions
nodes.description: Estimating a CPDAG remains challenging in high-dimensional settings, requiring many conditional independence tests whose errors can accumulate and undermine fairness guarantees.

nodes.name: Cluster CPDAG needs far fewer tests
nodes.description: Cluster CPDAG inference needs substantially fewer conditional independence tests than variable-level CPDAG inference because clustering reduces graph size.

nodes.name: Research question
nodes.description: Motivates the research question: can interventional fairness be achieved using a cluster CPDAG despite unknown within-cluster causal structure?

components.description: Interventional fairness definition and its identifiability advantage.

nodes.name: Interventional fairness definition
nodes.description: Prediction is interventionally fair if the interventional distribution of the outcome is invariant to interventions on sensitive features, holding admissible features fixed (Salimi et al. 2019).

nodes.name: Group-level, interventional (not counterfactual)
nodes.description: Interventional fairness is a group-level notion defined via interventional distributions, distinct from individual-level counterfactual fairness.

nodes.name: Identifiable from partial graph knowledge
nodes.description: Interventional distributions in the fairness definition can be identified using partial causal graph knowledge, formalized as a CPDAG.

nodes.name: Back-door adjustment applicability
nodes.description: Under acyclicity and no unobserved confounders, standard back-door adjustment can be applied to identify interventional distributions.

components.description: Cluster DAGs / cluster CPDAGs and the extra structure (independence arcs, marks) they require versus plain CPDAGs.

nodes.name: Cluster DAG construction
nodes.description: A cluster graph is built by grouping nodes of a variable-level DAG according to a partition; a directed edge exists between clusters if any variable-level edge crosses between them.

nodes.name: Admissible partition assumption
nodes.description: The resulting cluster graph is assumed to be a DAG, feasible via an admissible partition designed with domain knowledge.

nodes.name: Ambiguous within-cluster conditional independence
nodes.description: Even under acyclicity, a cluster graph can entail different conditional independence relations among clusters depending on unspecified variable-level structure inside clusters (e.g., collider vs non-collider).

nodes.name: Independence arcs / marks introduced
nodes.description: Anand et al. propose independence arcs (marg/cond/never) plus connection and separation marks to explicitly represent the within-cluster ambiguity.

nodes.name: Cluster CPDAG defined
nodes.description: A cluster CPDAG expresses a cluster Markov equivalence class using directed edges, independence arcs, and connection/separation marks common to all compatible cluster DAGs, plus undirected edges that vary.

nodes.name: CLOC inference method
nodes.description: CLOC (Anand et al. 2025) infers a cluster CPDAG without restrictive assumptions about within-cluster connectivity, motivating its use as the inference backbone here.

components.description: Why cluster CPDAGs make adjustment-set identification hard, and the two-step algorithm that solves it.

nodes.name: Single adjustment set unidentifiable
nodes.description: Because a cluster CPDAG represents multiple compatible DAGs, a single adjustment set Z cannot be identified for back-door adjustment.

nodes.name: Enumerate multiple candidate sets
nodes.description: The proposed solution is to enumerate adjustment sets Z1,...,ZM such that at least one is valid for the true cluster DAG.

nodes.name: Variable-level enumeration methods don't transfer
nodes.description: Efficient enumeration methods for variable-level CPDAGs rely on graphical properties (e.g., chordality) that cluster CPDAGs lack.

nodes.name: Novel enumeration algorithm needed
nodes.description: A novel adjustment-set enumeration algorithm is developed that explicitly accounts for independence arcs and separation/connection marks.

nodes.name: Step 1: Parent set enumeration
nodes.description: First enumerate candidate parent sets of sensitive features A (definite parents plus possible-parent subsets of siblings satisfying Theorem 3.5).

nodes.name: Step 2: Adjustment set completion
nodes.description: If parent sets contain connection-marked clusters, iteratively augment each candidate set via Algorithm 1's queue-based propagation to achieve d-separation.

nodes.name: Refinement fallback for FAIL cases
nodes.description: When Algorithm 1 cannot guarantee identifiability (FAIL), the cluster CPDAG is refined by splitting connection-marked clusters into singleton nodes and re-inferring, at worst reaching variable-level granularity.

components.description: Worst-case unfairness penalty and the computational bottleneck it creates.

nodes.name: True valid Zm unknown
nodes.description: It is uncertain which of Z1,...,ZM yields a valid adjustment for the true cluster DAG.

nodes.name: Worst-case penalty formulation
nodes.description: The unfairness penalty is defined as the maximum, over m, of the aggregated kernel MMD between interventional distribution pairs.

nodes.name: Naive computation is prohibitive
nodes.description: Naively computing this worst-case MMD requires O(M·NA^2·NXad·n^2) time, which is computationally prohibitive.

nodes.name: Need for efficient MMD estimation
nodes.description: This prohibitive cost motivates developing efficient estimation strategies for the penalty function.

components.description: The barycenter-MMD + random-Fourier-feature strategy that resolves the computational bottleneck.

nodes.name: Barycenter MMD decomposition
nodes.description: Pairwise MMD summation over sensitive-value pairs (a,a') is rewritten as a sum of MMDs to a barycenter (mixture) distribution, reducing O(NA^2) to O(NA).

nodes.name: RFF approximation of kernel
nodes.description: The feature map of the MMD kernel is approximated with dRFF-dimensional random Fourier features, reducing per-MMD cost from O(n^2) to O(n·dRFF).

nodes.name: IPW-weighted kernel mean embedding estimator
nodes.description: Combining inverse probability weighting with RFFs yields a weighted empirical estimator of the kernel mean embedding for each interventional distribution.

nodes.name: Overall complexity reduced
nodes.description: Combining barycenter decomposition and RFF approximation reduces overall worst-case MMD computation to O(M·NA·NXad·n·dRFF).

nodes.name: Mellowmax relaxation of max
nodes.description: Since the max over m in the penalty is non-differentiable, it is approximated with the Mellowmax function to enable gradient-based training.

components.description: Synthetic experiment results: C-IFair vs baselines across cluster counts and settings.

nodes.name: C-IFair best among practical baselines (synthetic)
nodes.description: Excluding Oracle and Full, C-IFair achieves the best RMSE and unfairness across all synthetic settings (d=5,10,15; linear and nonlinear).

nodes.name: C-IFair closest to Oracle
nodes.description: C-IFair achieves fairness closest to Oracle while maintaining high accuracy, despite Oracle requiring the unrealistic true variable-level DAG.

nodes.name: Unaware/No-DesCs insufficient
nodes.description: Unaware and No-DesCs exhibit high RMSE and unfairness, implying that simply discarding predictive features fails to remove indirect discriminatory effects.

nodes.name: ε-IFair/ℓ-IFair degrade at high dimension
nodes.description: ε-IFair and ℓ-IFair produce less fair predictions than C-IFair in high-dimensional setups (d=15), indicating inferred variable-level CPDAGs become unreliable there.

nodes.name: Cluster CPDAGs more reliable at scale
nodes.description: Cluster CPDAG inference is more reliable than variable-level CPDAG inference in high-dimensional setups, explaining C-IFair's relative advantage at d=15.

nodes.name: λ trade-off confirmed
nodes.description: Varying penalty weight λ from 0 to 200 shows increasing λ reduces unfairness at the cost of higher RMSE, confirming C-IFair can flexibly tune the fairness-accuracy trade-off.

components.description: Real-world dataset results and fairness illustration.

nodes.name: C-IFair best on real-world AUC/unfairness
nodes.description: Excluding Oracle and Full, C-IFair achieves the best AUC and unfairness among all baselines on Adult, German credit, and OULAD datasets.

nodes.name: Practical utility underscored
nodes.description: The real-world results underscore C-IFair's practical utility for real-world fairness applications.

nodes.name: Fairness illustration on Adult
nodes.description: Comparing inferred interventional distributions of Ŷ across sensitive-feature interventions on Adult shows C-IFair makes sufficiently fair predictions with respect to gender and race.

components.description: Contribution summary chain: cluster-graph algorithm -> learning framework -> empirical validation.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: adjustment cluster set algorithm
nodes.description: A graphical algorithm to enumerate adjustment cluster sets, at least one of which enables identification of interventional distributions for the true cluster DAG.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: worst-case fairness learning framework
nodes.description: A learning framework that achieves interventional fairness by penalizing worst-case unfairness across adjustment cluster sets, using an efficient barycenter kernel MMD.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: empirical validation
nodes.description: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate a better fairness-accuracy trade-off than existing approaches.

isolated_nodes.name: Legal alignment of causal fairness
isolated_nodes.description: Causal notions of fairness align with legal requirements since discrimination is often legally assessed via the causal relationship between decisions and sensitive attributes.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: cluster MPDAGs
isolated_nodes.description: Extending cluster CPDAGs to cluster MPDAGs is highly non-trivial but would further reduce structural uncertainty and improve the fairness-accuracy trade-off; left to future work.

nodes.name: Local DP strong observability
nodes.description: Local DP assumes adversaries can observe all local updates, which requires injecting substantial noise and degrades utility.

nodes.name: PN-DP relaxation
nodes.description: Pairwise Network DP (PN-DP) relaxes Local DP by modeling only pairwise observability between connected nodes, rather than full observability.

nodes.name: PN-DP amplification benefit
nodes.description: PN-DP's relaxed observability assumption enables privacy amplification by decentralization, improving utility in decentralized learning.

nodes.name: Existing PN-DP relies on RDP
nodes.description: Existing PN-DP analyses rely mainly on Renyi DP (PN-RDP), which often yields loose privacy bounds.

nodes.name: PN-f-DP introduction
nodes.description: The paper introduces Pairwise Network f-DP (PN-f-DP), extending PN-DP with the f-DP formalism for tighter, lossless privacy accounting via a hypothesis-testing interpretation.

nodes.name: PN-f-DP captures decentralization amplification
nodes.description: Unlike previous federated f-DP formulations, PN-f-DP captures additional privacy amplification arising from decentralization, random walks, and iterative communication.

nodes.name: SecLDP framework
nodes.description: Secret-based Local DP (SecLDP) considers user pairs that share secrets with neighbors and coordinate correlated noise injection to improve the privacy-utility trade-off under limited collusion.

nodes.name: Sec-f-LDP introduction
nodes.description: The paper introduces Secret-based f-Local DP (Sec-f-LDP), generalizing f-DP to regimes with correlated noise and shared secrets.

nodes.name: Sec-f-LDP amplification under collusion
nodes.description: Sec-f-LDP leverages shared secrets to incorporate correlated noise, achieving additional privacy amplification in structured collusion scenarios not addressed by standard Local DP.

nodes.name: Random walk first-visit mixture
nodes.description: The one-time snapshot observed by user j is a mixture distribution over first-visit times, since the model reaches j from i for the first time at a random step governed by the hitting time.

nodes.name: Joint concavity of trade-off functions
nodes.description: The paper leverages the joint concavity of trade-off functions to lower bound the privacy loss of the mixture mechanism by a convex combination of per-step trade-off functions.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.1 mixture bound
nodes.description: Lemma 4.1 establishes a lower bound on the trade-off function of the single-observation mechanism as a weighted combination of per-step trade-off functions, weighted by hitting-time probabilities.

nodes.name: Hitting-time weighting refinement
nodes.description: The paper defines the mixture weights based on the hitting-time distribution rather than matrix power entries (W^t)_ij, better capturing random walk dynamics and yielding tighter bounds.

nodes.name: Recursive computation of hitting weights
nodes.description: The hitting-time weights are computed recursively via the Markov property, based on the transition matrix W.

nodes.name: Per-step trade-off via composition
nodes.description: Each per-step trade-off function is computed using the composition rule of f-DP to account for the cumulative privacy effect of local SGD updates.

nodes.name: Amplification by iteration for strongly convex losses
nodes.description: For strongly convex and smooth loss functions, privacy amplification by iteration in f-DP is applied, using the contraction effect together with repeated noise injection to yield tighter trade-off functions (Lemma 4.2).

nodes.name: Standard composition for non-convex losses
nodes.description: For general non-convex loss functions, the standard f-DP composition rule is used instead, yielding a more conservative bound (Lemma 4.3).

nodes.name: Markov chain concentration for visit counts
nodes.description: A Hoeffding-type concentration inequality for Markov chains is used to bound the total number of times node j is visited during training.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1 user-level guarantee
nodes.description: Theorem 4.1 combines the single-visit mixture bound with the Markov concentration bound on visit counts to yield the final user-level PN-f-DP guarantee for Algorithm 1, computable numerically though lacking closed form.

nodes.name: Tighter RDP conversion from hitting times
nodes.description: Converting the f-DP guarantees back into RDP yields improved bounds compared to prior work, primarily due to the more accurate modeling of communication timing via hitting times.

nodes.name: Record-level adjacency
nodes.description: Record-level privacy considers datasets differing by a single record within one user's local dataset, rather than the entire user dataset.

nodes.name: Sub-sampling amplification
nodes.description: In the record-level setting, each user computes a gradient from a random subset of local data, reducing the probability a given record is selected and amplifying privacy via sub-sampling.

nodes.name: Sub-sampling interacts with iteration amplification
nodes.description: Sub-sampling interacts with privacy amplification by iteration, making the record-level analysis more intricate than the user-level analysis.

nodes.name: Lemma 4.4 record-level trade-off
nodes.description: Lemma 4.4 characterizes the record-level trade-off function using a sub-sampling operator applied to the per-step Gaussian trade-off bounds.

nodes.name: Record-level guarantee via substitution
nodes.description: The record-level privacy guarantee is obtained by substituting the record-level trade-off function from Lemma 4.4 into Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.1.

nodes.name: Honest-but-curious collusion model
nodes.description: The correlated-noise analysis models honest-but-curious collusion at level q, where a coalition of up to q users may pool information including shared secrets.

nodes.name: Algorithm 2 correlated + independent noise
nodes.description: Algorithm 2 (DecoR) incorporates both independent Gaussian noise and pairwise correlated noise via shared secrets before mixing via the transition matrix.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.2 Sec-GDP guarantee
nodes.description: Theorem 4.2 shows Algorithm 2 satisfies (mu, S)-SecGDP against colluding users, with mu expressed in terms of independent noise variance, correlated noise variance, collusion level, and the graph Laplacian's second eigenvalue.

nodes.name: Tighter (eps,delta) bounds vs RDP
nodes.description: Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show f-DP-based accounting yields consistently tighter (epsilon, delta) bounds than RDP-based approaches.

nodes.name: Tighter bounds require less noise
nodes.description: Tighter (epsilon, delta) bounds allow calibrating less noise for a given privacy level.

nodes.name: Improved utility
nodes.description: Requiring less noise for the same privacy guarantee leads to significantly improved model utility.

nodes.name: Hypercube graph pairwise comparison
nodes.description: On a hypercube graph with 32 nodes, PN-f-DP yields noticeably smaller pairwise privacy budgets epsilon than PN-RDP across nearly all node pairs.

nodes.name: Refined RDP hitting-time baseline still worse
nodes.description: Even against a refined RDP baseline using exact hitting times rather than an upper bound, PN-f-DP consistently yields the smallest epsilon.

nodes.name: MNIST/logistic regression accuracy gains
nodes.description: On MNIST classification and logistic regression tasks under an expander graph topology, the f-DP-calibrated method achieves consistently higher test accuracy than RDP-based methods across graph structures and privacy budgets.

nodes.name: Sec-f-LDP improved trade-off vs SecLDP and LDP
nodes.description: On ring and torus topologies with logistic regression on the a9a dataset, Sec-f-LDP achieves a better privacy-utility trade-off than both SecLDP and local DP baselines.

isolated_nodes.name: FL motivation
isolated_nodes.description: Federated Learning enables user devices to collaboratively train models without sharing raw data, useful when a central server is unavailable, untrusted, or communication is expensive.

isolated_nodes.name: Model updates leak information
isolated_nodes.description: Even without access to raw data, model updates can reveal sensitive information, especially under inference or reconstruction attacks.

isolated_nodes.name: DP-SGD baseline mechanism
isolated_nodes.description: DP-SGD adds noise to stochastic gradients to provide a formal differential privacy guarantee.

isolated_nodes.name: Privacy accounting affects utility
isolated_nodes.description: More accurate privacy accounting allows adding less noise for the same guarantee, improving utility.

isolated_nodes.name: Trade-off function definition
isolated_nodes.description: The trade-off function T(P,Q) denotes the minimal type II error at a given level of type I error in the hypothesis-testing formulation of differential privacy.

isolated_nodes.name: Gaussian DP special case
isolated_nodes.description: A mechanism satisfies mu-Gaussian DP if its trade-off function equals that of two unit-variance Gaussians separated by mu.

isolated_nodes.name: Tensor product composition
isolated_nodes.description: The composition of DP mechanisms corresponds to the tensor product of their trade-off functions.

isolated_nodes.name: User-level vs record-level DP granularity
isolated_nodes.description: User-level DP bounds the influence of an entire user's dataset, while record-level DP limits the impact of a single data point within a user's dataset.

isolated_nodes.name: Algorithm 1 decentralized DP-SGD
isolated_nodes.description: Algorithm 1 performs K local SGD steps with Gaussian-perturbed gradients at each active node, then sends the model to a randomly chosen neighbor via a random-walk transition matrix.

isolated_nodes.name: Privacy amplification by shuffling and decentralization
isolated_nodes.description: Privacy amplification can arise from both shuffling techniques and decentralization of communication.

isolated_nodes.name: Privacy amplification by iteration
isolated_nodes.description: In iterative processes, revealing only the final model parameter (not intermediates) contributes additional privacy amplification, previously extended to f-DP via a shifted interpolated process.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior random-walk analysis limited to RDP
isolated_nodes.description: The privacy impact of random walks had previously only been studied under RDP, leaving its characterization within f-DP an open question prior to this work.

isolated_nodes.name: Communication graph and transition matrix
isolated_nodes.description: Decentralized communication is modeled via a connected graph with an associated Markov transition matrix governing message-passing probabilities between nodes.

isolated_nodes.name: Remark 3.1 weak federated f-DP relaxation
isolated_nodes.description: Record-level PN-f-DP is shown to be a relaxation of weak federated f-DP from prior work, connected via a double convex conjugate operation.

isolated_nodes.name: Spectral gap assumption in Theorem 4.1
isolated_nodes.description: Theorem 4.1 assumes the transition matrix is irreducible, aperiodic, and symmetric with a positive spectral gap, used to bound the number of node visits with high probability.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework generalizes to dynamic graphs
isolated_nodes.description: The proposed framework generalizes to dynamic or time-varying graphs by updating the transition matrices each round, and extends to other decentralized protocols such as gossip-based or push-sum algorithms.

nodes.name: DP and fairness under-explored jointly
nodes.description: Although privacy and algorithmic fairness are each rapidly growing research areas, their joint effect remains comparatively under-explored.

nodes.name: DP can deteriorate fairness
nodes.description: Prior empirical work indicates that differential privacy can deteriorate fairness in various settings.

nodes.name: Prior work lacks joint theory in distributed setting
nodes.description: Most prior works on joint DP-fairness lack rigorous theoretical guarantees on both fairness and excess risk control, and are typically developed under a single-server centrally-stored data setting.

nodes.name: Paper proposes FDP-Fair
nodes.description: The paper proposes a two-step algorithm, FDP-Fair, targeting demographic disparity constrained classification under federated differential privacy in a multi-server distributed setting.

nodes.name: CDP-Fair as single-server alternative
nodes.description: In the special case where there is only one server, the paper further proposes CDP-Fair, a simple yet computationally-lightweight alternative to FDP-Fair.

nodes.name: Central DP definition
nodes.description: Central DP (CDP) requires that the privacy mechanism's output distribution changes by at most a multiplicative eps and additive delta factor between neighboring datasets differing in one entry.

nodes.name: Federated DP definition
nodes.description: Federated DP (FDP) requires that, in the non-interactive setting, each server's transcript shared to the central server individually satisfies an (eps_s, delta_s)-CDP constraint.

nodes.name: FDP built on per-server CDP
nodes.description: Federated DP is defined by requiring the privatized transcript output by each individual server to satisfy central DP, extending CDP to the non-interactive distributed setting.

nodes.name: Demographic disparity definition
nodes.description: Demographic disparity (DD) of a classifier is defined as the difference in probability of predicting the positive label between the two sensitive groups.

nodes.name: Alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier
nodes.description: The alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier minimizes misclassification error subject to the constraint that the absolute demographic disparity is at most alpha.

nodes.name: Optimal classifier via adjusted threshold
nodes.description: The alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier can be obtained by shifting the unconstrained Bayes decision rule through an adjusted threshold determined by a fairness parameter.

nodes.name: Goal: estimate fair classifier under FDP
nodes.description: The paper's goal is to construct an estimator for the alpha-fair Bayes optimal classifier under federated differential privacy constraints.

nodes.name: Gaussian mechanisms for scalars and functions
nodes.description: Step S1 of Algorithm 1 uses Gaussian mechanisms (univariate noise for scalars, Gaussian processes for functional outputs) to privately estimate class probabilities and regression functions.

nodes.name: Site-wise privatized estimators aggregated
nodes.description: Site-wise privatized estimators of class probabilities and regression functions are aggregated at the central server through weighted sums, yielding global estimators while maintaining FDP.

nodes.name: Discretisation of threshold search
nodes.description: To estimate the private fairness threshold, the continuous optimization problem is approximated by discretising the search interval into a fine evaluation grid.

nodes.name: Binary tree tail-count structure
nodes.description: Each discretised candidate is reduced to evaluating tail counts via binary trees, where counts in dyadic intervals are organized hierarchically to enable efficient privacy budget allocation.

nodes.name: Constant per-level sensitivity
nodes.description: In the binary tree construction, changing a single data point affects at most one node per tree level, resulting in constant-order L2-sensitivity for the Gaussian mechanism.

nodes.name: Logarithmic tree depth limits composition
nodes.description: Because the tree depth is selected to be logarithmic, only a logarithmic number of privacy compositions is required, unlike the polynomial compositions needed in standard discretisation approaches.

nodes.name: Improved accuracy from log composition
nodes.description: The combination of constant per-level sensitivity and logarithmic-depth composition leads to substantial accuracy improvement compared to standard private nonparametric discretisation approaches.

nodes.name: Site-wise trees aggregated by variance-weighting
nodes.description: The resulting site-wise binary trees are aggregated at the central server via weighted averaging, with weights chosen according to the variances of the corresponding site-level estimators.

nodes.name: Noise breaks DD monotonicity
nodes.description: Aggregating Gaussian noise across different leaves of the binary tree means the evaluated empirical DD across grids is no longer guaranteed to be monotonically non-increasing, unlike the true DD function.

nodes.name: Monotonicity correction algorithm
nodes.description: Algorithm 4 is introduced to fit, with high probability, a non-increasing sequence to the noisy DD evaluations while controlling the induced bias, restoring the structure needed for threshold search.

nodes.name: Single-server DD is monotone (Thm 12)
nodes.description: In the single-server case, the empirical demographic disparity function is monotonically non-increasing, as shown in Theorem 12.

nodes.name: Monotonicity enables vertical noise shift
nodes.description: Because the single-server empirical DD is monotone, the threshold optimization is equivalent to finding where DD first crosses the fairness level, allowing the DD curve itself (rather than the cutoff point directly) to be perturbed vertically with noise.

nodes.name: CDP-Fair simplified threshold estimation
nodes.description: Algorithm 5 (CDP-Fair) estimates the adjusted threshold by adding one correctly calibrated Gaussian noise term directly to the empirical DD function, avoiding the more complex noisy binary tree procedure.

nodes.name: Pointwise CDP implies cutoff-point CDP
nodes.description: By ensuring each pointwise release of the DD function at a given threshold satisfies CDP, the induced release of the resulting cutoff point also satisfies CDP.

nodes.name: Theorem 1: FDP-Fair and CDP-Fair satisfy privacy
nodes.description: Under the stated assumptions, Algorithm 1 (FDP-Fair) is (eps,delta)-FDP and Algorithm 5 (CDP-Fair) is (eps,delta)-CDP.

nodes.name: CDP-Fair disparity inflation bound
nodes.description: The population demographic disparity of the CDP-Fair output exceeds alpha by an offset of order N^{-1/2} plus (N*eps)^{-1}.

nodes.name: FDP-Fair disparity inflation bound (order rho)
nodes.description: Under additional conditions on server sample sizes and bandwidth, the population demographic disparity of the FDP-Fair output exceeds alpha by an offset of order rho, as defined via a combination of privacy and sample-size terms across servers.

nodes.name: CDP offset driven by empirical deviation and noise
nodes.description: The CDP-Fair offset term is determined by the high-probability bound on the deviation between the empirical and estimated DD at the threshold, capturing both sampling deviation and Gaussian noise variance.

nodes.name: Parametric plus private rate decomposition
nodes.description: The CDP-Fair offset combines the standard parametric rate N^{-1/2} for plug-in fairness estimators with an additional private parametric rate of order (N*eps)^{-1}.

nodes.name: FDP inflation larger due to composition limits
nodes.description: The FDP-Fair disparity inflation of order rho is larger than the CDP-Fair inflation in (5), because privacy compositions across server communications preclude direct infinite pointwise evaluation of DD, unlike in the single-server CDP case.

nodes.name: Higher inflation driven by binary tree discretisation error
nodes.description: The larger FDP-Fair inflation term is primarily driven by the discretisation error introduced by the noisy binary tree construction, corresponding to the estimation error of DD per evaluation grid point.

nodes.name: Fairness-aware excess risk decomposition
nodes.description: The absolute excess risk relative to the optimal fair classifier is bounded by the fairness-aware excess risk plus a disparity cost term.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 excess risk bound for FDP-Fair
nodes.description: Theorem 2 provides finite-sample fairness-aware excess risk bounds for Algorithm 1 under a chosen bandwidth and server weighting scheme, the first such guarantees for fairness-aware classification under FDP.

nodes.name: Excess risk decouples into four cost sources
nodes.description: The excess risk upper bound decomposes into the intrinsic cost of classification, the cost of privacy in classification, the non-private cost of fairness, and the private cost of fairness.

nodes.name: Automatically fair regime recovers non-fair minimax rate
nodes.description: When the fairness threshold parameter is zero (automatically fair regime), the excess risk bound recovers the minimax optimal rate for FDP non-parametric classification without fairness constraints.

nodes.name: Privacy cost reduces effective sample size
nodes.description: The cost of privacy in the excess risk bound manifests as a reduction of the effective sample size from SN to SN^2*eps^2, along with a loss in exponent due to added dimension dependence.

nodes.name: Fairness cost from threshold estimation
nodes.description: When fairness constraints are active, additional terms quantifying the cost of fairness arise from the estimation error of the adjusted threshold, split into non-private and FDP-induced components.

nodes.name: Binary tree construction necessary for fairness cost rate
nodes.description: The parametric rate inside the fairness-cost term highlights the importance of the binary-tree-based threshold construction, since a naive smoothing-based plug-in alternative would introduce non-parametric rates and yield strictly weaker guarantees.

nodes.name: Increasing alpha reduces misclassification error
nodes.description: Relaxing the fairness constraint (increasing alpha) yields a noticeable reduction in misclassification error while the fairness constraint remains active, until it becomes inactive and the error curve flattens.

nodes.name: Larger epsilon reduces excess risk
nodes.description: Weakening the privacy constraint (increasing epsilon) reduces the excess risk for each fixed alpha, with performance converging toward the oracle benchmark as epsilon grows.

nodes.name: Larger sample size reduces error
nodes.description: Under fixed privacy and fairness parameters, increasing the sample size N leads to uniformly smaller misclassification error.

nodes.name: More servers with fixed total data worsens FDP-Fair accuracy
nodes.description: When a fixed total sample size is distributed across more servers, the misclassification error of FDP-Fair deteriorates, since local per-server sample size decreases and cross-server aggregation introduces additional privacy-preserving noise.

nodes.name: S=1 FDP-Fair matches CDP-Fair
nodes.description: When there is only one server, FDP-Fair performs comparably to CDP-Fair, yielding nearly identical misclassification errors and empirical disparities.

nodes.name: Real-data results confirm privacy-fairness trade-off
nodes.description: On the AdultCensus and Law School datasets, CDP-Fair and FDP-Fair successfully control empirical disparity below the target level while incurring higher misclassification error than non-private classifiers, with the gap narrowing as epsilon increases.

isolated_nodes.name: DP has wide industry applications
isolated_nodes.description: Differential privacy has wide applications at Google, Meta, and the US Census Bureau, among others.

isolated_nodes.name: Fairness mitigation categorization
isolated_nodes.description: Existing approaches to algorithmic fairness are broadly categorised into pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing strategies depending on the stage at which fairness constraints are incorporated.

isolated_nodes.name: Randomised classifier definition
isolated_nodes.description: A randomised classifier is a measurable function giving the probability of predicting the positive label given the feature and sensitive attribute, with the predicted label drawn Bernoulli accordingly.

isolated_nodes.name: Assumption 1: class and feature probability
isolated_nodes.description: Class probabilities are bounded away from 0 and 1, and the per-sensitive-class feature density is Holder smooth and bounded below.

isolated_nodes.name: Assumption 2: kernel function conditions
isolated_nodes.description: The kernel function is bounded, Lipschitz, and adaptive to the Holder smoothness class used for the regression functions.

isolated_nodes.name: Assumption 3: regression function margin conditions
isolated_nodes.description: The class-wise regression functions are Holder continuous and satisfy margin conditions controlling the behavior of the regression function and DD near the optimal threshold.

isolated_nodes.name: Homogeneous setting corollary
isolated_nodes.description: Corollary 3 specializes the excess risk bound of Theorem 2 to the homogeneous setting where all servers have equal sample size and privacy parameters.

isolated_nodes.name: Bandwidth choice balances bias and variance
isolated_nodes.description: The bandwidth h is chosen to balance the bias-variance trade-off across privacy and fairness-induced variance terms, and server weights are chosen proportional to effective sample size.

isolated_nodes.name: Bin width balances discretisation bias and estimation error
isolated_nodes.description: The bin width theta in the binary tree construction is chosen to balance the discretisation bias in approximating the optimal threshold against the estimation error of the noisy DD estimate.

isolated_nodes.name: Simulated data generation setup
isolated_nodes.description: Simulated experiments generate sensitive features, standard features via Beta and Uniform distributions, and labels via an arctan-based regression function, across varying training sizes and privacy budgets.

isolated_nodes.name: Cross-fitting classifier construction
isolated_nodes.description: To mitigate randomness from data splitting between estimation and threshold calibration, a cross-fitting approach averages two classifiers with the roles of the two data splits reversed.

isolated_nodes.name: Real datasets used
isolated_nodes.description: The paper evaluates CDP-Fair and FDP-Fair on the AdultCensus dataset (income classification, gender as protected attribute) and the Law School entrance dataset (admission classification, race as protected attribute).

isolated_nodes.name: Future extension: unavailable sensitive features
isolated_nodes.description: The paper notes that when sensitive features are unavailable at test time, one could predict them from standard features, or apply a label local DP framework when sensitive features require additional privacy protection.

isolated_nodes.name: Future extension: data heterogeneity
isolated_nodes.description: The paper suggests investigating the effect of data heterogeneity across servers under fairness constraints as a direction for future work, connecting to differentially private transfer learning literature.
