components.name: Motivation: inconsistent evaluation protocols undermine adversarial GNN conclusions

nodes.name: GNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks
nodes.description: A series of recent works demonstrate that even minor perturbations to the input graph can significantly degrade GNN performance.

nodes.name: Many adversarial attack studies use differing experimental setups
nodes.description: Many studies report substantial gains using differing experimental setups, making results difficult to compare and conclusions potentially misleading.

nodes.name: The vision community's neglect of adaptive attacks and evaluation rigor is a cautionary precedent
nodes.description: Mujkanovic et al. warn that the graph community has yet to learn the 'bitter lesson' from the vision community, where overlooking adaptive attacks and evaluation rigor once led to a flood of unreliable defense evaluations.

nodes.name: GNNs are often trained with attack-specific hyperparameters or fixed splits, biasing results
nodes.description: GNNs are often trained using attack-specific hyperparameters or fixed data splits, biasing reported results.

nodes.name: New attacks are frequently tested under more favorable conditions than baselines
nodes.description: New attack models are frequently tested under more favorable conditions than their baselines, further biasing comparisons.

nodes.name: Target node selection commonly underrepresents high-degree nodes, which are harder to attack
nodes.description: Evaluations commonly select target nodes in a way that underrepresents high-degree nodes, which are typically more resistant to attacks.

nodes.name: These issues mean reported improvements may reflect favorable setups rather than true methodological advances
nodes.description: Because of biased hyperparameters/splits, favorable conditions for new attacks, and skewed target-node selection, reported improvements in the literature may reflect favorable experimental setups rather than genuine advances in method design.

nodes.name: This motivates a standardized, fair re-evaluation of widely used gray-box attacks
nodes.description: These recurring evaluation issues motivate re-evaluating several widely used gray-box attacks under a standardized, robust evaluation framework to demonstrate how variations in evaluation protocol produce inconsistent or overstated findings.

components.name: Positioning against prior evaluation frameworks and benchmarks

nodes.name: Errica et al. and Shchur et al. established rigorous model selection/assessment practices
nodes.description: Errica et al. and Shchur et al. standardize evaluation procedures and promote a reproducible experimental environment with rigorous model selection and assessment, focusing on graph classification and node classification respectively.

nodes.name: Shchur et al. showed train/val/test split choice significantly impacts performance ranking
nodes.description: Shchur et al. have shown that the train/validation/test split of choice used in evaluation significantly impacts the performance ranking, drawing community attention to the necessity of using multiple splits.

nodes.name: These works target rigorous GNN model evaluation generally, not adversarial attack evaluation specifically
nodes.description: Errica et al. and Shchur et al. focus on designing rigorous evaluation frameworks for GNN models generally, rather than on preventing biased estimates of adversarial attack performance specifically.

nodes.name: The Graph Robustness Benchmark (GRB) exists but omits targeted, poisoning, and homophily/heterophily scenarios
nodes.description: The Graph Robustness Benchmark focuses mainly on global evasion attacks and does not consider targeted attacks, poisoning scenarios, or the distinction between homophilic and heterophilic graphs.

nodes.name: This paper unifies rigorous model-selection practice with adversarial-attack-specific robust evaluation, filling GRB's gaps
nodes.description: By unifying the model-selection/assessment rigor of Errica et al. and Shchur et al. with an adversarial-attack-specific evaluation procedure, and by adding targeted evasion, poisoning, and homophily/heterophily coverage that GRB lacks, this paper's benchmark addresses the identified gaps in prior work.

components.name: Formalizing rigorous risk assessment: separating model selection from attack evaluation

nodes.name: Validation accuracy is often a biased estimator of generalization performance
nodes.description: Validation accuracy is often a biased estimator of generalization performance, and overreliance on it can lead to overfitting and inflated expectations of model quality.

nodes.name: Model selection and final evaluation are often conflated in adversarial GNN literature
nodes.description: In adversarial GNN literature, model selection and final evaluation are often conflated, undermining fair comparisons across attack strategies.

nodes.name: Proper separation between model selection and risk assessment is essential to avoid misleading conclusions
nodes.description: Because validation-based selection is a biased estimator and is often conflated with final evaluation in this literature, proper separation between model selection (choosing hyperparameters via validation) and risk assessment (estimating performance via held-out test splits) is essential to avoid misleading conclusions.

nodes.name: The proposed framework performs model selection on clean data only, before any attack is applied
nodes.description: The proposed evaluation formalizes this separation: model selection for victim models (and surrogate models) is performed solely on clean, unperturbed data via validation performance, prior to attacking, ensuring an unbiased risk estimate (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).

components.name: Diagnosing target-node-selection bias in the standard (Nettack) protocol

nodes.name: Most prior works select target nodes via the Nettack strategy (high/low margin plus random)
nodes.description: Most prior works follow the Nettack strategy for target node selection: 10 highest-margin nodes, 10 lowest-margin (but correctly classified) nodes, and 20 additional randomly chosen nodes.

nodes.name: This strategy ignores node degree, which strongly affects attack difficulty
nodes.description: The Nettack-style selection strategy ignores structural properties such as node degree, even though richer neighborhood context makes high-degree nodes harder to attack.

nodes.name: This selection strategy therefore underrepresents high-degree, attack-resistant nodes
nodes.description: Because the standard selection criteria (margin, random) do not account for degree, this strategy may systematically underrepresent high-degree nodes, which are typically more resistant to attacks.

nodes.name: This bias inflates measured attack performance and skews conclusions
nodes.description: By underrepresenting the harder-to-attack, attack-resistant high-degree nodes, the standard target-selection strategy inflates measured attack performance and skews the resulting conclusions about attack effectiveness.

nodes.name: A rigorous evaluation must therefore include target nodes with diverse structural types, including degree-based selection
nodes.description: To correct this bias, a high-quality evaluation should select target nodes to include diverse structural types (not just margin and random criteria), explicitly incorporating node degree as a selection axis.

components.name: Benchmark design: attacks, defenses, adaptive attacks, and the naive baseline

nodes.name: Seven widely cited attack methods are benchmarked, selected for review status, diversity, and citations
nodes.description: Seven widely cited attack methods (Nettack, FGA, SGA, GOttack, PR-BCD, PGD, and one more) are benchmarked, selected based on peer-review status, architectural diversity, and citation count.

nodes.name: Vanilla and nine defended victim models are evaluated to test both baseline and defended vulnerability
nodes.description: Four vanilla GNN victim models (GCN, GSAGE, GIN, PNA) and nine defended victim models are evaluated, so attacks against vanilla models establish baseline vulnerability while defended scenarios test the effectiveness of robustness interventions.

nodes.name: The gray-box, targeted attack setting is adopted to balance realism and diagnostic value
nodes.description: The gray-box setting (attacker has training data/labels to train a surrogate, but not full model parameters) is adopted as it balances realism with the ability to diagnose vulnerabilities, and targeted attacks on a node subset are used since they are harder to detect in real systems.

nodes.name: Adaptive attacks are included alongside fixed-surrogate attacks to simulate stronger adversaries
nodes.description: Unlike prior work using fixed surrogates only, adaptive attacks directly optimized against defended victim models are also evaluated (e.g., PR-BCD adaptive vs. non-adaptive variants), simulating stronger adversaries.

nodes.name: A naive L1_D-RND baseline is introduced to contextualize claimed improvements
nodes.description: A naive yet surprisingly effective baseline, L1_D-RND, which perturbs edges based on node degree and features rather than gradients or learned surrogates, is introduced to contextualize performance claims and enable basic sanity checks against complex new methods.

nodes.name: Together these design choices instantiate the evaluation criteria motivated by the earlier diagnoses
nodes.description: Diverse attacks/defenses, vanilla and defended victims, gray-box adaptive attacks, and a naive baseline together instantiate the rigorous evaluation criteria (model selection, multiple splits, diverse target nodes, vanilla and defended victims) called for by the preceding diagnostic sections.

components.name: Results: vanilla attack performance depends heavily on budget, homophily, and scale

nodes.name: No single attack dominates at low budget on homophily datasets; PR-BCD and L1_D-RND both lead in some cases
nodes.description: At budget ∆=1, PR-BCD (NA) has the highest misclassification rate in only 4 of 12 evasion scenarios on homophily datasets, with L1_D-RND surprisingly yielding the highest rate for PUBMED and CITESEER when PNA is the victim.

nodes.name: At higher budgets, Nettack becomes dominant on homophily datasets
nodes.description: When the budget increases (∆=2...5), Nettack demonstrates superior performance in 36 of 48 cases, while PR-BCD (NA) only remains best on CITESEER and CORA for GCN.

nodes.name: Poisoning attacks are substantially more effective than evasion attacks
nodes.description: Poisoning attacks are significantly more effective than evasion attacks: at ∆=1 Nettack's average misclassification rate rises 4.72% from evasion to poisoning, and even the naive L1_D-RND baseline improves by 8.9% under poisoning.

nodes.name: GraphSAGE is the most resilient vanilla victim model across both settings
nodes.description: GraphSAGE is the most resilient victim model in both evasion and poisoning attacks, with Nettack yielding the lowest average misclassification rate (44.8% evasion, 47.97% poisoning) against it compared to other victim models.

nodes.name: Perturbation impact differs qualitatively between homophily and heterophily graphs by budget regime
nodes.description: At budget 1, average misclassification rate is higher on heterophily (33.96%) than homophily (27.78%) datasets, but by budget 5 homophily datasets show the higher rate (52.21% vs 46.86%), indicating the first perturbation has greater impact under heterophily while later perturbations gain more under homophily.

nodes.name: Attack rankings shift substantially between homophily and heterophily settings
nodes.description: Nettack is best on homophily datasets (rank 1.64) but drops to rank 5.48 on heterophily datasets, while FGA rises from rank 3.10 on homophily to rank 1.92 (best) on heterophily, and the naive L1_D-RND similarly reverses from worst on homophily (rank 6.27) to competitive on heterophily (rank 2.33).

nodes.name: Most existing attacks fail to scale to even moderately large graphs like OGB-ARXIV
nodes.description: On the moderately sized OGB-ARXIV dataset (under 200K nodes), only three of seven attack methods and two of four victim models could be fully evaluated within the 120-hour compute limit, despite ample GPU resources, underscoring a critical scalability limitation.

nodes.name: Attack rankings and robustness conclusions are therefore highly protocol- and setting-dependent, not fixed properties of methods
nodes.description: Because attack effectiveness rankings, the evasion-vs-poisoning gap, and scalability all shift substantially across budget, homophily/heterophily, and dataset scale, no single attack or ranking generalizes across settings, confirming that prior single-setting evaluations risk overstated or misleading conclusions.

components.name: Results: defenses substantially reduce attack effectiveness, unevenly across settings

nodes.name: Defenses substantially reduce misclassification, with poisoning generally easier to defend than evasion
nodes.description: Defense models substantially reduce misclassification rates on homophily datasets, with poisoning attacks generally easier to defend against than evasion; e.g. Nettack's average rate drops from 49.1% to 32.2% under evasion and from 53.6% to 23.56% under poisoning with defenses applied.

nodes.name: GNNGuard is the most effective defense on homophily datasets
nodes.description: Among defense methods, GNNGuard is the most effective on homophily datasets, achieving average misclassification rates of just 5.01% (evasion) and 5.92% (poisoning) at ∆=1 across three datasets and seven attacks, with GRAND consistently second-best.

nodes.name: The naive L1_D-RND baseline often outperforms sophisticated attacks against defended models
nodes.description: The naive L1_D-RND baseline achieves the highest misclassification rate in 19 of 45 defended evasion settings and 18 of 45 defended poisoning settings, despite lacking any optimization or model-specific tuning.

nodes.name: This calls into question the actual gains offered by sophisticated adversarial attack methods
nodes.description: Because a simple degree/feature-based baseline frequently outperforms optimized, learned adversarial attacks against defended models, this raises doubt about how much genuine gain sophisticated attack methods actually provide over naive perturbation strategies.

nodes.name: Defenses are more effective on heterophily datasets than homophily datasets
nodes.description: Defenses are more effective on heterophily datasets than on homophily datasets: average misclassification rates under defense are substantially lower on heterophily ([16.08%,23.33%]) than homophily ([20.11%,40.82%]) across budgets, with the best defense (RUNG) reducing most heterophily attack rates to about 2%.

nodes.name: Some defenses that excel on homophily graphs become fragile or degenerate on heterophily graphs
nodes.description: Despite its strong homophily performance, GNNGuard becomes notably fragile under heterophily, in one case pruning all edges on Chameleon and producing uniformly zero misclassification rates regardless of attack, an artifact rather than genuine robustness.

nodes.name: Robustness conclusions about both attacks and defenses are highly setting-dependent and require standardized multi-setting evaluation
nodes.description: Because attack rankings against defenses, defense effectiveness, and even defense failure modes (e.g. GNNGuard's edge-pruning degeneracy) all vary sharply between homophily and heterophily graphs, and because a naive baseline frequently rivals sophisticated attacks, robustness conclusions cannot be generalized from a single dataset type or attack set, reinforcing the need for the standardized multi-setting evaluation this benchmark provides.

components.name: Empirically confirming the target-node-selection and victim-model-selection critiques

nodes.name: Degree-based target selection yields substantially lower attack success than margin/random selection
nodes.description: Using node degree as a selection criterion results in substantially lower attack success compared to margin-based or random selection, even in vanilla undefended settings, empirically confirming the earlier bias diagnosis.

nodes.name: High-degree nodes show alarmingly low misclassification rates across all attacks
nodes.description: All attack methods perform poorly on high-degree nodes, which exhibit misclassification rates of only 0.05 to 0.28 despite the complete absence of any defense, while low-degree and low-margin nodes remain vulnerable.

nodes.name: This vulnerability went undetected because attacks were developed/benchmarked mainly on small, low-average-degree graphs
nodes.description: Because most attacks were developed and benchmarked on small graphs with low average degree, and scalability limitations prevented testing on larger, high-degree networks, the high-degree robustness gap remained undetected in prior evaluations.

nodes.name: Evaluations ignoring node degree therefore systematically overstate attack effectiveness and GNN fragility
nodes.description: Because low-degree/margin-biased evaluations miss the strong inherent robustness of high-degree nodes, such evaluations systematically overstate both the effectiveness of attack models and the fragility of GNNs, especially given that real-world networks tend to have much higher average degree.

nodes.name: Incorporating victim-model selection significantly alters measured attack outcomes
nodes.description: Incorporating model selection into evaluation significantly alters attack outcomes: on CORA and CITESEER, model-selected victim models are generally more vulnerable (e.g. SGA's misclassification rate on GIN under poisoning differs by an average of 15.27% across budgets), while on PUBMED model selection sometimes yields more robust victims, particularly for GraphSAGE.

nodes.name: Perceived attack effectiveness therefore depends on whether the victim model is realistically (validation-)selected
nodes.description: Because incorporating realistic model selection can substantially shift measured attack success in either direction depending on the dataset, the perceived effectiveness of adversarial attacks depends not only on the attack method but also on whether the victim model is realistically selected, so omitting this step can overstate or understate GNN vulnerability.

isolated_nodes.name: Definition of node classification margin
isolated_nodes.description: The classification margin Mv for node v is defined as the difference between the model's output score for the true class and the highest score for any incorrect class (Eq. 1), with small/negative margins indicating uncertain or incorrect, more attackable predictions.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal definitions of evasion vs. poisoning attacker capacity
isolated_nodes.description: In the evasion setting the victim trains on clean data and is attacked only at inference; in the poisoning setting the attack modifies the graph before training, so the victim is trained on perturbed data.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal perturbation budget constraint
isolated_nodes.description: The perturbation budget ∆ bounds the total L1 change to node features and edges between the clean and perturbed graphs (Eq. 2).

isolated_nodes.name: Black-box, white-box, and gray-box attacker knowledge definitions
isolated_nodes.description: Black-box attackers lack access to model parameters and labels, white-box attackers have full access to both, and gray-box attackers can access training data and labels to train a surrogate model approximating the victim; this paper adopts the gray-box setting.

isolated_nodes.name: Dataset descriptions and statistics
isolated_nodes.description: The benchmark uses three homophilous datasets (CORA, CITESEER, PUBMED), two heterophilous datasets (SQUIRREL, CHAMELEON), and one large-scale dataset (OGB-ARXIV), with node/edge/feature/label counts given in Table 1.

isolated_nodes.name: Computational environment and scale of experiments
isolated_nodes.description: Experiments comprised up to 453,461 training runs, conducted on a Linux cluster with Intel Xeon Gold 6338 CPUs, 251GB RAM, and NVIDIA RTX A40 GPUs, using PyTorch/PyTorch Geometric, with a 120-hour per-run compute cap (OOR marking for runs exceeding it).

isolated_nodes.name: Feature-attack extension largely mirrors structural-attack trends
isolated_nodes.description: The pipeline was also extended to feature-based attacks, and results on homophily datasets largely mirror the trends observed for structural attacks, with Nettack and FGA remaining the best and second-best methods.

isolated_nodes.name: Explicit non-goal: fully adaptive attacks against every defense mechanism
isolated_nodes.description: The paper explicitly scopes out evaluating defenses against fully adaptive attacks specifically crafted to circumvent their core mechanisms, focusing instead on a practical setting where neither side has access to the opponent's backbone model or strategy.

structural_reasoning: The graph mirrors the paper's diagnose-then-fix-then-validate structure. C1 reconstructs the Introduction's cumulative case that inconsistent protocols (biased hyperparameters/splits, favorable new-attack conditions, skewed target selection) undermine adversarial GNN conclusions, directly motivating the re-evaluation. C2 captures the Related Work's positioning against Errica et al., Shchur et al., and GRB, showing this benchmark's novelty as filling specific gaps (adversarial-attack-specific rigor; targeted/poisoning/heterophily coverage). C3 and C4 formalize the paper's own Sections 3-4.1 diagnostic arguments (model-selection/risk-assessment conflation; Nettack-style target-selection bias) as self-contained derivations, since each grounds a distinct methodological fix embodied in Algorithm 1 and the expanded target-node criteria. C5 assembles these fixes into the concrete benchmark design (attacks, defenses, adaptive attacks, naive baseline). C6-C8 mirror the Results section's three empirical threads (vanilla-attack findings, defended-attack findings, and the explicit empirical validation of the target-node and victim-model-selection critiques from C3/C4), each chain culminating in the paper's own higher-level interpretive claim. Isolated nodes are limited to formal definitions (margin, evasion/poisoning, budget, attacker knowledge), dataset/compute descriptions, and explicitly scoped-out or secondary findings (feature-attack extension) that support but are not premises within the central argument chains.

note_on_evidence: Evidence fields cite paper sections/subsections/theorems/lemmas rather than sentence indices, since a sentence-indexed source was not available for this document.

components.name: Motivation: the oversmoothing/oversquashing tension and open complexity question

nodes.name: Oversmoothing mechanism
nodes.description: Oversmoothing occurs because GNN layers act as low-pass filters, so after many layers node representations become dominated by the principal eigenvector of the propagation matrix, converging to a uniform vector.

nodes.name: Oversmoothing rate governed by spectral gap
nodes.description: The rate of oversmoothing is governed by the spectral gap of the graph's propagation operator, and oversmoothing is inevitable for any fixed-spectrum graph as the number of layers grows.

nodes.name: Oversquashing mechanism
nodes.description: Oversquashing describes information from distant nodes failing to reach a target node because messages must flow through a narrow cut/bottleneck, compressing exponentially many messages into fixed-size vectors.

nodes.name: Oversquashing quantified by conductance/effective resistance
nodes.description: Oversquashing is a structural phenomenon quantified by the graph's conductance or effective resistance; a graph with a bottleneck forces information squashing regardless of layer count.

nodes.name: High connectivity mitigates oversquashing but worsens oversmoothing
nodes.description: Graphs that mitigate oversquashing (expanders, dense graphs) tend to have high connectivity, which accelerates oversmoothing.

nodes.name: Sparse/tree-like graphs resist oversmoothing but cause oversquashing
nodes.description: Sparse, tree-like graphs resist oversmoothing but create severe bottlenecks that cause oversquashing.

nodes.name: Tension motivates the optimal-rewiring question
nodes.description: Because oversmoothing- and oversquashing-mitigating graph properties conflict, this raises the natural question of whether graph structure can be optimized to strike an optimal balance between the two.

nodes.name: Complexity of graph rewiring optimization was previously unexplored
nodes.description: While heuristic rewiring methods (DIGL, SDRF) have shown empirical success, the fundamental computational complexity of the underlying graph optimization problems had remained unexplored prior to this paper.

components.name: Expander embedding construction (shared reduction tool)

nodes.name: Need for a bisection-to-conductance mapping construction
nodes.description: A construction is needed that maps a graph H to a new graph G such that the conductance of G is small if and only if H has a small bisection, to enable reductions from Minimum Bisection.

nodes.name: Expander Embedding lemma (Lemma 2)
nodes.description: There exists a polynomial-time algorithm that, given H with n vertices, outputs a 3-regular graph G with 2n vertices such that H is an induced subgraph of G, and cut conductance in G is tightly related to cut size in H in both directions (upper bound via part 2, and a converse via part 3 with a balancing procedure).

nodes.name: Embedding constants can be tuned via expander strength
nodes.description: The constants c1, c2, c3 in the Expander Embedding lemma can be made arbitrarily small or large by choosing a sufficiently strong or weak expander, allowing specific inequality conditions (e.g., c1 < 1/6, c2c3 < 1/2) to be satisfied.

nodes.name: Instance Scaling lemma (Lemma 3)
nodes.description: Any Minimum Bisection instance (H, B) can be transformed in polynomial time into an equivalent instance with convenient bounds relating B to the number of vertices n (either B >= 2n and B = O(n), or n/2 <= B <= 2n), preserving the yes/no answer.

components.name: Oversquashing mitigation formalized as conductance optimization (GROC) and its NP-completeness

nodes.name: Maximizing conductance minimizes oversquashing loss
nodes.description: The worst-case bottleneck is captured by conductance phi(G), and the oversquashing loss is defined as the negative conductance, so maximizing phi(G) minimizes oversquashing.

nodes.name: GROC decision problem definition
nodes.description: GROC asks: given graph G, integer budget K, and threshold phi0, does there exist G' with symmetric-difference edge budget at most K such that the conductance of G' is at least phi0.

nodes.name: GROC is in NP
nodes.description: Given a candidate graph G', its conductance can be computed exactly via a min-cut/max-flow computation in polynomial time, so GROC is in NP.

nodes.name: Reduction from Minimum Bisection to GROC
nodes.description: Using the Expander Embedding and Instance Scaling lemmas, a Minimum Bisection instance (H,B) is transformed into a 3-regular graph G with K=0 and a threshold phi0 = 1 - c1(B+n)/n, chosen so that phi0 > 1/2 using the constant bound c1 < 1/6.

nodes.name: Forward direction of the GROC reduction
nodes.description: If H has a bisection with at most B edges, Lemma 2(2) gives a cut in G with conductance at most 1-phi0, which is less than phi0, so (G,0,phi0) is a NO instance.

nodes.name: Reverse direction of the GROC reduction
nodes.description: If H has no bisection with at most B edges, assuming phi(G) < phi0 leads via Lemma 2(3) and the balancing procedure to a bisection of H with fewer than B edges, a contradiction; hence phi(G) >= phi0 and (G,0,phi0) is a YES instance.

nodes.name: GROC is NP-hard
nodes.description: Because Minimum Bisection reduces to GROC (with inverted YES/NO answers, invertible in polynomial time) and Minimum Bisection is NP-complete, GROC is NP-hard.

nodes.name: GROC is NP-complete (Theorem 4)
nodes.description: Since GROC is both in NP and NP-hard, it is NP-complete.

components.name: Oversmoothing mitigation formalized as spectral optimization (GROS) and its NP-completeness

nodes.name: Dirichlet energy decay bound
nodes.description: For a regular graph, the Dirichlet energy after L layers decays as E(X(L)) <= (mu2(P))^(2L) * E(X(0)), where mu2(P) is the second-largest eigenvalue of the propagation matrix.

nodes.name: Preventing oversmoothing requires minimizing mu2(P)
nodes.description: Because the Dirichlet energy decay rate is governed by mu2(P), preventing oversmoothing requires minimizing mu2(P).

nodes.name: Minimizing mu2(P) equivalent to maximizing spectral gap
nodes.description: Since mu2(P) = 1 - lambda2(L), minimizing mu2(P) is equivalent to maximizing lambda2(L), the spectral gap of the normalized Laplacian.

nodes.name: GROS decision problem definition
nodes.description: GROS asks: given graph G, integer budget K, and threshold tau, does there exist G' with symmetric-difference edge budget at most K such that mu2(P_G') <= tau.

nodes.name: GROS is in NP
nodes.description: A certificate is the target graph G'; the edge-budget constraint is checked directly, and mu2(P_G') <= tau can be decided in polynomial time via root isolation (e.g., Sturm sequences) since the propagation matrix has rational entries and polynomial-bit-length algebraic eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Reduction from Minimum Bisection to GROS
nodes.description: Using the same Expander Embedding (with constants satisfying c1 < 1/48, 2c2*sqrt(3c1) < 1/2) and Instance Scaling lemma (part 1), a Minimum Bisection instance is transformed into a 3-regular graph G with K=0 and threshold tau = 1 - 2c1(B+n)/n - epsilon for a suitably small rational epsilon.

nodes.name: Forward direction of the GROS reduction
nodes.description: If H has a bisection with at most B edges, Lemma 2(2) and Cheeger's inequality give mu2(P_G) >= 1 - 2c1(B+n)/n > tau, so (G,0,tau) is a NO instance.

nodes.name: Reverse direction of the GROS reduction
nodes.description: If H has no bisection with at most B edges, assuming mu2(P_G) > tau leads via Cheeger's inequality, Lemma 2(3), and the balancing procedure (using B >= 2n and c2*c3*sqrt(3c1) bounds) to a bisection of H with fewer than B edges, a contradiction; hence mu2(P_G) <= tau and (G,0,tau) is a YES instance.

nodes.name: GROS is NP-hard
nodes.description: Because Minimum Bisection reduces to GROS and Minimum Bisection is NP-complete, a polynomial algorithm for GROS would solve Minimum Bisection, so GROS is NP-hard.

nodes.name: GROS is NP-complete (Theorem 6)
nodes.description: Since GROS is both in NP and NP-hard, it is NP-complete.

components.name: Inapproximability and heuristic justification

nodes.name: Conductance is hard to approximate
nodes.description: Conductance phi(G) cannot be approximated within a factor of O(sqrt(log n)) unless P = NP.

nodes.name: Spectral gap is hard to approximate
nodes.description: The spectral gap lambda2(L) cannot be approximated within any constant factor for regular graphs.

nodes.name: Rewiring optimization likely also hard to approximate
nodes.description: These inapproximability results suggest that algorithms attempting to optimize graph structure for these measures under a limited edge-change budget will also be hard to approximate, though a formal proof for the rewiring problems themselves remains open.

nodes.name: SDRF and DIGL run in polynomial time
nodes.description: SDRF (iteratively removing most-negative-curvature edges and adding highest-effective-resistance edges, total O~(n^3)) and DIGL (graph diffusion via personalized PageRank, O(n^2 log n)) are existing heuristic rewiring methods shown to run in polynomial time.

nodes.name: NP-hardness justifies heuristic use
nodes.description: Because exact optimization of GROC and GROS is NP-hard/intractable while SDRF and DIGL run in polynomial time, the hardness results provide theoretical justification for using such heuristics rather than seeking exact solutions.

components.name: Discussion: duality between the two objectives

nodes.name: Cheeger's inequality links the two objectives for regular graphs
nodes.description: For regular graphs, mu2(P) = 1 - lambda2(L) and phi(G) lies between lambda2(L)/2 and sqrt(2*lambda2(L)), mathematically linking the oversmoothing objective (spectral gap) and the oversquashing objective (conductance).

nodes.name: High algebraic connectivity tends to raise conductance too
nodes.description: This mathematical relationship reflects a tangible tradeoff: a graph with high algebraic connectivity (good for oversmoothing) tends to have high conductance (good for oversquashing), but the exact relationship is constrained by the spectral gap.

nodes.name: Both exact optimizations are intractable, reinforcing reliance on heuristics
nodes.description: The NP-hardness results for both GROC and GROS show that optimizing either objective exactly is intractable in general, reinforcing that practical approaches must rely on approximations or heuristics.

nodes.name: Dense graphs mitigate both but are often impractical
nodes.description: A highly connected graph (e.g., complete graph) can simultaneously mitigate oversquashing (no bottlenecks) and oversmoothing (large spectral gap), but such graphs are often prohibitively dense for real-world applications.

nodes.name: Finding an optimal sparse balancing graph is computationally challenging
nodes.description: Because dense graphs mitigate both issues but are often impractical, while sparse graphs may suffer from both, finding an optimal sparse graph that strikes the right balance is computationally challenging, justifying iterative heuristic rewiring methods like SDRF and DIGL.

isolated_nodes.name: Normalized Laplacian and Fiedler value defined
isolated_nodes.description: The normalized Laplacian is L = I - D^(-1/2) A D^(-1/2), with eigenvalues 0 = lambda1(L) <= ... <= lambda_n(L) <= 2, and lambda2(L) (the Fiedler value) measures algebraic connectivity.

isolated_nodes.name: Symmetric normalized propagation matrix defined
isolated_nodes.description: For a GNN layer, the symmetric normalized propagation matrix is P = D-tilde^(-1/2) A-tilde D-tilde^(-1/2), where A-tilde = A + I and D-tilde = D + I, with eigenvalues in [-1, 1].

isolated_nodes.name: Conductance formally defined
isolated_nodes.description: For a subset S of vertices, conductance phi(S) = |boundary(S)| / min(vol(S), vol(V\S)), and the conductance of the graph phi(G) is the minimum over all such subsets with volume at most half the total volume.

isolated_nodes.name: Cheeger's inequality stated
isolated_nodes.description: Cheeger's inequality relates the spectral gap of the normalized Laplacian to conductance: phi(G)^2/2 <= lambda2(L) <= 2*phi(G).

isolated_nodes.name: Minimum Bisection is NP-complete
isolated_nodes.description: Minimum Bisection, the classical decision problem used as the basis for both reductions in this paper, is NP-complete (Garey, Johnson, and Stockmeyer).

isolated_nodes.name: Expander embeddings are a standard hardness-of-approximation tool
isolated_nodes.description: Expander embeddings, used to relate graph cuts between H and G in this paper's constructions, are a standard tool in hardness-of-approximation results.

isolated_nodes.name: GNNs are the de facto standard for graph-structured learning
isolated_nodes.description: Graph Neural Networks have become the de facto standard for learning on graph-structured data, with applications including fake news detection, drug discovery, and recommendation systems.

isolated_nodes.name: Message passing as GNNs' core operation
isolated_nodes.description: The core operation of GNNs, message passing, aggregates information from neighboring nodes, allowing the model to capture relational structure.

isolated_nodes.name: Existing mitigation strategies for oversmoothing
isolated_nodes.description: Prior work proposed mitigation strategies for oversmoothing such as residual/skip connections, normalization layers, and adaptive propagation schemes, but the underlying graph structure remains a key determinant of the effect.

isolated_nodes.name: SDRF algorithm description
isolated_nodes.description: SDRF (prior work) uses effective resistance to quantify oversquashing and adds edges with high effective resistance while removing edges with negative curvature.

isolated_nodes.name: DIGL algorithm description
isolated_nodes.description: DIGL (prior work) uses graph diffusion to densify the graph, adding edges based on personalized PageRank.

isolated_nodes.name: Bilevel graph structure learning as an alternative approach
isolated_nodes.description: Prior work introduced a bilevel optimization framework for learning the graph structure end-to-end, which is empirically effective but lacks theoretical hardness guarantees, unlike this paper's analysis.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: directed and weighted graphs
isolated_nodes.description: Extending the complexity analysis to directed and weighted graphs would broaden applicability, since many real-world graphs possess these properties.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: task-specific importance weights
isolated_nodes.description: Incorporating task-specific importance weights on node pairs could lead to more practical formulations aligning graph structure with the downstream learning objective.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: other GNN architectures
isolated_nodes.description: Different GNN architectures (e.g., Graph Attention Networks, Gated Graph Neural Networks) employ distinct propagation mechanisms that may alter the oversmoothing/oversquashing relationship, motivating complexity analysis for those architectures.

isolated_nodes.name: Future direction: empirical gap between worst case and heuristic practice
isolated_nodes.description: Empirical evaluation of the gap between theoretical worst-case complexity and actual heuristic rewiring performance would provide insight into how often hard instances occur in practice.

structural_reasoning: This graph is highly coherent, closely mirroring the paper's own logical structure. C1 establishes the motivating tension between oversmoothing and oversquashing mitigation as a clean causal chain leading to the open complexity question. C2 isolates the shared Expander Embedding and Instance Scaling machinery used by both subsequent reductions, avoiding duplication. C3 and C4 each trace a complete, tightly sequenced proof structure (formulation -> NP membership -> reduction construction -> forward direction -> reverse direction -> NP-hardness -> NP-completeness) that mirrors the paper's own Theorem 4 and Theorem 6 proofs almost line for line, with every edge corresponding to an explicit logical dependency in the proof. C5 (inapproximability/heuristics) and C6 (discussion of the duality) are compact but well-grounded in the paper's Sections 5 and 6. The isolated nodes are appropriately limited to genuine definitional/notational facts (Laplacian, propagation matrix, conductance, Cheeger's inequality), citations to external established results (Minimum Bisection's NP-completeness, expander embeddings as a general tool), background/related-work summaries, and forward-looking future-work suggestions -- none of which function as premises within the paper's own argumentative chain. This is a mathematically self-contained paper with an unusually explicit proof structure, which is why the graph achieves a higher structural score than the more narrative empirical papers analyzed previously.

components.description: Motivation: why hybrid interpretable models arise, and the overlooked distributive question this raises.

nodes.name: Post-hoc explanations can be unreliable
nodes.description: Post-hoc explanation techniques approximate black-box behavior after training, but can be unreliable and susceptible to manipulation, raising faithfulness concerns.

nodes.name: Inherently interpretable models trade off performance
nodes.description: Inherently interpretable models (decision trees, rule lists, rule sets, scoring systems) are easier to understand but may exhibit reduced predictive performance in complex settings.

nodes.name: Hybrid interpretable models proposed as compromise
nodes.description: This limitation motivated hybrid interpretable models, which combine an interpretable component with a black-box component via a gating mechanism assigning each example to one or the other.

nodes.name: Transparency level creates accuracy-interpretability trade-off
nodes.description: By varying the proportion of examples assigned to the interpretable component (transparency), hybrid models realize different trade-offs between interpretability and predictive performance.

nodes.name: Overlooked question: uneven interpretability distribution
nodes.description: Even when hybrid models improve the aggregate accuracy-interpretability trade-off, they may distribute interpretability unevenly across individuals or demographic groups — a largely overlooked question.

components.description: Positioning relative to prior procedural-fairness work (explanation quality, recourse) and the distinct nature of ICD/ICA.

nodes.name: Prior fairness work mostly targets predictive outputs
nodes.description: A large body of fairness-in-ML work focuses on fairness criteria defined with respect to a predictive model's outputs, intervening via pre-, in-, or post-processing.

nodes.name: Fairness in explanation quality studied separately
nodes.description: Fairness in explanation quality has been examined for post-hoc explanation methods (feature attribution, counterfactual explanations), revealing demographic disparities in properties like sparsity, robustness, and recourse cost.

nodes.name: Explanation-quality and recourse fairness are procedural but post-hoc
nodes.description: Fairness in explanation quality and recourse fairness both fall under procedure-oriented fairness, evaluating whether externally-produced reasoning is equally reliable across groups.

nodes.name: In hybrid models interpretability is allocated by the model itself
nodes.description: In hybrid interpretable models, interpretability is not provided by a separate post-hoc method; it is allocated by the model itself through its gating mechanism.

nodes.name: ICD/ICA measure allocation, not explanation quality
nodes.description: Unlike prior work on explanation quality or recourse, ICD and ICA measure how interpretability itself is allocated via the routing decision, not the quality of an explanation produced after a prediction.

nodes.name: ICD shifts focus to access rather than quality
nodes.description: This distinction means ICD shifts attention from whether explanations are equally good to whether different individuals/groups are equally likely to receive interpretable decisions in the first place.

components.description: Formal setup: hybrid interpretable model structure and transparency definition.

nodes.name: Hybrid model as triplet ⟨Ω, hs, hc⟩
nodes.description: A hybrid interpretable model is defined by a triplet ⟨Ω, hs, hc⟩ where Ω is the interpretable region handled by simple model hs, and examples outside Ω are deferred to black-box model hc.

nodes.name: Transparency defined as coverage fraction
nodes.description: The transparency C_Ω of a hybrid model on a dataset is the proportion of examples covered by the interpretable region Ω, with 0 = pure black-box and 1 = single interpretable model.

nodes.name: Rule-based interpretable component defines Ω
nodes.description: In practice, existing hybrid interpretable models use a set of rules r as the interpretable component, where the rules' support simultaneously defines Ω; examples not captured by any rule are deferred to the black-box.

components.description: Predictive multiplicity / Rashomon set background motivating the individual-level ICA metric and the need for approximation.

nodes.name: Predictive multiplicity: many near-optimal, disagreeing models
nodes.description: Several models can achieve nearly indistinguishable predictive performance while disagreeing on individual predictions — a phenomenon called predictive multiplicity.

nodes.name: Rashomon set formalizes the set of near-optimal models
nodes.description: The set of near-optimal models is formalized as the Rashomon set R(H, ε, S), those with loss within a factor (1+ε) of the reference model's loss.

nodes.name: Rashomon-set models can differ on other desiderata
nodes.description: Although models in the Rashomon set have comparable predictive performance, they can differ substantially on other desiderata, motivating evaluation across the whole set rather than a single arbitrary model.

nodes.name: Exact enumeration methods scale poorly / are narrow
nodes.description: Exact enumeration methods for constructing Rashomon sets exist only for specific simple hypothesis classes (rule lists, rule sets, decision trees) and scale poorly with ε and rule/feature counts; enumeration-free methods are similarly limited to particular model classes.

nodes.name: Exact Rashomon-set construction intractable for hybrid models
nodes.description: Building the exact Rashomon set is not tractable for black-box models, and even more so for hybrid interpretable models, whose interpretable component training often depends on a pre-trained black-box.

nodes.name: Bootstrap-based approximation adopted
nodes.description: Consistent with prior work showing model-sampling/bootstrapping provides useful Rashomon-set approximations, the paper replaces the exact Rashomon set with a bootstrap-based approximation for estimating interpretability-coverage statistics.

components.description: Formalization of the group-level Interpretability Coverage Disparity (ICD) metric.

nodes.name: Interpretability Coverage (IC) of a group defined
nodes.description: The Interpretability Coverage IC_p of protected group p is defined as the fraction of individuals from p that fall within the interpretable region Ω.

nodes.name: ICD defined as max pairwise IC gap
nodes.description: Interpretability Coverage Disparity (ICD) is defined as the maximum pairwise difference in IC across protected groups, equivalently max IC_p minus min IC_p.

nodes.name: ICD depends only on allocation, not predictions
nodes.description: ICD depends only on the allocation of individuals to interpretable vs. black-box regions, not on the predictions made by either component, making it a procedural fairness notion.

nodes.name: ICD conflates disparity magnitude with direction
nodes.description: ICD alone does not identify which groups are relatively advantaged or disadvantaged, since it only reflects the largest observed disparity, motivating reporting per-group coverage as well.

components.description: Formalization of the individual-level Interpretability Coverage Arbitrariness (ICA) metric.

nodes.name: Interpretability Coverage Frequency (ICF) defined
nodes.description: ICF(x) is defined as the fraction of models in the (approximate) Rashomon set for which example x falls within the interpretable region Ω.

nodes.name: ICA defined from ICF via distance from 1/2
nodes.description: ICA(x) = 1 - 2|ICF(x) - 1/2|, so ICA is high when x is assigned to the interpretable region for roughly half the Rashomon-set models and low when assignment is consistent.

nodes.name: ICA quantifies individual-level routing instability
nodes.description: Values close to 1 indicate high arbitrariness (unstable routing across the Rashomon set), while values close to 0 indicate consistent assignment to one component.

nodes.name: Exact R(H,ε,S) replaced by bootstrap approximation for ICF/ICA
nodes.description: Because exact Rashomon-set construction is intractable for hybrid models, ICF and ICA are computed using the bootstrap-based approximate Rashomon set instead of the exact one.

components.description: Experimental design: methods, datasets, and bootstrap Rashomon-set construction procedure.

nodes.name: Four hybrid learning methods compared
nodes.description: Four state-of-the-art hybrid interpretable learning methods are evaluated: HyRS, CRL (heuristic, simulated-annealing based), and HybridCORELSPre/Post (exact branch-and-bound based).

nodes.name: Heuristic methods lack optimality/transparency guarantees
nodes.description: HyRS and CRL optimize accuracy-transparency-sparsity trade-offs but do not provide optimality guarantees and cannot enforce a prescribed transparency level.

nodes.name: HybridCORELS variants enforce hard transparency constraints
nodes.description: HybridCORELSPre/Post rely on exact branch-and-bound to explore rule prefixes, with HybridCORELSPost optimizing accuracy+sparsity subject to a hard transparency constraint, and HybridCORELSPre learning the prefix before the black-box.

nodes.name: Three benchmark datasets used
nodes.description: Experiments use three datasets of varying size: COMPAS (recidivism), UCI Adult Income (earnings), and ACS Employment (employment status), each with Age/Gender/Race subgroups.

nodes.name: Bootstrap procedure generates approximate Rashomon sets
nodes.description: For each method/hyperparameter configuration, a reference model is trained plus 1000 bootstrap-resampled retrainings, yielding 1001 models per configuration (10,010 per method across 10 configurations), deduplicated and binned by transparency.

nodes.name: Filtering by Rashomon parameter ε yields final analysis sets
nodes.description: Within each transparency bin, unique models are filtered to keep only those satisfying the Rashomon parameter ε relative to the reference model, yielding the approximate Rashomon sets used for all downstream analyses.

components.description: Result 1: substantial group-level ICD, concentrated in intermediate transparency regimes.

nodes.name: ICD is substantial across nearly all settings
nodes.description: Results reveal substantial ICD across nearly all experimental settings, confirming hybrid interpretable models can distribute interpretability unevenly, with values approaching 1.0 in several cases.

nodes.name: Disparities consistently favor/disfavor specific subgroups
nodes.description: Within the same transparency bin, certain subgroups (e.g., African-American on COMPAS under HyRS) consistently receive lower interpretability coverage than others, not just larger variance.

nodes.name: Extreme transparency bins dominated by one component
nodes.description: In the lowest transparency bin most instances go to the black-box; in the highest bin most go to the interpretable component — both regimes are dominated by a single component.

nodes.name: Intermediate bins are the truly hybrid regime
nodes.description: Intermediate transparency bins (0.25-0.75) are where both components actively contribute to prediction, better characterizing the truly hybrid regime.

nodes.name: ICD follows a bell-like curve peaking at intermediate transparency
nodes.description: The largest ICD values occur in intermediate transparency bins, with ICD increasing from low to intermediate bins and then decreasing/stabilizing at higher bins.

nodes.name: Bell-like pattern statistically confirmed via Mann-Whitney tests
nodes.description: Non-parametric pairwise (Mann-Whitney U, Holm-corrected) tests across adjacent transparency bins confirm the bell-like ICD pattern is frequent and statistically significant across datasets/methods, strengthening at larger ε.

components.description: Result 2: individual-level ICA, also concentrated in intermediate transparency regimes.

nodes.name: Arbitrariness low at extreme transparency bins
nodes.description: Assignment arbitrariness (ICA) is generally limited in the lowest and highest transparency bins, where predictions are predominantly handled by a single component.

nodes.name: Arbitrariness high at intermediate transparency bins
nodes.description: Substantially higher ICA emerges in intermediate transparency bins where both components contribute to prediction, consistently across all evaluated methods.

nodes.name: Hybridization itself amplifies assignment uncertainty
nodes.description: The consistent pattern across methods supports the hypothesis that hybridization itself amplifies assignment uncertainty within Rashomon sets.

components.description: ICD mitigation methodology: constrained branch-and-bound extension of HybridCORELS.

nodes.name: High ICD + Rashomon variability motivates mitigation
nodes.description: The observed substantial ICD plus high within-Rashomon-set variability across transparency bins shows near-optimal models can induce very different ICD levels, motivating a predictive-multiplicity-based search for fairer models.

nodes.name: Maximum ICD constraint added to HybridCORELS branch-and-bound
nodes.description: ICD is mitigated by incorporating a maximum ICD constraint η into the HybridCORELS branch-and-bound algorithms: a candidate best prefix is retained only if it satisfies the constraint, otherwise discarded.

nodes.name: Existing bounds/data structures remain valid under new constraint
nodes.description: The bounds and symmetry-aware data structures used in HybridCORELSPre/Post remain valid and tight under the added maximum-ICD constraint.

components.description: Mitigation results (3-7): generalization, effect on ICA, effect on algorithmic fairness, effect on performance/sparsity, and dose-response with η.

nodes.name: Mitigation generalizes to test data
nodes.description: ICD mitigation applied during training consistently reduces both magnitude and variability of test-set ICD distributions across all sensitive attributes and transparency bins.

nodes.name: Mitigation has no clear effect on ICA
nodes.description: ICD mitigation produces no substantial change in the distribution of ICA, indicating it is effective at reducing group-level disparity but has limited impact on individual-level arbitrariness.

nodes.name: Mitigation frequently improves EO/SP despite not targeting them
nodes.description: Mitigated models frequently show lower median EO/SP disparities and reduced variability, despite these algorithmic fairness metrics not being directly targeted during training, though improvement is not uniform across settings.

nodes.name: Mitigation preserves sparsity and accuracy
nodes.description: Enforcing ICD constraints results in only minor increases in rule count and largely comparable accuracy distributions, occasionally even slightly improving accuracy (suggesting a regularization effect).

nodes.name: Relaxing η increases ICD magnitude/variability, accuracy stable
nodes.description: As the maximum ICD constraint η is relaxed from strict to unconstrained, ICD magnitude and variability consistently increase across Rashomon models, while test accuracy remains remarkably stable throughout.

nodes.name: Fairness gains concentrated at high-transparency bins
nodes.description: Bin-level analysis shows the largest EO/SP improvements from tightening η occur in higher-transparency bins, where interpretability coverage is greatest and the constraint most strongly affects routing (e.g., HybridCORELSPost's EO from ~0.25 to ~0.18 as η tightens from 0.25 to 0.05).

nodes.name: Reduced ICD achievable without sacrificing accuracy
nodes.description: Combined with stable predictive performance across mitigation strengths, results show substantially lower ICD can be selected from the Rashomon set without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: ICD and ICA metrics introduced
nodes.description: ICD (demographic-parity-style group disparity) and ICA (predictive-multiplicity-based individual arbitrariness) are introduced as procedural fairness notions for interpretability allocation.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: extensive empirical demonstration of ICD/ICA
nodes.description: Extensive experiments across four hybrid methods show substantial ICD/ICA can arise on real-world datasets, with some individuals arbitrarily assigned and some groups systematically routed to the black-box.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: mitigation methods and trade-off analysis
nodes.description: Existing hybrid interpretable learning methods are extended to mitigate ICD, with the resulting impact on sparsity, predictive performance, and algorithmic fairness investigated.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: characteristics driving individual ICA
isolated_nodes.description: Future work includes investigating which characteristics make an example more or less likely to be affected by ICA, and designing mitigation mechanisms for such arbitrariness, possibly drawing on the stability literature.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: downstream privacy and robustness effects of ICD
isolated_nodes.description: Investigating downstream effects of ICD on privacy (black-box-deferred examples may be more vulnerable to inference attacks) and robustness (harder to audit black-box-deferred examples for adversarial vulnerability) is an interesting future research avenue.

correction_notes: Initial graph build (not a correction pass). Evidence uses paraphrase-anchored tags (E<n>) keyed to paper sections/paragraphs, since no sentence-indexed source was provided. Edges reflect explicit causal/support language in the text (e.g., 'because', 'this suggests', ablation deltas); coordinate/parallel statements joined by 'and' without dependency language are left as separate isolated nodes rather than force-linked.

nodes.name: Encoder-decoder decoupling
nodes.description: LaMaTE decouples encoding and decoding from language modeling by using an LLM as the NMT encoder and leaving the NMT decoder unchanged.

nodes.name: Modeling flexibility
nodes.description: Decoupling encoding and decoding confers modeling flexibility, allowing a deep complex encoder paired with a lightweight decoder.

nodes.name: Heterogeneous architecture suitability
nodes.description: The heterogeneous architecture (powerful encoder, lightweight decoder) is well-suited for MT, using a powerful encoder to understand input while generating translations at lower decoding cost.

nodes.name: Inference speedup result
nodes.description: LaMaTE achieves 2.4-6.5x inference speedups over baselines.

nodes.name: KV cache memory reduction result
nodes.description: LaMaTE achieves a 75% reduction in KV cache memory footprint.

nodes.name: LLM decoder as unidirectional encoder
nodes.description: The function Dec_theta( , [c,x]) serves as a unidirectional encoder in LaMaTE.

nodes.name: Whole model as hybrid LM
nodes.description: Because both the LaMaTE encoder and decoder are unidirectional, the whole model can roughly be thought of as a hybrid language model: a large model for prefilling, a small model for decoding.

nodes.name: Dimensionality mismatch problem
nodes.description: The LLM decoder may have a larger hidden size than the NMT decoder, creating a mismatch.

nodes.name: Adaptor introduced
nodes.description: An adaptor is added to the output of the LLM decoder to reduce its dimensionality to match the NMT decoder.

nodes.name: Plain linear adaptor insufficient
nodes.description: A simple linear mapping adaptor falls short because LLMs are too big, making it difficult for untrained smaller models to use the transformed representations directly.

nodes.name: Three-component adaptor design
nodes.description: An adaptor with three components (layer fusion, MLP, EncStack) is designed to make better use of LLM outputs for the NMT decoder.

nodes.name: Layer fusion mechanism
nodes.description: LLM layers are divided into K groups and their outputs fused via a learnable weighted sum plus layer norm (Hfuse).

nodes.name: Layer fusion motivation
nodes.description: Fusing outputs of intermediate layers (rather than only the final layer) forms a finer-grained output, a method found beneficial to deep-to-shallow architectures in prior NMT work.

nodes.name: MLP dimensionality reduction
nodes.description: A 2-layer MLP is placed after layer fusion to reduce hidden size from d1 to d2, matching the NMT decoder's hidden size.

nodes.name: EncStack bidirectional learning
nodes.description: A stack of Transformer encoder layers (EncStack) is used to learn bidirectional representations from the unidirectional adaptor output, added with small computational overhead.

nodes.name: Ablation: no layer fusion
nodes.description: Removing layer fusion causes a COMET drop of 0.24 and BLEU drop of 0.71 relative to full LaMaTE.

nodes.name: Ablation: no EncStack
nodes.description: Removing EncStack causes a COMET drop of 0.30 and BLEU drop of 0.53 relative to full LaMaTE.

nodes.name: Layer fusion informativeness conclusion
nodes.description: Fusing intermediate LLM layers provides a more informative representation than relying solely on the final layer.

nodes.name: Adaptor enhances LLM representations conclusion
nodes.description: The adaptor enhances the native representations of LLMs, rendering them more suitable for the NMT decoder.

flagged_edges: P18,P19 left unconnected to other nodes within component: parallel adaptor sub-components with no stated dependency ordering

nodes.name: Fine-tuning LLMs is costly
nodes.description: Fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs is costly, making it generally favorable to use less labeled data.

nodes.name: Less data causes inadequate learning
nodes.description: Using less labeled data can lead to inadequate learning of the new parameters (adaptor and NMT decoder).

nodes.name: Extensive fine-tuning causes forgetting
nodes.description: Extensive fine-tuning may cause the LLM to forget its original knowledge encoded in its parameters.

nodes.name: Two-stage training method introduced
nodes.description: A two-stage training method is presented to perform more efficient learning for different types of parameters.

nodes.name: Stage 1: frozen LLM pretraining
nodes.description: In stage 1, the LLM decoder is frozen while the adaptor and NMT decoder are pre-trained on a standard translation task.

nodes.name: Stage 1 avoids backward pass
nodes.description: Because the LLM decoder parameters are frozen in stage 1, only a forward pass through the large network is needed, avoiding the backward pass.

nodes.name: Stage 1 is less computationally expensive
nodes.description: Avoiding the backward pass through the LLM makes stage 1 less computationally expensive than full LLM fine-tuning, enabling scaling to large datasets.

nodes.name: Stage 2: joint fine-tuning
nodes.description: In stage 2, the LLM decoder, NMT decoder, and adaptor are fine-tuned together on various tasks using the ComMT dataset.

nodes.name: Ablation: without stage 2
nodes.description: Training with only stage 1 (W/o S2) results in a substantial performance drop (COMET -2.25, BLEU -4.18).

nodes.name: Ablation: stage 2 with frozen LLM
nodes.description: Incorporating stage 2 while freezing LLM parameters yields improvements over stage-1-only but still falls short of full LaMaTE performance (COMET -0.16, BLEU -0.12).

nodes.name: Both data and LLM tuning matter conclusion
nodes.description: The ablation results underscore the importance of both high-quality data and LLM parameter tuning in maximizing model performance.

nodes.name: Gap in universal translation data resources
nodes.description: There remains a notable gap in comprehensive, high-quality data resources tailored to developing universal translation models.

nodes.name: ComMT benchmark developed
nodes.description: ComMT, a new comprehensive evaluation/training benchmark spanning five diverse translation-related tasks, is developed to generalize and evaluate LaMaTE.

nodes.name: ComMT task set
nodes.description: ComMT comprises five tasks: General Translation, Document-level Translation, Domain Translation, Terminology-constrained Translation, and Automatic Post-editing.

nodes.name: ComMT training set size
nodes.description: ComMT's training set totals 239,661 samples across four languages (German, Czech, Russian, Chinese).

nodes.name: ComMT quality verification setup
nodes.description: Llama3-8B was fine-tuned on ComMT and compared against WMT17-20 and TowerBlock datasets, evaluated on the WMT23 test set.

nodes.name: ComMT outperforms WMT17-20
nodes.description: ComMT surpasses WMT17-WMT20 in both En->X and X->En directions.

nodes.name: ComMT underperforms TowerBlock on X->En
nodes.description: ComMT excels in En->X but underperforms TowerBlock in the X->En direction.

nodes.name: TowerBlock size/composition explanation
nodes.description: The X->En discrepancy versus TowerBlock may be attributed to TowerBlock's larger dataset size and its inclusion of additional general task data predominantly in English.

nodes.name: LaMaTE vs encoder-decoder baselines
nodes.description: LaMaTE surpasses NLLB-3.3B, NMT, and mT5-Large across all evaluated ComMT tasks.

nodes.name: LLMs as high-capacity encoders conclusion
nodes.description: This result highlights the potential of LLMs as high-capacity encoders, capable of producing more expressive and informative representations.

nodes.name: Better representations improve decoder foundation
nodes.description: The enhanced representations from LLM encoding provide a solid foundation for the decoder, ultimately improving translation quality.

nodes.name: LaMaTE comparable to Llama3-8B-SFT
nodes.description: LaMaTE achieves comparable overall performance to Llama3-8B-SFT, a fully fine-tuned decoder-only LLM.

nodes.name: LLMs as effective MT encoders conclusion
nodes.description: The comparability to Llama3-8B-SFT demonstrates that LLMs can serve as effective MT encoders, offering an efficient alternative to fine-tuning LLMs as direct generators.

nodes.name: Encoder-decoder models show lower misalignment
nodes.description: Encoder-decoder models (mT5-large, LaMaTE) consistently exhibit lower off-target rate, unaligned source words, and unaligned target words than decoder-only models.

nodes.name: LaMaTE mitigates misalignment
nodes.description: LaMaTE follows the encoder-decoder paradigm, which also helps mitigate misalignment issues as an added bonus.

nodes.name: Cross-attention hypothesis
nodes.description: The misalignment improvement is speculated to be attributable to the cross-attention mechanism in the NMT decoder, which allows direct token-wise interaction between target and source.

nodes.name: Cross-attention enhances alignment
nodes.description: Cross-attention enhances source-target alignment, in contrast to LLMs relying on a single attention mechanism over concatenated source and target text.

nodes.name: Single attention causes lost focus
nodes.description: Relying on a single attention mechanism to jointly process concatenated source and target text could potentially cause a loss of attention focus.

flagged_edges: P60->P58 direction inferred: text presents cross-attention hypothesis first, then contrasts with single-attention/lost-focus explanation for decoder-only models; causal ordering between P58 and P60 is not fully explicit

nodes.name: Ablation: Concat Decoder variant
nodes.description: The Concat Decoder variant, which removes cross-attention, underperforms the standard decoder (COMET -0.80, BLEU -2.34).

nodes.name: Ablation: Prefix Decoder variant
nodes.description: The Prefix Decoder variant, which also removes cross-attention, underperforms the standard decoder (COMET -0.66, BLEU -1.47).

nodes.name: Standard decoder superiority conclusion
nodes.description: The standard decoder proves superior to the alternative cross-attention-free decoder designs.

nodes.name: Cross-attention beneficial for alignment-demanding tasks
nodes.description: Together with the misalignment findings, maintaining cross-attention in the decoder is argued to be particularly beneficial for translation tasks that demand strong alignment.

nodes.name: Decoder depth increases quality but reduces speed
nodes.description: Increasing decoder layers significantly improves translation performance, particularly En->X, but decoding speed drops sharply as depth increases, with a 39% reduction from 8 to 16 layers.

nodes.name: Encoder scaling offers better trade-off conclusion
nodes.description: Because decoder depth improves quality but sharply hurts speed while EncStack depth gives only modest gains with minimal efficiency cost, scaling the encoder offers a more effective trade-off between performance and computational efficiency than scaling the decoder.

nodes.name: EncStack depth gives modest gains
nodes.description: Adding more EncStack layers leads to modest improvements in both translation directions, with relatively small gains compared to decoder variations.

nodes.name: EncStack depth has minimal efficiency impact
nodes.description: Since EncStack operates only on the encoder side, its impact on decoding efficiency is minimal.

nodes.name: LaMaTE underperforms on low-resource languages
nodes.description: LaMaTE underperforms compared to mT5-large in low- and very-low-resource languages in the large-scale 99-language evaluation.

nodes.name: Limited pretraining data explanation
nodes.description: The low-resource underperformance is likely due to limited pre-training data for these languages in the Llama3-base model.

nodes.name: Stronger multilingual encoder suggestion
nodes.description: Using a model with stronger multilingual capabilities as the encoder could further improve performance on low-resource languages.

nodes.name: Decoder lightweight design
nodes.description: The NMT decoder in LaMaTE is intentionally lightweight relative to the LLM encoder.

nodes.name: Lightweight decoder may bottleneck many-target-language generation
nodes.description: Because the decoder is lightweight, it may become a bottleneck when generating translations into many target languages.

nodes.name: Expanding decoder capacity essential
nodes.description: Expanding decoder capacity is essential for better performance given this potential bottleneck.

nodes.name: MoE scaling suggestion
nodes.description: A more effective strategy might involve scaling the decoder's capacity with Mixture-of-Experts instead of adding more layers, boosting performance without compromising efficiency.

nodes.name: Randomly initialized decoder requires stage-1 pretraining
nodes.description: The approach requires pre-training the decoder's parameters using large-scale bilingual data in stage 1 because the decoder is randomly initialized.

nodes.name: Stage-1 pretraining may be inefficient
nodes.description: The requirement to pre-train a randomly initialized decoder on large-scale bilingual data may not be the most efficient process.

nodes.name: Alternative initialization suggestion
nodes.description: Future work could explore initializing decoder parameters from the encoder or leveraging a small pre-trained language model to reduce the state gap between encoder and decoder.

nodes.name: Llama3-8B best multilingual backbone
nodes.description: Llama3-8B consistently outperformed XGLM-7.5B, Bloom-7B, Falcon-7B, and Qwen2-7B in 0-shot and 3-shot translation across En<->De/Cs/Ru/Zh.

nodes.name: Stronger multilingual capability inference
nodes.description: Llama3-8B's superior cross-lingual performance suggests it possesses stronger multilingual capabilities.

nodes.name: Llama3-8B selected as backbone
nodes.description: Based on the evaluation results, Llama3-8B was selected as the backbone model for subsequent LaMaTE experiments.

isolated_nodes.name: NLP focus on decoder-only models
isolated_nodes.description: Much recent NLP emphasis has been on modeling MT and other problems using a single pre-trained Transformer decoder.

isolated_nodes.name: Encoder-decoder architectures receive less attention
isolated_nodes.description: Encoder-decoder architectures, standard in earlier NMT models, have received relatively less attention.

isolated_nodes.name: LLMs computationally expensive
isolated_nodes.description: LLMs are computationally expensive and pose challenges for applications requiring low latency and small memory footprint.

isolated_nodes.name: Analyze-then-generate paradigm
isolated_nodes.description: Most MT models, traditional and LLM-based, operate on an analyze-then-generate paradigm.

isolated_nodes.name: BERT-style encoder pretraining
isolated_nodes.description: A large body of NLP work has focused on pretraining and applying text encoders such as BERT for language understanding.

isolated_nodes.name: LLMs as text encoders for embeddings
isolated_nodes.description: Recent work has fine-tuned LLMs for text encoding and shown they can produce high-quality representations for embedding tasks.

isolated_nodes.name: Rarity of LLM encoders for generation
isolated_nodes.description: It is rare to see studies incorporating LLMs in the encoding side for NMT or other language generation tasks.

isolated_nodes.name: MT research shift to LLM adaptation
isolated_nodes.description: The focus of MT research has shifted toward adapting LLMs (prompting, fine-tuning) rather than improving model architectures.

isolated_nodes.name: Complementarity with efficiency methods
isolated_nodes.description: Quantization, pruning, and speculative decoding methods are not contradictory with LaMaTE and can be combined with it.

isolated_nodes.name: Two-stage architecture as hybrid LM framing
isolated_nodes.description: The whole LaMaTE system can be viewed as a single language model since both encoder and decoder are language-model-based.

isolated_nodes.name: Prompt-guided task control
isolated_nodes.description: By giving an appropriate prompt, the system can be guided to produce outputs following specific needs or contexts, giving LaMaTE an advantage over traditional NMT models.

isolated_nodes.name: ComMT collection goals
isolated_nodes.description: ComMT data was collected with two goals: maximizing data source diversity and maximizing high-quality manually annotated data.

isolated_nodes.name: ComMT covers four languages
isolated_nodes.description: ComMT is multilingual and supports four languages: German, Czech, Russian, and Chinese.

isolated_nodes.name: Original source language requirement
isolated_nodes.description: The test set ensures the source language is original in each case to avoid translationese issues.

isolated_nodes.name: Some languages lack test sets
isolated_nodes.description: Some languages currently lack test sets in ComMT because obtaining task data is challenging.

isolated_nodes.name: Efficient methods compatibility
isolated_nodes.description: Since LaMaTE follows standard encoding/decoding, it can be easily combined with various efficient inference methods.

structural_reasoning: The graph captures LaMaTE's main argumentative chains: architecture motivation -> speed/memory results (C1); the LLM-decoder-as-encoder framing and adaptor necessity (C2); the three-part adaptor design and its ablations (C3); the two-stage training rationale and its ablations (C4); the ComMT benchmark motivation and quality-verification results (C5); main results and the 'LLMs as encoders' interpretive claims (C6); misalignment analysis with a speculative causal mechanism (C7, lower confidence since the causal direction between cross-attention and single-attention explanations is somewhat inferred); decoder-variant ablations reinforcing the cross-attention claim (C8); depth-vs-efficiency trade-off reasoning (C9); low-resource underperformance diagnosis (C10); and two limitations chains (C11 decoder bottleneck, C12 stage-1 initialization cost). Background/related-work statements and standalone descriptive facts (dataset composition, prior-work framing) are left as isolated nodes since the text does not present them as premises feeding a specific downstream claim.
