components.description: Motivation: LLM opacity, its real-world stakes, and the limits of existing explainability approaches.

nodes.name: LLM inference is opaque
nodes.description: LLMs exhibit broad capabilities, yet their inference remains opaque: decision factors are unobservable and generated explanations often lack faithfulness.

nodes.name: Opacity hinders high-stakes adoption
nodes.description: This opacity hinders adoption in high-stakes domains, risking confident hallucinations and biases in medicine and fictitious legal precedents that undermine accountability.

nodes.name: Attribution/attention methods are correlational
nodes.description: Attribution and attention-based explainability methods are primarily correlational, whereas faithful explanations require causal evidence.

nodes.name: Counterfactual causal-graph methods remain local/input-centered
nodes.description: Counterfactual methods using causal graphs over textual variables provide stronger causal evidence but typically remain local and input-centered: they quantify a given factor's causal effect but do not recover the model's high-level inference.

nodes.name: Mechanistic interpretability is low-level and often misaligned with stakeholder needs
nodes.description: Mechanistic interpretability targets internal components like neurons and circuits, providing a valuable low-level science but is often misaligned with the explanations stakeholders actually need.

nodes.name: Missing: global causal account of concept organization
nodes.description: What remains missing is an applicable explainability method providing a global, causal account of how a model organizes human-interpretable concepts and reduces them to a prediction.

components.description: Core reframing: using causal graphs to model LLM inference itself rather than the external world.

nodes.name: Prior causal-graph work models external-world processes
nodes.description: Prior work uses causal graphs, and sometimes LLMs, to recover causal graphs of external-world processes (concepts → text → prediction, graph usually assumed a priori).

nodes.name: This paper models LLM inference itself
nodes.description: Instead, this paper uses causal graphs to model LLM inference itself (text → concepts → prediction), providing a transparent view of how the model perceives and organizes high-level concepts to produce a prediction.

nodes.name: The graph is itself the explanation; nothing assumed a priori
nodes.description: In this new setting, the graph is itself the explanation, and both the relevant concepts and their causal relations must be inferred rather than assumed in advance.

components.description: Positioning relative to the three senses of causal graphs in LLM interpretability, and relative to the closest related work (COAT).

nodes.name: Sense 1: mechanistic-interpretability graphs over model internals
nodes.description: In mechanistic interpretability, causal graphs are defined over model-internal components (attention heads, neurons, residual-stream directions), abstracting away the complete computation to retain only components hypothesized to mediate a targeted behavior.

nodes.name: Sense 2: graphs enabling causal-effect estimation of concepts on predictions
nodes.description: Causal graphs are also used to enable estimation of causal effects of high-level concepts on predictions (via counterfactuals, matching, adjustment), where the graph is usually assumed in advance and describes concepts → text → prediction.

nodes.name: Sense 3 (this paper): graphs describing the model's high-level reasoning
nodes.description: The paper introduces a third utility: causal graphs describing the model's high-level reasoning (text → concepts → prediction), where the graph is the explanation and has received no prior attention in the literature.

nodes.name: COAT is the closest related work but targets real-world structure
nodes.description: COAT (Liu et al. 2024) also uses an LLM to propose concepts and applies causal discovery, but aims to recover real-world causal structures and focuses on local Markov blankets for causal effect estimation.

nodes.name: Departure 1: recover the full graph, not a local Markov blanket
nodes.description: Because the goal is to characterize the model's internal reasoning rather than estimate a real-world effect, this work recovers the full graph from text to prediction rather than only a local Markov blanket, to capture the complete reasoning process.

nodes.name: Departure 2: MCMC-inspired counterfactual augmentation for sparse coverage
nodes.description: Because observational data sparsely cover the model's internal decision space, this work introduces an MCMC-inspired counterfactual augmentation procedure to actively expand the concept space for more robust graph discovery.

components.description: The data-coverage bottleneck in causal discovery and why the LLM setting makes it tractable.

nodes.name: Reliable structure learning needs representative coverage
nodes.description: A central challenge in causal discovery is data coverage: reliable structure learning requires a representative sample spanning diverse combinations of concept values.

nodes.name: Achieving coverage often requires costly/impractical/unethical interventions
nodes.description: In many domains, obtaining such coverage requires costly, impractical, or unethical interventions.

nodes.name: LLM mechanism makes counterfactual generation cheap
nodes.description: Because the mechanism under study is an LLM, the model itself can be prompted to generate counterfactual texts in which a targeted concept is altered while the remaining context stays stable, making the coverage bottleneck more tractable.

nodes.name: MCMC-inspired algorithm iteratively expands and filters
nodes.description: The MCMC-inspired algorithm iteratively proposes counterfactual chains and rejects unfaithful candidates, producing a denser, higher-quality concept space for robust causal discovery.

components.description: Formal setup: concept vectors, the LLM-inference causal graph, and its structural constraints.

nodes.name: Causal Graph framework adopted, relaxed to allow cycles
nodes.description: The method adopts Pearl's Causal Graph framework, relaxed to admit cyclic dependencies, acknowledging potential reciprocal influences among concepts an LLM uses internally.

nodes.name: Concept-extraction function maps text to a concept vector
nodes.description: A concept-extraction function ϕ maps input text x to a concept vector [l_c1,...,l_cn], where each l_ci is a categorical variable over subsets S ⊆ Y indicating which classes the LLM perceives concept ci to support (∅ = absent, Y = non-discriminative).

nodes.name: Graph defined over text, concepts, and prediction
nodes.description: The LLM's inference process is represented as a directed graph G=(V,E) with V = {X} ∪ C ∪ {Ŷ}, capturing high-level causal flow from input text through LLM-perceived concepts to the prediction.

nodes.name: Structural constraints: X is root, Ŷ is sink
nodes.description: Three structural constraints are imposed: X has only outgoing edges (root), Ŷ has only incoming edges (sink), and the text's effect on prediction is mediated by the concept variables.

nodes.name: Task reduces to recovering C and E
nodes.description: Given these constraints, the task reduces to recovering the concept set C and edge set E.

components.description: Phase 1-2 of the pipeline: label prediction and discriminative concept discovery/filtering.

nodes.name: Label Prediction substitutes LLM predictions for ground truth
nodes.description: Ground-truth labels in D are replaced with the LLM's own predictions ŷ=f(x); all downstream phases use these predicted labels so the recovered graph reflects the model's perspective rather than dataset labels.

nodes.name: Concepts proposed iteratively over class-balanced batches
nodes.description: Discriminative Concept Discovery processes training data in small, class-balanced batches; for each batch, the model proposes new candidate concepts which are added to the accumulating concept set C.

nodes.name: Concepts periodically filtered by relevance and discriminativeness
nodes.description: Every ten batches, accumulated concepts are annotated and filtered, retaining only concepts whose assigned value maps to a strictly partial subset of classes (neither ∅ nor Y) in a fraction of examples exceeding threshold τ=1/|Y|.

nodes.name: Filtering removes non-expressed and non-discriminative concepts
nodes.description: This filtering removes concepts that are rarely expressed in text (providing little evidence for a text-to-concept edge) and concepts broadly aligned with all classes (providing little evidence for a concept-to-prediction edge).

nodes.name: Final concept set fixed after test-set filtering pass
nodes.description: After processing all training batches, test examples are annotated with concept vectors and the same filtering criterion is applied once more, yielding the final concept set C.

components.description: Phase 3 of the pipeline: MCMC-inspired counterfactual data expansion, including the Metropolis-Hastings-like acceptance test.

nodes.name: Expansion operates in text space, not directly in concept space
nodes.description: Rather than operating directly in the discrete concept space, the algorithm operates in raw text space: the LLM proposes a textual perturbation, which is mapped to a concept vector by ϕ and retained only if it induces the intended conceptual shift.

nodes.name: Operating in text space preserves linguistic coherence
nodes.description: Operating in text space preserves linguistic coherence while allowing exploration of realizable regions of the concept space, i.e., configurations expressible by natural text.

nodes.name: Each example initiates an independent expansion chain
nodes.description: Each original training example initiates an independent expansion process lasting K=11 steps, iterating through concepts and sampling a target class y* to determine a directional shift (MORE/LESS).

nodes.name: Acceptance test requires target alignment and minimal side effects
nodes.description: A proposal is accepted (akin to a Metropolis-Hastings test) if it achieves the intended target alignment for the targeted concept and the count of drifted non-target concepts is bounded by a small tolerance ϵ.

nodes.name: Recursive refinement re-prompts on failure
nodes.description: If a proposal fails either acceptance condition, the LLM is re-prompted with feedback on which criterion was violated, up to R=5 regeneration attempts per concept; if all fail, no sample is appended for that concept.

nodes.name: Expansion densifies the concept manifold for causal discovery
nodes.description: The MCMC-inspired expansion densifies the latent concept space by exploring combinations beyond the original dataset, stochastically exploring the valid concept manifold and providing richer support for causal discovery.

components.description: Phase 4 of the pipeline: causal discovery via σ-CG, and why σ-CG was chosen.

nodes.name: σ-CG chosen for cyclic, discrete-variable compatibility
nodes.description: σ-CG (Forré and Mooij 2018) is chosen because it accommodates cyclic causal structures, which may arise in LLM inference and cannot be ruled out a priori, and it supports the discrete variables produced by the concept annotations.

nodes.name: σ-CG applied to the expanded dataset
nodes.description: σ-CG is applied to the expanded, annotated dataset D_mcmc, obtaining a directed graph G over the variables V.

nodes.name: Ŷ enforced as the unique sink during orientation
nodes.description: As background knowledge, the algorithm imposes that ŷ is the unique sink node and enforces this constraint during edge orientation.

components.description: Predictive fidelity evaluation: rationale, protocol, and headline result.

nodes.name: No ground-truth graph exists for direct evaluation
nodes.description: Because the goal is to recover a causal graph over the LLM's latent inference process, there is no ground-truth graph available for direct evaluation.

nodes.name: Predictive fidelity rationale: parents should screen off indirect variables
nodes.description: The learned graphs are evaluated via predictive fidelity: if a graph captures meaningful dependencies, direct causal parents should screen off indirect variables, making them more predictive of a node than other concept subsets.

nodes.name: Post-hoc prediction task compares parent set to all other subsets
nodes.description: For each target node, a multinomial logistic regression is trained to predict it from its graph-based parent set, compared via 10-fold CV to models trained on all other concept subsets that do not fully contain the parent set.

nodes.name: Graph-based predictors outperform average alternative subset in every setting
nodes.description: Graph-based predictors outperform the average alternative subset in every setting, across all models, datasets, and target types, indicating discovered parent sets capture relevant information.

nodes.name: Parent set ranks in Top-3 in most settings
nodes.description: In every setting but one, the causal-graph parent set ranks among the best predictors (Top-3) in a majority of CV cases, despite being compared against tens of alternatives, further strengthening the conclusion.

components.description: Qualitative analysis of learned graphs: convergence vs. divergence across LLMs by task naturalism.

nodes.name: Synthetic Disease Diagnosis concepts consistent across LLMs
nodes.description: On the synthetic Disease Diagnosis dataset, extracted concepts are consistent across LLMs and successfully recover the ground-truth variables (specific symptoms) defining the dataset's generative causal graph.

nodes.name: Even with similar concepts, causal topologies differ
nodes.description: The learned graphs reveal that different LLMs can follow different concept-level reasoning patterns: even when models rely on similar concepts, their causal topologies differ.

nodes.name: Naturalistic tasks show model-specific concept sets, not just topologies
nodes.description: This model-specific structure is even more pronounced in naturalistic Sentiment Analysis and LLM-as-a-Judge tasks, where the extracted concepts themselves vary across models, suggesting models rely on different reasoning mechanisms.

nodes.name: Reasoning differences matter for deployment decisions
nodes.description: These differences matter for deployment: choosing among models requires understanding not only their performance but also whether their underlying reasoning aligns with stakeholders' expectations and constraints.

components.description: MCMC convergence diagnostics: why naive KL decrease is insufficient and the bounded trajectory used instead.

nodes.name: Multi-chain diagnostics inapplicable in single-chain-per-instance setting
nodes.description: Multi-chain diagnostics such as the Gelman-Rubin statistic are not directly applicable because the setting uses a single chain per instance; convergence is instead monitored via the empirical KL divergence over the combinatorial concept-state distribution across iterations.

nodes.name: Naive KL decrease is not sufficient evidence of convergence
nodes.description: A naive KL decrease is not sufficient evidence of convergence, since as the sample pool grows each new counterfactual carries diminishing marginal weight, mechanically reducing KL regardless of genuine stabilization.

nodes.name: Empirical KL bounded between orthogonal-expansion and perfect-overlap extremes
nodes.description: To separate genuine convergence from this artifact, the empirical KL is bounded between an orthogonal-expansion upper bound (every new sample unseen) and a perfect-overlap lower bound (every new sample duplicates an existing one).

nodes.name: Desirable trajectory moves from upper bound toward lower bound
nodes.description: A desirable trajectory begins near the upper bound (actively discovering new valid concept states) and gradually approaches the lower bound (samples increasingly come from a stable, realizable region).

nodes.name: Empirical KL follows the desired trajectory
nodes.description: The empirical KL curve on Sentiment Analysis for GPT-OSS-20B follows precisely this desired trajectory.

nodes.name: Structural stability confirmed once KL stabilizes
nodes.description: Once the KL stabilizes, the Hamming distance between causal edge sets recovered across successive iterations drops to zero, suggesting additional augmentation no longer changes the learned graph.

components.description: Ablation on the contribution of MCMC counterfactual augmentation itself.

nodes.name: Three data regimes compared
nodes.description: The contribution of MCMC expansion is evaluated by comparing three data regimes: All Original, Original Seed (subset seeding the chains), and Seed + Counterfactuals.

nodes.name: Counterfactuals achieve highest predictive accuracy
nodes.description: The counterfactual-augmented regime achieves the highest predictive accuracy for both concept nodes and prediction across all models.

nodes.name: MCMC introduces concept-state combinations absent from original data
nodes.description: The MCMC-generated counterfactuals introduce concept-state combinations absent in the original data, enabling more accurate estimation of dependencies between concepts.

nodes.name: Causal-graph parent subsets outperform average subset (replicated)
nodes.description: Consistent with the predictive fidelity evaluation, the causal graph's parent subsets outperform the average over all concept subsets in this ablation as well.

nodes.name: Together, results demonstrate necessity of the augmentation stage
nodes.description: Together, these two patterns (counterfactual benefit and parent-subset superiority) demonstrate the necessity of the counterfactual augmentation stage.

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: causal paradigm for global concept-based explainability
nodes.description: A causal paradigm is introduced for global, concept-based explainability that maps LLM reasoning to causal graphs.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: MCMC-inspired counterfactual augmentation framework
nodes.description: An MCMC-inspired data augmentation framework is proposed that generates counterfactuals to better cover the concept space, enabling robust causal discovery.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: evaluation protocol for structural stability and predictive fidelity
nodes.description: An evaluation protocol is developed for assessing both the structural stability and predictive fidelity of the resulting causal graphs, addressing the absence of gold-standard reasoning graphs.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: sensitivity to batch pairing in concept extraction
isolated_nodes.description: Concept extraction runs only once in small batches due to token limits and cost; different batch assignments could highlight distinct contrastive features and yield a different concept set, a limitation future work could mitigate with multiple shuffled extraction passes.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: validation restricted to local parents, not full multi-hop chains
isolated_nodes.description: The current validation protocol primarily evaluates local predictive fidelity through discovered parent sets, demonstrating immediate predictors are informative and stable but not directly verifying longer multi-hop causal chains or the broader graph hierarchy.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: dependence on self-annotation and generation faithfulness
isolated_nodes.description: The framework relies on the target LLM to annotate concepts, generate counterfactuals, and judge whether edits satisfy constraints; since LLM self-assessments are not guaranteed faithful, errors may propagate despite acceptance criteria mitigating this risk, motivating future external validation or human audits.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: languages, open-ended generation, multimodal domains
isolated_nodes.description: Future work plans to extend the framework to additional languages, open-ended generation settings, and multimodal domains, broadening evaluation toward standardized, stakeholder-oriented explainability frameworks.

nodes.description: σ-CG (Forré and Mooij 2018) is chosen because it accommodates cyclic causal structures, which may arise in LLM inference and cannot be ruled out a priori, and it supports the discrete variables produced by the concept annotations.

nodes.name: σ-CG applied to the expanded dataset
nodes.description: σ-CG is applied to the expanded, annotated dataset D_mcmc, obtaining a directed graph G over the variables V.

nodes.name: Ŷ enforced as the unique sink during orientation
nodes.description: As background knowledge, the algorithm imposes that ŷ is the unique sink node and enforces this constraint during edge orientation.

components.description: Predictive fidelity evaluation: rationale, protocol, and headline result.

nodes.name: No ground-truth graph exists for direct evaluation
nodes.description: Because the goal is to recover a causal graph over the LLM's latent inference process, there is no ground-truth graph available for direct evaluation.

nodes.name: Predictive fidelity rationale: parents should screen off indirect variables
nodes.description: The learned graphs are evaluated via predictive fidelity: if a graph captures meaningful dependencies, direct causal parents should screen off indirect variables, making them more predictive of a node than other concept subsets.

nodes.name: Post-hoc prediction task compares parent set to all other subsets
nodes.description: For each target node, a multinomial logistic regression is trained to predict it from its graph-based parent set, compared via 10-fold CV to models trained on all other concept subsets that do not fully contain the parent set.

nodes.name: Graph-based predictors outperform average alternative subset in every setting
nodes.description: Graph-based predictors outperform the average alternative subset in every setting, across all models, datasets, and target types, indicating discovered parent sets capture relevant information.

nodes.name: Parent set ranks in Top-3 in most settings
nodes.description: In every setting but one, the causal-graph parent set ranks among the best predictors (Top-3) in a majority of CV cases, despite being compared against tens of alternatives, further strengthening the conclusion.

components.description: Qualitative analysis of learned graphs: convergence vs. divergence across LLMs by task naturalism.

nodes.name: Synthetic Disease Diagnosis concepts consistent across LLMs
nodes.description: On the synthetic Disease Diagnosis dataset, extracted concepts are consistent across LLMs and successfully recover the ground-truth variables (specific symptoms) defining the dataset's generative causal graph.

nodes.name: Even with similar concepts, causal topologies differ
nodes.description: The learned graphs reveal that different LLMs can follow different concept-level reasoning patterns: even when models rely on similar concepts, their causal topologies differ.

nodes.name: Naturalistic tasks show model-specific concept sets, not just topologies
nodes.description: This model-specific structure is even more pronounced in naturalistic Sentiment Analysis and LLM-as-a-Judge tasks, where the extracted concepts themselves vary across models, suggesting models rely on different reasoning mechanisms.

nodes.name: Reasoning differences matter for deployment decisions
nodes.description: These differences matter for deployment: choosing among models requires understanding not only their performance but also whether their underlying reasoning aligns with stakeholders' expectations and constraints.

components.description: MCMC convergence diagnostics: why naive KL decrease is insufficient and the bounded trajectory used instead.

nodes.name: Multi-chain diagnostics inapplicable in single-chain-per-instance setting
nodes.description: Multi-chain diagnostics such as the Gelman-Rubin statistic are not directly applicable because the setting uses a single chain per instance; convergence is instead monitored via the empirical KL divergence over the combinatorial concept-state distribution across iterations.

nodes.name: Naive KL decrease is not sufficient evidence of convergence
nodes.description: A naive KL decrease is not sufficient evidence of convergence, since as the sample pool grows each new counterfactual carries diminishing marginal weight, mechanically reducing KL regardless of genuine stabilization.

nodes.name: Empirical KL bounded between orthogonal-expansion and perfect-overlap extremes
nodes.description: To separate genuine convergence from this artifact, the empirical KL is bounded between an orthogonal-expansion upper bound (every new sample unseen) and a perfect-overlap lower bound (every new sample duplicates an existing one).

nodes.name: Desirable trajectory moves from upper bound toward lower bound
nodes.description: A desirable trajectory begins near the upper bound (actively discovering new valid concept states) and gradually approaches the lower bound (samples increasingly come from a stable, realizable region).

nodes.name: Empirical KL follows the desired trajectory
nodes.description: The empirical KL curve on Sentiment Analysis for GPT-OSS-20B follows precisely this desired trajectory.

nodes.name: Structural stability confirmed once KL stabilizes
nodes.description: Once the KL stabilizes, the Hamming distance between causal edge sets recovered across successive iterations drops to zero, suggesting additional augmentation no longer changes the learned graph.

components.description: Ablation on the contribution of MCMC counterfactual augmentation itself.

nodes.name: Three data regimes compared
nodes.description: The contribution of MCMC expansion is evaluated by comparing three data regimes: All Original, Original Seed (subset seeding the chains), and Seed + Counterfactuals.

nodes.name: Counterfactuals achieve highest predictive accuracy
nodes.description: The counterfactual-augmented regime achieves the highest predictive accuracy for both concept nodes and prediction across all models.

nodes.name: MCMC introduces concept-state combinations absent from original data
nodes.description: The MCMC-generated counterfactuals introduce concept-state combinations absent in the original data, enabling more accurate estimation of dependencies between concepts.

nodes.name: Causal-graph parent subsets outperform average subset (replicated)
nodes.description: Consistent with the predictive fidelity evaluation, the causal graph's parent subsets outperform the average over all concept subsets in this ablation as well.

nodes.name: Together, results demonstrate necessity of the augmentation stage
nodes.description: Together, these two patterns (counterfactual benefit and parent-subset superiority) demonstrate the necessity of the counterfactual augmentation stage.

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: causal paradigm for global concept-based explainability
nodes.description: A causal paradigm is introduced for global, concept-based explainability that maps LLM reasoning to causal graphs.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: MCMC-inspired counterfactual augmentation framework
nodes.description: An MCMC-inspired data augmentation framework is proposed that generates counterfactuals to better cover the concept space, enabling robust causal discovery.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: evaluation protocol for structural stability and predictive fidelity
nodes.description: An evaluation protocol is developed for assessing both the structural stability and predictive fidelity of the resulting causal graphs, addressing the absence of gold-standard reasoning graphs.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: sensitivity to batch pairing in concept extraction
isolated_nodes.description: Concept extraction runs only once in small batches due to token limits and cost; different batch assignments could highlight distinct contrastive features and yield a different concept set, a limitation future work could mitigate with multiple shuffled extraction passes.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: validation restricted to local parents, not full multi-hop chains
isolated_nodes.description: The current validation protocol primarily evaluates local predictive fidelity through discovered parent sets, demonstrating immediate predictors are informative and stable but not directly verifying longer multi-hop causal chains or the broader graph hierarchy.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: dependence on self-annotation and generation faithfulness
isolated_nodes.description: The framework relies on the target LLM to annotate concepts, generate counterfactuals, and judge whether edits satisfy constraints; since LLM self-assessments are not guaranteed faithful, errors may propagate despite acceptance criteria mitigating this risk, motivating future external validation or human audits.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: languages, open-ended generation, multimodal domains
isolated_nodes.description: Future work plans to extend the framework to additional languages, open-ended generation settings, and multimodal domains, broadening evaluation toward standardized, stakeholder-oriented explainability frameworks.

note_on_evidence: Evidence fields cite paper sections/subsections/figures/tables rather than sentence indices, since a sentence-indexed source was not available for this document. This is a broad survey rather than a single-argument paper, so many nodes are definitional/categorical rather than links in one causal chain; edges are included only where the survey itself states a dependency, trade-off, or motivating relationship.

components.name: Motivation: why robustness evaluation is needed beyond accuracy

nodes.name: Accuracy alone is insufficient for reliability
nodes.description: Although accuracy is the most fundamental evaluation metric, it is insufficient to ensure reliability in real-world LLM applications.

nodes.name: Deep models are easily fooled by imperceptible perturbations
nodes.description: Despite improved accuracy, deep neural network models, including LLMs, have been shown to be easily fooled by specific imperceptible input perturbations.

nodes.name: Lack of robustness causes unintended harms in high-stakes domains
nodes.description: A lack of robustness may result in unintended biases, incorrect predictions, or overreliance on spurious correlations, raising reliability concerns in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, complex reasoning, code generation, and finance.

nodes.name: A thorough robustness assessment beyond accuracy is required
nodes.description: Because of the risks in high-stakes domains, a thorough and exacting assessment of LLM robustness that goes beyond conventional accuracy criteria is required.

nodes.name: No standardized robustness definitions/categorizations
nodes.description: The absence of standardized definitions and categorizations of robustness complicates cross-study comparisons, as research efforts differ in how they frame scope and components.

nodes.name: Root causes of non-robustness are hard to disentangle
nodes.description: Pinpointing the root causes of non-robustness (data biases, unstable training dynamics, architectural limitations, inference inefficiencies) requires disentangling complex interactions across these factors.

nodes.name: Mitigation effectiveness does not generalize across vulnerabilities
nodes.description: While numerous mitigation strategies exist, their effectiveness often depends on addressing specific vulnerabilities, making it difficult to generalize solutions.

nodes.name: Evaluation of robustness remains fragmented
nodes.description: Evaluating robustness remains fragmented, with no unified metrics or benchmarks to holistically assess performance under diverse real-world conditions.

nodes.name: Existing literature is scattered across domains
nodes.description: Existing literature on LLM robustness is scattered across domains, limiting cross-pollination of insights and hindering cohesive solutions.

nodes.name: These challenges motivate this comprehensive survey
nodes.description: The combination of definitional fragmentation, disentangling root causes, non-generalizing mitigations, fragmented evaluation, and scattered literature motivates this survey's comprehensive overview to unify perspectives and accelerate progress.

components.name: Defining robustness and its interdependent dimensions

nodes.name: Robustness is stability of output under perturbation or distribution shift
nodes.description: Robustness is conceptualized as the degree to which a model's output remains stable or correct when the input is perturbed or drawn from a test distribution different from the training distribution.

nodes.name: Working definition synthesizing core themes
nodes.description: The survey's working definition is that LLM robustness is the model's ability to maintain consistent performance, reliability, and adherence to intended behaviour despite variations in inputs, contexts, or data distributions, encompassing resilience to noise, paraphrasing, distribution shifts, incomplete information, reasoning perturbations, instruction variations, and adversarial manipulations.

nodes.name: Eight (overlapping) key dimensions identified
nodes.description: The survey delineates key dimensions of robustness: resilience to adversarial attacks, OOD generalization, sensitivity to prompt variations, handling noisy input, fairness under stress, consistency/reliability of outputs, and task-specific robustness, noting these categories overlap and interact.

nodes.name: Spurious-correlation reliance links OOD, adversarial, and prompt sensitivity
nodes.description: A model prone to spurious correlations (an OOD issue) is often more vulnerable to adversarial attacks that exploit those patterns and more sensitive to prompt variations that shift these cues.

nodes.name: Improving consistency lowers adversarial vulnerability
nodes.description: Enhancing consistency (e.g., reducing prompt sensitivity) can lower adversarial vulnerability.

nodes.name: Stronger OOD generalization reduces hallucination and reinforces consistency
nodes.description: Stronger OOD generalization reduces hallucination risks and may indirectly reinforce consistency.

nodes.name: Noise robustness may strengthen consistency
nodes.description: Robustness to noise may also strengthen consistency.

nodes.name: Rigid consistency enforcement can limit adaptability
nodes.description: Enforcing consistency too rigidly may limit adaptability to novel inputs, illustrating a trade-off between dimensions.

nodes.name: Fairness-improving alignment can weaken OOD generalization (alignment tax)
nodes.description: Alignment methods aimed at improving fairness may weaken OOD generalization, a phenomenon also known as the alignment tax.

nodes.name: OOD inputs push models beyond knowledge boundaries, raising hallucination risk
nodes.description: OOD inputs can push models beyond their knowledge boundaries, increasing hallucination risks.

nodes.name: Over-optimizing one dimension can undermine others
nodes.description: Overall, robustness requires balanced strategies, since over-optimizing a single dimension can undermine other dimensions.

components.name: Sources of non-robustness across the LLM lifecycle

nodes.name: Non-robustness sources span the full model lifecycle
nodes.description: Failures in robustness can be broadly categorized as stemming from data, model architecture, the training/learning process, or inference, spanning the entire lifecycle from data collection to deployment.

nodes.name: Spurious correlations are a primary data-related cause
nodes.description: Instead of learning intended causal relationships, models learn to rely on simpler, superficial patterns (shortcuts) that correlate with correct outputs in training data but do not hold universally, causing performance collapse when such correlations are absent or altered.

nodes.name: Dataset biases and annotation artifacts propagate into model behavior
nodes.description: Training data reflects societal biases and superficial annotation patterns (e.g., crowd-sourced shortcut labeling), which LLMs learn and amplify, perpetuating robustness failures across training, evaluation, and deployment.

nodes.name: Data poisoning/backdoors can be intentionally injected
nodes.description: Adversaries can inject malicious examples into training or fine-tuning data to create hidden backdoors triggered by specific inputs at inference time, often without noticeably degrading general performance.

nodes.name: Standard training objectives (NTP/ERM) optimize average performance, not robustness
nodes.description: Standard pre-training (next-token prediction) and fine-tuning (ERM) objectives primarily optimize average performance on the training distribution and may not explicitly encourage robustness to distribution shifts or perturbations, potentially encouraging shortcut reliance.

nodes.name: RLHF introduces reward hacking and bias amplification risks
nodes.description: RLHF can cause the model to exploit weaknesses/biases in the reward model (reward hacking) and can amplify biases present in inconsistent or incomplete human feedback (bias amplification).

nodes.name: Alignment tax trades general capability for alignment
nodes.description: Improving alignment (helpfulness, harmlessness) can come at the cost of reduced performance on general knowledge benchmarks, worse calibration, or new vulnerabilities -- termed the alignment tax.

nodes.name: Fine-tuning can reduce OOD robustness and increase noise/instruction brittleness
nodes.description: Fine-tuning can cause overfitting to fine-tuning-data-specific patterns (harming OOD generalization), high sensitivity to noise in instruction/preference data, and brittleness to instruction phrasing variations at test time.

nodes.name: Transformer architecture has inherent vulnerable components
nodes.description: Specific Transformer components, such as the self-attention mechanism, can be points of failure, and expanding model depth can particularly disrupt attention mechanisms.

nodes.name: Efficiency modifications (quantization, pruning) can cascade into robustness loss
nodes.description: Deployment modifications like quantization and pruning can induce information-loss cascades that significantly degrade robustness, with extreme cases like bit-flip attacks showing catastrophic sensitivity.

nodes.name: Decoding strategy choice affects consistency and robustness
nodes.description: The algorithm used to select the next token (greedy, beam search, sampling) has a major impact on model performance and consistency, with deterministic vs. stochastic strategies offering different trade-offs and hyperparameters like temperature/beam width strongly affecting robustness.

nodes.name: Calibration errors undermine reliable use of confidence scores
nodes.description: LLM confidence scores frequently fail to accurately reflect true correctness likelihood, especially after RLHF fine-tuning (overconfidence), hindering reliable decision-making based on model outputs.

nodes.name: RAG robustness depends on retriever quality
nodes.description: RAG systems' robustness depends heavily on the quality and relevance of retrieved context; inaccurate or noisy retrieval can significantly compromise final output quality, sometimes worse than no retrieval at all.

components.name: Mitigation strategies organized by pipeline stage

nodes.name: Four-stage pipeline categorization of mitigations
nodes.description: Mitigation strategies are categorized by deployment stage: pre-processing (data-stage interventions), in-processing (training/fine-tuning interventions), intra-processing (inference-time adaptations), and post-processing (output validation/filtering).

nodes.name: Pre-processing targets data-stage vulnerabilities before training
nodes.description: Pre-processing strategies (data augmentation, data filtering) intervene at the data stage before training/fine-tuning, aiming to prevent the model from inheriting or amplifying data biases and vulnerabilities.

nodes.name: In-processing builds robustness into model parameters during training
nodes.description: In-processing strategies (adversarial training, regularization, alignment) integrate directly into the training/fine-tuning loop, actively guiding learning to develop more robust representations and counter training-induced non-robustness.

nodes.name: Intra-processing adapts inference without retraining
nodes.description: Intra-processing strategies (robust prompting, weight redistribution, modified decoding, inference-time adaptation) dynamically adjust how models interpret inputs or produce outputs during inference, addressing data/training/inference-related non-robustness without retraining, though not root causes in training data or parameters.

nodes.name: Post-processing is the final output-stage defence
nodes.description: Post-processing strategies (output filtering/validation, LLM-as-a-judge) scrutinize, filter, validate, or transform generated text after generation but before delivery, catching harmful content, inaccuracies, biases, or outputs from attacks that bypassed earlier defences.

nodes.name: Data filtering involves a harm-removal vs. diversity trade-off
nodes.description: Overly strict data filtering to remove toxic content or bias can inadvertently harm general performance or erase valid examples from underrepresented groups, creating a data-quality-vs-quantity trade-off.

nodes.name: Adversarial training is a minimax optimization with scaling limitations
nodes.description: Adversarial training formulates an inner loop that maximizes loss via worst-case perturbations and an outer loop that minimizes loss on these examples, but scaling it to LLMs faces challenges: discrete-text gradient mismatches, high computational overhead, a robustness-utility trade-off, and attack-specific (non-transferable) robustness gains.

nodes.name: Alignment improves robustness against certain attacks but introduces new challenges
nodes.description: Alignment techniques (SFT, RLHF, DPO variants) contribute to robustness against attacks eliciting harmful/biased content, but introduce challenges: over-sensitivity to prompt phrasing causing unnecessary refusals, failure to anticipate post-alignment vulnerabilities, reward hacking, and high computational/data requirements.

nodes.name: Intra-processing trades robustness gains for coverage of root causes
nodes.description: Intra-processing strategies are cost-effective (avoiding retraining) and adaptable to emerging risks, but because they act at inference time, they do not address root causes in the training data or model parameters.

nodes.name: LLM-as-a-judge introduces its own manipulation and bias risks
nodes.description: Using an LLM to judge another model's outputs enables scalable assessment of bias, safety, and factuality, but judge evaluations can be inconsistent due to prompt sensitivity and inherent biases, and judge models themselves can be manipulated by adversarial stylistic cues.

components.name: Metrics, benchmarks, and their evaluation gaps

nodes.name: No single metric captures robustness holistically
nodes.description: Effective robustness evaluation requires combining complementary metrics across multiple dimensions, since no single metric tells the whole story.

nodes.name: Performance degradation metrics quantify clean-vs-stressed gaps
nodes.description: Metrics like Accuracy/F1 Drop, Attack Success Rate, and Compliance/Refusal Rate quantify how much performance or safety degrades when moving from clean to challenging (adversarial/noisy) conditions.

nodes.name: OOD performance metrics assess generalization to shifted distributions
nodes.description: Metrics like OOD Accuracy/F1, ID-OOD Performance Gap, and OOD Detection (AUROC, Energy Score) assess how well models perform on and detect distribution-shifted inputs, using benchmarks such as BOSS, ANLI, Dynasent, and WANLI.

nodes.name: Consistency metrics test output stability across equivalent inputs
nodes.description: Metrics like Semantic Consistency, Consistency Rate, Response Consistency, and LLM-based Consistency Score assess whether outputs remain stable under paraphrasing, sampling variation, or answer-choice reordering.

nodes.name: Calibration metrics assess confidence-accuracy alignment
nodes.description: Expected Calibration Error and its OOD-shifted variant assess whether a model's predicted confidence reliably reflects actual correctness likelihood, which is particularly important given RLHF-induced overconfidence (linking to P33 in C3).

nodes.name: Fairness-under-stress metrics test bias amplification under adversarial prompting
nodes.description: Fairness metrics (e.g., FLEX-derived measures) evaluate whether disparities in ASR, refusal rate, or accuracy across demographic groups emerge specifically under bias-inducing adversarial prompts.

nodes.name: Hallucination/factuality metrics measure stress-induced factual degradation
nodes.description: Metrics like FactScore, FEWL, SelfCheckGPT-style consistency checks, and Hallucination Rate Increase (HRI) measure factual correctness and how much hallucination tendency increases specifically under stress conditions relative to standard conditions.

nodes.name: ID-OOD performance gap does not always follow from ID performance
nodes.description: Studies using benchmarks like BOSS show the ID-OOD performance gap can vary in complex, non-monotonic patterns depending on model scale, training steps, and task type, indicating that improving ID performance does not always guarantee better OOD performance.

nodes.name: Adversarial benchmarks can inadvertently induce hallucinations
nodes.description: Adversarial benchmarks primarily focused on inducing misclassification or safety failures can inadvertently trigger hallucinations, since attacks that manipulate reasoning or push models into unusual states via jailbreaking may cause factually incorrect outputs as a byproduct.

nodes.name: Trend toward dynamic, LLM-free benchmarks to reduce contamination/judge bias
nodes.description: The field is trending toward benchmarks that are dynamic (generating test cases on-the-fly, e.g., ODE, DyVal) and LLM-free (avoiding reliance on potentially unreliable LLM judges, e.g., AMBER) to improve reliability and validity of robustness evaluation.

components.name: Persistent challenges and future research priorities

nodes.name: Robustness does not consistently correlate with model scale
nodes.description: Larger models are not inherently more robust; scaling trends for robustness often show weak or inconsistent patterns.

nodes.name: Safety-aligned models remain vulnerable to sophisticated jailbreaks
nodes.description: Despite safety alignment, models remain susceptible to sophisticated jailbreaking attempts and can deteriorate sharply under minor distribution shifts or input perturbations.

nodes.name: Robustness defences face scalability limits
nodes.description: Many promising defences (adversarial training, complex inference-time checks) are computationally expensive and may not scale efficiently to trillion-parameter models.

nodes.name: Robustness-utility trade-offs remain unresolved
nodes.description: Aggressively optimizing for robustness often negatively impacts general capabilities or clean-task performance, exemplified by the RLHF alignment tax; balancing the two remains a critical ongoing challenge.

nodes.name: Evaluation methodology gaps persist
nodes.description: Current evaluation lacks comprehensive benchmarks covering multiple robustness dimensions simultaneously and subtle failure modes, and evaluating generative-task robustness remains harder than classification-task robustness.

nodes.name: Theoretical understanding of robustness failures is still developing
nodes.description: Theoretical understanding of why LLMs exhibit shortcut learning, how architecture influences vulnerabilities, and why certain defences work is still developing, limiting principled mitigation design.

nodes.name: Static benchmark gains may not transfer to real-world deployment
nodes.description: Translating robustness improvements observed on static benchmarks into reliable performance under continuous real-world distribution shifts and novel threats remains a significant hurdle.

nodes.name: These challenges motivate causal/invariant learning and adaptive evaluation as priorities
nodes.description: The combination of scale-independence, unresolved trade-offs, evaluation gaps, and limited theory motivates future priorities: causal/invariant learning, efficient robust training, adaptive/automated evaluation, improved benchmarks, and extending robustness research to multimodal and agentic systems.

isolated_nodes.name: Systematic PRISMA-style search methodology
isolated_nodes.description: The survey conducted a systematic search across six databases (arXiv, ACL Anthology, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, OpenReview, GitHub) covering January 2020-June 2025, screening 337 records and including 209 new studies after applying inclusion/exclusion criteria and backward snowballing.

isolated_nodes.name: Robustness as a component of broader AI Trustworthiness
isolated_nodes.description: Robustness is frequently discussed as a critical component within the broader framework of AI Trustworthiness, which also expects reliability, safety, fairness, transparency, and accountability.

isolated_nodes.name: Task-specific robustness spans domain-specific failure modes
isolated_nodes.description: Task-specific robustness addresses unique challenges in particular applications, such as logical-consistency failures in reasoning benchmarks (e.g., FOLIO) or functionally incorrect/insecure generated code.

isolated_nodes.name: Decision matrix maps threat models to recommended mitigations
isolated_nodes.description: The survey provides a decision matrix (Table 3) and actionable flowchart (Figure 6) mapping specific threat models/metric thresholds (e.g., high ASR, large OOD gap, low consistency rate, high ECE) to recommended mitigation strategies and their trade-offs, intended as practitioner guidance.

isolated_nodes.name: Comprehensive LLM robustness pipeline diagram
isolated_nodes.description: Figure 5 presents a comprehensive multi-stage pipeline diagram showing how pre-, in-, intra-, and post-processing mitigation stages map onto the data collection, training/alignment, inference, and output stages of the LLM lifecycle.

isolated_nodes.name: Specific mitigation technique catalog
isolated_nodes.description: The survey catalogs numerous specific techniques within each mitigation category, including ME-ADA, ACL, A3, SALAD, and HarmAug for data augmentation; rule-based filtering, Data-Juicer, and RAZOR for data filtering; ALUM, C-AdvUL, and CAPO for adversarial training; BSR, LAAT, and DBL for regularization; DPO, ORPO, KTO, and Safe RLHF variants for alignment; and self-denoising, referenced instruction tracking, and RMOD for intra-processing.

isolated_nodes.name: Specific benchmark catalog across dimensions
isolated_nodes.description: The survey catalogs benchmarks by target dimension, including AdvGLUE++, PromptBench, and JailbreakBench for adversarial resilience; BOSS, ANLI, and OODRobustBench for OOD generalization; SCORE for prompt/sampling consistency; FLEX for fairness under stress; ReClor-plus and R2ATA for task-specific reasoning robustness; and TruthfulQA, HaluEval, FACTOR, DefAn, UMWP, and AMBER for hallucination/factuality.

structural_reasoning: As a broad survey rather than a single-thesis paper, this graph necessarily differs in character from the theoretical/empirical papers analyzed previously: most of its content is definitional and taxonomic rather than a single chain of argument, so edges are sparser relative to node count and many nodes are appropriately isolated (search methodology, technique/benchmark catalogs, pipeline diagrams). Within that constraint, the graph captures the survey's genuine argumentative structure where it exists: C1 traces the stated motivation for the survey itself; C2 captures the explicit dimension-interdependency claims from Figure 3/Section 2.2 (the survey's most causally dense passage); C3 organizes sources of non-robustness by lifecycle stage with a few explicit causal chains (e.g., RLHF -> alignment tax -> fine-tuning brittleness) the survey itself draws; C4 mirrors the four-stage mitigation taxonomy and the specific trade-offs the survey names for each stage; C5 connects metrics/benchmarks to the 'no single metric suffices' framing and highlights the two explicit gap-claims the survey makes (ID-OOD gap non-monotonicity, adversarial benchmarks inducing hallucination); C6 synthesizes the challenges section into a fan-in structure toward future priorities, matching the survey's own concluding logic. The moderate structural score (lower than the proof-driven papers, higher than a purely descriptive listing) reflects that a survey's value lies primarily in comprehensive categorization rather than a tight deductive chain, so full argumentative connectivity is not the right bar to hold it to.

nodes.name: Communication complexity governed by kappa and spectral gap
nodes.description: For strongly convex problems, communication complexity is governed by the condition number kappa=L/mu and the spectral gap 1-beta of the mixing matrix.

nodes.name: Large kappa or beta inflates communication rounds
nodes.description: A large condition number (ill-conditioned objective) or beta close to 1 (poorly connected network) can each independently inflate communication rounds by orders of magnitude.

nodes.name: Deterministic acceleration achieves both improvements
nodes.description: In the deterministic setting, prior work established that incorporating Nesterov-type momentum can attain communication complexities with accelerated sqrt(kappa) dependence and accelerated 1/sqrt(1-beta) dependence simultaneously.

nodes.name: Whether stochastic setting can match deterministic acceleration is open
nodes.description: Whether the same simultaneous acceleration achievable deterministically is also achievable in the stochastic setting, where gradient noise couples with both optimization dynamics and consensus, remains an open question.

nodes.name: D-MASG accelerates kappa but worsens communication
nodes.description: The D-MASG method accelerates optimization updates and improves condition-number dependence, but its communication complexity is paradoxically worse than non-accelerated decentralized SGD because acceleration amplifies consensus error.

nodes.name: LMT improves spectral gap but not condition number
nodes.description: The LMT method incorporates accelerated gossip to improve the spectral-gap dependence to 1/sqrt(1-beta), but does not improve the condition-number dependence beyond sqrt(kappa).

nodes.name: No prior stochastic method achieves both accelerations
nodes.description: To the authors' knowledge, no existing decentralized stochastic method achieves accelerated sqrt(kappa) and 1/sqrt(1-beta) dependence simultaneously in communication complexity for strongly convex optimization.

nodes.name: Paper proposes MG-ADSGD to close the gap
nodes.description: This paper proposes Multi-Gossip Accelerated DSGD (MG-ADSGD) to close the gap of achieving both accelerated dependences simultaneously in the stochastic decentralized setting.

nodes.name: FGA accelerates consensus via Chebyshev-type recurrence
nodes.description: Fast Gossip Average (FGA) accelerates consensus over a network by performing multiple rounds of weighted neighbor averaging using an accelerated Chebyshev-type recurrence, rather than standard repeated gossip steps.

nodes.name: FGA compresses many consensus steps into few rounds
nodes.description: FGA's accelerated recurrence significantly reduces disagreement among nodes after a fixed number of communication rounds, enabling the network to approximate the global average much faster than plain gossip.

nodes.name: Design idea: invoke FGA twice per outer iteration with tunable depth R
nodes.description: The key design idea of MG-ADSGD is to invoke the FGA operator twice per outer iteration with a tunable gossip depth R controlling the number of internal communication rounds.

nodes.name: Coupling mini-batch size B=R with gossip depth
nodes.description: MG-ADSGD couples the mini-batch size B with the gossip depth R (B=R), so that increasing R simultaneously improves communication accuracy and reduces gradient variance.

nodes.name: Three-sequence accelerated structure (X,Y,Z)
nodes.description: MG-ADSGD adopts a three-sequence accelerated structure where Y is the extrapolated query point for gradient evaluation, Z is an auxiliary descent variable, and X is the primal iterate, reminiscent of Nesterov-type accelerated schemes.

nodes.name: Consensus enforced via FGA on both Z- and X-updates
nodes.description: Unlike single-mixing-step designs, MG-ADSGD applies the accelerated FGA_R primitive to both the Z-update and the X-update, reflecting the principle that optimization error and consensus error must be controlled simultaneously.

nodes.name: Shared R couples statistical and communication accuracy
nodes.description: Using the same parameter R for both mini-batch size and gossip rounds deliberately couples statistical and communication accuracy: increasing R reduces gradient variance through averaging while also improving consensus through deeper accelerated mixing.

nodes.name: MG-ADSGD jointly balances three mechanisms
nodes.description: As a result of the coupled design (accelerated optimization dynamics, accelerated consensus, coupled batch/gossip size), MG-ADSGD jointly balances optimization acceleration, consensus acceleration, and stochastic variance reduction.

nodes.name: Communication budget T=KR
nodes.description: Since each outer iteration requires R communication rounds, the total communication budget after K outer iterations is T=KR, which serves as the complexity measure in the analysis.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.1: MG-ADSGD communication complexity bound
nodes.description: Theorem 5.1 establishes that, under standard smoothness, strong convexity, unbiased bounded-variance gradient, and gossip-matrix assumptions, MG-ADSGD's total gossip rounds needed to reach accuracy epsilon is order (sigma^2/(mu*n*epsilon))*log(L*Delta_x/epsilon) + sqrt((L/mu)/(1-beta))*log(L*Delta_x/epsilon).

nodes.name: Bound achieves both accelerated dependences simultaneously
nodes.description: The bound in Theorem 5.1 matches the canonical stochastic term sigma^2/(mu*n*epsilon) and the accelerated network term sqrt((L/mu)/(1-beta)), giving the best currently available communication complexity by simultaneously achieving accelerated sqrt(kappa) and accelerated 1/sqrt(1-beta) dependence.

nodes.name: Noise-free case recovers deterministic accelerated rate
nodes.description: When the stochastic noise vanishes (sigma^2=0), Theorem 5.1's bound simplifies to the deterministic accelerated communication rate, recovering (up to logarithmic factors) the optimal complexity established by prior deterministic work (MSDA).

nodes.name: Recovery of deterministic rate confirms tightness
nodes.description: Because the bound reduces exactly to the known optimal deterministic rate in the noise-free limit, this confirms the bound is tight in this sense and validates the overall communication complexity claim.

nodes.name: Modest additional cost in gradient computation complexity
nodes.description: The improved communication complexity comes at the cost of only a modest additional log(1/epsilon) factor in stochastic-gradient complexity over the optimal centralized stochastic rate, which is typically acceptable since communication is the primary bottleneck.

nodes.name: MSDA established tight deterministic lower bound
nodes.description: The MSDA work established a tight lower bound of order sqrt(kappa/(1-beta))*log(1/epsilon) for smooth and strongly convex deterministic decentralized optimization and proposed the Multi-Step Dual Accelerated method to attain it.

nodes.name: APM achieves optimal rate with single consensus step
nodes.description: Subsequent work introduced APM, which achieves the same optimal deterministic rate using only a single consensus step per iteration through an increasing penalty schedule, seeking simpler designs than MSDA.

nodes.name: Existing stochastic algorithms remain worse than deterministic counterparts
nodes.description: Despite advances like D-MASG and LMT, the communication complexity of existing stochastic decentralized algorithms remains worse than that of their deterministic counterparts.

nodes.name: This work targets matching deterministic complexity stochastically
nodes.description: Motivated by the persistent gap between stochastic and deterministic decentralized communication complexity, this work aims to design an algorithm achieving the same communication complexity as deterministic counterparts in the strongly-convex stochastic setting.

isolated_nodes.name: Decentralized architecture avoids single-point bottleneck
isolated_nodes.description: Decentralized optimization eliminates the single-point communication bottleneck, improves robustness to node failures, and naturally accommodates edge-generated and edge-stored data.

isolated_nodes.name: Steady-state bias from data heterogeneity
isolated_nodes.description: A common drawback of foundational decentralized methods (DGD, diffusion, dual averaging) is a steady-state bias arising from data heterogeneity across agents.

isolated_nodes.name: Bias-corrected exact convergence methods
isolated_nodes.description: To overcome steady-state bias, a rich line of work developed bias-corrected and exactly convergent algorithms, including ADMM-based primal-dual methods, explicit correction methods, and gradient-tracking approaches.

isolated_nodes.name: Decentralized SGD achieves linear speedup
isolated_nodes.description: Seminal prior work showed that decentralized SGD achieves linear speedup with respect to the number of workers.

isolated_nodes.name: Unified framework for time-varying topologies
isolated_nodes.description: Subsequent work developed a unified analytical framework for decentralized methods over time-varying communication topologies.

isolated_nodes.name: Data heterogeneity exacerbates sparse-network effects
isolated_nodes.description: More recent works demonstrated that data heterogeneity can significantly exacerbate the detrimental effect of sparse network connectivity in decentralized SGD, leading to inferior communication complexity, motivating correction and variance-reduction mechanisms.

isolated_nodes.name: Problem setup: distributed empirical objective
isolated_nodes.description: The paper considers minimizing the average of n local objectives f_i, each defined as an expectation over a local data distribution, with each node accessing only its local objective, stochastic gradient oracle, and neighbor messages.

isolated_nodes.name: Standard assumptions: smoothness, strong convexity, bounded variance, doubly stochastic mixing matrix
isolated_nodes.description: The analysis relies on four standard assumptions: L-smoothness and mu-strong convexity of each local objective, unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded variance sigma^2, and a symmetric doubly stochastic communication matrix with spectral parameter beta.

structural_reasoning: The graph is coherent across its major clusters: the motivational gap between deterministic and stochastic decentralized acceleration that directly motivates MG-ADSGD (C1), the fast-gossip-averaging primitive and its coupling design (C2), the detailed three-sequence algorithmic mechanism (C3), the main convergence theorem and its consequences including tightness and cost trade-offs (C4), and the related-work lineage of accelerated deterministic methods that frames the paper's targeted improvement (C5). Edge confidence is high throughout because the paper's introduction and algorithm sections explicitly state each design choice's motivation and each theorem's implications in a clear expository chain. The isolated-node set captures background context (decentralized optimization history, bias-correction methods, problem formalization, and standard assumptions) that supports but is not part of the central argument connecting the acceleration gap to the paper's proposed algorithm and its proven guarantees. No cycles or contested edge directions were identified in this construction.

notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the DecomposeRL example graph. This source document was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Core position statement and its five concrete disclosure requirements.

nodes.name: MI increasingly uses causal vocabulary
nodes.description: Mechanistic interpretability papers increasingly use causal vocabulary: circuits, mediators, causal abstraction, monosemanticity.

nodes.name: Causal claims require identification assumptions
nodes.description: Such causal claims require explicit identification assumptions to be meaningful.

nodes.name: Position: MI must disclose identification assumptions
nodes.description: Mechanistic interpretability research using causal language must disclose identification assumptions: state whether a claim is causal, name the identification strategy, enumerate assumptions, stress at least one, and explain how conclusions shift if assumptions fail.

nodes.name: Validation is not identification
nodes.description: Validation metrics report what the data show under assumed conditions, while identification assumptions are the conditions under which a causal claim follows; the two are not interchangeable.

components.description: Motivating case sequence: a recurring pattern of undisclosed assumptions followed by downstream diagnosis, across multiple prior works.

nodes.name: Wang et al. circuit claim without stated assumptions
nodes.description: Wang et al. [2023] identified a GPT-2 circuit for indirect object identification using activation patching but did not state the assumptions under which the circuit claim was identified.

nodes.name: Makelov et al. diagnose a failure mode a year later
nodes.description: Makelov et al. [2024] diagnosed a failure mode showing naive subspace patching can produce interpretability illusions where the patched direction is not the direction the behavior actually depends on.

nodes.name: Makelov et al. don't generalize the diagnosis into a protocol
nodes.description: Makelov et al.'s paper is careful and self-aware but does not generalize its diagnosis into a field-wide assumption-disclosure protocol applicable before failure shows up downstream.

nodes.name: Leask et al. produce an analogous SAE correction
nodes.description: Leask et al. [2025] showed approximately one-third of features in a larger SAE are absent from a smaller one trained on the same data, directly pressuring the dictionary-basis-recoverability assumption monosemanticity work relied on without stating.

nodes.name: Canby et al. surface undeclared probing assumptions
nodes.description: Canby et al. [2024] formalized completeness and selectivity for causal probing as competing desiderata, surfacing assumptions the underlying probing literature had not declared.

nodes.name: Field absorbs corrections as hazards, not as a disclosure lesson
nodes.description: This sequence recurs: causal vocabulary is adopted enthusiastically, assumptions are left implicit, downstream work diagnoses a specific identification failure, and the field absorbs the correction as a methodological hazard rather than evidence that disclosure should have come first.

edges.note: cross-component link into C1: recurring pattern motivates the position

components.description: Validation-metric-substitution phenomenon and empirical demonstration that it can mask failed identification.

nodes.name: Validation-metric substitution defined
nodes.description: The repeated audit finding is 'validation metric substitution': faithfulness, completeness, monosemanticity, behavioral alignment, or alignment-search accuracy are reported in support of causal claims without a separate statement of the identification assumptions those claims require.

nodes.name: Consistency does not establish causal attribution
nodes.description: A faithful, complete, monosemantic, or behaviorally aligned description is consistent with the model and with itself, but consistency does not establish that the proposed mechanism is the cause rather than a correlate.

nodes.name: High validation scores can coexist with failed identification
nodes.description: Makelov et al. [2024] and Canby et al. [2024] demonstrate empirically that high validation scores can co-exist with failed identification.

components.description: Econometrics precedent: why the paper borrows the disclosure norm rather than a specific causal framework.

nodes.name: Econometrics institutionalized assumption-based evaluation
nodes.description: Econometrics did not eliminate identification disputes; it institutionalized the norm that causal claims are evaluated through stated assumptions.

nodes.name: Meta-practice imported, not a specific framework
nodes.description: The paper imports the meta-practice of stating identification assumptions and offering falsifiability/sensitivity tests, not any specific causal framework (instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, etc.).

nodes.name: Two frameworks converge on assumption disclosure
nodes.description: The potential-outcomes framework (SUTVA, unconfoundedness) and the DAG framework (causal graph, Markov/d-separation assumptions) differ in technical detail but converge on the same meta-practice: explicit assumption disclosure as a prerequisite for any causal claim.

nodes.name: Assumption disclosure is a logical requirement, not just convention
nodes.description: This convergence is not merely disciplinary convention; it is a logical requirement because a causal claim has no meaning without specifying the conditions under which the causal quantity is identified.

nodes.name: MI methods have direct assumption parallels
nodes.description: For LLM interpretability the parallel is direct: activation patching assumes interventions isolate causal pathways, SAEs assume learned features correspond to the true representational basis, causal abstraction assumes distributed representations align with higher-level causal structures, and probing assumes localized causal interventions are possible.

nodes.name: MI literature almost never states these assumptions
nodes.description: These are identification assumptions that must hold for causal claims to follow, yet the LLM interpretability literature almost never states them.

components.description: Enumeration of strand-specific identification assumptions and their observed non-disclosure.

nodes.name: Activation patching assumptions: completeness, exclusivity, sufficiency
nodes.description: Activation patching's identification assumptions are circuit completeness (targeted components account for all causal pathways), pathway exclusivity (patching doesn't activate dormant parallel circuits), and metric sufficiency (the behavioral metric reflects the causal property of interest).

nodes.name: SAE assumptions: basis recoverability, atomicity, monosemanticity, completeness
nodes.description: Sparse autoencoders' assumptions are dictionary basis recoverability, feature atomicity, monosemanticity, and feature completeness.

nodes.name: Causal abstraction assumptions: alignment faithfulness, optimization validity
nodes.description: Causal abstraction's assumptions are alignment faithfulness (structural correspondence preserved under intervention) and optimization validity (gradient search finds genuine alignments, not artifacts).

nodes.name: Probing assumptions: causal locality, intervention completeness, behavioral sufficiency
nodes.description: Probing's assumptions are causal locality, intervention completeness (ablation removes the full representational content of the target concept), and behavioral sufficiency.

nodes.name: None of these assumptions formally stated in the reviewed works
nodes.description: Across the reviewed activation-patching, SAE, causal-abstraction, and probing papers (Wang et al., Makelov et al., Bricken et al., Templeton et al., Wu/Geiger et al., Geiger et al., Huang et al., Canby et al.), none of these assumptions were formally/numerically stated.

components.description: Audit design (n=10): sample, coding dimensions, and the Dim A coding-rule sensitivity check.

nodes.name: n=10 purposive sample across four strands
nodes.description: The audit covers ten papers spanning four methodological strands (circuit discovery, SAEs, causal abstraction, probing) across NeurIPS, ICLR, CLeaR, BlackboxNLP, and the Anthropic Transformer Circuits Thread, purposively rather than randomly selected.

nodes.name: Purposive sampling limits prevalence claims but supports the position
nodes.description: The audit is meant to support the position rather than estimate prevalence in the broader MI literature; the position depends on the conceptual point, not prevalence statistics, but the audit shows the gap is widespread enough across major venues/strands to warrant a community standard.

nodes.name: Four coding dimensions defined
nodes.description: Each paper is coded on Dim A (abstract claim type: causal w/ID, causal w/o ID, implicit causal, association only), Dim B (main-text identification-assumptions statement: dedicated section, partial, none), Dim C (falsifiability: yes/partial/no), and Dim D (validation-metric substitution: yes/partial/no).

nodes.name: Single-coder audit; no inter-rater stats reported for n=10
nodes.description: The n=10 audit is transparent but single-coder, so Cohen's κ and other inter-rater statistics are not reported for it, since computing κ from a single coder would be unsound.

nodes.name: Dim A hardest call has a uniform decision rule
nodes.description: The hardest coding call — whether 'causal interventions'/'causal model' language constitutes a causal claim or a method label — is resolved with a uniform decision rule distinguishing method labels, unsupported causal claims, causal claims with named ID strategy, and non-causal language.

nodes.name: Permissive re-coding doesn't change the main argument
nodes.description: Under a more permissive Dim A rule, three III-coded papers could be re-coded II, but this doesn't affect the main argument since II papers also fail the disclosure protocol and no paper reaches I under either rule.

components.description: Audit results (n=10): aggregate findings and concentration of validation-metric substitution.

nodes.name: 0/10 dedicated identification-assumptions sections
nodes.description: Aggregate Dim B results: 0/10 papers contain a dedicated Identification Assumptions section, 6/10 partial discussion, 4/10 no explicit statement.

nodes.name: Majority implicit causal claims, none fully disclosed
nodes.description: Aggregate Dim A results: 0/10 explicit causal with ID basis, 2/10 explicit without, 8/10 implicit, 0/10 association-only.

nodes.name: No paper has a falsifiability test
nodes.description: Aggregate Dim C results: 0/10 falsifiability test, 3/10 partial sensitivity, 7/10 no falsifiability evidence.

nodes.name: 8/10 fully or partially substitute validation for identification
nodes.description: Aggregate Dim D results: 5/10 fully substitute a validation metric for causal support (Yes), 3/10 partially (discuss with caveats but don't separate), 2/10 clearly separate validation from identification (No).

nodes.name: The 2 clean-separation papers are exactly the failure-mode papers
nodes.description: The two papers that cleanly separate validation from identification are Makelov et al. [2024] and Canby et al. [2024], both of whose primary contribution is to demonstrate failure modes of the validation criteria.

nodes.name: Separation only arises when it is itself the research question
nodes.description: This concentration supports reading identification-validation separation as not a baseline practice, but something that arises only when separation itself is the research question.

components.description: Anchor cases from the n=10 audit illustrating the pattern concretely: Makelov et al. and Leask et al.

nodes.name: Makelov et al.: orthogonal direction produces same effect
nodes.description: Patching what appeared to be the correct direction for a known feature produced the expected behavioral change, but activating an orthogonal direction in the same subspace produced the same change, showing the effect was not uniquely attributable to the feature direction.

nodes.name: Even Makelov et al. doesn't formally enumerate its assumptions
nodes.description: Even Makelov et al., the most methodologically self-aware paper in the sample, does not formally enumerate the assumptions underlying its own critique; the assumptions are described rather than declared.

nodes.name: Leask et al.: stitching experiments challenge basis recoverability
nodes.description: Leask et al. [2025] ran stitching experiments showing ~1/3 of larger-SAE features are absent from smaller SAEs, directly challenging dictionary basis recoverability.

nodes.name: Leask et al.: meta-SAE experiments challenge feature atomicity
nodes.description: Leask et al.'s meta-SAE experiments showed larger-SAE features decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE features, challenging feature atomicity.

nodes.name: Unstated SAE assumptions could not be anticipated or hedged
nodes.description: Both findings invalidate assumptions that the audited SAE papers never stated, so those papers could not anticipate or hedge against these failure modes.

edges.note: cross-component link from C2: elaborates the Makelov failure-mode finding
cross-component link from C2: elaborates Leask finding
cross-component link into C6: even the best paper's implicit assumptions motivate systematic single-coder auditing

components.description: n=30 two-human-coder audit: design, inter-rater reliability, and robustness relative to n=10.

nodes.name: n=30 audit designed to probe robustness of n=10
nodes.description: To probe robustness of the n=10 single-coder audit and estimate inter-coder agreement, a two-human-coder audit was conducted on n=30 MI papers spanning the four strands plus circuit-discovery scaling work, from additional venues.

nodes.name: Two independent coders, abstract-layer information only
nodes.description: Two independent bilingual coders coded the n=30 records from title, abstract, strand, venue, and year using the same rubric, without seeing each other's labels or the n=10 codings; this suits auditing the most visible reporting layer but is not full-text recoding.

nodes.name: Agreement moderate on A/C, lower on B/D
nodes.description: Inter-rater agreement (κ) is moderate on Dim A (0.56) and Dim C (0.52) but lower on Dim B (0.26) and Dim D (0.43).

nodes.name: Low Dim B agreement itself supports the disclosure recommendation
