nodes.description: Coders disagreed on whether informal limitation language counts as partial assumption disclosure; this ambiguity strengthens rather than weakens the disclosure recommendation, since current papers do not provide stable, easily identifiable assumption statements.

nodes.name: 0/30 dedicated identification sections under any rule or coder
nodes.description: On Dim B, no paper is coded I (dedicated identification-assumptions section) under either the strict or permissive rule, by either coder — 0/30.

nodes.name: Dim D count is coding-rule sensitive: 19/30 strict vs 26/30 permissive
nodes.description: Disagreements on Dim D were resolved with two rules: a strict rule yields Dim D=Yes on 19/30 papers, a permissive rule yields 26/30; this count should be read as a moderate-confidence structural pattern, not a precise prevalence estimate.

nodes.name: n=30 reproduces direction of n=10 findings and reveals strand heterogeneity
nodes.description: The n=30 audit reproduces the direction of all n=10 findings and surfaces strand heterogeneity the n=10 obscured: SAE and causal-abstraction strands show stronger substitution than activation patching, where the illusion-and-failure-modes literature has a partial protective effect.

edges.note: cross-component link from C8: activation patching's partial protection linked to illusion-literature within that strand

components.description: Further sensitivity checks: single-rater n=20 human audit and second human-coder re-coding.

nodes.name: n=20 single-rater human audit reproduces the headline result
nodes.description: A stratified n=20 single-rater human audit (Dim B + Dim D, abstracts only) finds Dim B=I: 0/20 and Dim D=Yes: 16/20, reproducing the 0-dedicated-section finding exactly and the substitution direction.

nodes.name: Author-vs-strict-adjudication agreement moderate
nodes.description: Agreement between the author's n=20 ratings and strict adjudication is 80% on Dim B and 65% on Dim D.

nodes.name: Second human-coder re-coding is more conservative on Dim D
nodes.description: A second human-coder re-coding of Dim B/D on the n=20 sample shows 80% agreement (κ=0.49) on Dim B and 70% agreement (κ=0.46) on Dim D, with the second coder more conservative (some Dim D labels move from Yes to Partial).

nodes.name: Second coder differs more on n=30 records
nodes.description: On the n=30 records, the second coder differs more from the existing strict adjudication (κ=0.08 on Dim B, κ=0.25 on Dim D), using Partial much more often.

nodes.name: 0/N structural finding survives all sensitivity checks; exact substitution count is only moderate-confidence
nodes.description: The low Dim B κ (0.26) means the precise 19-26/30 Dim D count is better read as a moderate-confidence point estimate, but the 0/30 structural finding (no dedicated identification sections) is not threatened by this and is reproduced across all human raters.

components.description: The proposed disclosure protocol and its worked example.

nodes.name: Protocol adapts the econometrics norm without prescribing a framework
nodes.description: The protocol adapts the causal-inference convention of opening-section assumption disclosure to MI without prescribing a specific causal framework, requiring only that whatever framework a paper adopts, its core assumptions be stated explicitly.

nodes.name: Five concrete requirements specified
nodes.description: The five requirements are: (1) state in the abstract whether the claim is causal or associational; (2) if causal, name the identification strategy; (3) include a numbered Identification Assumptions section stating what each assumption asserts, why it's plausible, and what evidence supports it; (4) provide a falsifiability test, sensitivity analysis, or counter-evidence statement for each core assumption; (5) discuss substantively how conclusions change if key assumptions fail.

nodes.name: Worked example: Wang et al. under the protocol
nodes.description: Applying the protocol to Wang et al. [2023] would require stating the causal claim under circuit completeness and pathway exclusivity, enumerating and testing these assumptions, addressing the parallel-pathway concern Makelov et al. later raised but Wang et al. never engaged with.

nodes.name: Recommendation to incorporate protocol into venue checklists
nodes.description: The recommendation to NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, and comparable venues is to incorporate the protocol into existing submission checklists.

edges.note: cross-component link from C10: robust audit finding motivates the venue recommendation

components.description: Validation-metric-vs-identification-gap table logic: why specific metrics fail to test specific assumptions.

nodes.name: Reporting validation metrics is necessary but not sufficient
nodes.description: Reporting metrics like patch effect, steering behavior change, alignment score, or ablation effect is necessary but not sufficient for the causal claims the corresponding methods are typically used to support.

nodes.name: Patch effect doesn't test pathway exclusivity/completeness
nodes.description: A measurable patch effect can flow through dormant or parallel pathways, so patch-effect/logit-difference metrics do not test pathway exclusivity or circuit completeness.

nodes.name: Steering doesn't test canonical basis/atomicity
nodes.description: SAE steering shows a feature is causally relevant, but not that the basis is canonical or that features are atomic.

nodes.name: Alignment score doesn't test optimization validity/faithfulness
nodes.description: High interchange-intervention-accuracy (IIA)/alignment score can reflect spurious alignments learned by the optimizer rather than a faithful abstraction.

nodes.name: Ablation effect doesn't test causal locality/completeness
nodes.description: A null ablation effect can reflect distributed representation rather than absence of the underlying structure, so ablation effect does not test causal locality or intervention completeness.

components.description: Anticipated objections and the paper's responses.

nodes.name: Objection: MI is engineering, not causal science
nodes.description: One view is that MI is engineering rather than causal science, so causal-claim disclosure requirements shouldn't apply broadly.

nodes.name: Response: protocol only applies to causal-vocabulary papers
nodes.description: The protocol applies only when papers use causal vocabulary; non-causal papers can avoid the requirement by framing claims descriptively.

nodes.name: Objection: formal disclosure is premature
nodes.description: A second view is that formal assumption disclosure is premature for the field.

nodes.name: Response: protocol only asks authors to state assumptions their methods already require
nodes.description: The response is that the protocol does not impose econometric estimators or a single causal framework; it asks authors to state the assumptions their own interventions already require.

nodes.name: Objection: boilerplate sections could become performative
nodes.description: A third view is that mandated identification-assumptions sections could become performative boilerplate rather than substantive.

nodes.name: Response: reviewer guidance plus templates distinguish substance from checklist
nodes.description: The response is that reviewer guidance should distinguish substantive assumptions, falsifiers, and sensitivity statements from perfunctory checklists, and method-specific templates are provided to make the norm concrete.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior evaluation-practice critiques exist but don't target MI identification disclosure specifically
isolated_nodes.description: Schaeffer et al. [2023] showed claimed emergent abilities often vanish under careful evaluation, and Pearl [2009]/Pearl and Mackenzie [2018] established formal foundations arguing causal claims require explicit assumptions, but none of these prior works focused specifically on identification-assumption disclosure in mechanistic interpretability.

isolated_nodes.name: Leask et al. is the only prior work directly testing an unstated MI identification assumption
isolated_nodes.description: Leask et al. [2025] is characterized as the only prior work that directly identifies an unstated identification assumption in interpretability and tests it; this paper's contribution is to make such assumption-checking standard practice rather than a post-hoc discovery.

nodes.name: LLMs excel in English NLU
nodes.description: LLMs pretrained with language modeling on trillions of tokens excel at complex NLU tasks with minimal or no labeled data, predominantly in English.

nodes.name: English-dominant pretraining
nodes.description: Widely used LLMs are predominantly trained on English data, with English text typically comprising more than 80% of their pretraining corpora.

nodes.name: LLM degradation on distant/unseen languages
nodes.description: LLM performance degrades in cross-lingual transfer to languages that are typologically distant from English or virtually unseen at pretraining.

nodes.name: LLM effectiveness restricted to high-resource languages
nodes.description: The cross-lingual performance degradation restricts LLM effectiveness primarily to English and a small subset of high-resource languages, amplifying the cross-lingual technology gap.

nodes.name: MT models are inclusive by design
nodes.description: Publicly available MT models like NLLB and MADLAD-400 are designed for inclusiveness, providing translation between 200+ and 400+ languages respectively.

nodes.name: MT encoders semantically align representations
nodes.description: Unlike LLMs, MT models (specifically MT encoders) are designed to semantically align textual representations in a unified embedding space, as demonstrated by sentence retrieval performance on FLORES 200.

nodes.name: MT encoders lack world/commonsense knowledge
nodes.description: MT models lack various types of knowledge (world knowledge, commonsense knowledge) commonly acquired through large-scale language modeling pretraining.

nodes.name: MT encoders underperform on multilingual NLU
nodes.description: Because they lack LM-acquired knowledge, MT encoders underperform even smaller multilingual encoders like XLM-R on multilingual NLU tasks and cross-lingual transfer.

nodes.name: Proposal: merge MT encoders with LLMs (MT-LLM)
nodes.description: The paper proposes merging MT encoders directly with LLMs into a unified multilingual model (MT-LLM) to combine the LLM's general knowledge with the MT encoder's multilingual representational alignment.

nodes.name: TTRAIN requires LLM support for target language
nodes.description: Translating training data (TTRAIN) yields strong XLT performance but requires LLMs to support the target languages, which does not hold for low-resource languages.

nodes.name: TTEST enables ZS-XLT with monolingual LMs
nodes.description: Translating test data (TTEST) enables zero-shot cross-lingual transfer with monolingual LMs, but incurs additional inference overhead from MT and generally offers performance slightly inferior to TTRAIN.

nodes.name: TTRAIN/TTEST rely on discrete MT decoder output
nodes.description: Both TTRAIN and TTEST align input to accommodate LLM representation-space shortcomings by resorting to discrete natural language translations from the MT decoder.

nodes.name: Discrete translation propagates errors, loses latent info
nodes.description: Because TTRAIN and TTEST rely on discrete MT decoder output, they fail to preserve the rich latent representations from the MT encoder and propagate translation errors to LLMs, reducing downstream performance.

nodes.name: Proposal: align latent MT encoder representations
nodes.description: In contrast to discrete translation-based methods, the paper proposes aligning the latent representations produced by the MT encoder directly to the LLM's representation space via self-distillation, bypassing MT-decoder translation errors.

nodes.name: Latent alignment reduces inference cost vs TTEST
nodes.description: By retaining continuous MT encoder representations and avoiding discretization in the MT decoder, the proposed approach reduces inference time and cost relative to TTEST.

nodes.name: Vertical fusion of MT encoder and LLM
nodes.description: The MT-LLM approach 'vertically' fuses a multilingual MT encoder E and an LLM M by introducing a projection U mapping the MT encoder's output space into the LLM's input embedding space, plus LoRA adapters inserted into the LLM's linear layers.

nodes.name: Frozen base parameters, trainable Θ only
nodes.description: All other parameters of the MT encoder and LLM are frozen; only the new projection and LoRA parameters are trained.

nodes.name: Self-distillation with original LLM as teacher
nodes.description: The new modular parameters are trained using the original (unmodified) LLM as a teacher, guiding the self-supervised training of the stacked MT-LLM.

nodes.name: Stage 1: minimize MSE between pooled outputs
nodes.description: In Stage 1, the sequence embedding from feeding input through the original LLM is compared, via mean-squared error, to the sequence embedding obtained from feeding MT-encoder output embeddings through the LLM (with projection and LoRA), training only the projection and LoRA parameters.

nodes.name: General adaptation less sample-efficient than task-specific
nodes.description: The authors hypothesize that optimizing MT-LLM representation alignment on general-purpose data is less sample-efficient than task-specific alignment.

nodes.name: Task fine-tuning reduces LLM output complexity
nodes.description: Fine-tuning the base LLM with a classification head on labeled task data reduces the complexity of the LLM's output representations to encode only task-specific features.

nodes.name: Reduced complexity facilitates task-specific alignment
nodes.description: Because task fine-tuning reduces the LLM's output representations to task-specific features, this facilitates task-specific representational alignment for the MT-LLM.

nodes.name: Stage 2: continue training LoRA adapters on task alignment
nodes.description: Building on Stage 1's task-agnostic adaptation, Stage 2 continues training only the LoRA adapters to again minimize MSE between the MT-LLM's and fine-tuned LLM's task-specific output representations.

nodes.name: Two-stage alignment extends LLM knowledge access
nodes.description: Both alignment stages together ensure that MT encoder latent translations integrate seamlessly as LLM input representations, extending access to the LLM's embedded knowledge to all languages supported by the MT model.

nodes.name: NLLB-Encoder alone lacks NLU on complex tasks
nodes.description: The NLLB encoder alone shows strong ZS-XLT performance on sentiment classification (NusaX) but performs worse on NLI and degrades on the more intricate Belebele MRC task.

nodes.name: NLLB-LLM2Vec outperforms both components
nodes.description: The integrated NLLB-LLM2Vec variants substantially outperform both standalone LLM2Vec and the standalone NLLB encoder on all NLU tasks, with Belebele gains of 12% and 30% respectively.

nodes.name: S1+FT already competitive with TTEST
nodes.description: Fine-tuning NLLB-LLM2Vec adapted only via task-agnostic Stage 1 (S1+FT) is already competitive with the more computationally involved TTEST baseline.

nodes.name: S1+S2 substantially improves over S1+FT
nodes.description: Adding task-specific distillation (S1+S2) substantially and consistently improves performance over direct fine-tuning (S1+FT), with the largest gains on NusaX (+9.4%), the dataset with the smallest training set.

nodes.name: S1+S2 consistently beats TTEST on same MT model
nodes.description: The full NLLB-LLM2Vec S1+S2 consistently beats TTEST based on the same NLLB 600M model by sizable margins of 3-11%.

nodes.name: S1+S2 matches or beats TTEST with larger MT model
nodes.description: NLLB-LLM2Vec S1+S2 frequently performs on par with or better than TTEST using higher-quality translations from the larger NLLB 3B model, because MT improvements propagate to ZS-XLT via favorable model selection on T-DEV.

nodes.name: LLM2Vec strong English but weak ZS-XLT
nodes.description: Despite strong English performance, the English-centric LLM2Vec model underperforms all other models in ZS-XLT, with even the much smaller NLLB-Encoder outperforming it on NLI and NusaX.

nodes.name: TTEST significantly improves over LLM2Vec ZS-XLT
nodes.description: TTEST significantly improves upon the ZS-XLT performance of LLM2Vec, especially on datasets predominantly featuring lower-resource languages (AmNLI, Kardeş-NLU).

nodes.name: Larger MT model improves TTEST
nodes.description: Consistent with related work, the larger NLLB 3B model improves TTEST performance on all tasks compared to NLLB 600M.

nodes.name: MT-LLM alignment outperforms TTEST and cuts inference cost
nodes.description: The alignment procedure effectively merges NLLB into LLM2Vec to enable ZS-XLT that both outperforms TTEST and reduces inference cost by avoiding MT decoding.

nodes.name: Task-agnostic adaptation is sample-efficient
nodes.description: Stage 1 alignment is highly sample-efficient: the largest relative ZS-XLT gains are obtained after only 3K training steps (e.g., +10.5% for Belebele) and then marginalize with further training.

nodes.name: Adaptation important for both English and ZS-XLT
nodes.description: Task-agnostic adaptation steps are important for both English performance and ZS-XLT performance, with similar trends observed for English gains (e.g., +15% on Belebele from 3K steps).

nodes.name: Negligible computational cost relative to pretraining
nodes.description: Because alignment gains saturate after only a few thousand steps, LLMs and MT encoders can be tied into a unified MT-LLM at computational cost negligible relative to both LLM and MT pretraining.

nodes.name: NusaX ZS-XLT does not improve with prolonged adaptation
nodes.description: On NusaX, prolonged task-agnostic adaptation benefits in-language English performance but does not improve ZS-XLT results, because the NLLB encoder already solves the simpler sentiment task well, requiring little additional LLM knowledge.

nodes.name: GPT-2 lacks EOS token pretraining
nodes.description: Due to the absence of an EOS token in GPT-2's pretraining, task-agnostic self-distillation for NLLB-GPT-2 uses mean-pooled token representations instead.

nodes.name: NLLB-GPT-2 outperforms standalone NLLB and fair TTEST
nodes.description: NLLB-GPT-2 successfully taps into GPT-2's knowledge to outperform both the standalone NLLB encoder and the fair TTEST baseline using the same NLLB-600M model in ZS-XLT across all datasets.

nodes.name: Encoder-to-decoder conversion causes suboptimal alignment
nodes.description: Despite outperforming baselines, NLLB-GPT-2 shows a notable performance gap to fine-tuned GPT-2 on English, likely stemming from challenges in converting encoder representations into a decoder model.

nodes.name: Approach generalizes to decoder-only backbones
nodes.description: The successful (though suboptimal) alignment of NLLB with GPT-2 demonstrates that the self-distillation MT-LLM approach benefits both encoder-only and decoder-only LLM backbones.

isolated_nodes.name: Better generation does not mean better NLU
isolated_nodes.description: Recent work shows that methods improving a model's target-language generation capabilities (continued pretraining, self-instruction, vocabulary extension) do not necessarily translate to stronger NLU performance.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior MT-representation integration was task-specific only
isolated_nodes.description: Few prior studies investigated integrating rich MT representations into language models, but these efforts generally focused on task-specific integration without achieving global representation alignment between the MT encoder and the LLM.

isolated_nodes.name: MT-LLM enables TTRAIN unlike standalone LLM
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike an English-centric standalone LLM, the inherently multilingual MT-LLM can further benefit from training on translated training data (TTRAIN), since it was trained on both MT and denoising autoencoding objectives.

isolated_nodes.name: Evaluation tasks and datasets
isolated_nodes.description: The paper evaluates on three NLU tasks: Natural Language Inference (XNLI, AmericasNLI, Kardeş-NLU), Sentiment Classification (NusaX), and multiple-choice Machine Reading Comprehension (Belebele), covering 127 predominantly low-resource languages.

isolated_nodes.name: LLM2Vec conversion recipe
isolated_nodes.description: LLM2Vec converts decoder-only LLMs into sequence encoders via bidirectional attention, self-supervised masked next-token prediction, and SimCSE training.

isolated_nodes.name: Buginese excluded as outlier
isolated_nodes.description: ZS-XLT performance for Buginese progressively deteriorated with more distillation, an unusual behavior consistent with other reported work using NLLB, leading the authors to exclude it from the main discussion.

isolated_nodes.name: Numerical instability from merging LoRA sets
isolated_nodes.description: Preliminary experiments found that merging the Stage 1 adaptation LoRAs with new fine-tuning LoRA adapters led to numerical instabilities due to quantization, severely degrading task performance, motivating separate continued training of the same LoRA set.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: token-level alignment and MT encoder extension
isolated_nodes.description: Future work directions include incorporating token-level alignment objectives to further improve MT-LLM generalization, and extending the MT-LLM to additional languages via post-hoc adaptation of the MT encoder.

structural_reasoning: The graph is coherent across its major clusters: the motivation contrasting LLM English-centricity with MT multilinguality that drives the MT-LLM proposal (C1), the critique of discrete translation-based baselines motivating latent representation alignment (C2), the two-stage self-distillation methodology (C3, C4), the main NLLB-LLM2Vec results chain (C5), the LLM2Vec-specific comparative results (C6), the sample-efficiency analysis of adaptation (C7), and the decoder-backbone generalization experiment with GPT-2 (C8). Edge confidence is generally high because the paper's argumentative structure directly motivates each design choice with an explicit problem-solution narrative, and the results sections explicitly connect ablation findings to the paper's central claims about sample efficiency and performance gains. The isolated-node set captures supporting details (specific datasets, technical recipes, minor outlier observations, future work) that contextualize but are not tightly chained into the central technical and empirical narrative. No cycles or contested edge directions were identified in this construction.

note_on_evidence: Evidence fields cite paper sections/subsections/tables rather than sentence indices, since a sentence-indexed source was not available for this document.

components.name: Task-conditional learning setup via task embeddings

nodes.name: First task-conditional RL competition
nodes.description: To the organizers' knowledge, this is the first RL competition on task-conditional learning, where submitted agents are given the task to solve at inference time instead of a single fixed objective.

nodes.name: Neural MMO 2.0 task system enables arbitrary conditions
nodes.description: Neural MMO 2.0's new task system allows checking nearly arbitrary conditions on the agent, environment, and other agents, which is what makes task-conditional learning possible for this competition.

nodes.name: Tasks specified as predicate functions
nodes.description: Individual tasks are specified in plain code as predicate functions called with specific arguments.

nodes.name: Tasks embeddable via language model
nodes.description: Because tasks are specified as code, it is possible to embed tasks into a fixed-length vector by feeding their implementation into a language model.

nodes.name: Predicate-based embeddings cluster meaningfully
nodes.description: When encoded with an LLM, different predicates produce distant embeddings, while the same predicate with different arguments produces similar embeddings.

nodes.name: Simple, cheap model input for task-conditional agents
nodes.description: Task embeddings give a simple model input for training task-conditional agents, without requiring a large model to be run during inference (unlike LLM agents); capable models are only millions to low tens of millions of parameters.

nodes.name: Small but significant train/eval task embedding gap
nodes.description: There is a small but significant gap between most training and evaluation task embeddings, with a 22.3% overlap considering only predicates and 2.1% overlap considering both predicate and arguments.

nodes.name: Curriculum needed for hard evaluation tasks
nodes.description: Some evaluation tasks are too hard to solve without a guiding curriculum; e.g., agents perform poorly on training tasks like equipping medium-level items, and training directly on hard evaluation tasks (e.g., equipping high-level items) would not help since prerequisites cannot be completed.

components.name: Baseline architecture and Clean PuffeRL modification

nodes.name: Neural MMO has variable agent count
nodes.description: Neural MMO has a variable number of agents, since agents can die during an episode.

nodes.name: Most RL libraries expect fixed-size observations
nodes.description: Most learning libraries, including CleanRL, expect fixed-size observations, which is incompatible with a variable number of agents.

nodes.name: Zero-padding used to reconcile the mismatch
nodes.description: It is common practice to zero-pad observations to reconcile variable agent counts with fixed-size observation requirements.

nodes.name: Heavy padding occurs late in episodes
nodes.description: Because many agents die near the start of the game, it is common for the last quarter of the game to be 90% padding.

nodes.name: Padding destabilizes learning
nodes.description: Heavy zero-padding destabilizes learning by lowering and randomizing the effective batch size.

nodes.name: Clean PuffeRL introduced to omit padding
nodes.description: Clean PuffeRL, PufferLib's variant of CleanRL's PPO implementation, alters CleanRL's data structures to omit padding.

nodes.name: Padding removal was key usability improvement
nodes.description: Omitting padding via Clean PuffeRL was the key modification that allowed the organizers to improve the usability of their baselines this year.

components.name: Evaluation methodology

nodes.name: Two-stage evaluation design
nodes.description: Evaluation consisted of two stages: PvE (all agents controlled by the same submitted policy) and PvP (top policies loaded together into shared environments).

nodes.name: Strong opponents can suppress PvE-style scores
nodes.description: The PvE evaluation score can be underestimated for a strong policy because each agent is evaluated on its own without cooperative or competitive interaction with distinct opponents.

nodes.name: PvP scores exceed PvE for top policy
nodes.description: The top score in PvE was 17.09%, but rose to 25.21% in PvP, consistent with PvE potentially underestimating strong policies.

nodes.name: PvE used to select candidates for PvP
nodes.description: Based on PvE results, policies performing better than or comparable to the baseline (max 1 per participant) were selected for the PvP evaluation stage.

nodes.name: Lifespan correlates with task completion rank
nodes.description: Across 86 submissions, a correlation of 0.91 (p<0.001) was found between rank by average agent lifespan and rank by tasks completed, used as a sanity check on the evaluation.

components.name: Takeru (co-winner) approach

nodes.name: Baseline training instability observed
nodes.description: The Takeru team observed instability in baseline training, where value loss could become excessively large and policy entropy would collapse to 0 early.

nodes.name: Unscaled continuous item features suspected cause
nodes.description: One possible reason for the observed instability is that the baseline model did not properly scale continuous features for items.

nodes.name: Continuous features scaled to [0,1]
nodes.description: Takeru addressed the suspected scaling issue by scaling all continuous features to the [0,1] range.

nodes.name: Modified baseline significantly outperforms original
nodes.description: The modified baseline model (with feature scaling and other simplifications) significantly outperforms the original baseline model under the same training configuration, and became the basis of Takeru's final solution.

nodes.name: Difficult-task sparse rewards identified as bottleneck
nodes.description: Takeru analyzed that the bottleneck for further improvement lies in sparse rewards for difficult tasks, and therefore did not invest much time in trying alternative model structures (e.g., Transformer or ResNet encoders).

nodes.name: Early-stop agent threshold set to 0
nodes.description: Takeru set the early-stop agent number to 0 (vs. the baseline's 8) after finding the baseline setting caused loss of reward signal for difficult tasks late in the game, which hindered learning those tasks.

nodes.name: Exploration reward found broadly beneficial
nodes.description: Takeru found that the exploration reward, which encourages generating more game events, had a noticeable positive effect on learning across various tasks, partly by assisting agents in acquiring general skills like using gold.

components.name: Yao Feng (co-winner) approach

nodes.name: Goals: expressiveness, exploration ease, generalization
nodes.description: Given the complex environment and restricted training time, Yao Feng's goal was to increase policy expressiveness, decrease exploration difficulty, and help generalization.

nodes.name: Encoder architecture modifications
nodes.description: Yao Feng modified encoders (adding ReLU activations, a ResNet block for tiles, normalized absolute position, removing unused player/item features, shared embeddings across attributes, added MLP and layer norm, LSTM cells for historical information, orthogonal initialization).

nodes.name: Historical information considered important
nodes.description: Because agents can only see a nearby area, taking historical information into account (via added LSTM cells) is considered important.

nodes.name: Restricted action space to reduce exploration difficulty
nodes.description: Yao Feng restricted the action space (disabling giving items/gold and attacking neutral NPCs) specifically to reduce exploration difficulty and avoid agent deaths from attacking NPCs.

nodes.name: Custom reward set replaces baseline's HP/meander/explore rewards
nodes.description: Yao Feng designed a custom reward set (HP, Experience, Defense, Attack, Gold) after finding the baseline's given HP restoration, meander, and explore rewards not very useful.

components.name: Saidinesh Pola approach

nodes.name: Baseline lacked LSTM and inter-agent coordination
nodes.description: Saidinesh Pola identified that the baseline model lacked LSTM layers (hindering use of sequential information) and lacked effective coordination among agents.

nodes.name: Exploration of alternative architectures had stability issues
nodes.description: Experimentation with cross-attention networks, Transformer architectures, ResNet-18/34, and ViT-tiny encountered training stability challenges, such as zero entropy in early training steps.

nodes.name: Final architecture adds multi-head attention, extra conv layer, and 5 LSTM layers
nodes.description: The final submission integrated PyTorch multi-head attention between agent tiles, an additional convolutional layer, five LSTM layers with SiLU activations for temporal dependencies.

nodes.name: Multi-head attention used as inter-agent communication channel
nodes.description: Cross-attention mechanisms were used not only for action decoding but as a communication channel between agents, allowing exchange of task-relevant information for more coordinated decision-making.

components.name: Mori approach and post-hoc metric discovery

nodes.name: Mori optimized TotalScore instead of true metric
nodes.description: Mori initially aimed to optimize TotalScore, before belatedly discovering that CompletedTaskCount was the true evaluation metric.

nodes.name: Late discovery limited impact of corrected design
nodes.description: Because the true-metric realization came near the contest's end, the second-stage reward design informed by it did not affect Mori's final competition results, though it showed promise for TotalScore performance.

nodes.name: Reward mechanisms adapted from prior winner
nodes.description: Mori's Stage One reward mechanisms were adopted and empirically validated from a previous winner's ('realikun') reward design.

nodes.name: Seed choice affects training outcomes
nodes.description: Mori observed that model training outcomes are highly dependent on seed choice, motivating treating seeds as a tunable variable searched via automatic algorithms to boost scores, though this does not enhance underlying model ability.

components.name: Jimyhzhu approach

nodes.name: Baseline weaknesses identified
nodes.description: Jimyhzhu identified baseline weaknesses: lack of pre-processing for categorical data, a continuous-data scaling issue, and lack of global information about other agents.

nodes.name: One-hot encoding used for categorical attributes
nodes.description: One-hot encoding was introduced for categorical attributes to avoid the model assuming a natural ordering between categories.

nodes.name: Continuous data downscaled instead of upscaled
nodes.description: Jimyhzhu replaced the baseline's upscaling of continuous data ([0,100] to [0,10000]) with downscaling to [0,1] for more balanced feature representation.

nodes.name: Average pooling used instead of MLP for market/item embeddings
nodes.description: Average pooling was applied to market and item embeddings instead of an MLP, since the strategic significance of items/players often does not depend on their order of appearance.

nodes.name: Cross-attention in action decoder tested but not adopted
nodes.description: Cross-attention was tested in the action decoder (using the observation as query and specific embeddings as key/value) but showed no major improvement, possibly because the specific embeddings were not rich or diverse enough, so it was not used in the final design.

components.name: Fair evaluation and reproducibility verification

nodes.name: Top-5 submissions retrained from scratch for verification
nodes.description: Source code from the top 5 prize-eligible participants was collected, manually inspected, and retrained from scratch for 8 hours on organizer hardware.

nodes.name: Retraining used more steps than original baseline
nodes.description: The retrained models were trained between 15M and 22M steps (depending on speed), more than the 10M steps used in the original baseline, because faster hardware was available.

nodes.name: Four of five models reproduced original ranking
nodes.description: Four of the top 5 models matched their original ranks and matched or exceeded original training performance upon reproduction.

nodes.name: Mori's model did not fully reproduce due to seed instability
nodes.description: One model (Mori's) did not quite reproduce original performance, but after investigation this was attributed to seed instability rather than manipulation, and the discrepancy was not substantial enough to affect prize awarding.

nodes.name: No cheating found in post-competition investigation
nodes.description: Post-competition investigations, including this reproduction exercise, revealed no instances of cheating among winners.

isolated_nodes.name: Competition attracted 200+ participants
isolated_nodes.description: The NeurIPS 2023 Neural MMO Competition attracted over 200 participants and submissions.

isolated_nodes.name: Top solution scored 4x baseline in 8 hours on one GPU
isolated_nodes.description: The top solution achieved a score 4x higher than the baseline within 8 hours of training on a single 4090 GPU.

isolated_nodes.name: Everything open-sourced under MIT license
isolated_nodes.description: The organizers open-source everything relating to Neural MMO and the competition under the MIT license, including policy weights and training code for the baseline and top submissions.

isolated_nodes.name: Neural MMO 2.0 environment description
isolated_nodes.description: Neural MMO 2.0 simulates 128 agents on procedurally generated maps with terrain, resources, rock-paper-scissors-style combat types, foraging/combat skill leveling, items, and a global agent-to-agent market.

isolated_nodes.name: 1297 training tasks vs 63 evaluation tasks
isolated_nodes.description: The baseline training curriculum has 1297 tasks (including easy 'scaffolding' goals sampled more frequently), while there are only 63 evaluation tasks focused on measuring performance on hard goals.

isolated_nodes.name: Compute and hyperparameter rules
isolated_nodes.description: Participants were capped to 8 A100-hours-equivalent of training compute and 12 CPU cores, with large hyperparameter sweeps disallowed and scrutiny applied to overly precisely tuned hyperparameters.

isolated_nodes.name: Baseline model size and architecture components
isolated_nodes.description: The released baseline is a 3.9 million parameter model (1 million in the task embedding projection layer), using a small CNN subnetwork for terrain, linear layers for agent/item/market embeddings, and pointer networks for target/item selection.

isolated_nodes.name: PvP evaluation protocol details
isolated_nodes.description: In PvP, 9 top policies were each placed in one of 9 groups of 14 agents within a shared 128-agent environment (with 2 agents controlled by an untrained baseline), using 256 held-out maps, 200 episodes per round, and 9 seed rounds (1800 episodes total) to determine winners.

isolated_nodes.name: Top-2 policies tied as co-winners after extended evaluation
isolated_nodes.description: After participants were given a chance to challenge results and extended evaluation was performed, there was enough contention between the top 2 policies that they were declared co-winners.

isolated_nodes.name: Competition preparation and scope reduction
isolated_nodes.description: After 6 months of preparation and 1000+ volunteer hours, 90% of promised compute and devops support was pulled, forcing elimination of the curriculum track and a live rewrite of the evaluation procedure.

isolated_nodes.name: Manual evaluation offered as compensation
isolated_nodes.description: To compensate participants for difficulties from live changes to the evaluation procedure, the organizers manually evaluated checkpoints that failed in automatic evaluation.

structural_reasoning: The graph is coherent within each thematic component. C1 (task embeddings enabling task-conditional learning) and C2 (the padding problem motivating Clean PuffeRL) each form clean causal chains grounded in the paper's own stated reasoning. C3 (evaluation methodology) captures the PvE/PvP relationship and the lifespan sanity check as a small, well-supported set of edges. Components C4-C8, one per winning team, each independently trace that team's own stated diagnosis-to-modification reasoning (e.g., Takeru's training-instability diagnosis leading to feature scaling and reward choices; Yao Feng's stated goals driving architecture and reward changes), which is why they remain separate components rather than being merged: the five teams' design processes are largely independent narratives with no stated cross-team dependencies, aside from Mori explicitly building on a prior winner's reward design (captured within C7). C9 (reproducibility verification) forms a clear chain from retraining methodology to the ranking-reproduction and no-cheating findings. A substantial set of purely descriptive facts (competition scale, environment mechanics, task counts, compute rules, evaluation protocol parameters, and post-hoc organizational remarks) are left as isolated nodes since they are specifications rather than argumentative claims with premise-conclusion links elsewhere in the paper.
