components.description: Defining citation hallucination: a conservative, identity-level notion excluding ordinary bibliographic drift.

nodes.name: Two roles of a citation: social gesture and auditable pointer
nodes.description: A citation is both a social gesture (crediting prior work) and a pointer giving readers enough information to recover the cited artifact from the public record; LLM-assisted authoring can quietly destabilize the pointer role.

nodes.name: Fabrication defined
nodes.description: Fabrication: the cited work does not exist at all — no indexed artifact matches the title, and the listed authors never produced anything matching it.

nodes.name: Author-identity corruption defined
nodes.description: Author-identity corruption: a real paper exists, but the citation assigns it to a substantially different set of authors.

nodes.name: Both are treated as one phenomenon
nodes.description: Fabrication and author-identity corruption are treated as two faces of one phenomenon and both counted, because from a reader's perspective the reference fails to point to the work it claims to credit either way, leaving an unverifiable intellectual debt.

nodes.name: Ordinary bibliographic drift explicitly excluded
nodes.description: Minor name variants, spelling mistakes, and venue/year/publication-status changes (e.g., preprint to proceedings) are not counted as hallucination unless author evidence no longer matches at a substantial level.

nodes.name: Definition intentionally narrow: no claims about truth or authorship
nodes.description: The measure makes no claim about whether the surrounding text was LLM-generated or whether the cited result is true; it asks only whether the bibliography points to a real work by the named authors.

components.description: Positioning relative to related work: closest comparators and how this study differs.

nodes.name: Zhao et al. audits preprints, not camera-ready proceedings
nodes.description: Zhao et al. audit 111M references across 2.5M arXiv/bioRxiv/SSRN/PubMed papers, but their corpus is dominated by preprints rather than camera-ready proceedings.

nodes.name: GhostCite is comparable but less conservative and less structured
nodes.description: GhostCite audits 2.2M citations across 56,381 AI/ML and security-venue papers (2020-2025), finding 1.07% of papers carry an invalid citation and 76.7% of surveyed reviewers report not checking references; it is less conservative in selecting candidates and needs more manual filtering.

nodes.name: This work differs by auditing camera-ready proceedings with more conservative precision
nodes.description: This study differs from Zhao et al. by auditing camera-ready proceedings rather than preprints, and from GhostCite on precision, paper-level structure (affected-paper prevalence, high-count tail), and reported per-paper cost.

nodes.name: Prior controlled-prompting studies characterize models in isolation
nodes.description: Studies like Naser (11.4-56.8% hallucination rates across models/domains under direct prompting) characterize models in isolation, whereas this work measures what survives peer review into the archival record.

nodes.name: Convergence of independent measurements supports the phenomenon's reality
nodes.description: Reading the convergence of this and other independent, concurrent measurements (Zhao et al., GhostCite, Ansari, Sakai et al., GPTZero disclosures) is taken as evidence that the citation-hallucination phenomenon is real and growing.

components.description: RefChecker pipeline architecture: extraction, multi-source verification, and escalation logic.

nodes.name: Corpus restricted to venue/platform-controlled camera-ready PDFs
nodes.description: The corpus includes only accepted papers whose camera-ready PDFs are openly accessible via OpenReview or official proceedings pages, excluding author-hosted substitutes, to ensure every analyzed manuscript is tied to a controlled publication record.

nodes.name: References extracted and normalized from multiple input formats
nodes.description: RefChecker extracts bibliographies from PDFs (primary input here), parsing fields (title, authors, year, venue, DOI, arXiv ID, URL) using LLM-assisted parsing (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) or GROBID fallback, preserving the original string for auditability, then normalizing fields to absorb harmless formatting variation.

nodes.name: Multi-source verification needed due to variable coverage/quality
nodes.description: Each normalized reference is checked against multiple bibliographic sources (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, CrossRef, DBLP, ACL Anthology) because coverage and metadata quality vary significantly across venues, years, and publication types; disagreements are preserved rather than treating one source as absolute ground truth.

nodes.name: Deterministic filters trigger escalation to deep web search
nodes.description: A reference is escalated when unverifiable, when author overlap falls below a 60% default threshold (for 3+ author references), when a DOI/arXiv ID resolves to a different work, or when a cited URL fails/misdirects; minor year/venue variation alone does not trigger escalation.

nodes.name: Escalated references undergo constrained LLM web search plus re-verification
nodes.description: Escalated references are sent to an LLM with web-search capability, constrained to find a dedicated source page (not merely another paper repeating the citation); if found, RefChecker re-verifies cited metadata against that source before clearing or retaining suspicion.

nodes.name: LLMs used as evidence-gathering escalation step, not sole authority
nodes.description: LLMs help parse noisy bibliographies and perform targeted searches, but the final decision is constrained by external evidence (database matches, identifiers, discovered pages, re-verified metadata); this design reduces but does not eliminate model risk (missing obscure sources, over-trusting low-quality pages).

nodes.name: Only LIKELY verdicts surviving re-verification count as hallucinated
nodes.description: Of the three-layer label system (final status, issue value, hallucination verdict), only references with a positive hallucination outcome after re-verification (LIKELY, surviving metadata re-check) are counted in the aggregate hallucination measurements; errors, warnings, suggestions, and unverified cases inform triage but are not automatically counted.

edges.note: cross-component link from C1: the checkability property is what makes this pipeline design possible

components.description: The core denominator argument: sub-1% reference-level rates translate to high paper-level prevalence at proceedings scale.

nodes.name: Reference-level rate is small in essentially every venue-year
nodes.description: Across the 48,095-paper, 2,614,992-reference corpus, the reference-level likely-hallucinated rate stays below 1% in essentially every venue-year (e.g., 2025: 0.38% ICLR, 0.54% ICML, 0.68% NeurIPS, 0.81% USENIX Security on all references).

nodes.name: A conference is not a single bibliography
nodes.description: A sub-1% rate sounds negligible for one bibliography, but a full proceedings contains thousands of papers and hundreds of thousands of references (e.g., ICLR 2025: 221,281 references across 3,703 papers), so even a small rate reaches a large absolute number of flagged references and distinct papers (835 flagged references, 692 papers for ICLR 2025 alone).

nodes.name: Paper-level prevalence is large: roughly 1-in-4 to 1-in-3 for at least one flag
nodes.description: At the paper level, at least one likely hallucinated reference appears in 18.7% of ICLR 2025, 23.3% of ICML 2025, 26.2% of NeurIPS 2025, and 34.9% of USENIX Security 2025 accepted papers.

nodes.name: Raising the threshold to two doesn't flatten the signal
nodes.description: Requiring at least two academic-paper-like likely hallucinated references (a more conservative, false-positive-resistant threshold) still yields 1.9% (ICLR), 3.4% (ICML), 5.1% (NeurIPS), and 4.8% (USENIX Security) for 2025 — roughly one in twenty accepted papers at NeurIPS/USENIX Security.

nodes.name: Post-ChatGPT rise visible at the two-threshold level but not the raw reference level
nodes.description: The post-ChatGPT trend does not show clearly at the raw reference-level rate (where false-positive noise dominates), but sharpens once focus shifts to papers with several likely hallucinated references, which are far less likely to be false positives.

components.description: Distribution shape: most affected papers have one bad pointer, but a long tail concentrates risk and confidence.

nodes.name: Most affected papers carry just one flagged reference
nodes.description: Among affected papers in 2025, exactly one likely hallucinated reference accounts for 87% (ICLR), 81% (ICML), 74% (NeurIPS), and 65% (USENIX Security), arguing against framing affected papers as generally compromised manuscripts.

nodes.name: A visible high-count tail exists nonetheless
nodes.description: Despite the single-reference majority, a visible tail of papers carries 5+ hallucinated citations in a single bibliography, with USENIX Security 2025 showing 34.6% of affected papers with ≥2 and 2.0% with ≥5, and NeurIPS 2025 showing 1,545 affected papers, 407 with ≥2, and 30 with ≥5.

nodes.name: Higher counts per paper increase confidence the flags are genuine
nodes.description: The more failures a single bibliography accumulates, the less plausible it is that every one is a false positive, so 5+-reference papers are the cases the authors can most safely call genuine.

nodes.name: The tail is rare by paper-rate but not by reference-count
nodes.description: Papers with 5+ flagged references are rare on a paper-rate basis (≤1%, often zero pre-2022) but contribute a disproportionate share of all flagged references (e.g., 11.7% at USENIX Security 2024, 9.6% at NeurIPS 2025), so even a tail-only check would intercept a non-trivial fraction of hallucinated citations.

nodes.name: Per-paper maxima reach double digits
nodes.description: The single-paper maximum observed is 20 (NeurIPS), 13 (ICML and USENIX Security), and 8 (ICLR) — a bibliography with 20 likely hallucinated references is not a borderline case.

components.description: Ruling out ordinary bibliographic drift as the explanation for the observed rates.

nodes.name: Natural objection: maybe this is just citation noise, not hallucination
nodes.description: A natural objection is that the measured rates reflect ordinary bibliographic drift (e.g., an arXiv year instead of venue year, a transliterated name, an outdated URL) rather than genuine hallucination.

nodes.name: Failures decompose into identity-level buckets, not drift categories
nodes.description: Across every venue family, likely hallucinated references decompose into three identity-level failure buckets — unresolved references, multi-field failures, and substantial author-list mismatches — with ordinary venue/year/publication-status drift logged separately and never entering any rate.

edges.note: cross-component link from C2: definition already excludes drift, and the measurement confirms this in practice

components.description: Peer review does not catch hallucinated citations: rating, tier, and area analyses all show no relationship.

nodes.name: Mean reviewer rating is nearly identical for clean vs. affected papers
nodes.description: Joining hallucination counts to mean reviewer rating for the OpenReview-covered subset (22,764 papers) shows the difference between clean (0 hallucinated refs) and affected (≥1) papers is almost negligible: Δ=+0.02 ICLR, +0.005 ICML, +0.04 NeurIPS — if anything affected papers rate marginally higher.

nodes.name: Acceptance tier is uncorrelated with hallucination prevalence
nodes.description: Slicing by acceptance tier instead of rating shows posters affected at 20.4%, spotlights at 23.5%, orals at 20.3% — acceptance into the most selective tier does not lower hallucinated-citation prevalence.

nodes.name: Every research area is affected within a narrow band
nodes.description: Across 14 research areas with ≥100 papers, affected-paper prevalence sits in a narrow 15.5%-25.7% band; the problem cannot be reduced to a particular community's authoring practices, though LLM/foundation-model researchers appear slightly less prone (16.1%), possibly from more careful reference checking.

nodes.name: Accepted and rejected ICLR 2023 papers show nearly identical hallucination rates despite a 2-point rating gap
nodes.description: Accepted ICLR 2023 papers (mean rating 6.61) are affected 16.0% of the time; rejected papers (mean rating 4.67, nearly two points lower) are affected 16.9% of the time — a negligible integrity gap despite a large assessment gap.

nodes.name: Hallucination rate reflects authoring practice, not paper quality
nodes.description: Because a paper judged much weaker by reviewers is not, in expectation, much more likely to carry hallucinated citations, the hallucinated-citation rate is driven by authoring practice rather than overall paper quality.

nodes.name: Reviewers' rating signal is orthogonal to bibliographic integrity
nodes.description: Together, these results show reviewers' rating signal carries essentially no information about whether a paper's bibliography survives verification — the signal exists in the published record but is invisible to the process deciding what gets published.

nodes.name: Governance policies (desk rejection) respond to exactly this gap
nodes.description: Recent ICLR 2026 and ICML 2026 policies explicitly listing hallucinated references as desk-rejection grounds are responding to precisely this invisibility of the signal to ordinary review.

components.description: Manual adjudication of true and false positives, revealing the genuine difficulty of the boundary.

nodes.name: An automated flag is a starting point, not a verdict
nodes.description: The single most consistent lesson from the audit is that manual inspection is needed: across manually verified references, most flags were not hallucinations but mangled author strings, truncated titles, or PDF-extraction corruption.

nodes.name: True positives share a sharp identity-failure property
nodes.description: The flags that survived scrutiny shared a sharper property: no corresponding work could be found, or a real title was bound to an unrelated authorship record — illustrated by cases where no source anywhere matches a well-formed cited title/authors, and where a real title (e.g., 'Compressive Transformers...') is bound to a wrong author list.

nodes.name: False positives arise from editor-as-coauthor, parsing artifacts, and title collisions
nodes.description: Documented false-positive patterns include an editor's name miscounted as a coauthor, a title fragment parsed as part of the author field (e.g., 'Jimmy Ba Adam'), and two genuinely distinct real papers sharing an identical title where the tool matched the wrong one.

nodes.name: Author-list-mismatch thresholds are inherently fragile
nodes.description: Deciding how much author-list divergence counts as fabrication is hard: on a two-author reference a single wrong name already crosses a 'half the names' cutoff, yet one wrong name is exactly what an ordinary copy-paste slip produces; the kind of difference (transposition vs. genuinely different person) matters as much as its size.

nodes.name: Metadata alone can't reliably separate error from fabrication
nodes.description: At this resolution, metadata alone almost never separates an erroneous copy-paste from deliberate or machine-generated fabrication, so the tool's output remains a set of candidates requiring human verification and final decision.

edges.note: cross-component link from C4: candidates flagged by the pipeline are what gets manually adjudicated here

components.description: Author-contact validation study: authors' own explanations converge on workflow breakdown, not intentional fabrication.

nodes.name: Authors of heavily-flagged papers were contacted for validation
nodes.description: To further check results, authors of accepted papers with at least five likely hallucinated references were contacted directly and shown the tool's output for their paper.

nodes.name: Authors attribute failures to bibliography-construction errors
nodes.description: Across responses, authors consistently attribute citation hallucinations to errors introduced during bibliography construction (often LLM-based generation/reformatting not subsequently verified, sometimes specifically at the camera-ready stage) rather than intentional fabrication.

nodes.name: Some cases involve corrupted metadata on real works or valid false positives
nodes.description: Other authors clarify that cited works were real but had corrupted metadata (author lists, titles, venues), while a smaller subset disputed certain flags as false positives (e.g., webpage references or valid but misidentified papers).

nodes.name: No author claimed deliberate fabrication; most corrected promptly
nodes.description: No response claimed deliberate fabrication; where errors were acknowledged, authors uniformly reported correcting the citations and, in several cases, proactively notifying program chairs or updating public versions.

nodes.name: Findings support framing as workflow breakdown, not misconduct
nodes.description: Read together, these responses match the paper's framing of the failure as an unchecked, machine-completed reference that no pipeline stage was responsible for validating, rather than deliberate misconduct.

edges.note: cross-component link from C6: the high-count tail is the population selected for author contact

components.description: Practical response: low-cost automated verification integrated into submission workflow, with human oversight preserved.

nodes.name: Auditing is cheap at venue scale
nodes.description: In one venue-scale scan, auditing 3,703 accepted papers and 221,281 references cost approximately $157, or roughly four cents per paper.

nodes.name: Verification can be run repeatedly without material budget impact
nodes.description: At this price, verification can be run at submission (to inform review) and again at camera-ready (to catch revision-introduced references) without materially affecting a conference's budget.

nodes.name: Proposed workflow: flag a small set, attach evidence, keep humans in the loop
nodes.description: The practical implication is not a manual gate but a standardized check folded into submission infrastructure: run the tool at submission/camera-ready, surface only failing references with supporting evidence and the search trail, and let a human confirm or dismiss each flag.

nodes.name: Design respects reviewers' already-strained voluntary workload
nodes.description: This design is motivated by respect for reviewers' workload, since reviewing is voluntary and already strained by rising submission volumes, and manually resolving every reference is neither reasonable nor scalable.

nodes.name: Desk rejection should preserve room for author justification
nodes.description: Even though the underlying signal is real and large enough to matter, and desk-rejection policies are a reasonable deterrent, flags should inform an evidence-backed, human-reviewed process giving authors a chance to justify or correct before punitive action, given cases like not-yet-indexed works.

edges.note: cross-component link from C9: fragility of automated adjudication motivates keeping humans in the loop
cross-component link from C10: workflow-breakdown framing motivates justification-before-punishment

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: conservative auditable hallucination definition
nodes.description: A conservative, externally auditable notion of hallucinated citation is defined, based on non-existent works and substantial author-identity mismatch, explicitly excluding ordinary venue/year/publication-status drift.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: RefChecker pipeline
nodes.description: RefChecker, a scalable open-source reference-verification pipeline combining multiple authoritative bibliographic sources with deep web-search re-verification, is built.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: large-scale audit across top venues
nodes.description: A large-scale audit of likely hallucinated citations is conducted across accepted papers from top AI and security venues.

nodes.name: Contribution 4: demonstration that hallucinated citations survive peer review
nodes.description: The audit shows likely hallucinated citations survive peer review and appear in camera-ready proceedings, including award-winning papers and papers with multiple failures in one bibliography.

nodes.name: Contribution 5: quantified trends and low-cost auditability
nodes.description: The post-ChatGPT increase, paper-level prevalence, error composition, and high-count tail are quantified, and conference-scale auditing is shown to be performable at low cost.

isolated_nodes.name: Results reported in aggregate only, deliberately withholding paper/author identity
isolated_nodes.description: No specific paper, author, or institution is identified; all results are aggregate, motivated by concern that public identification could cause reputational harm disproportionate to what the audit can establish, especially where failures reflect workflow breakdown rather than individual misconduct.

isolated_nodes.name: Results depend on the configured LLM provider and change over time
isolated_nodes.description: The extraction and deep-search stages inherit the strengths/weaknesses of the configured LLM provider (stronger models reduce false positives/negatives but cost more); model behavior also changes as providers roll out updates, so a scan run today may not reproduce identically under a future model release.

isolated_nodes.name: Extraction noise is a leading cause of false positives; source .bib files would help
isolated_nodes.description: PDF reference extraction is the noisiest pipeline step (merged/split fields, mangled strings, truncated titles); collecting source bibliographies (.bib files) directly at submission would let the pipeline skip this noisiest stage and reduce false positives.

isolated_nodes.name: Unpublished or not-yet-indexed works are near-certain false positives
isolated_nodes.description: Genuinely unpublished or very recently accepted work not yet indexed by aggregators can be impossible to confirm at scan time even though real, since no tool can distinguish 'does not exist' from 'not yet indexed' — a structural reason to keep humans in the loop.

isolated_nodes.name: Citation-layer verification is necessary but not sufficient for paper integrity
isolated_nodes.description: The audit verifies only whether a cited work exists and its authorship matches; it does not verify whether the citing sentence is faithfully supported by the cited work or whether scientific claims are correct, so it complements rather than replaces claim-level fact-checking.

isolated_nodes.name: A shared, canonical citation-verification layer is proposed as a more durable fix
isolated_nodes.description: Much of the friction and false positives stem from bibliographic identity being fragmented across disagreeing sources; a continuously updated canonical citation service unifying these records would raise precision/recall of any checker and help authors fetch correct entries at the point of writing.

notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the DecomposeRL example graph. This source document was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Motivation: SSL's success in language transfers to vision, but existing vision-SSL methods struggle with structured/compositional understanding.

nodes.name: SSL underlies LLM success via representation learning without annotation
nodes.description: LLMs like GPT, BERT, and LLaMA demonstrate remarkable performance largely due to self-supervised learning, training models to predict parts of input from other parts without human annotations.

nodes.name: Vision SSL methods learn global representations via auxiliary similarity tasks
nodes.description: SSL approaches like DINO, iBOT, and BEiT extend these ideas to vision, mostly using large Transformer (ViT) architectures and learning global representations by solving auxiliary tasks like predicting similarities between augmented views.

nodes.name: These global methods struggle to capture compositional object structure
nodes.description: While effective for image classification and matching, these global-representation methods often struggle to capture the compositional structure of objects in scenes.

nodes.name: Existing grouping methods have partial coverage: single-object or implicit-only
nodes.description: Methods like CutLER typically identify only a single dominant foreground region and struggle to isolate multiple objects without costly iterative training, while Slot Attention/SlotCon produce structured representations via implicit grouping but lack explicit hierarchical organization and instance-level decomposition.

nodes.name: Limitation 1: representations lack multi-level structure
nodes.description: Current methods tend to produce whole-scene representations with limited capacity for structured object understanding, even though an image contains objects, parts, and spatial relationships that a meaningful representation should reflect at local, intermediate, and global scales.

nodes.name: Limitation 2: dense-prediction fine-tuning is resource-intensive
nodes.description: Fine-tuning these SSL models for dense prediction tasks often demands substantial computational resources and extensive annotated data, making deployment challenging in resource-constrained settings.

components.description: Design response: ProtoScale's guiding intuition and the resulting deviations from SOTA practice.

nodes.name: ProtoScale introduced to progressively build structured representations
nodes.description: An SSL approach based on a new ProtoScale module is introduced, designed to overcome these limitations by progressively constructing a structured visual representation combining semantic abstraction, instance separation, and hierarchical organization.

nodes.name: Three-part guiding intuition: group, separate instances, organize
nodes.description: The approach builds on the intuition that an effective representation should be able to (i) group pixels by semantic meaning, (ii) identify distinct instance parts, and (iii) organize them coherently into complete objects.

nodes.name: Object detection chosen as the evaluation task
nodes.description: Object detection is chosen as the evaluation task because it offers a good balance between local and global scene complexity for testing this hypothesis.

nodes.name: Full scene context preserved instead of disruptive cropping
nodes.description: Unlike SOTA methods that rely on disruptive cropping strategies, the full scene context is preserved across views to ensure instance consistency while maintaining spatial structure.

nodes.name: Lightweight hybrid encoder adopted for computational efficiency
nodes.description: A lightweight hybrid CNN/Transformer encoder is adopted to reduce computational cost and improve feature scalability.

nodes.name: DETR-like architecture chosen over Mask R-CNN for evaluation
nodes.description: Unlike traditional downstream pipelines based on Mask R-CNN (which rely on NMS post-processing and are often less efficient), a DETR-like architecture is adopted for a fully end-to-end, NMS-free formulation better aligned with evaluating structured object-centric representations.

components.description: Positioning within related work: contrastive, dense, and slot-based SSL each fall short in a specific way.

nodes.name: Contrastive SSL maximizes cross-view similarity for a global vector
nodes.description: Contrastive methods (SimCLR, MoCo) maximize similarity between two views' representations in latent space; DINO extends this with a teacher-student EMA framework leading to spontaneous emergence of structured patterns like foreground/background.

nodes.name: Contrastive methods target a global image vector, unsuitable for dense prediction
nodes.description: Their primary goal is to encode an entire image as a global vector, suitable for image-level tasks like classification but falling short for dense prediction.

nodes.name: Unsupervised object-discovery methods limited by pseudo-label quality and single-object focus
nodes.description: Object-discovery methods (MOST via clustering, CutLER via iterative supervised loops) are effective at discovering salient regions but remain limited by initial pseudo-label quality and often focus on a single dominant object per image.

nodes.name: Dense SSL methods align features spatially but don't structure objects explicitly
nodes.description: Dense SSL methods (DetCon, SoCo) learn features preserving spatial coherence and local consistency, but do not explicitly structure objects.

nodes.name: Slot-based methods offer structure but lack explicit hierarchy
nodes.description: Slot Attention assigns pixels to abstract instances via iterative attention; SlotCon combines semantic grouping with contrastive learning for object-centric representations — but ProtoScale extends SlotCon's formulation by modifying semantic grouping and explicitly modeling hierarchical relationships between instances.

nodes.name: Pure ViT architectures are computationally costly and fragment local spatial continuity
nodes.description: Most recent SSL methods rely on pure ViT architectures, which are computationally expensive and whose patch-based processing fragments the input, limiting the ability to capture small or occluded objects.

nodes.name: Overall gap: no method combines modularity, hierarchy, and generalization
nodes.description: Contrastive methods yield effective global/local representations but lack grouping; latent slot models offer encouraging directions but still fall short on hierarchy, modularity, and generalization — this gap is what ProtoScale's modular, hierarchical, shared-prototype grouping mechanism addresses.

components.description: Student-teacher framework: architecture and the multi-scale encoder that underlies ProtoScale's multi-level operation.

nodes.name: Shared encoder, asymmetric roles: student trained, teacher EMA-updated
nodes.description: Both student and teacher networks share the same encoder architecture but differ in input processing and training role; the teacher's parameters are updated via exponential moving average (EMA) of the student weights and serves as a stable label generator.

nodes.name: Three losses align student predictions across views to the teacher output
nodes.description: Training encourages student predictions across all views to align with the teacher output using three loss terms, promoting view-consistent grouping, tightly integrated with the ProtoScale module.

nodes.name: Shared multi-scale encoder enables ProtoScale to operate at three resolutions
nodes.description: Both models share a multi-scale encoder extracting feature maps at three spatial resolutions, enabling ProtoScale to operate simultaneously at fine, intermediate, and global scales, helping discover small object parts, full objects, and global scene structure in a unified representation.

components.description: Multi-view learning strategy: asymmetric augmentation designed to preserve spatial structure while introducing appearance variability.

nodes.name: Teacher sees a single strongly-augmented global view
nodes.description: The teacher processes a single globally augmented image (random cropping, zoom out, horizontal flip, photometric distortions), serving as the stable training target and base input for generating student views.

nodes.name: Student sees four spatially-coherent, appearance-varied views
nodes.description: The student is exposed to four distinct views from a different transformation pipeline (Gaussian blur, random spatial masking, color jitter) designed to be spatially coherent, preserving object layout and relative positioning while introducing appearance variability.

nodes.name: SOTA cropping strategies disrupt spatial distribution and dense-prediction performance
nodes.description: SOTA methods relying heavily on random cropping strategies disrupt the spatial distribution of objects and degrade dense prediction performance.

nodes.name: Full-context preservation promotes instance consistency without sacrificing structure
nodes.description: By adopting a strategy that preserves full scene context across views instead, instance consistency is promoted without compromising the underlying spatial structure.

components.description: Hybrid CNN-Transformer pyramid encoder: how global attention and local convolution are fused for efficient dense representation.

nodes.name: Hybrid encoder adopted, inspired by RT-DETR
nodes.description: Unlike previous SSL methods, a hybrid CNN/Transformer encoder inspired by RT-DETR is employed, processing multi-scale features extracted from a ResNet backbone.

nodes.name: Lowest-resolution map gets full self-attention for global guidance
nodes.description: The lowest resolution feature map is passed through a full self-attention transformer, capturing long-range spatial dependencies and providing coarse guidance on where the model should focus.

nodes.name: Low-res attention fused top-down/bottom-up with CNN features
nodes.description: The resulting low-resolution attention is progressively fused with intermediate and high-resolution convolution features through top-down and bottom-up fusion paths, relying on CNN local precision to determine what is present in the identified regions.

nodes.name: Hybrid design balances accuracy and computational cost
nodes.description: This hybrid design enables accurate dense representation while reducing the computational cost associated with full-resolution attention.

components.description: ProtoScale module internals: the three sequential grouping stages (semantic, instance, hierarchical).

nodes.name: ProtoScale has three sequential components
nodes.description: ProtoScale consists of three sequential components: semantic clustering per feature map, aggregation into shared instance-level prototypes across the batch, and a hierarchical module inferring relationships between instances.

nodes.name: Semantic grouping via learnable-prototype attention
nodes.description: At each encoder scale, spatial features are fed into a semantic grouping module computing softmax dot-product attention between 256 learnable semantic prototypes and spatial features, each prototype aggregating features into semantic queries via weighted attention.

nodes.name: Centered Gaussian prior and auxiliary noise-absorbing prototypes prevent collapse
nodes.description: A centered Gaussian prior (μ=0.5, σ=0.7) is applied to attention maps to reduce collapse and bias toward generic representations (encouraging local-structure focus), and a set of auxiliary prototypes R, excluded from the loss, absorb noisy activations to stabilize learning.

nodes.name: Semantic grouping alone fails in crowded/occluded scenes
nodes.description: While semantic grouping isolates regions, it fails in crowded or occluded scenes, motivating a differentiable instance grouping stage.

nodes.name: Instance grouping via shared latent prototypes across the batch
nodes.description: Instance grouping introduces shared latent prototypes I_k learned across the batch; each semantic slot is softly assigned to 32 learnable instance prototypes, scaling the corresponding attention map before summation over semantic prototypes, trained with consistency and sparsity regularization to encourage specialization and spatial diversity.

nodes.name: Hierarchical relations modeled via prototype affinity matrix
nodes.description: Beyond instance-level attention, ProtoScale models object relationships via a relation (affinity) matrix between instance prototypes, predicted by a shallow MLP with sigmoid activation; thresholding low-affinity pairs at 0.5 lets the model merge overlapping/related instances, capturing part-whole and object-group structure.

edges.note: cross-component link from C2: three-stage design directly instantiates the group/separate/organize intuition

components.description: The self-supervised training objective combining the three ProtoScale stages.

nodes.name: Weighted three-term loss trains student to match teacher
nodes.description: The student is trained via a weighted objective L_total = λ_sem L_sem + λ_inst L_inst + λ_hier L_hier, with (λ_sem, λ_inst, λ_hier) = (1, 2, 1) found to yield the best experimental results.

nodes.name: Each loss term uses KL divergence between attention maps
nodes.description: Each loss term includes a KL-divergence term computed between corresponding student and teacher attention maps, chosen to encourage matching the entire probability distribution rather than only the highest-probability regions.

nodes.name: All modules operate across three spatial scales for object-centric reasoning
nodes.description: All modules operate at three spatial scales, enabling rich object-centric reasoning across fine, intermediate, and global resolutions.

components.description: Experimental design: baseline/framework choice and low-resource evaluation setup.

nodes.name: RT-DETR chosen over Mask R-CNN for evaluation
nodes.description: SSL encoders are typically evaluated via downstream fine-tuning using Mask R-CNN, but this work adopts RT-DETR, an end-to-end detection pipeline without NMS post-processing that achieves significantly better performance than Mask R-CNN.

nodes.name: RT-DETR's lack of instance segmentation restricts scope to detection
nodes.description: Because RT-DETR does not support instance segmentation, evaluation focuses exclusively on object detection as the downstream task.

nodes.name: Strong SSL baselines selected and integrated fairly
nodes.description: A set of strong SSL baselines (DINOv1, DINOv2, iBOT, TEC, SlotCon) are selected, with each method's encoder backbone attached to a shared projection module outputting multi-scale features, integrated into the same student-teacher method for fair comparison under identical training configurations; a fully supervised RT-DETR baseline is also included as reference.

nodes.name: Two datasets chosen for complementary diversity/density characteristics
nodes.description: COCO (high scene diversity) and UA-DETRAC (high object density) are used, with class labels redefined into a fine-grained 17-class taxonomy and images filtered to those containing at least two such classes, yielding 50,022 combined training and 5,555 combined validation images.

nodes.name: Low-resource evaluation simulates realistic deployment constraints
nodes.description: Evaluation varies fine-tuning epoch count and the proportion of labeled training data (always testing on the full validation set), reflecting realistic conditions where high computing infrastructure and large annotated datasets are often unavailable.

components.description: Results: sensitivity to fine-tuning epochs, showing ProtoScale's efficiency advantage.

nodes.name: ProtoScale outperforms SOTA SSL and supervised baseline across epochs
nodes.description: ProtoScale significantly outperforms current SOTA SSL approaches and the supervised RT-DETR (random init) baseline, consistently achieving higher performance even versus models pretrained on much larger datasets (ImageNet-1K, LVD-142M).

nodes.name: ProtoScale needs far fewer pretraining epochs than comparable methods
nodes.description: ProtoScale, pretrained for only 35 epochs on COCO, outperforms methods like SlotCon which requires up to 800 pretraining epochs to achieve competitive results.

nodes.name: ProtoScale is especially strong on small/medium objects
nodes.description: The method demonstrates strong performance specifically on small and medium objects, even with fewer fine-tuning epochs.

nodes.name: DINOv2 slightly outperforms on large objects, plausibly due to scale of pretraining data
nodes.description: DINOv2 slightly outperforms ProtoScale on large objects, likely due to the strong generalization capabilities of transformer architectures trained on a massive 142-million-image dataset.

components.description: Results: influence of labeled data availability, comparing ProtoScale against the strongest baseline (DINOv2) under data scarcity.

nodes.name: Data-fraction sweep compares the two best methods from the epoch experiment
nodes.description: Different training-set fractions (10%, 30%, 50%, 70%) are used to simulate low-resource scenarios, comparing the two best-performing methods (ProtoScale and DINOv2) for robustness under varying data availability.

nodes.name: ProtoScale requires less labeled data for competitive performance
nodes.description: Although overall performance decreases relative to 100%-data fine-tuning for both methods, results show ProtoScale requires less labeled data to achieve competitive performance.

nodes.name: ProtoScale outperforms DINOv2 on small/medium objects across data fractions
nodes.description: ProtoScale consistently outperforms DINOv2 on small and medium objects across the tested data fractions, while DINOv2 performs slightly better on large objects.

nodes.name: ProtoScale achieves this with fewer parameters than DINOv2's encoder
nodes.description: The performance advantage is achieved despite ProtoScale using only about 12 million parameters, compared to DINOv2's ViT-Small encoder's approximately 21 million parameters.

components.description: Contribution summary chain.

nodes.name: Contribution 1: annotation-free SSL combining grouping, instance clustering, hierarchy
nodes.description: An SSL approach is proposed that combines semantic grouping, instance-level clustering, and hierarchical reasoning to build structured visual representations without any annotations.

nodes.name: Contribution 2: ProtoScale multi-scale grouping module
nodes.description: ProtoScale, a modular grouping module operating at multiple spatial scales, is introduced, capable of organizing pixels into instances and instances into structured groups.

nodes.name: Contribution 3: full-scene-context preservation for dense-prediction consistency
nodes.description: Full scene context is preserved across views by avoiding disruptive cropping, improving consistency in dense prediction tasks.

nodes.name: Contribution 4: lightweight hybrid encoder
nodes.description: A lightweight hybrid CNN/Transformer encoder, adapted from RT-DETR, is leveraged to balance feature precision and reduce computational overhead.

nodes.name: Contribution 5: validation against SOTA under realistic low-resource constraints
nodes.description: The proposed approach is validated through downstream object detection experiments, comparing against SOTA methods and evaluating under realistic constraints of small annotated datasets and limited training epochs.

isolated_nodes.name: Under review at ISVC since August 20, 2025
isolated_nodes.description: The manuscript has been submitted to the International Symposium on Visual Computing (ISVC) and has been under review since August 20, 2025.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: scale to larger datasets and other dense-prediction tasks
isolated_nodes.description: Future work will investigate the effectiveness of the method on larger datasets and explore applicability to other dense prediction tasks.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work: SSL decoder for human-interpretable representations
isolated_nodes.description: Future work aims to design an SSL decoder to enhance the interpretability of the learned representations in a human-understandable manner.

nodes.name: LLM hallucination and knowledge limitations
nodes.description: LLMs have catalyzed NLP advances but encounter challenges such as hallucination and the need for domain-specific knowledge, and cannot promptly update their knowledge.

nodes.name: Retrieval integration mitigates limitations
nodes.description: Recent methodologies integrate information retrieved from external resources with LLMs, substantially enhancing their performance across NLP tasks.

nodes.name: Existing RAG surveys are incomplete
nodes.description: Existing surveys on RAG are limited in scope: some do not cover all relevant domains or lack developmental timelines, some introduce retrievers and generators independently limiting insight into their interaction, and some focus narrowly on text generation with limited illustrative detail.

nodes.name: RAG surveys tell only half the story
nodes.description: Existing surveys on RAG only address NLG-oriented retrieval augmentation, neglecting that NLU tasks also necessitate external information, leaving a scarcity of comprehensive surveys spanning the full spectrum of NLP.

nodes.name: Survey introduces RALM framing
nodes.description: This survey addresses the gap by covering both Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Retrieval-Augmented Understanding (RAU) under the unified concept of Retrieval-Augmented Language Models (RALM), aligning generation work with NLG and the rest with NLU.

nodes.name: RALM basic architecture y=F(x,z)
nodes.description: RALM is defined by the basic architecture y = F(x, z), where x is the input, z is the retrieved message, and F is a language model or data processing function.

nodes.name: Sequential single interaction
nodes.description: In sequential single interaction, a retriever finds top-K relevant documents z for input x, and the language model then receives x and z to generate output tokens.

nodes.name: Single interaction insufficient for long/multi-hop tasks
nodes.description: Researchers discovered that a single retriever-LM interaction is insufficient for long dialogue generation and solving multi-hop problems.

nodes.name: Sequential multiple interactions
nodes.description: To address the insufficiency of single interaction, a method with multiple interactions between retriever and language model was proposed, where the LM generates output first and the outputted content is used for subsequent retrieval steps.

nodes.name: Sequential structure may not be optimal
nodes.description: The strictly sequential flow of information (retriever-to-LM or LM-to-retriever) may not be optimal in all domains and may be less extensible.

nodes.name: Parallel interaction
nodes.description: As an alternative to sequential structures, researchers proposed a parallel interaction structure where the retriever and language model work independently on the input, with the output determined by weighted interpolation of their respective outputs.

nodes.name: Sparse retrieval simplicity
nodes.description: Sparse retrieval's main advantage is simplicity, allowing easy integration into existing indexing systems due to fewer dimensions, and it is easier to generalise and more efficient.

nodes.name: Term matching insufficient, motivates sparse vectors
nodes.description: Simple term matching methods (TF-IDF, BM25) became insufficient to meet retrieval demands, motivating the use of machine-learning-based sparse vector representations that capture semantic essence rather than exact term overlap.

nodes.name: Deep learning transforms retrieval toward dense methods
nodes.description: The emergence of deep learning techniques significantly transformed retrieval, driving growing interest in dense retrieval methods that sacrifice some comprehensibility for enhanced accuracy.

nodes.name: Dual-encoder architecture underlies dense retrieval
nodes.description: The dual encoder architecture, comprising two networks that independently generate dense embeddings for queries and documents, is the common design for dense retrieval models, favored for its high accuracy and suitability for RALM.

nodes.name: Knowledge distillation streamlines retrieval database
nodes.description: Knowledge distillation is a technique for gradually filtering and streamlining a large retrieval database to make it more suitable for a user's query, transferring data from larger pre-trained models to smaller ones.

nodes.name: Internet retrieval as plug-and-play but noisy
nodes.description: Internet retrieval offers a plug-and-play approach well-suited to open-domain generalisation without requiring real-time database updates, but the presence of irrelevant or harmful web information can significantly reduce RALM effectiveness without proper screening.

nodes.name: Hybrid retrieval combines technique strengths
nodes.description: As researchers gained better understanding of individual retrieval techniques' strengths and weaknesses, they increasingly combined them into hybrid approaches to improve effectiveness and robustness of the RALM architecture.

nodes.name: AutoEncoder LM independence assumption limitation
nodes.description: AutoEncoder language models introduce an independence assumption during pre-training that means correlations between predicted [MASK] tokens are not considered, and the [MASK] marker creates inconsistency between pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

nodes.name: AutoEncoder models suited to NLU
nodes.description: Because AutoEncoder language models are highly generalisable, unsupervised, and naturally incorporate contextual semantic information, self-encoding models are commonly used in RALM architectures for natural language understanding tasks.

nodes.name: AutoRegressive left-to-right prediction
nodes.description: AutoRegressive language models predict the next word based only on preceding words (left-to-right modelling), making them well-suited to generative NLG tasks like dialogue generation and machine translation.

nodes.name: AutoRegressive models popular for RALM NLG
nodes.description: Because of their left-to-right generative advantage, AutoRegressive language models are a popular choice for NLG tasks in the RALM field.

nodes.name: Encoder-Decoder architecture enables parallel computation
nodes.description: The Transformer encoder-decoder architecture divides input into source and destination sequences processed by encoder and decoder respectively, enabling parallel computation and significantly increasing training and inference speed.

nodes.name: Retrieved documents can harm output quality
nodes.description: Retrieval can produce documents that not only fail to provide helpful information but can also compromise the quality of the language model output, motivating research on retrieval quality control.

nodes.name: Instruction-tuning improves query encoder relevance
nodes.description: An instruction-tuning approach updates the query encoder using a generalised supervised retrieval training target, enabling the retriever to produce more contextually relevant results consistent with LLM preferences.

nodes.name: SELF-RAG builds on instruction-tuning idea
nodes.description: Inspired by the instruction-tuning approach to retrieval quality, SELF-RAG proposes a more sophisticated model trained on an instruction-tracking dataset, retrieving and selecting outputs via fine-grained self-reflection.

nodes.name: Correction strategy improves on SELF-RAG
nodes.description: A further method improves on SELF-RAG by designing a correction strategy that classifies retrieved information into CORRECT, INCORRECT, and AMBIGUOUS categories to address inaccurate retriever results.

nodes.name: Single-document retrieval augmentation limited
nodes.description: The RALM architecture initially used a single document for retrieval augmentation, but performance significantly improved when the number of retrieved paragraphs was increased.

nodes.name: Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) proposed
nodes.description: Because increasing retrieved paragraphs improved performance, Fusion-in-Decoder was proposed: keeping the retriever unchanged, encoding related documents individually, then connecting them for decoder output.

nodes.name: FiD-Light constrains information flow
nodes.description: An improvement on FiD constrains the information flow from encoder to decoder and tunes source pointers to improve topmost source accuracy.

nodes.name: FiD-KD applies knowledge distillation to FiD
nodes.description: Knowledge distillation was applied to the FiD model (FiD-KD), using cross-attention scores from a sequence-to-sequence reader to obtain synthetic targets for the retriever.

nodes.name: KNN-LM linear interpolation with neighbors
nodes.description: The KNN-LM approach linearly interpolates an extended neural language model's predictions with K-nearest-neighbours in the pre-trained LM embedding space.

nodes.name: Not all tokens need retrieval (adaptive retrieval)
nodes.description: It was proposed that not all generated tokens need to be retrieved; a lightweight neural network can be trained to aid KNN-LM in adaptive retrieval, improving efficiency.

nodes.name: RETOMATON improves on adaptive retrieval
nodes.description: RETOMATON, an unsupervised weighted finite automaton built on the datastore using saved pointers and clustering, is more effective than the adaptive retrieval approach in improving accuracy while requiring no additional training data.

nodes.name: REALM end-to-end trainable retriever
nodes.description: REALM used masked language training in pre-training and included a retriever trainable end-to-end, targeting only the QA task with a frozen retriever during fine-tuning.

nodes.name: RAG uses pre-trained retriever with partial end-to-end training
nodes.description: Unlike REALM, RAG used an already-trained retriever (DPR) and only employed BART for partial end-to-end training.

nodes.name: End-to-end retriever training improves performance
nodes.description: Building on REALM's approach with an unsupervised pre-training and supervised fine-tuning pipeline, subsequent work found that using end-to-end trained retrievers resulted in significant performance improvement across tasks.

nodes.name: Simple prefix attacks degrade RALM
nodes.description: Exceedingly simple prefix attacks can diminish the relevance and accuracy of RALM output and even alter the retriever's retrieval strategy, revealing poor robustness as a limitation.

nodes.name: Robustness limitation motivates GGPP defense
nodes.description: In response to prefix-attack vulnerability, Gradient Guided Prompt Perturbation (GGPP) is proposed as a method to perturb RALM and detect such perturbations by prompting the internal state of the perturbed model.

nodes.name: Internet quality variance causes noisy retrieval
nodes.description: When using the Internet as a retrieval tool, the quality of sources can vary widely, and merging this data without proper consideration can introduce noise or misleading information, contributing to poor retrieval-result quality.

nodes.name: Poor retrieval quality motivates future retrieval improvement
nodes.description: The persistent uncertainty that retrieval outcomes fully align with the LM, and the noise introduced by variable-quality Internet sources, motivates the proposed future direction of improving retrieval quality via better datasets and re-ranking techniques.

nodes.name: Extensive model changes increase overhead
nodes.description: Some existing RALMs require extensive model changes and complex pre-training/fine-tuning, increasing time and space overhead and reducing scalability as retrieval scale grows.

nodes.name: Overhead motivates plug-and-play and in-context solutions
nodes.description: The overhead limitation motivates proposed future solutions such as plug-and-play intermediate modules, greater use of Internet retrieval, and in-context learning to reduce the cost of improving language models.

isolated_nodes.name: NLP multidisciplinary goal
isolated_nodes.description: NLP is a multidisciplinary field integrating linguistics, computer science, and mathematics, aiming to enable mutual transformation between human language and computer data.

isolated_nodes.name: Transformer architecture rise
isolated_nodes.description: The transformer architecture has grown significantly in popularity as a leading representative of NLP and large language models.

isolated_nodes.name: GPT and BERT families dominance
isolated_nodes.description: The most prevalent language models are the GPT families and BERT families, demonstrated to excel across many NLP tasks.

isolated_nodes.name: Semiparametric memory concept
isolated_nodes.description: RALM integrates the nonparametric memory acquired by the retriever with the parametric memory of the language model to create a semiparametric memory, enhancing performance.

isolated_nodes.name: DPR indexes passages in continuous space
isolated_nodes.description: DPR indexes all passages in a low-dimensional continuous space using a dense encoder, allowing efficient retrieval of top-k passages associated with an input query at runtime.

isolated_nodes.name: Contriever uses unsupervised dual-encoder training
isolated_nodes.description: Contriever is trained using unsupervised data with a dual-encoder architecture and average pooling to reduce reliance on manual annotation.

isolated_nodes.name: Multimodal retrieval bridges modalities
isolated_nodes.description: Multimodal retrieval techniques encode textual and visual information into a shared latent space to bridge different modalities for tasks like image-text retrieval.

isolated_nodes.name: GPT family architecture evolution
isolated_nodes.description: The GPT family evolved from unsupervised pre-training plus fine-tuning, to zero-shot learning, to GPT-3's scaled-up approach abandoning fine-tuning, with later variants incorporating RLHF.

isolated_nodes.name: Llama family design choices
isolated_nodes.description: The Llama family introduced RMSNorm, SwiGLU activation, and rotary position embeddings, with Llama2 adding supervised fine-tuning, iterative reward modelling, RLHF, and Ghost Attention for multi-turn dialogue control.

isolated_nodes.name: T5 unified text-to-text framework
isolated_nodes.description: T5 introduces a unified framework converting all text-based language problems into text-to-text format to explore transfer learning potential in NLP.

isolated_nodes.name: BART arbitrary noise transformations
isolated_nodes.description: BART is an encoder-decoder model that allows arbitrary noise transformations to the input document during pre-training, including token masking, deletion, text infilling, sentence permutation, and document rotation.

isolated_nodes.name: FLAN systematic instruction tuning
isolated_nodes.description: FLAN is one of the most systematic and comprehensive approaches to instruction tuning, fine-tuning on instruction-optimised datasets while scaling task count, model size, and incorporating chain-of-thought data.

isolated_nodes.name: Structured vs unstructured data sources
isolated_nodes.description: RALM data sources are categorised into structured data (tables, knowledge graphs) with clearly defined fields, and unstructured data (text, images, audio, video) lacking a clearly defined structure.

isolated_nodes.name: RALM applications span NLG, NLU, and both
isolated_nodes.description: RALM downstream applications are categorized by whether task completion depends primarily on generative capability (NLG, e.g., machine translation, dialogue generation), comprehension capability (NLU, e.g., slot filling, fact checking), or both (e.g., question answering, summarization).

isolated_nodes.name: RAGAS evaluates faithfulness and relevance
isolated_nodes.description: RAGAS employs the WikiEval dataset to assess RALM faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance, using an automated LLM-based evaluation process.

isolated_nodes.name: RGB evaluates robustness dimensions
isolated_nodes.description: RGB is a bilingual Chinese-English evaluation system using accuracy, rejection rate, and error detection rate metrics to assess noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness.

isolated_nodes.name: MIRAGE targets medical domain evaluation
isolated_nodes.description: MIRAGE integrates data from five datasets including MMLU-Med to evaluate zero-shot learning, multi-choice evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation, and question-only retrieval ideation capabilities of medical RALMs, discovering log-linear scaling and a lost-in-the-middle effect.

isolated_nodes.name: Few application domains limitation
isolated_nodes.description: Despite improving LM performance, RALMs have seen limited improvement from an application perspective, still mostly performing routine tasks like question answering and summarization rather than more diverse applications.

structural_reasoning: As a broad survey rather than a single unified technical contribution, this paper's content is naturally structured as many largely independent thematic strands (interaction paradigms, retriever categories, language model families, enhancement techniques, applications, evaluation methods, limitations) rather than one tightly chained argument. The extracted components each capture locally coherent motivation-to-solution chains within a subsection (e.g., single-interaction limitations motivating multi-interaction and parallel designs; single-document retrieval limitations motivating FiD and its extensions; prefix-attack vulnerabilities motivating GGPP). However, edges connecting across major sections (e.g., linking retriever categories to specific LM families, or linking data sources to particular applications) are largely absent from the graph because the survey treats these as a taxonomy rather than asserting causal or dependency relationships between them. This structural characteristic of survey papers, combined with the very large number of enumerated techniques described in parallel (particularly in Related Work-style catalog sections and the large summary tables), results in a substantial isolated-node set and a moderate structural score reflecting genuine catalog-style organization rather than a flaw in extraction.

note_on_evidence: Evidence fields cite paper sections/subsections/tables/equations rather than sentence indices, since a sentence-indexed source was not available for this document.

components.name: Motivation: absence of reliable reward signals for CUA reinforcement learning

nodes.name: Desktop task success is implicit and visually grounded
nodes.description: Unlike robotics simulators or game environments with explicit machine-readable success criteria, desktop applications rarely expose clear, machine-readable indicators of task completion; objectives are typically implicit, visually grounded, and unstructured.

nodes.name: RL for GUI agents is constrained by lack of reward signals
nodes.description: Applying reinforcement learning to GUI-based environments remains fundamentally constrained by the absence of reliable, scalable reward signals.

nodes.name: Prior work relies on brittle heuristics or manual labels
nodes.description: Prior work often relies on brittle, task-specific heuristics (e.g., DOM element checks in web environments) or manually annotated success labels to supply a reward/success signal.

nodes.name: Heuristics/manual labels fail to scale and generalize
nodes.description: Brittle heuristics and manual success labels fail to scale across different applications, operating systems, and task distributions, substantially limiting generalization beyond narrowly defined settings.

nodes.name: Self-judging agents introduce reliability concerns
nodes.description: Defining task success internally within the computer-use agent itself introduces additional reliability concerns, since the agent's own perception and reasoning are imperfect and are exactly what RL aims to improve.

nodes.name: Lack of scalable reliable reward mechanism is a central bottleneck
nodes.description: The lack of a scalable and reliable reward mechanism remains a central bottleneck for effective RL fine-tuning of computer-use agents.

nodes.name: SOTA desktop agents underperform in real-world settings
nodes.description: State-of-the-art desktop agents achieve success rates of only around 60% on OSWorld and approximately 40% on macOSWorld, highlighting a significant gap between current capability and practical deployment.

components.name: Noisy autonomous evaluator and noise-corrected reward estimator derivation

nodes.name: Autonomous VLM evaluators achieve high accuracy but introduce noise
nodes.description: Autonomous evaluators based on Vision-Language Models can achieve high accuracy and generalize across diverse applications, but inevitably introduce noise via false positives (labeling unsuccessful executions as completed) and false negatives (failing to detect success).

nodes.name: Naive evaluator-as-reward use causes bias/instability
nodes.description: Naively using evaluator outputs as reward signals can introduce bias and lead to unstable reinforcement learning.

nodes.name: Evaluator modeled as noisy binary reward channel
nodes.description: The paper models the autonomous evaluator's feedback as a noisy binary reward channel, characterized by false-negative rate e+ and false-positive rate e-.

nodes.name: Separability constant D defined and assumed positive
nodes.description: The separability constant D := 1 - e+ - e- is defined and assumed positive, ensuring the evaluator gives informative feedback beyond random guessing.

nodes.name: Conditional expectation of noisy signal derived
nodes.description: Because the observed evaluator output is binary, its conditional expectation given the true label satisfies E[r~ | r*] = e- + D * r*.

nodes.name: Corrected reward estimator derived by solving for r*
nodes.description: Solving the conditional-expectation equation for the true label r* yields the corrected reward estimator r-hat := (r~ - e-) / D.

nodes.name: Corrected estimator is asymptotically unbiased
nodes.description: The corrected reward estimator r-hat satisfies E[r-hat | trajectory] = r*, making it an asymptotically unbiased estimator of true task completion.

nodes.name: Plug-in estimator using empirical error rates
nodes.description: Because true error rates e+ and e- are unknown in practice, empirical estimates from a held-out calibration split are substituted to form a plug-in estimator, asymptotically unbiased as calibration data grows and the estimated separability stays bounded away from zero.

nodes.name: Corrected reward integrated into PPO via terminal discounted return
nodes.description: The corrected terminal reward is propagated backward through the trajectory as a discounted return and used as the training signal for Proximal Policy Optimization, enabling stable policy-gradient updates despite evaluator-induced noise.

components.name: Dataset and evaluator calibration design

nodes.name: Synthetic dataset of 7,560 tasks across 42 applications/OS
nodes.description: The authors construct a synthetic dataset of computer-use tasks spanning 42 applications per OS, with 60 natural-language task descriptions per application, totaling 7,560 tasks across macOS, Windows, and Linux.

nodes.name: Three-way disjoint split per application
nodes.description: Tasks per application are randomly partitioned into three disjoint splits of 20 tasks each: two splits (40 tasks, two-thirds) for RL fine-tuning and one split (one-third) reserved for evaluator calibration.

nodes.name: Disjoint splits prevent information leakage
nodes.description: Separating evaluator calibration and policy optimization onto disjoint task sets ensures evaluator calibration and policy optimization are conducted without information leakage between them.

nodes.name: Ground-truth labels reserved for evaluator assessment and benchmarking only
nodes.description: Ground-truth success labels for the calibration and RL test splits are used exclusively for evaluator assessment and final benchmarking, and are never exposed to the agent during training.

components.name: Evaluator error asymmetry and its consequences for RL

nodes.name: Evaluator behavior varies by operating system
nodes.description: While the vision-based evaluator achieves high accuracy overall, its behavior (error profile) varies by operating system, as shown in the normalized confusion matrices (Table 2).

nodes.name: False positives reinforce incorrect behaviors
nodes.description: False positives are particularly harmful for reinforcement learning because they assign high reward to unsuccessful trajectories, reinforcing incorrect behaviors.

nodes.name: False negatives slow learning by reducing reward frequency
nodes.description: False negatives primarily reduce the effective reward frequency, which can slow learning, but do not reinforce incorrect behavior the way false positives do.

nodes.name: Per-OS error rates estimated for reward correction
nodes.description: Because evaluator error rates vary by OS, (e+, e-) were estimated separately per OS from the evaluator calibration split and used to compute the corrected reward estimator during PPO fine-tuning.

components.name: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning results

nodes.name: Evaluator-based RL improves over zero-shot baseline
nodes.description: Across all three benchmarks (macOSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, OSWorld), reinforcement learning with evaluator feedback (raw or corrected) improves performance over the zero-shot baseline.

nodes.name: Raw evaluator rewards yield moderate, inconsistent gains
nodes.description: Using raw evaluator rewards yields moderate gains in most settings, but these gains are consistently smaller than those from the corrected reward estimator, and in some cases raw rewards reduce generalization.

nodes.name: Corrected reward achieves strongest performance with per-OS models
nodes.description: The noise-corrected reward achieves the strongest performance across all three benchmarks when combined with per-OS fine-tuning: 0.084->0.203 on macOSWorld, 0.331->0.442 on Windows Agent Arena, and 0.283->0.432 on OSWorld.

nodes.name: Corrected reward outperforms raw reward most clearly on OSWorld
nodes.description: The effect of the corrected estimator's advantage over raw rewards is most evident on OSWorld, where it consistently outperforms raw rewards under both unified and per-OS training.

nodes.name: Ignoring evaluator error introduces distribution-shift bias
nodes.description: These results indicate that ignoring evaluator error can introduce bias that negatively impacts reinforcement learning, particularly under distribution shift.

nodes.name: Per-OS models generalize more reliably than unified models
nodes.description: The ablation comparing per-OS and unified fine-tuning suggests OS-specific policies provide more reliable generalization overall, supporting the use of per-OS models in the main experiments.

components.name: Limitations of the noise-correction framework

nodes.name: Assumption of fixed error rates may not hold
nodes.description: The approach assumes evaluator false-negative and false-positive rates are approximately fixed for a given model/protocol, but in practice evaluator behavior may be non-stationary, varying with task type, UI complexity, phrasing, visual themes, and OS-specific conventions.

nodes.name: Policy improvement may shift visited-state distribution
nodes.description: As the agent improves during training, the distribution of visited GUI states may shift, potentially changing the evaluator's error profile and introducing residual bias in the plug-in error-rate estimates.

nodes.name: Binary terminal signal is sparse and limits exploration
nodes.description: The formulation relies on a binary, effectively terminal success signal, which is inherently sparse; while PPO can learn under sparse rewards, exploration remains challenging for long-horizon GUI tasks with delayed success.

nodes.name: Correction improves accuracy but not reward density
nodes.description: The proposed correction improves reward accuracy but does not increase reward density, and therefore cannot by itself resolve exploration difficulties.

nodes.name: Small separability D amplifies correction variance
nodes.description: With limited calibration data or a small separability term D, statistical uncertainty in the error-rate estimates can propagate into the corrected reward and increase the variance of policy-gradient updates.

nodes.name: Corrected reward can fall outside [0,1], affecting PPO scale
nodes.description: The corrected reward r-hat is real-valued and can fall outside the [0,1] range, altering the scale of advantages, which may affect PPO optimization in finite-sample settings despite policy-gradient methods being invariant to affine reward transforms in expectation.

nodes.name: Vision-based evaluators have inherent blind spots
nodes.description: Vision-based evaluators may miss semantically correct outcomes that are visually subtle or overestimate success from superficial visual cues, and binary labels ignore partial progress and alternative valid solutions.

isolated_nodes.name: RL framing as principled improvement mechanism
isolated_nodes.description: Reinforcement learning provides a principled framework for improving agent behavior via exploration, error recovery, and interaction, rather than reliance on static demonstrations.

isolated_nodes.name: CUA definition and interaction model
isolated_nodes.description: Computer-Use Agents are end-to-end autonomous systems that complete natural-language tasks by perceiving the rendered desktop GUI (typically via screenshots) and executing actions such as clicking, typing, scrolling, and dragging, without requiring explicit service/API integrations.

isolated_nodes.name: CUA MDP formulation
isolated_nodes.description: A CUA is formulated as a Markov Decision Process with state defined as the rendered screen image plus the fixed task description, and an action space of click, type, scroll, and drag operations.

isolated_nodes.name: Terminal-only reward setting
isolated_nodes.description: Reward in this setting is terminal-only: the true task-completion signal is defined only at the end of the episode and is never directly observed.

isolated_nodes.name: Qwen2-VL-7B used as the evaluator
isolated_nodes.description: The autonomous evaluator uses the Qwen2-VL-7B model, chosen for its strong multimodal reasoning and demonstrated superiority as a vision-based evaluator among open-source models.

isolated_nodes.name: Evaluator decoupled from acting agent
isolated_nodes.description: The evaluator operates zero-shot and is fully decoupled from the acting agent, observing neither its action history nor internal reasoning, basing judgment solely on the final screenshot and instruction.

isolated_nodes.name: Five training configurations compared
isolated_nodes.description: The experiments compare five training configurations: zero-shot baseline, PPO with raw rewards (unified model), PPO with corrected rewards (unified model), PPO with raw rewards (per-OS models), and PPO with corrected rewards (per-OS models).

isolated_nodes.name: Additional external datasets incorporated for RL diversity
isolated_nodes.description: Task descriptions from OmniAct, GUI-World, and GUIDE are incorporated alongside the authors' own dataset to further diversify the task distribution used for RL fine-tuning, using only their natural-language task specifications.

isolated_nodes.name: Execution logs recorded from base and fine-tuned agents
isolated_nodes.description: The dataset includes execution logs of the base UI-TARS agent and of RL-fine-tuned agents, recording complete trajectories including screenshots, actions, and intermediate reasoning steps.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: reward corruption correction via confusion matrix
isolated_nodes.description: Prior work (Wang et al. 2020a) formalizes reward corruption using a confusion matrix over discrete reward values and shows that, given an estimate of the corruption process, an unbiased reward estimator can be constructed.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: CANDERE-COACH online denoising
isolated_nodes.description: CANDERE-COACH considers unreliable binary approve/disapprove human feedback and proposes online denoising mechanisms that filter feedback before policy updates, at the data level rather than the reward level.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: RL with verifiable noisy rewards
isolated_nodes.description: Cai et al. study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards from noisy binary automated verifiers, modeling asymmetric false-positive/false-negative errors and deriving correction strategies that debias policy-gradient updates, most closely related to this paper's setting.

isolated_nodes.name: This work's correction operates at the reward level
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike approaches that denoise feedback at the data level, this paper's correction operates at the reward level, making it straightforward to plug into standard policy-gradient fine-tuning such as PPO.

isolated_nodes.name: Future extension: conditional error-rate estimation
isolated_nodes.description: A suggested extension is to estimate evaluator error rates conditionally, e.g., per task family or application type, to address non-stationary evaluator behavior.

isolated_nodes.name: Future extension: richer feedback signals
isolated_nodes.description: Extending evaluators to produce calibrated confidence scores, multi-level outcomes, or preference-based feedback could provide richer learning signals, but would require revisiting both the noise model and correction mechanism.

isolated_nodes.name: Open research direction: robustness under broader distribution shift
isolated_nodes.description: Robustness under broader distribution shifts, such as new application versions, different screen resolutions, or accessibility settings, remains an open direction for future work.

structural_reasoning: The graph is highly coherent within its components. C1 traces a clean motivational chain from the implicit/visually-grounded nature of desktop task success through to the central reward-signal bottleneck, closely following the paper's own introduction narrative. C2 is the strongest and most central component, tightly mirroring the paper's formal derivation from the noisy-channel model through the separability constant, conditional expectation, corrected estimator, unbiasedness proof, plug-in estimator, and integration into PPO -- each step is an explicit mathematical consequence of the prior one (Equations 3-11). C3 (dataset/calibration split design) and C4 (error asymmetry and its RL consequences) are compact, well-evidenced chains directly grounded in Sections 3.1 and 4.1. C5 (main results) follows the paper's own results narrative from evaluator-based improvement over baseline, through the raw-vs-corrected comparison, to the per-OS vs. unified ablation conclusion. C6 (limitations) is intentionally left as a small set of largely independent point-claims (non-stationarity, sparse terminal signal, small-D variance, out-of-range reward scale) since the paper itself presents these as a list of separate caveats rather than a single dependency chain. A substantial number of foundational/definitional facts (MDP formulation, evaluator model choice, dataset composition, and related-work summaries) are correctly left as isolated nodes, as they are descriptive/contextual rather than argumentative premises feeding into other propositions.

nodes.name: CLIP not optimized for neural alignment
