C6 is the paper's own explicit synthesis, and its cross-component edges into C7 correctly reflect that the empirical unevenness (both cross-dimension and cross-model) is the paper's stated motivation for a taxonomy rather than a fixed checklist. C7's internal structure (TRAILS-D/TRAILS-R split, then three prioritization heuristics) mirrors Section 5's own organization, including a cross-component edge from the cross-model finding (P30) to the heuristic it directly motivates (P40). C8 mirrors the paper's explicit numbered objection-response pairs, with edges back into C3 and C7 where the paper explicitly invokes its own framework as the response. The isolated nodes are appropriately limited to scope/definitional setup, prior-work context, experimental configuration details, and the concluding calls to action, none of which function as premises within the paper's central argument chain.

notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the prior example graphs. Evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text.

components.description: Motivation: object grouping as a shared challenge for brains and AI, and the gap in testing naturalistic alignment.

nodes.name: Grouping visual input into objects is fundamental for both brains and AI
nodes.description: Grouping visual input into coherent whole objects is a fundamental problem for the brain and AI systems, with the human visual system relying on cues from part-whole/Gestalt processes to prior semantic knowledge of object categories.

nodes.name: Association fields model grouping via long-range feature-similarity-dependent connections
nodes.description: Visual integration has been proposed to be mediated by association fields, long-range lateral connections in retinotopic visual cortex whose effective connectivity depends on similarity between locally represented features.

nodes.name: Prior modeling work focused on Gestalt cues with clear object boundaries, not natural scenes
nodes.description: Most behavioral and modeling experiments in this domain have focused on Gestalt cues and objects with clear boundaries, not natural contexts where objects are less spatially separated or have unclear contours.

nodes.name: Self-attention in vision transformers resembles association fields and yields emergent grouping
nodes.description: Self-supervised training of transformer models produces object grouping properties, with self-attention forming dynamic contextual connections analogous to association fields; contour integration also emerges and improves with training data/model scale.

nodes.name: Contour integration is a low-level Gestalt cue; naturalistic generalization is untested
nodes.description: Contour integration is a hallmark of human object perception but remains a low-level Gestalt cue, and it remains untested whether these findings extend to naturalistic settings.

nodes.name: This paper tests whether vision foundation models' object grouping aligns with human perception in naturalistic scenes
nodes.description: The paper addresses this gap by testing whether the object grouping properties of vision foundation models align with human object perception, using a naturalistic behavioral benchmark and model representation readouts.

components.description: Positioning against related work on self-supervised transformers and object/part discovery.

nodes.name: Self-distillation objectives (DINO family) yield object-centric attention without labels
nodes.description: Vision transformers trained with self-distillation losses (DINO, DINOv2, DINOv3) develop attention maps containing explicit semantic segmentation information for foreground objects and parts, without label supervision, unlike classification-trained models.

nodes.name: These models also excel at predicting visual-cortex brain activity
nodes.description: Self-distillation-trained models have also been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance predicting brain activity in visual areas responding to complex scenes, further supporting their plausibility as models of human-like visual processing.

nodes.name: MAE learns object-centric features via masked reconstruction
nodes.description: In masked autoencoding, heavy occlusion forces the model to reconstruct the full image from few visible patches, and minimizing this loss enables learning object-centric features useful for downstream tasks.

nodes.name: Unsupervised object/part discovery methods confirm patch-affinity reflects object identity
nodes.description: Methods like LOST and TokenCut use similarity graphs for unsupervised object discovery (successful with one salient object), and other work uses feature similarity for part co-segmentation, corroborating that self-supervised transformers represent object-centric information at the patch level.

nodes.name: Visual-anagram probes show global, configural shape sensitivity emerging across layers
nodes.description: Work using visual anagrams shows self-supervised transformers exhibit strong sensitivity to global part configuration via long-range interactions, transitioning from local to global coding across layers, suggesting integration of spatially distributed part information rather than reliance on local texture alone.

components.description: The two-dot behavioral paradigm design, scaled up from prior small psychophysics studies.

nodes.name: Two-dot same/different object judgment paradigm directly probes grouping
nodes.description: A two-dot paradigm places two dots on an image and has participants indicate by button press whether they lie on the same object or two different objects, with one dot fixed at image center and the other peripheral.

nodes.name: Reaction time indexes grouping difficulty and tracks known Gestalt effects
nodes.description: Reaction time is the primary measure and has been shown to track known perceptual grouping effects such as the same-object advantage and Gestalt cues, supporting its use as a measure of object segmentation difficulty.

nodes.name: Prior work using this paradigm was small-scale or used simple stimuli
nodes.description: Previous two-dot paradigm studies were limited in scale or focused on simpler stimuli, e.g. one prior study used only 24 hand-selected images of two vehicle or animal instances.

nodes.name: This study scales the paradigm to over 1000 trials on naturalistic COCO images
nodes.description: The present work significantly scales up this effort, using naturalistic scenes and collecting over 1000 trials, an order of magnitude beyond prior small-stimulus-set studies.

components.description: Stimulus construction and experimental procedure, ensuring dots fall on well-defined, distance-matched object locations.

nodes.name: Images selected from COCO2017 with center dot always on a well-bounded object
nodes.description: Images were selected from COCO2017 validation using object-level annotations, first requiring an object overlapping the image center (where the center dot was placed) to ensure a well-defined object boundary.

nodes.name: Peripheral markers algorithmically placed with distance matched across same/different conditions
nodes.description: Four peripheral markers (same/different x close/far) were placed algorithmically with distances matched between same and different conditions to prevent judgments based on distance alone, retaining only images with valid locations for all four conditions.

nodes.name: Manual inspection excluded ambiguous or annotation-inaccurate placements, yielding 255 experimental images / 1020 trials
nodes.description: After manual inspection excluding images with dots outside object boundaries or ambiguous intended objects, 288 images remained (32 practice, 256 experimental); one further image was excluded for ambiguous ground truth, leaving 255 experimental images and 1020 trials (255×4 conditions).

nodes.name: Fixation was gaze-tracked and enforced throughout each trial
nodes.description: Participants maintained gaze on the center dot throughout the trial (recorded via EyeLink 1000 eye-tracking at 1000 Hz), with trials terminated on excessive gaze deviation; 7% of trials were excluded due to fixation breaks.

nodes.name: 72 participants, counterbalanced condition assignment, average 90% accuracy
nodes.description: 72 undergraduates (mean age 20.4) participated, with image-to-condition assignment counterbalanced across groups of four participants, and average subject accuracy on the task was 90%.

components.description: Core behavioral findings: same-object advantage and its interaction with dot distance.

nodes.name: Subjects respond faster when dots are on the same object (same-object advantage)
nodes.description: Subjects were faster to respond when the two dots were on the same object than when the peripheral dot was on a different object, an effect known as the same-object advantage, indicating the first dot facilitates selection of the whole object.

nodes.name: Distance effect is specific to the same-object condition
nodes.description: The same-object advantage interacted with dot distance: the fastest RTs occurred in the close-separation same-object condition, whereas dot separation had little effect on RTs when dots were on different objects, consistent with prior work.

nodes.name: Within-condition RT variability reflects finer-grained grouping difficulty factors
nodes.description: Task difficulty and RTs increase with within-object part boundaries, differing textures between dot locations, narrower object parts, proximity to object boundaries, or presence of multiple same-category objects, capturing variable real-world grouping conditions.

components.description: Modeling setup: diverse vision models and the MLP readout used to predict human same/different judgments.

nodes.name: Diverse model set spans Transformer/CNN architectures and self-supervised/supervised/distilled objectives
nodes.description: The study evaluates ViT-Base models trained with self-distillation (DINO, DINOv2, DINOv3), masked autoencoding (MAE), and supervised ImageNet training (with/without IN-21K), alongside ConvNext-Base models trained supervised or distilled from a DINOv3 transformer.

nodes.name: Patch features extracted from final layer/last convolutional layer, matched spatial resolution
nodes.description: Patch features are extracted from the last Transformer layer or last convolutional layer, with convolutional input sizes adjusted so feature-map dimensions match a ViT-Base patch-16 model.

nodes.name: Two-layer MLP readout predicts same/different from concatenated center+peripheral patch features
nodes.description: A two-layer MLP readout is trained to predict same/different responses from the concatenation of central and peripheral patch features, trained on ~30,000 auto-generated trials from COCO2017 training images and evaluated on the 1,020 held-out behavioral trials.

components.description: Grouping-accuracy results: DINO-objective transformers dominate; objective matters more than architecture.

nodes.name: DINOv3 ViT B achieves the highest grouping accuracy (91.9%)
nodes.description: Self-supervised Transformer models trained with the DINO objective achieve the strongest grouping-task performance, with DINOv3 ViT B reaching 91.9% accuracy.

nodes.name: Supervised transformers of identical architecture perform far worse
nodes.description: Supervised Transformer models (IN21k/IN1K ViT B: 72.2%/70.6%) perform considerably lower than DINO models despite sharing the same architecture, suggesting training objective rather than architecture alone drives object-centric representations.

nodes.name: MAE ViT B falls between DINO and supervised models (80.7%)
nodes.description: MAE ViT B's 80.7% grouping accuracy falls between self-supervised DINO models and supervised models, consistent with learning some object-centric structure via reconstruction but not to the same degree as self-distillation.

nodes.name: DINOv3-distilled ConvNext substantially outperforms supervised ConvNext counterparts
nodes.description: Among convolutional models, DINOv3 ConvNext B (86.7%) substantially outperforms its supervised counterparts (IN21k/IN1K ConvNext B: 67.4%/60.0%), further highlighting the quality of DINOv3's dense features regardless of architecture.

components.description: Behavior-prediction (reaction time) results using noise-ceiling-normalized correlation, confirming the grouping-accuracy pattern.

nodes.name: Noise ceiling computed via split-half subject correlation for fair normalization
nodes.description: A human noise ceiling is estimated independently of any model by splitting subjects into two halves 20 times, computing the Spearman correlation of mean RTs between halves each time, and averaging; model-human correlations are then normalized by this ceiling.

nodes.name: DINOv3 ViT B again achieves the highest normalized behavioral alignment
nodes.description: The same DINO-objective advantage observed in the grouping task holds for RT prediction: self-supervised DINO-trained transformers achieve the strongest behavioral alignment, with DINOv3 ViT B reaching the highest normalized Spearman correlation among all models.

nodes.name: Supervised models again show weaker alignment; MAE intermediate; ConvNext weakest except DINOv3-distilled
nodes.description: Supervised models show considerably weaker alignment despite identical architecture, MAE ViT B falls intermediate, and convolutional models are weakest overall except for the DINOv3 ConvNext B exception, mirroring the grouping-accuracy ordering.

nodes.name: DINOv3 ViT B's predicted RTs reproduce the same-object advantage and same-object distance effect
nodes.description: The mean RTs predicted by DINOv3 ViT B, broken down by condition, reproduce the same-object advantage and the distance effect specific to the same-object condition observed in human behavior, confirming the model captures the qualitative structure of grouping behavior.

components.description: Object-centric affinity/ROC metric: definition, layer/head analysis, and its role in explaining alignment.

nodes.name: Affinity maps and ROC analysis quantify how well patch similarity tracks true object boundaries
nodes.description: Affinity maps are computed via cosine similarity between a patch's feature and all other patches; ROC analysis across trials computes TPR (within-object patches above threshold) and FPR (outside-object patches above threshold) across a range of similarity thresholds.

nodes.name: TPR rises sharply before FPR for DINOv3, indicating strong object-centric signal
nodes.description: In a sample trial, TPR increases substantially as the threshold decreases while FPR remains low, and only once TPR is high does FPR begin to rise, reflecting a strong object-centric signal in DINOv3's affinity map.

nodes.name: Object-centric structure strengthens in deeper DINOv3 layers
nodes.description: ROC curves across all 12 DINOv3 ViT B layers show deeper layers have progressively stronger object-centric structure (higher AUC).

nodes.name: Object-centricity is broadly distributed across attention heads in the last layer
nodes.description: ROC curves across the 12 attention heads of DINOv3's last layer show broadly similar object-centricity across heads, each contributing similarly to patch-level object representation.

nodes.name: AUC-based model comparison replicates the DINO-objective ordering seen in behavior
nodes.description: Comparing last-layer AUC across all evaluated models, self-supervised DINO-trained models achieve the highest object-centricity, DINOv3 ViT B leading, followed by DINOv2 ViT B, with supervised models progressively weaker and MAE intermediate, mirroring the grouping-accuracy/behavioral-alignment ordering; DINOv3 ConvNext B again substantially outperforms supervised ConvNext counterparts.

nodes.name: Object-centric AUC strongly predicts behavioral alignment across models (r=0.950)
nodes.description: Across all 9 models, object-centricity AUC correlates strongly with noise-normalized behavioral alignment (Spearman r=0.950, p=0.0001), a relationship holding across both Transformer and convolutional architectures, suggesting object-centricity is a general principle linking representations to human perceptual behavior.

components.description: Gram matrix alignment intervention: distilling pairwise similarity structure into supervised models improves all three metrics.

nodes.name: The Gram matrix captures pairwise patch similarity structure, revealing object-block patterns
nodes.description: The Gram matrix is the full (h×w)×(h×w) pairwise cosine-similarity matrix across patch tokens; in models with strong object-centric representations, same-object patches show higher mutual similarity, producing block-like structure reflecting object boundaries.

nodes.name: Four supervised models are fine-tuned to distill DINOv3's Gram matrix structure while retaining classification training
nodes.description: IN21k ViT B, IN1K ViT B, IN21k ConvNext B, and IN1K ConvNext B are fine-tuned on ImageNet classification while simultaneously distilling the Gram matrix structure from DINOv3 ViT B.

nodes.name: Gram alignment improves grouping accuracy by 8-18 percentage points across all four models
nodes.description: Gram alignment consistently improves grouping accuracy across all four fine-tuned models, with gains ranging from approximately 8 to 18 percentage points.

nodes.name: Gram alignment raises object-centric AUC close to self-supervised DINO levels
nodes.description: Object-centric AUC improves substantially and consistently after Gram alignment for all four models, approaching the AUC values of self-supervised DINO models.

nodes.name: Gram alignment improves behavioral alignment, with larger gains for Transformers than ConvNext
nodes.description: Behavioral alignment with human RTs improves across all four Gram-aligned models, though the two Transformer models show larger gains than the ConvNext models across all three metrics.

nodes.name: Transformer architecture is more responsive to Gram alignment, plausibly due to self-attention already encoding pairwise relations
nodes.description: The Transformer architecture's greater responsiveness to Gram matrix alignment suggests the self-attention mechanism provides a particularly natural substrate for encoding pairwise patch relationships, unlike convolutional architectures.

nodes.name: Gram alignment gains hold even without large-scale pretraining
nodes.description: The gains from Gram alignment are substantial even for models without large-scale pretraining, suggesting Gram alignment can partially compensate for the absence of large dataset training, particularly in Transformer models.

nodes.name: Finding converges with DINOv3's own use of Gram anchoring to improve dense feature quality
nodes.description: The improvement from matching Gram matrix structure converges with the independent prior finding that Gram anchoring improves DINOv3's own dense feature quality, pointing to feature correlation structure across patches as a key mechanism underlying human-like object representations.

components.description: Conclusion synthesis: theoretical implications, model-design guidance, and the remaining gap to human performance.

nodes.name: Self-supervised transformers implicitly instantiate classical feature-similarity binding principles
nodes.description: Classical perceptual-grouping theories emphasize feature similarity in binding image regions into objects (Gestalt principles, association fields, lateral connectivity); the results show self-supervised transformers implement a similar computational principle where same-object patches develop highly similar representations.

nodes.name: Emergent alignment supports self-supervised objectives as better approximations of perceptual organization than supervised classification
nodes.description: The emergent alignment between self-supervised training objectives and human object perception supports the view that these objectives better approximate the organizational principles of perception than supervised classification.

nodes.name: A gap remains between best models and the human noise ceiling
nodes.description: Despite strong alignment, a gap nonetheless remains between the best-performing model and the human noise ceiling, leaving room for future models to close this distance.

nodes.name: Training objective is a major factor beyond architecture for object-centric representations
nodes.description: The consistent advantage of DINO-trained models over supervised counterparts with identical architectures demonstrates that training objective is a major factor beyond architecture alone, though DINOv3 ConvNext B's strong performance shows convolutional architectures can also instantiate such representations.

nodes.name: Perfect object-centricity is not the goal; behaviorally aligned models likely balance object organization and fine-grained feature sensitivity
nodes.description: Representations entirely organized around object boundaries would resemble semantic segmentation maps, losing fine-grained feature structure useful for other visual tasks; the most behaviorally aligned models may strike an optimal balance between object-level organization and feature sensitivity.

nodes.name: Path to more perceptually aligned models lies in shaping representational similarity structure, not scaling classification objectives
nodes.description: The Gram alignment finding suggests the path toward more perceptually aligned vision models lies not in scaling classification objectives but in explicitly shaping the similarity structure of learned representations to reflect object-level organization of natural scenes.

isolated_nodes.name: RT patterns hold whether or not incorrect trials are included
isolated_nodes.description: Analyses were reported only for correct trials, but the same behavioral patterns were largely observed when both correct and incorrect trials were included.

isolated_nodes.name: A CLS-token distillation baseline is used to isolate Gram structure as the active ingredient
isolated_nodes.description: A separate CLS token distillation baseline, isolating Gram structure specifically as the active ingredient behind the observed improvements, is reported in the supplementary results section.

correction_notes: Initial graph build (not a correction pass). Evidence uses paraphrase-anchored tags (E<n>) since no sentence-indexed source was provided. Edges follow explicit motivational/derivational language ('we pose our question', 'this allows us to', 'by combining', ablation-style comparisons to prior bounds). Two independent theoretical tracks (sub-Weibull SsGD; p-BCM clipped-SsGD) are kept as separate components since the paper studies them as parallel, largely independent contributions sharing only background/motivation.

nodes.name: Weakly convex definition
nodes.description: A function f is rho-weakly convex iff f(x) + (rho/2)||x||^2 is convex, for rho >= 0.

nodes.name: Composition proposition
nodes.description: The composition of an L-Lipschitz convex function h and a beta-smooth function c is a beta*L-weakly convex function.

nodes.name: Weakly convex includes Lipschitz-convex and smooth
nodes.description: By letting h and c be the identity function, weakly convex functions include all Lipschitz continuous convex functions and smooth functions.

nodes.name: Neural net loss connection
nodes.description: The composition function structure connects to neural network architecture: the sample loss of a network with sigmoid/tanh activations and logistic loss is weakly convex while being non-convex and non-smooth.

nodes.name: Prior weakly convex analyses assume light-tailed noise
nodes.description: Prior works on SFOM convergence in weakly convex optimization key on the gradient noise being variance-bounded or sub-Gaussian (light-tailed).

nodes.name: Empirical evidence of heavy-tailed gradient noise
nodes.description: Recent observations empirically show gradient noise distributions may be heavy-tailed, in training CNNs and BERT.

nodes.name: Motivation for weaker noise assumptions
nodes.description: These observations motivate assuming gradient noises satisfy weaker assumptions than variance boundedness or sub-Gaussianity.

nodes.name: Paper considers heavy-tailed noise in weakly convex optimization
nodes.description: The paper considers heavy-tailed gradient noises in weakly convex optimization.

nodes.name: Sub-Weibull definition
nodes.description: X follows sigma-sub-Weibull(theta) if E[exp((|X|/sigma)^(1/theta))] <= 2, with tail parameter theta >= 1/2.

nodes.name: Sub-Weibull generalizes sub-Gaussian/sub-exponential
nodes.description: Sub-Weibull is more general than sub-Gaussian; theta=1/2 reduces to sub-Gaussian, theta=1 corresponds to sub-exponential, and heavier tails occur as theta increases.

nodes.name: Prior sub-Weibull SFOM work limited to smooth/convex
nodes.description: Prior works studying high-probability convergence of SFOMs under sub-Weibull noise have done so in smooth optimization.

nodes.name: Gap: sub-Weibull SsGD for weakly convex unknown
nodes.description: For stochastic weakly convex optimization under sub-Weibull noise, whether SGD/SsGD exhibits worse dependence on iterations and failure probability than in the smooth case is unknown (Q1).

nodes.name: SGD becomes SsGD under non-differentiability
nodes.description: Due to possible non-differentiability of weakly convex functions, the SGD method specifically refers to stochastic sub-gradient descent (SsGD).

nodes.name: p-BCM definition
nodes.description: A centralized random vector X has bounded p-th central moment if E[||X||^p] <= sigma^p for p in (1,2].

nodes.name: p-BCM strictly weaker than variance-bounded
nodes.description: If gradient noise satisfies p-BCM for p<2, the second central moment could be infinite, so p-BCM is strictly weaker than variance-boundedness.

nodes.name: Vanilla SGD may diverge under p-BCM
nodes.description: For p in (1,2), existing theory shows vanilla SGD may diverge under p-BCM noise, making this case much more complicated.

nodes.name: Gradient clipping enables convergence under p-BCM
nodes.description: Prior works demonstrate that through gradient clipping (restricting stochastic gradient norm to a threshold), SFOMs can be proven to converge under p-BCM noise in smooth or convex optimization.

nodes.name: Extension to weakly convex motivated
nodes.description: The demonstrated success of clipping in smooth/convex settings motivates extending the analysis to the weakly convex scenario.

nodes.name: Gap: clipped-SGD weakly convex high-probability under p-BCM unknown
nodes.description: Whether clipped-SGD exhibits worse dependence on iterations and failure probability than the smooth case for weakly convex optimization under p-BCM noise is unknown (Q2).

nodes.name: Theorem 1: sub-Weibull SsGD high-probability rate
nodes.description: Under Assumptions 3.1-3.5, projected SsGD achieves stated high-probability convergence bounds on the Moreau-envelope gradient norm for theta=1/2, theta in (1/2,1], and theta>1.

nodes.name: Rate matches smooth case (theta general)
nodes.description: The dependence on iteration number and failure probability delta in the O(1/sqrt(T)) unknown-horizon rate aligns with that of the smooth case in prior work.

nodes.name: No degradation conclusion (Q1 answer)
nodes.description: Under sub-Weibull noise, the theoretical convergence rate of SGD/SsGD for non-convex, non-smooth yet weakly convex objectives does not degrade compared to the smooth case.

nodes.name: Degradation as theta increases
nodes.description: As theta increases (heavier tail), the iteration complexity of SsGD deteriorates, consistent with empirical observations of SsGD handling heavy-tailed noise.

nodes.name: Extra log(1/delta)log(T/delta)^(theta-1) term for theta>1
nodes.description: When theta>1, an extra term log(1/delta)log(T/delta)^(theta-1) emerges in the upper bound complexity.

nodes.name: Sub-Weibull Freedman inequality use
nodes.description: The extra term for theta>1 arises because the analysis employs the sub-Weibull Freedman inequality (an extension of the sub-Gaussian Freedman inequality).

nodes.name: Gamma-function coefficient grows large
nodes.description: The constant coefficient preceding sigma^2 in the theta>1 case is Gamma(3theta+1), which grows extremely large as theta increases.

nodes.name: SsGD performs poorly for theta>1 conclusion
nodes.description: Despite the noise-norm square remaining bounded, SsGD performs poorly with sigma-sub-Weibull(theta)-type noise when theta>1, due to the large Gamma-function coefficient.

nodes.name: Corollary 1: fixed eta_t = gamma/sqrt(t)
nodes.description: Setting eta_t = gamma/sqrt(t) in Theorem 1 yields explicit O(1/sqrt(T)) rates for each theta regime.

nodes.name: Reduces to deterministic case when sigma=0
nodes.description: Corollary 1's result reduces to the deterministic rate O((Delta_1 + rho*G^2*logT)/sqrt(T)) when sigma=0 for any theta>1.

nodes.name: theta=1/2 aligns with Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2018b)
nodes.description: For theta=1/2 (sub-Gaussian case), disregarding log(1/delta) and logT, the result aligns with the in-expectation results in Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2018b).

nodes.name: Comparison to Madden 2020 / Li and Liu 2022 (non-convex smooth)
nodes.description: For theta>=1/2, the results share the same order of T and log(1/delta) as prior high-probability bounds for non-convex smooth SGD under sub-Weibull noise.

nodes.name: Key difference: G-Lipschitz condition needed
nodes.description: Unlike Li and Liu (2022), which only requires eta_t||grad f(x_t)||<=G, this analysis (like Madden et al. 2020) relies on a globally bounded (sub-)gradient norm, because weakly convex analysis via Moreau envelopes makes it difficult to remove the G-Lipschitz condition.

nodes.name: Corollary 2: fixed time-horizon T with tuned step-size
nodes.description: Fixing the time horizon T and assuming access to parameters Delta_1, G, sigma allows a refined step-size choice and tighter bound than Corollary 1.

nodes.name: Deterministic reduction (sigma=0)
nodes.description: When sigma=0, Corollary 2's bound reduces to the deterministic case O(sqrt(rho*Delta_1*G^2/T)).

nodes.name: Alignment with Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2018b) at theta=1/2
nodes.description: For theta=1/2, ignoring the log(1/delta) factor, the iteration complexity aligns with the in-expectation result in Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2018b).

nodes.name: Similarity to Liu et al. (2023a)
nodes.description: For theta=1/2, the result is similar to the high-probability convergence of SsGD for convex, G-Lipschitz functions with unbounded constrained domain in Liu et al. (2023a).

nodes.name: log(T/delta) persists for theta>1 even with fixed T
nodes.description: Even with constant step-size and fixed time horizon T, a log(T/delta) term still emerges for theta>1.

nodes.name: log(T/delta) dependency may be inherent to sub-Weibull noise
nodes.description: The persistence of log(T/delta) for theta>1 despite fixing T suggests this dependency may be inherent to sub-Weibull-type gradient noise rather than an artifact of the analysis technique.

nodes.name: Lemma 1: fundamental descent inequality
nodes.description: For projection-SsGD, a descent-type inequality bounds eta_t||grad f_{1/rho-bar}(x_t)||^2 in terms of Delta_t - Delta_{t+1} plus a martingale-type inner product term and noise terms.

nodes.name: Distinction from L-smooth descent lemma
nodes.description: Lemma 1 is analogous to the descent lemma for L-smooth functions, but the inner product term involves x-hat_t - x_t rather than x_{t+1} - x_t.

nodes.name: Martingale term cannot be ignored in high-probability analysis
nodes.description: Unlike in-expectation analysis where the martingale term has zero expectation and can be ignored, high-probability analysis requires concentration inequalities to bound it.

nodes.name: Sub-Weibull has no MGF for theta>1
nodes.description: Bakhshizadeh et al. (2022) proved a sub-Weibull random variable does not have a moment generating function when theta>1, making concentration inequalities challenging to establish.

nodes.name: Bernstein-type concentration inequality (Madden et al. 2024)
nodes.description: Madden et al. (2024) developed a Bernstein-type concentration inequality extending the Freedman sub-Gaussian inequality, which can be applied despite the MGF non-existence issue.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 derived from concentration inequality
nodes.description: A usable concentration lemma (Lemma 2) for sums of sub-Weibull martingale differences is directly derived from the Madden et al. (2024) inequality.

nodes.name: Need to bound rho-bar*eta_t*||x-hat_t - x_t||*sigma by M_t
nodes.description: Applying Lemma 2 requires the term rho-bar*eta_t*||x-hat_t - x_t||*sigma to be upper-bounded by M_t when theta>1/2.

nodes.name: Lemma 3: Moreau envelope displacement bound
nodes.description: For a rho-weakly convex function, the displacement ||x-hat - x|| is bounded by 2||g||/(rho-bar - rho) for g in the sub-differential.

nodes.name: Combining Lemma 3 and G-Lipschitz bounds the needed quantity
nodes.description: Combining Lemma 3 with the G-Lipschitz Assumption 3.3 upper-bounds rho-bar*eta_t*||x-hat_t-x_t||*sigma, enabling application of the concentration inequality.

nodes.name: Concentration inequality bounds the martingale term
nodes.description: This allows bounding rho-bar*eta_t*<x_{t+1}-x_t, xi_t> by O(eta_t^2 ||grad f_{1/rho-bar}(x_t)||^2), which acts as a descent term.

nodes.name: Telescoping yields Delta_1 bound
nodes.description: By telescoping the sum, Delta_t - Delta_{t+1} can be upper-bounded by Delta_1.

flagged_edges: P60->P25 links the proof-sketch component to the theorem-statement component; included since the proof sketch is explicitly presented as sketching Theorem 1's derivation.

nodes.name: Clipping introduced for p-BCM setting
nodes.description: The clipping technique is introduced because existing works have shown vanilla SsGD may diverge when p in (1,2) under the p-BCM assumption.

nodes.name: Theorem 2: clipped-SsGD high-probability rate (unknown horizon)
nodes.description: Under Assumptions 3.1-3.4 and 3.6, with specified lambda_t and eta_t, projected clipped-SsGD achieves a stated high-probability bound on the average squared Moreau-envelope gradient norm.

nodes.name: Rate is O(T^{(1-p)/p}) regardless of sigma known
nodes.description: The high-probability convergence rate is O(T^{(1-p)/p}) in T regardless of whether sigma is known.

nodes.name: Deterministic reduction reduces to vanilla GD
nodes.description: When sigma=0, the step-size and clipping level simplify so that Algorithm 2 reduces to the vanilla projected GD method with rate O(1/sqrt(T)).

nodes.name: log T attributed to time-varying step-size
nodes.description: The emergence of log T in Theorem 2 is solely attributed to the use of a time-varying step-size.

nodes.name: Theorem 3: fixed time-horizon removes log T
nodes.description: By fixing the time horizon T (Theorem 3), the log T factor present in Theorem 2 can be eliminated, yielding dependence log(1/delta) instead of log(T/delta).

nodes.name: Improved delta-dependence vs Hong and Lin (2025)
nodes.description: The log(1/delta) dependence in Theorem 3 is more optimal than the log(T/delta) dependence in Hong and Lin (2025), which analyzes AdaGrad-norm for weakly convex, G-Lipschitz functions with sub-Gaussian noise.

nodes.name: Theorem 4/5: in-expectation upper bounds
nodes.description: In-expectation upper bounds for mini-batch clipped-SsGD in weakly convex optimization under p-BCM noise are derived, paralleling Theorems 2 and 3 (Theorem 5 fixes T to remove log(eT)).

nodes.name: Sample complexity O(eps^{-2p/(p-1)})
nodes.description: From Theorem 5, finding an eps-stationary point (in expectation) requires at most O(eps^{-2p/(p-1)}) sub-gradient evaluations.

nodes.name: Zhang et al. (2020b) lower bound for smooth L-smooth case
nodes.description: Zhang et al. (2020b) showed the sample-complexity lower bound for any stochastic algorithm under p-BCM noise when minimizing L-smooth functions cannot be lower than Omega(eps^{-(3p-2)/(p-1)}).

nodes.name: Derived sample complexity exceeds the smooth lower bound
nodes.description: The paper's sample complexity O(eps^{-2p/(p-1)}) exceeds (is worse than) the Zhang et al. (2020b) lower bound for L-smooth optimization.

nodes.name: No existing lower bound for weakly convex under p-BCM
nodes.description: No existing work provides a lower sample complexity (or convergence rate) for SFOMs under the p-BCM assumption when minimizing weakly convex functions.

nodes.name: Unclear whether weakly convex shares smooth lower bound
nodes.description: It remains unclear whether stochastic gradient methods for non-smooth, non-convex yet weakly convex functions enjoy the same lower sample complexity as smooth functions.

nodes.name: Results still valuable despite apparent suboptimality
nodes.description: Given the unresolved lower-bound question, the authors argue their results still demonstrate value for weakly convex optimization even though the rate may not seem optimal compared to L-smooth optimization results.

nodes.name: Hu et al. (2025) prior in-expectation result
nodes.description: Hu et al. (2025) provided the first in-expectation convergence analysis for clipped-SGD under p-BCM noise in weakly convex optimization, in a distributed setting.

nodes.name: Hu et al. (2025) lacks concrete rate
nodes.description: Hu et al. (2025) only provides a general in-expectation upper bound without specifying convergence rate/complexity or concrete choices of eta_t and lambda_t, limiting practical insight.

nodes.name: Hu et al. (2025) clipping level cannot adapt to sigma
nodes.description: In Hu et al. (2025), the clipping level lambda_t cannot adapt to sigma; convergence requires lambda_t increasing to infinity regardless of whether sigma=0.

nodes.name: This paper's lambda_t adapts to sigma
nodes.description: In this paper's analysis, lambda_t is set to max{sigma*t^{1/p}, 2G}, which is fixed at 2G when sigma=0, so clipping has no effect and clipped-SsGD reduces to vanilla GD in that case.

nodes.name: Hu et al. (2025) example achieves only O(1/logT)
nodes.description: Hu et al. (2025) give an example with eta_t=1/(t+1), lambda_t=2G(t+1)^0.4, achieving convergence rate O(1/logT).

nodes.name: This paper's rate is significantly better
nodes.description: The O(1/logT) rate from Hu et al. (2025)'s example is significantly worse than this paper's O(T^{-(p-1)/p}) rate for any p in (1,2].

nodes.name: This paper additionally provides high-probability bounds
nodes.description: Unlike Hu et al. (2025), which only gives in-expectation guarantees, this paper establishes high-probability upper bounds for non-smooth weakly convex clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise, inspired by prior high-probability analyses in smooth/convex settings.

nodes.name: High-probability bounds more practical
nodes.description: High-probability bounds are argued to be more practical for real-world applications compared to in-expectation upper bounds.

nodes.name: Unbiased clipped gradient no longer holds
nodes.description: Unlike unclipped SsGD, the clipped stochastic sub-gradient g_t is no longer an unbiased estimator of the sub-gradient of f at x_t.

nodes.name: Martingale term challenge under clipping
nodes.description: Because clipping introduces bias, the inner-product term in the descent inequality is not a martingale, complicating the high-probability analysis.

nodes.name: Bias-variance decomposition of xi_t
nodes.description: The noise term xi_t is decomposed into an unbiased part xi_t^u and a biased part xi_t^b, following Cutkosky and Mehta (2021).

nodes.name: Decomposition restores a martingale term
nodes.description: After decomposition, the term involving xi_t^u is a martingale, allowing concentration inequalities to bound its summation again.

nodes.name: Lemma 4: bounds on xi_t^u and xi_t^b
nodes.description: For lambda_t >= 2G, explicit bounds on ||xi_t^u||, ||xi_t^b||, and their second moments are established in terms of sigma, lambda_t, B, and p.

nodes.name: Trade-off between xi_t^u and xi_t^b via lambda_t
nodes.description: Increasing lambda_t increases the norm of xi_t^u while decreasing the norm of xi_t^b, motivating a careful choice of lambda_t to balance the two.

nodes.name: Setting eta_t*lambda_t <= eta_0 balances terms
nodes.description: Following Liu and Zhou (2023), bounding eta_t*lambda_t <= eta_0 balances the orders of xi_t^u and xi_t^b and is important for applying concentration inequalities to the martingale terms.

isolated_nodes.name: SFOM definition
isolated_nodes.description: Stochastic first-order optimization methods use unbiased or biased estimators of the true gradient to improve training efficiency, unlike deterministic gradient-based methods.

isolated_nodes.name: High-probability vs in-expectation convergence
isolated_nodes.description: High-probability convergence bounds the iterations/oracle calls needed so that a single run satisfies the target accuracy with probability at least 1-delta, and is more informative for practical single-run applications than in-expectation convergence.

isolated_nodes.name: Fréchet sub-differential definition
isolated_nodes.description: The Fréchet sub-differential extends the classical convex sub-differential/gradient to non-smooth, non-convex functions via a liminf inequality condition.

isolated_nodes.name: Fréchet sub-gradient reduces to standard cases
isolated_nodes.description: If f is convex, the Fréchet sub-differential reduces to the classical convex sub-differential; if f is differentiable, it collapses to the singleton gradient set.

isolated_nodes.name: Moreau envelope definition
isolated_nodes.description: For a rho-weakly convex f, its Moreau envelope f_{1/rho-bar} is defined via a proximal minimization with rho-bar > rho.

isolated_nodes.name: Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2018b) originates Moreau envelope approach
isolated_nodes.description: Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2018b) were first to use the gradient of the Moreau envelope of a weakly convex function to analyze convergence of the stochastic sub-gradient method.

isolated_nodes.name: Moreau envelope properties enable stationarity via nearby point
isolated_nodes.description: If the Moreau envelope gradient norm at x is small, there exists a nearby point x-hat that is approximately stationary for f, motivating use of the Moreau envelope gradient as the convergence measure.

isolated_nodes.name: Assumptions 3.1-3.6 listed
isolated_nodes.description: Standard assumptions are stated: weak convexity (3.1), existence of finite local minimum (3.2), bounded sub-gradient norm G (3.3), unbiased oracle (3.4), sub-Weibull noise (3.5), p-BCM noise (3.6).

isolated_nodes.name: Algorithm 1: projected SsGD
isolated_nodes.description: The projected SsGD algorithm iterates x_{t+1} = Proj_X(x_t - eta_t g_t) using an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle.

isolated_nodes.name: Algorithm 2: projected clipped-SsGD
isolated_nodes.description: The projected clipped-SsGD algorithm additionally computes a mini-batch gradient estimate and clips its norm to a threshold lambda_t before the projected update.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: sub-Weibull SFOM survey
isolated_nodes.description: Multiple prior works (Madden et al. 2020, Li and Liu 2022, Liu et al. 2022, Liu and Zhou 2024, Li et al. 2025, Ospina et al. 2022, Yu et al. 2025, Chen et al. 2025) studied SFOM convergence under sub-Weibull noise in convex/smooth/online/distributed settings.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: p-BCM clipped-SFOM survey
isolated_nodes.description: Multiple prior works (Zhang et al. 2020b, Cutkosky and Mehta 2021, Nguyen et al. 2023, Sadiev et al. 2023, Gorbunov et al. 2024, Liu and Zhou 2023, Liu et al. 2023b, Chezhegov et al. 2025a/b, Li and Liu 2023) studied clipped-SFOM convergence under p-BCM noise in smooth/convex/non-convex settings.

isolated_nodes.name: Zhang et al. (2020b) strongly convex lower bound
isolated_nodes.description: Zhang et al. (2020b) also shows that for strongly convex optimization under p-BCM noise, no SFOM can converge faster than Omega(T^{-2(p-1)/p}).

isolated_nodes.name: Vural et al. (2022) convex lower bound
isolated_nodes.description: Vural et al. (2022) establishes that for convex optimization under p-BCM noise, any SFOM's convergence rate is bounded below by Omega(T^{-(p-1)/p}).

isolated_nodes.name: No prior lower bounds for weakly convex heavy-tailed
isolated_nodes.description: No existing work has established lower bounds on the convergence rate of SFOMs under heavy-tailed noises for weakly convex optimization.

isolated_nodes.name: Liu et al. (2024) related online setting
isolated_nodes.description: Liu et al. (2024) developed a first-order online optimization algorithm with high-probability convergence under p-BCM noise for non-smooth, non-convex online optimization, but still requires continuous differentiability.

isolated_nodes.name: Contribution summary: sub-Weibull SsGD rate
isolated_nodes.description: The paper establishes the first high-probability convergence rate of SsGD for weakly convex optimization under sub-Weibull noise.

isolated_nodes.name: Contribution summary: p-BCM clipped-SsGD rate
isolated_nodes.description: The paper establishes the first high-probability convergence rate of mini-batch clipped-SsGD for weakly convex optimization under p-BCM noise, with delta-dependence O(log(T/delta)) consistent with prior smooth-optimization work.

isolated_nodes.name: log T eliminable by fixing horizon in both analyses
isolated_nodes.description: In both the high-probability and in-expectation analyses, the logarithmic term log T can be eliminated by fixing the time horizon T.

structural_reasoning: The graph separates the paper's two parallel theoretical tracks (sub-Weibull SsGD: C3, C5, C6, C7, C8; p-BCM clipped-SsGD: C4, C9, C10, C11, C12) which share only background motivation (C1, C2) and are not otherwise causally linked, matching how the paper itself frames them as answering two independent research questions (Q1, Q2). Proof-sketch components (C8, C12) are kept separate from the theorem-statement components they support, with a single connecting edge (P60->P25) rather than merging them, since the proof sketch is explicitly presented as a derivation route rather than additional claims. Comparison-to-prior-work nodes (C6, C7, C10, C11) are attached where the text makes an explicit comparative or explanatory claim (e.g. 'aligns with', 'is significantly worse than', 'is more optimal than'); background survey material (related-work lists, standard definitions, assumption statements, algorithm listings) is left isolated since it is descriptive scaffolding rather than a premise feeding a specific downstream inference. All edges are single_run confidence since this is a single extraction pass with no multi-run voting.

note_on_evidence: Evidence fields cite paper sections/subsections/theorems/definitions rather than sentence indices, since a sentence-indexed source was not available for this document.

components.name: Motivation: gap between expressivity and learnability in neural algorithmic reasoning

nodes.name: MPNNs are a natural NAR backbone
nodes.description: MPNNs' close correspondence with iterative, local graph computation makes them a natural architectural backbone for learning graph algorithms such as shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, and dynamic programming.

nodes.name: Prior NAR theory is either empirical or purely expressivity-focused
nodes.description: Existing theoretical work on neural algorithmic reasoning is either purely empirical, lacking formal guarantees, or focuses on existential expressivity questions (which algorithms can in principle be represented), abstracting away the learning process.

nodes.name: Expressivity analyses give little insight into generalization
nodes.description: Expressivity-focused analyses provide little insight into sample efficiency or generalization beyond the training distribution, so they do not explain when learned models provably generalize to larger or structurally different graphs.

nodes.name: Nerem et al. [2025] is a notable exception but limited
nodes.description: Nerem et al. [2025] provides theoretical learning guarantees for MPNNs, but is restricted to a single algorithm (Bellman-Ford) and enforces correctness via a non-differentiable regularization term, limiting applicability to broader algorithm classes and standard gradient-based training.

nodes.name: Need for a general, differentiable learning framework
nodes.description: These limitations motivate developing a general theoretical framework for learning algorithms with MPNNs that covers a broad class of algorithms while remaining compatible with fully differentiable training objectives.

components.name: Regularization-induced extrapolation framework (finite Lipschitz classes, Theorem 3)

nodes.name: Finite Lipschitz class defined
nodes.description: A hypothesis class is a finite Lipschitz class if there exists a pseudo-metric on the input space such that every hypothesis is Lipschitz with a finite (certifiable) constant, and the space has finite covering number for every epsilon > 0.

nodes.name: Lipschitz certificate concept
nodes.description: A Lipschitz certificate is a computable upper bound on a hypothesis's true (possibly intractable) Lipschitz constant, derivable directly from the hypothesis's parameters (e.g., via operator-norm bounds).

nodes.name: Regularization term defined via certificate gap
nodes.description: The regularization term is defined as a scaled ReLU of the gap between the hypothesis's Lipschitz certificate and the target function's Lipschitz certificate.

nodes.name: Theorem 3: regularized empirical loss implies uniform approximation
nodes.description: For a finite Lipschitz class with certificates and a Lipschitz target approximable with a certificate, there exists a dataset of bounded, computable size such that sufficiently small regularized loss on that dataset implies the learned hypothesis approximates the target uniformly over the entire input space, including larger instances than seen in training.

nodes.name: Certificate control, not true Lipschitz constant, is the key requirement
nodes.description: The key assumption in Theorem 3 is that the computable Lipschitz certificate of the learned hypothesis stays controlled, not that its true (possibly intractable) Lipschitz constant does, making the regularizer practically usable even when the true constant is unknown.

nodes.name: Distinguishability is a necessary condition for learnability under Theorem 3
nodes.description: If Theorem 3's conclusion holds, then whenever the hypothesis class cannot distinguish two inputs, the target function must also assign them the same value, restricting uniform learnability to targets whose distinguishing power does not exceed the model class's.

components.name: MPNN aggregation satisfies finite Lipschitzness, enabling learnability of specific algorithms

nodes.name: Theorem 4: normalized-sum, mean, and max/min aggregation MPNNs satisfy finite Lipschitzness
nodes.description: The hypothesis class induced by MPNNs using normalized sum aggregation, mean aggregation, or max/min aggregation satisfies the finite Lipschitz class definition, with max/min aggregation being the first architectures given explicit Lipschitzness guarantees despite widespread use of related stability arguments.

nodes.name: Finite Lipschitzness plus Theorem 3 yields learnability for expressible algorithms
nodes.description: Given Theorem 4 (finite Lipschitzness of these MPNN classes) and Theorem 3 (regularized loss implies uniform approximation), any graph algorithm expressible by one of these MPNN architectures is learnable from finite data with extrapolation to arbitrary graph size.

nodes.name: Truncated PageRank exactly representable by mean-aggregation MPNN
nodes.description: The K-truncated weighted PageRank recurrence is represented exactly by a K-layer mean-aggregation MPNN, with the update function matching the PageRank recursion term for term.

nodes.name: PageRank truncation depth is size-independent
nodes.description: Because PageRank is a contraction with factor equal to the damping factor, the truncation depth K needed for a given error epsilon depends only on epsilon and the damping factor, not on the number of vertices in the graph.

nodes.name: Truncated PageRank is learnable and extrapolates to arbitrary graph size
nodes.description: Because truncated PageRank is representable by a mean-aggregation MPNN (finite Lipschitz class) with size-independent truncation depth, Theorem 3 implies a finite training set with regularization suffices to learn it and extrapolate to graphs of arbitrary size with error independent of graph size.

nodes.name: Bellman-Ford exactly representable by min-aggregation MPNN
nodes.description: The K-step Bellman-Ford recurrence for single-source shortest paths is represented exactly by a K-layer min-aggregation MPNN, with the update function implementing the identity and the aggregation function implementing the Bellman-Ford relaxation step.

nodes.name: Required Bellman-Ford iteration count is diameter-bounded
nodes.description: The number of iterations K needed to compute shortest paths is at most the graph diameter, which is independent of graph size for bounded-diameter graph families.

nodes.name: Bellman-Ford is learnable and extrapolates to arbitrary graph size
nodes.description: Because Bellman-Ford is representable by a min-aggregation MPNN (finite Lipschitz class) with diameter-bounded iteration count, Theorem 3 implies a finite training set with regularization can train an MPNN to learn Bellman-Ford and extrapolate to graphs of arbitrary size.

nodes.name: Generalized Bellman-Ford invariants also fall in finite Lipschitz classes
nodes.description: A generalized Bellman-Ford algorithm based on path formulations captures invariants such as the Katz index, widest path, and most reliable path, which can likewise be represented by mean/max-aggregation MPNNs and thus fall into a finite Lipschitz hypothesis class.

nodes.name: Dynamic programs reducible to shortest-path problems on transformed graphs
nodes.description: Many dynamic programming problems, including the 0-1 knapsack problem, can be cast as a shortest-path problem on a suitably constructed (transformed) directed acyclic graph.

nodes.name: Knapsack recurrence exactly representable by min-aggregation MPNN with layers = number of items
nodes.description: The standard knapsack recurrence is exactly the shortest-path relaxation on the transformed graph, representable by a min-aggregation MPNN with K equal to the number of items n, using the same identity/relaxation update as Bellman-Ford.

nodes.name: Bounded-stage dynamic programs are learnable and extrapolate to arbitrary problem size
nodes.description: For families where the number of dynamic-programming stages n is bounded (so K is independent of the transformed graph's size, which grows with capacity), the finite Lipschitzness result implies learnability from a finite training set with extrapolation to arbitrarily large problem instances (e.g., knapsack capacities), and the same reasoning extends to other DP problems like longest increasing subsequence or edit distance.

components.name: Improved, explicit training-set guarantee for Bellman-Ford (Theorem 5)

nodes.name: General framework does not give explicit training set construction
nodes.description: The general finite-Lipschitz-class results demonstrate existence of a finite training set for learning various algorithms, but do not explicitly show how to construct this training set or bound its size.

nodes.name: Explicit constant-size training set derived for Bellman-Ford
nodes.description: For a K-layer min-aggregation MPNN learning K-step Bellman-Ford with m-layer feed-forward networks, an explicit training set of size K+1 can be constructed together with a differentiable weighted ell-1 regularization term.

nodes.name: Theorem 5: small regularized loss implies bounded approximation error
nodes.description: If the K-layer min-aggregation MPNN achieves a loss within epsilon < 1/2 of its global minimum on the constructed size-(K+1) training set, then for any SSSP instance, the MPNN approximates every K-step shortest path distance within additive error epsilon*(x^(K)+1).

nodes.name: Result uses smaller training set and differentiable regularizer than Nerem et al.
nodes.description: Compared to Nerem et al. [2025], this result uses a smaller training set (K+1 path instances) and replaces their non-differentiable ell-0 penalty with a differentiable ell-1 regularizer with layer-specific weights, allowing direct gradient-based optimization of the loss.

nodes.name: Trade-off: more restricted model assumptions
nodes.description: In exchange for the smaller training set and differentiability, the analysis assumes a more restricted model: depth fixed to exactly K layers matching K Bellman-Ford steps, and aggregation dimension assumed to be 1.

components.name: Impossibility results: expressivity and covering-number limitations

nodes.name: Standard MPNNs cannot approximate SSSP or MST cost
nodes.description: No standard MPNN architecture (Equation 1) can approximate the SSSP cost invariant or the MST cost invariant arbitrarily well.

nodes.name: More expressive (1-iWL/(1,1)-WL) MPNNs overcome this for SSSP/MST
nodes.description: There exist 1-iWL-expressive and (1,1)-WL-expressive MPNN architectures that can approximate the SSSP and MST invariants respectively, overcoming the expressivity limitation of standard MPNNs; the MST limitation persists even for 1-iWL-simulating MPNNs specifically.

nodes.name: Some expressible invariants still lack a finite-covering-number metric
nodes.description: Beyond expressivity limits, there exist invariants representable by MPNNs for which the sufficient learnability conditions do not apply, because the obstruction is the absence of a metric structure yielding finite covering numbers, not a lack of expressive power.

nodes.name: Unnormalized-sum MPNN can express the degree invariant
nodes.description: A one-layer MPNN variant with unnormalized-sum aggregation (on graphs without vertex/edge features) exactly computes the vertex degree invariant.

nodes.name: Unbounded-degree families make the degree invariant's covering number infinite
nodes.description: If the graph space is not restricted to bounded maximum degree, any pseudo-metric under which the degree invariant is Lipschitz with a finite constant necessarily has infinite covering number for sufficiently small radius (Lemma 7), so no hypothesis class containing the degree invariant can satisfy the finite Lipschitz class definition on such a space.

nodes.name: Same covering-number pathology extends to all 1-WL-equivalent invariants
nodes.description: Because the first iteration of 1-WL already captures the degree invariant, any hypothesis class expressive enough to represent all 1-WL invariants inherits the same covering-number pathology on graph spaces with unbounded degrees.

components.name: Experimental validation of the theoretical framework

nodes.name: Experiments target the explicit SSSP construction from Theorem 5
nodes.description: Because Theorem 5 gives an explicit training set construction, experiments are conducted on the SSSP problem outlined in Section 3.3, training a two-layer MPNN to predict two steps of Bellman-Ford on synthetic Erdos-Renyi and path-graph datasets.

nodes.name: Size generalization holds empirically (Q1)
nodes.description: Test error does not increase with vertex count across test sets of 64, 256, and 1024 vertices, and average vertex degree (bounded vs. unbounded) does not affect test set performance, supporting the theoretical size-generalization guarantee.

nodes.name: More expressive (1-iWL) MPNNs greatly outperform standard MPNNs in practice (Q2)
nodes.description: A standard MPNN is unable to generalize to unseen test graphs at all, whereas a 1-iWL-equivalent MPNN achieves much lower test error and significantly lower training loss, empirically corroborating the expressivity limitation shown in Proposition 6/C5.

nodes.name: Proposed differentiable regularizer matches or improves on p-norm regularization (Q3)
nodes.description: Replacing the proposed differentiable ell-1-based regularization term with standard ell_1 gives similar results, but size generalization improves with the proposed regularizer across graph sizes, while ell_2 regularization is noticeably less stable and yields slightly worse test performance.

isolated_nodes.name: MPNN formal definition via UPDATE/AGGREGATE
isolated_nodes.description: An L-layer MPNN computes, at each layer, a vertex feature via an UPDATE function applied to the previous feature and an AGGREGATE function applied to the multiset of neighbor features and incident edge weights.

isolated_nodes.name: 1-WL graph-distinguishing power upper bounds MPNNs
isolated_nodes.description: Prior work (Morris et al. 2019, Xu et al. 2019) established that the graph-distinguishing power of any MPNN architecture is upper bounded by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm, and sum-aggregation MPNNs can match 1-WL's expressivity on any finite graph set.

isolated_nodes.name: 1-iWL and (1,1)-WL defined as more expressive variants
isolated_nodes.description: The 1-iWL individualizes a root vertex before running 1-WL, and the (1,1)-WL extends this by trying every possible individualization placement, yielding strictly more expressive graph-distinguishing variants than plain 1-WL.

isolated_nodes.name: Proposition 1: separation entails approximation under mild conditions
isolated_nodes.description: Under mild regularity assumptions and for graphs of fixed order with attributes in a compact domain, if an algorithm's induced equivalence relation is coarser than that of a simulating class (1-WL/1-iWL/(1,1)-WL), an MPNN in that class can approximate the algorithm arbitrarily well -- but this notion of approximation is non-uniform across graph sizes.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-uniform approximation does not imply learnability across sizes
isolated_nodes.description: Proposition 1's approximation results do not explain how to choose a function in the hypothesis class that approximates a given algorithm, and apply only to graphs of fixed size, so they do not by themselves imply learnability, particularly for larger instances -- motivating the paper's own framework in Section 3.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal definitions of SSSP, MST, and knapsack problems
isolated_nodes.description: The paper formally defines the single-source shortest path problem, minimum spanning tree problem, and 0-1 knapsack problem as the graph/combinatorial problems studied throughout.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: PAC-style sample complexity for algorithm learning (Xu et al. 2020)
isolated_nodes.description: Xu et al. [2020] proposed PAC-style sample-complexity bounds for learning common graph algorithms with MPNNs, showing architectural alignment with the target algorithm can improve sample efficiency.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: VC dimension and generalization bounds for MPNNs
isolated_nodes.description: A body of prior work (Scarselli et al., Garg et al., Morris et al. 2023, and others) studies MPNN generalization via VC dimension, Rademacher complexity, and PAC-Bayesian analyses, primarily in the classical uniform-convergence regime, in contrast to this paper's focus on generalizing a single learned function to larger graphs than seen in training.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: negative/necessary generalization results for larger graphs
isolated_nodes.description: Yehudai et al. [2021] derived negative generalization results for larger graphs than seen in training, while Levin et al. [2025] derived necessary conditions for generalization to larger graphs.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: reliance on carefully constructed covering datasets
isolated_nodes.description: The framework assumes access to carefully constructed training datasets forming suitable covers of the underlying graph space, which may not arise naturally in practice, motivating future work on high-probability sampling-based dataset construction.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: no guarantee that gradient descent finds the required parameters
isolated_nodes.description: The framework's guarantees are stated in terms of achieving sufficiently small regularized training loss, but do not guarantee that standard gradient-based optimization will reliably converge to parameters achieving that loss.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: restricted to polynomial-time algorithms
isolated_nodes.description: The current analysis is restricted to polynomial-time algorithms; extending the framework to approximation algorithms for computationally hard problems is left as future work.

structural_reasoning: The graph closely tracks the paper's own logical progression. C1 establishes the expressivity-vs-learnability gap that motivates the whole paper. C2 captures the core theoretical machinery (finite Lipschitz classes, certificates, the regularizer, and Theorem 3) as a tight derivation chain. C3 is the largest and most interconnected component, since Theorem 4 (aggregation types satisfy finite Lipschitzness) is the shared premise that, combined with Theorem 3 from C2, unlocks learnability for three distinct algorithm families (PageRank, Bellman-Ford, and dynamic programming/knapsack) -- each traced as its own sub-chain of exact-representation -> size-independent iteration bound -> learnability conclusion. C4 documents the refined, explicit Bellman-Ford construction (Theorem 5) as an improvement over the general existence result of C3/Nerem et al., correctly capturing both its advantages (smaller set, differentiable regularizer) and its cost (more restrictive model assumptions) as one causal chain. C5 mirrors the paper's impossibility results, distinguishing two independent obstructions (expressivity limits in Proposition 6, and covering-number pathology in Lemma 7) that are structurally analogous but not causally linked to each other, hence kept as parallel sub-chains within one component. C6 ties the empirical section back to the theoretical claims from C2-C5 via a few cross-component edges (e.g., the expressivity limitation of C5 explaining the Q2 experimental gap). Isolated nodes are limited to genuine background/definitional material (MPNN formalism, 1-WL variants, Proposition 1, problem definitions, related work, and stated limitations) that does not function as an argumentative premise elsewhere in the paper's own chain of reasoning.

components.description: Central thesis: sparse multi-agent competitive reward vs. dense single-agent reward

nodes.name: Sparse competitive reward
nodes.description: Agents are rewarded only for finishing a lap or passing a gate before their opponent, with no reward term prescribing specific flight behavior.

nodes.name: Emergent agile flight
nodes.description: High-speed, physically aggressive flight emerges from the sparse competitive reward without any explicit speed-shaping term.

nodes.name: Emergent strategic behavior
nodes.description: Tactical behaviors such as overtaking, blocking, and adapting to an opponent's crash emerge without explicit reward terms for these skills.

nodes.name: Dense progress reward limits exploration
nodes.description: Dense, race-line progress-based rewards are prescriptive and constrain exploration, discouraging deviations needed for obstacle avoidance.

nodes.name: Complexity-dependent degradation of dense rewards
nodes.description: The prescriptive structure of dense rewards causes performance to degrade specifically as environment complexity increases (e.g., obstacles present).

nodes.name: Sparse multi-agent outperforms dense single-agent
nodes.description: The sparse multi-agent (Ours) approach outperforms the common dense, single-agent progress-reward paradigm, especially as environment complexity increases.

evidence: Sec III-A Comparison to Existing Rewards

components.description: Single-agent baseline limitations (obstacles)

nodes.name: Dense single-agent success without obstacles
nodes.description: Dense single-agent (DS) policies achieve high success rates (100% LT, 98% CT) when no obstacles are present.

nodes.name: Dense single-agent failure with obstacles
nodes.description: Dense single-agent (DS) policies achieve a 0% success rate on both tracks once obstacles are introduced, failing to complete even a single lap.

nodes.name: Progress reward penalizes gate-moving-away
nodes.description: The progress reward (Eq. 7) discourages the drone from moving away from the next gate, which is required to avoid obstacles.

nodes.name: Sparse single-agent (SS) lower speed but some obstacle tolerance
nodes.description: Sparse single-agent (SS) policies show lower speed than DS on obstacle-free tracks but retain non-zero, sometimes near-perfect, success with obstacles present on the lemniscate track.

nodes.name: Sparse reward reliability across obstacle settings
nodes.description: Sparse (competitive or not) rewards more consistently discover obstacle-free/obstacle-tolerant trajectories than dense rewards, though at a training-stability cost in the single-agent case.

components.description: Head-to-head competitive evaluation

nodes.name: Ours highest average win rate
nodes.description: The Sparse Multi-Agent (Ours) policy achieves the highest average win rate (91.17%) across all simulated head-to-head matchups.

nodes.name: Ours beats DS even on obstacle-free tracks
nodes.description: Ours wins 100% of races against DS on the lemniscate track and 84% on the complex track, even though those are DS's best-case conditions.

nodes.name: Adding overtaking reward to DM does not help
nodes.description: Extending the dense single-agent reward to multi-agent (DM) by adding a dense overtaking term does not improve performance and often results in more losses than DS.

nodes.name: DM balancing difficulty
nodes.description: DM's underperformance likely stems from the difficulty of balancing two dense reward terms, causing convergence to a suboptimal local minimum.

nodes.name: Competitive pressure broadens discovered behaviors
nodes.description: Competitive pressure among agents broadens the range of behaviors discovered during training, most visible when Ours is compared against SS (identical except for the presence of a competitor).

components.description: Sim-to-real transfer

nodes.name: Shared sim/hardware setup
nodes.description: DS and Ours use the same simulation environment, randomization strategy, policy structure, and physical hardware, isolating reward design as the variable.

nodes.name: Smaller sim-to-real speed gap for Ours
nodes.description: Ours shows a 44.7% smaller gap between simulated and real-world average flight speed (0.43 m/s vs. 0.76 m/s for DS).

nodes.name: Lower real-world failure/collision rate for Ours
nodes.description: Ours exhibits substantially lower real-world failure and collision rates than DS, despite both having zero failure/collision rates in simulation.

nodes.name: Sparse competitive rewards improve transfer
nodes.description: Sparse, competition-based rewards lead to improved simulation-to-reality transfer relative to dense progress-based rewards.

nodes.name: Only Ours clears real-world obstacle track
nodes.description: Ours is the only method that successfully completes the real-world lemniscate track in the presence of obstacles.

components.description: Generalization and real-world head-to-head

nodes.name: Generalization to unseen opponents
nodes.description: Ours generalizes well across different real-world opponents, achieving the highest win rate, on par with DS.

nodes.name: Ours vs DS head-to-head advantage
nodes.description: Despite equal average win rates with DS, Ours outperforms DS specifically in direct head-to-head real-world races.

nodes.name: DM poor transfer explains draws
nodes.description: Ours' equal average win rate (despite head-to-head superiority over DS) is explained by draws against the poorly-transferring DM policy, whose erratic behavior knocked Ours out of distribution.

nodes.name: Cross-agent dependency complicates real-world prediction
nodes.description: Because outcomes depend on the behavior of another agent, predicting a policy's real-world performance against new opponents is inherently more challenging in multi-agent settings.

components.description: Emergent strategic behavior analysis

nodes.name: More aggressive flight vs. competitive opponent
nodes.description: The agent flies a significantly more aggressive trajectory (higher max/mean velocity) against a competitive opponent than against a crashed one.

nodes.name: Risk-averse behavior once opponent forfeits
nodes.description: The agent reduces speed once the opponent has crashed, since gate-pass and lap-bonus rewards become effectively guaranteed.

nodes.name: Blocking maneuvers observed
nodes.description: Real-world trajectories show learned blocking maneuvers, e.g., an agent flying a wide trajectory to defend a lead and force a collision on the opponent.

nodes.name: Strategic behavior beyond raw speed
nodes.description: The agent learns strategic behaviors (risk-averse adaptation, blocking) beyond simply flying fast.

components.description: Training stability

nodes.name: Single-agent training stability
nodes.description: Single-agent (dense) training is stable and smooth across seeds, with low variance in cumulative reward.

nodes.name: Multi-agent training variability
nodes.description: Multi-agent (sparse, competitive) training curves show greater variability across seeds than single-agent training.

nodes.name: Multi-agent variability reflects competitive alternation
nodes.description: The alternating higher-cumulative-reward phases between the two competing agents reflect the inherently competitive, shifting-balance nature of multi-agent training.

nodes.name: Multi-agent training still consistently competitive
nodes.description: Despite greater variance, all multi-agent training runs converge to consistently competitive policies.

components.description: Methodology: reward and optimization design choices

nodes.name: General-sum Dec-MDP formulation
nodes.description: Racing is formulated as a two-agent, finite-horizon decentralized Markov decision process (general-sum game) between an ego and adversary policy.

nodes.name: Sparse reward composition
nodes.description: The task reward combines gate-passing precedence, a lap-completion bonus, an energy-minimization penalty, and a crash penalty — with no explicit behavior-shaping term.

nodes.name: IPPO used for joint optimization
nodes.description: Policies are jointly trained with IPPO, a multi-agent PPO variant without a shared critic, chosen for empirical performance and simplicity over MAPPO.

nodes.name: No explicit behavior reward needed
nodes.description: Because the reward is purely outcome-based, no reward term explicitly encodes agile flight or tactical behavior.

isolated_nodes.name: MPC/MPCC accuracy dependence
isolated_nodes.description: Classical MPC/MPCC controllers require an accurate drone model, which is difficult to obtain especially under aerodynamic effects during complex maneuvers.

isolated_nodes.name: MPC/MPCC compute cost
isolated_nodes.description: Classical MPC/MPCC controllers require significant online computation, limiting them to relatively short-horizon objectives.

isolated_nodes.name: Multi-agent MPC/game-theoretic scalability limits
isolated_nodes.description: Multi-drone MPC or game-theoretic formulations face severe scalability issues as environment complexity grows, limiting them to low-speed racing.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior multi-agent RL racing adds overtaking term
isolated_nodes.description: Prior multi-agent RL racing work augments single-agent dense rewards with an additional overtaking term, following approaches used in Gran Turismo.

isolated_nodes.name: Related work: emergent behavior in abstract multi-agent games
isolated_nodes.description: Prior multi-agent RL research (Capture the Flag, StarCraft, hide-and-seek, autonomous driving) shows complex emergent behavior from simple adversarial rewards, but mostly in abstract or simplified environments.

isolated_nodes.name: This work extends emergence to embodied real-world control
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike prior abstract multi-agent emergence studies, this work demonstrates similar emergent effects in a physically realistic setting deployable to real hardware.

isolated_nodes.name: Domain randomization used for transfer
isolated_nodes.description: Training relies on domain randomization and rapid test-time adaptation rather than extensive system identification for sim-to-real transfer.

isolated_nodes.name: Deeper critic improves performance
isolated_nodes.description: Empirically, making the critic network deeper than the actor network improves performance.

isolated_nodes.name: Track design rationale
isolated_nodes.description: The Complex Track and Lemniscate Track were designed to require agile motion even without obstacles, and obstacle placement forces drones away from the direct gate line.

isolated_nodes.name: Adversarial domain randomization hypothesis
isolated_nodes.description: The improved sim-to-real transfer of the competitive multi-agent approach is hypothesized to relate to adversarial domain randomization, though this is left to future work.

structural_reasoning: The graph is organized around one central causal chain (C1): sparse multi-agent competition removes prescriptive behavior shaping, which lets agile flight and strategy emerge, and this becomes advantageous specifically as track complexity increases (obstacles). This connects downstream to three empirically supported consequences: (C2/C3) competitive/tournament superiority in simulation, (C4/C5) improved and more predictable-in-aggregate sim-to-real transfer, and (C6) directly observable strategic behaviors (risk-aversion, blocking). C7 (training stability) is a secondary, partially countervailing thread — multi-agent training is noisier, which is acknowledged but doesn't undermine the main thesis. C8 covers methodological scaffolding (Dec-MDP formulation, reward terms, IPPO) that underlies all empirical components but has no direct causal claims linking it to specific result nodes beyond enabling them. Several background/motivational claims about classical control baselines and related work (isolated_nodes) are contextual rather than argumentatively load-bearing for the paper's core empirical claims.
