components.description: Motivation: PFN paradigm doesn't transfer naturally to time series

nodes.name: Forecasting models are typically dataset-specific
nodes.description: Most existing forecasting models are trained in a dataset-specific supervised manner, optimized separately for each target dataset, limiting their ability to learn a general forecasting mechanism transferable across tasks.

nodes.name: PFNs learn transferable inference from synthetic tasks
nodes.description: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs), e.g., TabPFN, learn an inference strategy from large-scale synthetic tasks generated by a prior distribution and transfer this strategy to unseen tasks, instead of training from scratch per dataset.

nodes.name: Tabular priors don't naturally capture time-series structure
nodes.description: Directly extending tabular PFN models to time series is insufficient because tabular data do not explicitly contain temporal order, dynamic lagged dependencies, or historical input-output correspondences.

nodes.name: Time-series forecasting requires joint reasoning over three structures
nodes.description: Time-series forecasting requires models to reason jointly over temporal dynamics, cross-variable structures, and sample-level historical patterns — none of which are natively present in tabular priors.

nodes.name: Modest reframed question: explicit reuse of historical input-output examples
nodes.description: Motivated by PFN-style learning but tempered by the tabular-transfer gap, the paper studies a more modest question: how can a forecasting model explicitly reuse historical input-output examples within a long time-series context?

components.description: Trio's three-dimensional attention design rationale

nodes.name: Trio decomposes modeling into temporal, spatial, sample dimensions
nodes.description: Trio is proposed as a sample-aware forecasting architecture that decomposes multivariate time-series modeling into temporal attention (within-window dynamics), spatial attention (inter-variable dependencies), and sample attention (retrieval of relevant historical lookback-future pairs).

nodes.name: History treated as structured examples, not flat context
nodes.description: Rather than treating long historical context as a flat sequence, the model uses historical segments as structured examples that encode how past inputs evolve into future outcomes.

nodes.name: Not claiming a fully general PFN-style forecaster
nodes.description: The paper explicitly does not claim a fully general PFN-style forecaster; its goal is narrower — studying how historical input-output examples can be explicitly organized and reused within a forecasting model.

components.description: Strict temporal ordering of historical pairs and current window

nodes.name: Historical context reorganized into lookback-future pairs
nodes.description: Instead of treating historical context as one continuous sequence, it is reorganized into S non-overlapping historical blocks, each an explicit (lookback, future) pair, plus one current query window (Eqs. 1-3).

nodes.name: Historical pairs placed strictly before current window
nodes.description: All historical lookback-future pairs are strictly placed before the current query window to avoid information leakage, with explicit index formulas ensuring max index of any historical future segment is less than the min index of the current input (Eqs. 4-6).

nodes.name: No leakage of current target guaranteed
nodes.description: This strict ordering ensures historical future prompts are past observations relative to the current window and never contain the target future of the current input.

components.description: Patch tokenization and historical prompt construction

nodes.name: Current and historical lookback segments patch-embedded
nodes.description: Both the current input window and historical lookback segments are converted into patch-level token representations via a shared patch embedding layer (Eqs. 7-9).

nodes.name: Historical future segments preserved as patch-wise tokens, not compressed
nodes.description: Unlike compressing the historical future into a single vector, the historical future segment is encoded by a separate future patch embedding layer, preserving patch-wise structure and producing tokens that act as historical prediction prompts (Eq. 10).

nodes.name: Lightweight pre-encoders improve intra-window representation
nodes.description: Self-attention-based pre-encoders operate along the patch dimension to enhance local lookback and future-prompt representations before cross-window interaction (Eqs. 11-12).

nodes.name: Historical window tokens concatenate lookback and future-prompt tokens
nodes.description: For each historical window, encoded lookback tokens and future-prompt tokens are concatenated into a single window token tensor (Eq. 13).

nodes.name: Current window uses learnable query tokens as future placeholders
nodes.description: Since the current window's future is unknown, learnable query tokens are appended in place of future tokens, acting as future placeholders that later query historical future-prompt tokens during sample-level retrieval (Eqs. 14-15).

nodes.name: All windows stacked into a unified tensor
nodes.description: All historical window tokens and the current window tokens are stacked along the sample/window dimension into a single tensor Z(0) containing temporal, spatial, and sample-level dependencies (Eq. 16).

components.description: Temporal-Spatial-Sample alternating encoder rationale

nodes.name: Full attention over all axes is expensive and uncontrolled
nodes.description: The constructed tensor contains three types of dependencies (temporal, spatial, sample-level); directly applying full attention over all axes jointly is computationally expensive and introduces uncontrolled interactions.

nodes.name: Alternating axis-wise attention decomposition proposed
nodes.description: This motivates a Temporal-Spatial-Sample alternating encoder that decomposes modeling into separate axis-wise attention operations, applied as an ordered composition per encoder block (Eq. 17).

components.description: Spatial attention module

nodes.name: Spatial attention models cross-variable dependencies
nodes.description: The spatial module reshapes the tensor and applies non-causal self-attention along the variable dimension, letting each variable dynamically aggregate information from other variables at the same sample and patch position (Eqs. 18-19).

nodes.name: Optional zero-gradient strategy reduces memory cost
nodes.description: For long-context supervised training, spatial attention for historical windows can optionally be computed under no-grad while only the current window is recomputed with gradient tracking, treating historical windows as contextual evidence and letting parameter updates be mainly driven by the current prediction loss.

components.description: Temporal attention module

nodes.name: Temporal attention captures within-window patch dependencies
nodes.description: The temporal module reshapes the tensor and applies causal self-attention along the patch dimension for each variable and sample, with a causal mask preventing later tokens from being accessed by earlier tokens (Eqs. 20-21).

nodes.name: Same zero-gradient strategy applies to temporal attention
nodes.description: When the optional zero-gradient strategy is enabled, historical windows are processed under no-grad in the temporal module too, while the current window is recomputed with gradients and replaces its position in the output.

components.description: Sample attention module (history-first, current-only retrieval)

nodes.name: Sample module retrieves historical input-output mappings
nodes.description: The sample module is designed to retrieve useful historical input-output mappings for the current prediction, performing patch-wise sample retrieval over future-query tokens rather than using a single CLS token.

nodes.name: Sample self-attention aggregates historical future-prompt tokens
nodes.description: Historical future-prompt tokens (excluding the current window) are extracted and rearranged so that sample self-attention is independently performed per variable and future-patch position, producing a memory bank of historical future-prompt representations (Eqs. 22-25).

nodes.name: Current future-query tokens cross-attend to historical memory bank
nodes.description: Current future-query tokens are extracted and used as the query in cross-attention against the aggregated historical tokens (keys/values), realizing history-first aggregation with current-only retrieval (Eqs. 26-27).

nodes.name: Only current tokens updated, avoiding bidirectional mixing
nodes.description: Only the current future-query tokens are updated and written back into the tensor, avoiding bidirectional mixing between historical and current windows while letting current prediction tokens selectively retrieve relevant historical patterns (Eq. 28).

components.description: Prediction head and training objective

nodes.name: All current-window tokens extracted and flattened
nodes.description: After the TSS encoder, all tokens from the current window are extracted and flattened per variable rather than using only a single CLS representation (Eqs. 29-30).

nodes.name: Shared linear head maps to prediction horizon
nodes.description: A shared linear head maps the flattened per-variable representation to the prediction horizon, either as a point forecast or as Q quantiles for probabilistic forecasting (Eqs. 31-32).

nodes.name: Input normalization and inverse normalization applied
nodes.description: Following common practice in non-stationary forecasting, each input sequence is normalized before tokenization using lookback-derived mean/std, with inverse normalization applied to the prediction (Eq. 33).

nodes.name: MSE (or pinball loss) used for training
nodes.description: For deterministic forecasting, the model minimizes mean squared error; for quantile forecasting, this is replaced by the standard pinball loss over all quantile levels (Eq. 34).

components.description: TS-SCM generator motivation and graph/node/edge mechanisms

nodes.name: GP-based synthetic priors define distribution over functions only
nodes.description: Unlike GP-based synthetic priors that mainly define a distribution over temporal functions, TS-SCM defines a distribution over multivariate causal dynamical systems.

nodes.name: TS-SCM specifies a directed causal graph with heterogeneous mechanisms
nodes.description: Each TS-SCM task is specified by a directed graph, heterogeneous node mechanisms, edge-level lag functions, noise processes, and optional mechanism drift.

nodes.name: Root vs. affected variable structure
nodes.description: TS-SCM samples root variables (exogenous driving processes from periodic functions, Fourier components, trends, GP-like priors, square waves, or chaotic systems) and affected variables generated by node-wise mechanisms receiving delayed parent inputs (Eq. 35).

nodes.name: Edge-level causal messages transform and deliver parent information
nodes.description: Each directed edge specifies an edge weight, optional nonlinear transform, lag function, reduce policy, and fill policy governing how information is transformed and delivered from parent to child (Eq. 36).

components.description: Dynamic, edge-level lag scheduling mechanism

nodes.name: Lags defined at edge level, not by global delay matrix
nodes.description: A central design of TS-SCM is that lags are defined per edge rather than by a global delay matrix, allowing the lag to be fixed, state-dependent, history-dependent, sampled, or expression-defined (Eq. 37).

nodes.name: Push-based event calendar avoids rounding of continuous lags
nodes.description: Rather than the child pulling a parent value from a fixed past index, a push-based event calendar computes a future arrival trajectory for each parent value and schedules interpolated events at crossed integer time buckets, avoiding crude rounding of continuous lags (Eqs. 38-39).

nodes.name: Enables smooth delayed propagation under time-varying lags
nodes.description: This push-based, interpolated event-scheduling design enables smooth delayed propagation even when lag functions vary over time or state.

components.description: Cycle handling, drift, noise, and stability control

nodes.name: Zero-lag edges restricted to acyclic subgraph
nodes.description: Zero-lag edges are allowed only when explicitly specified, and the zero-lag subgraph is constrained to be acyclic so that same-time-step nodes have a valid computation order.

nodes.name: Positive-lag edges can form recurrent feedback
nodes.description: Positive-lag edges can form recurrent feedback loops, including self-loops and reverse-direction effects, because their messages are delivered to future time steps, avoiding ill-defined simultaneous cycles.

nodes.name: Piecewise mechanism drift simulates nonstationarity
nodes.description: TS-SCM supports piecewise drift modifying node parameters, global linear scales, or edge weights over time, along with Gaussian, Student-t, autoregressive, or mixture noise, to simulate nonstationary real-world systems.

nodes.name: Stability-aware graph sampling prevents unstable trajectories
nodes.description: To prevent randomly sampled recurrent systems from becoming unstable, incoming edge gains are controlled by a child-wise budget, with self-feedback edges given a stricter gain budget than cross-variable delayed edges, producing diverse yet learnable synthetic systems.

components.description: Forecasting episode construction aligning TS-SCM with Trio

nodes.name: Generated trajectories converted into forecasting episodes
nodes.description: Each generated TS-SCM trajectory is converted into forecasting episodes consisting of multiple historical lookback-future pairs and a current query window (Eq. 40).

nodes.name: Episode format aligns directly with Trio's architecture
nodes.description: This episode format is directly aligned with the three-dimensional attention architecture: historical pairs provide sample-level evidence while the current window retrieves relevant input-output mappings, making TS-SCM both a trajectory generator and a forecasting-oriented task generator.

components.description: Synthetic delayed-dependency experiments

nodes.name: Synthetic Dataset #1 tests variable temporal delay
nodes.description: In Synthetic Dataset #1, the target Y is an M-step delayed version of input X with M~U(20,60), testing whether a model can capture variable temporal delays.

nodes.name: Synthetic Dataset #2 additionally tests source-variable identification
nodes.description: In Synthetic Dataset #2, Y is an M-step delayed version of one randomly selected variable among five inputs (M~U(20,30)), requiring the model to identify both delay length and the relevant source variable, making it more challenging.

nodes.name: Standard baselines show limited performance under delayed dependencies
nodes.description: Standard forecasting baselines (TimesNet, Crossformer, TimeXer) show limited performance under both delayed-dependency synthetic settings (Table 1).

nodes.name: Sample Attention improves the base model on both synthetic datasets
nodes.description: Adding Sample Attention consistently improves the base model: MSE drops from 0.706 to 0.298 on Dataset #1, and from 1.011 to 0.644 on Dataset #2 (Table 1).

nodes.name: Larger improvement on the harder, variable-selection dataset
nodes.description: The improvement from Sample Attention is more pronounced on Dataset #2, suggesting sample-level retrieval is particularly useful when the model must infer both temporal delay and variable relevance.

components.description: Public benchmark comparison results

nodes.name: Trio achieves best average MSE on 3 of 4 benchmarks
nodes.description: Trio achieves the best average MSE on ETTm1 (0.358), ETTm2 (0.255), and Electricity (0.164), out of four evaluated public benchmarks (Table 2).

nodes.name: Trio is not best on Weather but remains competitive
nodes.description: On Weather, Trio's average MSE (0.249) is not the best overall (TimeMixer++ achieves 0.226), but Trio remains competitive and achieves the best result at the short H=96 horizon.

nodes.name: Trio's advantage varies by dataset temporal characteristics
nodes.description: These results suggest Trio can effectively exploit historical input-output correspondences on most benchmarks, while its advantage may vary across datasets with different temporal characteristics.

components.description: Comparison against ICTSP (long-context baseline)

nodes.name: ICTSP uses long context without explicit input-output structuring
nodes.description: ICTSP also attempts to use long historical context for forecasting but does not explicitly organize historical segments as input-output examples.

nodes.name: Trio's explicit pairing outperforms ICTSP's undifferentiated long context
nodes.description: Trio, using historical lookback-future pairs and sample-level retrieval, achieves better best performance than ICTSP on both ETTm1 and ETTm2 across different context lengths (Table 3).

nodes.name: Supports explicit structuring over merely lengthening context
nodes.description: This comparison supports the advantage of explicitly modeling historical input-output mappings rather than simply increasing the context length.

components.description: Ablation: effectiveness of Sample Attention on real benchmarks

nodes.name: Base Model defined as Trio minus Sample Attention
nodes.description: The Base Model shares all of Trio's backbone (patch embeddings, pre-encoders, temporal/spatial attention, prediction head, normalization, depth, hidden dim, training protocol) except that current future-query tokens do not retrieve historical future prompts via the sample dimension.

nodes.name: This isolates the contribution of sample-level retrieval
nodes.description: Because the Base Model and Base+Sample-Attention comparison differs only in sample-level retrieval, it isolates the specific contribution of historical input-output retrieval from all other architectural components.

nodes.name: Sample Attention consistently improves performance across horizons
nodes.description: Across all tested horizons on ETTm1 and ETTm2, adding Sample Attention consistently improves the base model, e.g. MSE from 0.512 to 0.424 on ETTm1 H=720, and from 0.294 to 0.230 on ETTm2 H=192 (Table 4).

nodes.name: Confirms retrieval helps capture long-range/delayed dependencies
nodes.description: These consistent improvements demonstrate that retrieving relevant historical lookback-future pairs helps the model capture long-range and delayed temporal dependencies.

components.description: Scalability to long contexts

nodes.name: Longer context generally improves performance
nodes.description: Increasing the context length generally improves forecasting performance across default input lengths of both 96 and 336, showing the benefit of longer historical contexts (Tables 5-6).

nodes.name: Optimal context length varies by dataset and input setting
nodes.description: The best context length varies across datasets and input settings: for input length 96, moderate lengths (L=1000-2000) already give strong performance with little further gain; for input length 336, ETTm1/ETTm2 peak around L=3000 before performance drops.

nodes.name: Excessive context may reduce training samples / add noise
nodes.description: Performance drops at very long context lengths may occur because longer input windows reduce the number of available training samples and may introduce redundant or noisy historical information.

nodes.name: Moderate long-context modeling is useful but not unconditionally
nodes.description: Overall, moderate long-context modeling is useful, but blindly increasing context length is not always beneficial.

components.description: Exploratory zero-shot transfer using TS-SCM

nodes.name: Zero-shot setting assesses transfer potential, not full solution
nodes.description: The zero-shot experiment (train only on synthetic tasks, evaluate on real ETT benchmarks with no target-dataset fine-tuning) is explicitly framed as assessing the transfer potential of synthetic generation strategies, not as claiming a complete zero-shot forecasting solution.

nodes.name: TS-SCM achieves best MAE on all four ETT datasets
nodes.description: TS-SCM achieves the best MAE on all four evaluated ETT datasets when compared to CausalDynamics and LMC Synth synthetic generators (Table 7).

nodes.name: TS-SCM achieves best MSE on 3 of 4 datasets
nodes.description: TS-SCM achieves the best MSE on three of four datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, ETTm2), while CausalDynamics obtains a slightly lower MSE on ETTh2 (Table 7).

nodes.name: TS-SCM provides more transferable priors in most settings
nodes.description: These results suggest the forecasting-oriented TS-SCM task construction provides more transferable temporal priors than the compared generators in most evaluated settings.

nodes.name: Advantage not uniform; different priors capture different dynamics
nodes.description: The non-uniform advantage (ETTh2 MSE exception) indicates different synthetic priors may capture different aspects of real-world temporal dynamics, so results are interpreted as encouraging rather than conclusive evidence.

isolated_nodes.name: Three input paradigms illustrated
isolated_nodes.description: Figure 1 contrasts three input paradigms: short historical input, long contextual input without distinguishing input-output relationships, and the paper's approach leveraging long context with explicit input-output correspondences.

isolated_nodes.name: Comparison baselines used
isolated_nodes.description: Trio is compared against TimeMixer++, Patch-wise Structural, TIMEKAN, MOIRAI, TimesFM, TimeMixer, iTransformer, PatchTST, and DLinear, covering Transformer-based, patch-based, decomposition-based, MLP-based, and foundation-style methods.

isolated_nodes.name: Standard train/val/test protocol and training details
isolated_nodes.description: Public benchmark evaluation follows standard train/validation/test splits from prior long-term forecasting studies, using Adam with initial learning rate 1e-4, MSE loss, early stopping on validation loss, and fixed random seeds with best-validation-checkpoint reporting.

isolated_nodes.name: Zero-shot evaluation protocol details
isolated_nodes.description: Zero-shot test instances use seven context samples (lookback 96, future 48 each), with the model predicting the next 48 steps given a length-96 target input, using average MSE as the main metric.

isolated_nodes.name: Compared synthetic generators for zero-shot
isolated_nodes.description: TS-SCM is compared against Causal Dynamics and LMC Synth as representative synthetic data generation strategies for the zero-shot transfer experiment.

isolated_nodes.name: Future work directions
isolated_nodes.description: Future work will focus on stronger zero-shot evaluation, synthetic-data realism diagnostics, efficiency improvements, and broader comparisons with temporal causal priors.

structural_reasoning: The graph follows two parallel design-to-validation arcs unified by a shared motivation. The motivation (C1: PFN paradigm doesn't transfer to time series) leads to a re-scoped goal of explicit historical example reuse (C2), realized architecturally through strict temporal ordering (C3), patch tokenization with preserved future-prompt structure (C4), and a three-way alternating encoder (C5) whose spatial (C6), temporal (C7), and sample (C8) attention modules are each individually justified, feeding a shared prediction head and training objective (C9). In parallel, the same motivation supports a second contribution: the TS-SCM synthetic task generator, whose design (C10: causal graph/node/edge mechanisms; C11: dynamic edge-level lag scheduling; C12: cycle handling, drift, and stability control) culminates in an episode format explicitly aligned with Trio's three-dimensional architecture (C13), tying the two contributions together. The experimental components (C14-C19) each validate a specific claim: synthetic delayed-dependency experiments (C14) directly validate the sample-attention design from C8; public benchmark results (C15) and the ICTSP comparison (C16) validate the overall architecture and its explicit-pairing rationale from C2/C3; the ablation (C17) isolates and re-confirms C14's finding on real data; the scalability study (C18) tests the boundary conditions of the long-context design from C3/C4; and the zero-shot transfer experiment (C19) validates the TS-SCM generator's transfer utility from C10-C13. Figure illustrations, baseline/protocol details, and future work are treated as isolated nodes since they are supporting context rather than embedded in a specific argumentative chain.

nodes.name: Non-verbal behaviors underexplored
nodes.description: Existing studies mainly focus on simulating human dialogue; non-verbal behaviors like item clicking in recommender systems, though implicitly exhibiting user preferences, have not been deeply explored.

nodes.name: Gap between language and behavior modeling
nodes.description: The gap between universal language modeling and personalized behavior modeling, plus LLMs' incomprehension of user-item relations, is a main reason non-verbal behaviors are underexplored.

nodes.name: Verbalized interaction text fails to capture patterns
nodes.description: Verbalizing interaction records into natural language text to prompt LLMs struggles to capture underlying behavioral patterns, since semantically unrelated items (e.g., diapers and beer) can be behaviorally correlated in ways that confuse LLMs.

nodes.name: Item-side modeling neglected in prior work
nodes.description: Prior agent-based recommendation studies (e.g., RecAgent) mainly characterize user-side behaviors using universal LLMs, neglecting the effect of item-side modeling in the two-sided interaction process.

nodes.name: AgentCF proposal
nodes.description: AgentCF is proposed as an agent-based collaborative filtering approach that considers both users and items as agents, collaboratively optimized together, inspired by collaborative learning in traditional recommenders like BPR and NCF.

nodes.name: User and item memory modules
nodes.description: Both user and item agents are equipped with memory modules maintaining simulated preferences and tastes, including intrinsic features and acquired behavioral information.

nodes.name: User short-term and long-term memory
nodes.description: User agents are equipped with short-term memory (recently updated preference text) and long-term memory (a pool of historical preference texts) to reflect dynamically changing preferences.

nodes.name: Item unified memory
nodes.description: Item agents are equipped with a single unified memory module recording their characteristics and adopter preferences, since item information is relatively stable through time.

nodes.name: Autonomous interaction for contrastive item selection
nodes.description: User agents are presented with a contrastive pair of a positive and negative item candidate and tasked with selecting an item and providing an explanation, analogous to the forward computation of models like BPR.

nodes.name: Popularity and position bias introduced
nodes.description: To increase discrimination difficulty, a negative item with high popularity is sampled and placed before the positive item in the selection list, deliberately introducing popularity and position bias.

nodes.name: Collaborative reflection mechanism
nodes.description: Based on the disparity between an agent's decision and real-world interaction records, user and item agents are prompted to reflect on and adjust their memories in a mutual manner, serving as the 'backward update' analogous to gradient-based learning.

nodes.name: Negative item agent memory not modified
nodes.description: The memory of the negative item agent is not modified during reflection, because LLMs tend to over-complain about the negative item's drawbacks despite it possibly being attractive to other users.

nodes.name: Implicit preference propagation
nodes.description: Because memory of both user and item agents is updated for each interaction record, item memory becomes injected with adopter preferences, which propagate to subsequent users interacting with that item (and vice versa for users), implicitly modeling collaborative filtering.

nodes.name: Analogy to classical recommendation models
nodes.description: User and item memories serve as language-based parameters (embeddings); the selection process corresponds to forward preference evaluation and collaborative reflection corresponds to backward parameter update, with reflection acting as a 'semantic gradient'.

nodes.name: AgentCF outperforms baselines in most scenarios
nodes.description: AgentCF outperforms other baselines in most scenarios, highlighting the effectiveness of collaborative learning for simulating personalized agents.

nodes.name: AgentCF-B demonstrates preference propagation efficacy
nodes.description: The performance of the basic AgentCF-B variant, acting as a collaborative filtering recommender, demonstrates the efficacy of preference propagation in modeling the collaborative filtering idea.

nodes.name: AgentCF-B+R improves personalization
nodes.description: Retrieving user agents' specialized preferences toward candidates (AgentCF-B+R) enables more personalized inferences.

nodes.name: AgentCF-B+H better on sparse data
nodes.description: In sparse interaction cases (Office dataset), incorporating user historical interactions to enable LLMs as sequential recommenders (AgentCF-B+H) achieves better performance.

nodes.name: AgentCF comparable to full-dataset traditional recommenders
nodes.description: AgentCF achieves comparable performance to traditional recommenders trained on full datasets in sparse scenarios, despite being trained on only ~0.07% of the complete dataset.

nodes.name: Tuning-free baselines underperform
nodes.description: Existing tuning-free methods (Pop, BM25, LLMRank) exhibit unsatisfactory performance, with LLMRank falling significantly behind traditional models despite using ChatGPT with user historical interactions.

nodes.name: Removing autonomous interaction degrades performance
nodes.description: Without autonomous interaction (directly providing real interaction records to agents), performance drops, showing that comparing autonomous interactions to real-world records generates more comprehensive feedback for reflection.

nodes.name: Removing user agent optimization degrades performance
nodes.description: Without user agent memory updates (representing users by raw historical interactions), performance declines, showing simple verbalized interaction text cannot reflect underlying user preferences.

nodes.name: Removing item agent optimization degrades performance
nodes.description: Without item agent optimization (representing items by identity information only), performance also declines, highlighting the effectiveness of behavior-involved item-side modeling for capturing two-sided relations.

nodes.name: LLMRank susceptible to popularity/position bias
nodes.description: An LLM prompted by user historical interactions (LLMRank) is influenced by both popularity bias and position bias, tending to select popular and higher-positioned items.

nodes.name: AgentCF shows enhanced stability against bias
nodes.description: AgentCF, although inevitably affected by popularity and position bias, performs with enhanced stability compared to LLMRank, confirming it ranks candidates based on personalized preferences rather than general knowledge alone.

nodes.name: Continuous optimization improves agent-user alignment
nodes.description: Continuous optimization across steps enables user agents to align their preferences with real users, leading to an increasing number making correct choices on initial attempts before optimization at each step.

nodes.name: High post-reflection accuracy
nodes.description: Around 95% of user agents can make correct choices after collaborative reflection, highlighting its effectiveness.

nodes.name: User-user interaction via reviews
nodes.description: User agents can read and write reviews about items, simulating user-user social behaviors where test users read reviews from other user agents before deciding.

nodes.name: Simulated agents behave like real users toward reviews
nodes.description: Simulated user agents show a growing inclination to purchase items after positive reviews, refrain from purchasing after negative reviews, and trust reviews from users with similar preferences, akin to real-user behavior.

nodes.name: Item-item interaction alleviates cold-start
nodes.description: New item agents are prompted to interact with and learn from popular item agents with extensive interaction records, warming up cold-start items by estimating adopter preferences.

nodes.name: Item-item interaction improves ranking performance
nodes.description: The item-item interaction process enhances propagation of collected user preferences to new items and improves their ranking performance compared to using cold-start memory alone.

nodes.name: Dissimilar item interactions also help
nodes.description: Even interactions with item agents that differ in identity information can alleviate the cold-start problem to some extent, implying new item agents comprehend the relationship between identity information and personalized memory rather than simply replicating other agents' memories.

nodes.name: Seed preference propagation experiment
nodes.description: A seed user agent is initialized with special preference descriptions not spontaneously emerging during normal optimization, then agents autonomously interact and optimize memories to observe propagation.

nodes.name: Propagation increases then decays with scope
nodes.description: Through continuous interactions, an increasing number of user agents with similar behaviors to the seed user express similar preferences, but the proportion gradually decreases as interaction scope expands, indicating information decay consistent with real-world diffusion principles.

isolated_nodes.name: LLM agents exhibit emergent human-like behavior
isolated_nodes.description: By scaling their numbers, LLM-powered agents exhibit the emergence of human-like behaviors at both individual and population levels, motivating simulation of human social behaviors.

isolated_nodes.name: Collaborative filtering inspiration from BPR/NCF
isolated_nodes.description: AgentCF's solution is inspired by the collaborative learning idea from traditional recommendation models such as BPR and NCF, where user and item parameters are collaboratively optimized.

isolated_nodes.name: Task-focused reflection differs from collaborative reflection
isolated_nodes.description: Methods like Reflexion and Self-Refine optimize general-purpose agents through self-learning based on their own exploration, which differs from the collaborative learning emphasized in AgentCF.

isolated_nodes.name: Dataset construction
isolated_nodes.description: Experiments use sampled dense and sparse subsets (100 users each) from Amazon 'CDs and Vinyl' and 'Office Products' review datasets due to expensive API call costs.

isolated_nodes.name: Evaluation protocol
isolated_nodes.description: Performance is evaluated using NDCG@1/5/10 with a leave-one-out strategy, ranking the ground-truth last item alongside nine randomly sampled negative items, averaged over three repetitions.

isolated_nodes.name: Baseline models
isolated_nodes.description: AgentCF is compared against BPR, SASRec, Pop, BM25, and LLMRank as baseline recommendation methods.

isolated_nodes.name: Collaborative advertisement creation
isolated_nodes.description: Multiple advertiser agents proficient in different aspects (personalization, creativity, attractiveness) critique and refine an advertisement draft, producing more appealing advertisements through collaboration, illustrating collective intelligence potential.

components.description: Motivation: state representation as an overlooked component of CMAB recommenders

nodes.name: Recommender systems increasingly rely on CMABs for real-time personalization
nodes.description: Due to the continuous stream of user interactions and feedback in web-based systems, recommenders increasingly rely on contextual multi-armed bandits (CMABs), which encode users and items as feature vectors, select an item to recommend, and update incrementally from feedback.

nodes.name: CMAB research has concentrated on model, exploration, inference, and reward aspects
nodes.description: Most CMAB research has concentrated on four aspects: the underlying model consuming user state, the exploration strategy, the inference procedure for producing recommendations, and reward modeling for learning and evaluation.

nodes.name: State representation is a critical but neglected aspect of CMABs
nodes.description: Current literature often neglects the state representation — the contextual encoding of user interaction history (one-hot vectors, item metadata summaries, or more commonly embeddings) — with most CMAB studies treating it as a given design choice rather than investigating its impact.

nodes.name: Paper investigates how embedding-based state representations impact CMAB performance
nodes.description: The paper investigates the impact of different embedding-based state representations derived from matrix factorization models on the performance of traditional CMAB algorithms, hypothesizing that this seemingly minor design choice substantially influences final performance.

components.description: Contributions of the study

nodes.name: First large-scale empirical comparison of state representations in CMABs
nodes.description: The paper presents the first large-scale empirical comparison of state representations in contextual multi-armed bandits, evaluating six recommendation datasets, two matrix factorization models, three representation strategies, and three CMAB models, systematically varying both embedding method and representation formulation to isolate their impact.

nodes.name: State representation choice often outweighs bandit algorithm choice
nodes.description: The study shows that the choice of bandit algorithm often results in minor performance differences compared to the substantial impact of the selected context representation strategy.

nodes.name: Identification of a literature gap around state representation design
nodes.description: The paper identifies a prominent gap in the literature: while much research emphasizes new algorithms, reward modeling, and evaluation methods, the design of the environment's state representation remains largely overlooked.

components.description: Related work: content-based vs. embedding-based context strategies and their limitations

nodes.name: Content-based representations use demographic/metadata features but suffer from noise and unavailability
nodes.description: Content-based CMAB context uses user demographic information and item metadata, useful for cold-start and explainability, but such features are not always available and are often subject to noise and inconsistencies, limiting applicability.

nodes.name: Embedding-based context is a common alternative using latent factorization
nodes.description: Due to content-feature limitations, a common strategy represents users and items via latent embeddings capturing preferences and characteristics in a shared latent space, exemplified by warm-up ALS initialization, Latent Contextual Bandits, BanditMF, and deep-learning healthcare recommenders that concatenate learned embeddings as bandit input.

nodes.name: Many embedding-based recommenders rely on static offline-pretrained embeddings
nodes.description: Many existing recommenders using item/user embeddings as context rely on offline pre-trained embeddings that remain static during online interactions, simplifying modeling but potentially failing to capture evolving real-time dynamics.

nodes.name: Some studies instead learn evolving embeddings dynamically
nodes.description: To address the static-embedding limitation, studies like COFIBA (dynamic user clustering with LinUCB), Alternating Linear Bandits (continuously retrained MF embeddings), and Khosravi et al.'s work explore evolving user states and their representation.

nodes.name: Most studies still treat state representation as given, with limited focus on its construction
nodes.description: Even accounting for dynamic embeddings, the vast majority of studies pay limited attention to how item/user feature vectors are obtained and state representations constructed, treating context as given without describing how to build it.

nodes.name: Studies that prioritize state representation design achieve more impactful results
nodes.description: Studies emphasizing state representation — dynamically learned variable-sized embeddings (He et al.), bandit-based denoising and diffusion-enhanced contrastive learning for sequential recommendation (Feng et al., Cui et al.), and knowledge-graph embeddings (Gan and Kwon) — demonstrate that state-representation decisions can outweigh algorithm choice in impact.

components.description: Experimental protocol: continuous temporal evaluation with static embeddings to isolate representation effects

nodes.name: Temporal split into historical warm-up and online evaluation phases
nodes.description: Interaction logs are ordered by timestamp; the first 50% of interactions form historical data for model initialization (with a 10% slice for hyperparameter tuning and the remainder for learning embeddings and warming up CMABs), while the second half is dedicated exclusively to online evaluation (Fig. 1).

nodes.name: Static, non-incremental embeddings chosen to isolate representation effects
nodes.description: Embeddings are generated in a single non-incremental pass and kept static (not dynamically learned) to prevent effects related to temporal drift and model coupling, deliberately isolating the influence of state representation for a controlled comparison.

nodes.name: Cold-start items excluded to ensure consistent evaluation
nodes.description: Since the static embedding space was generated in a single pass, unseen test-set items lacked vector representations; interactions involving those items were excluded to avoid the cold-start issue and ensure consistent evaluation.

nodes.name: Online evaluation proceeds over 10 chronological windows
nodes.description: In the online stage, test data is processed in 10 equally-sized chronological windows; in each window, models generate ranked recommendations, observe actual user choices, and update their linear predictors with the new feedback.

components.description: Method: two matrix factorization embedding models (ALS and BPR)

nodes.name: Matrix factorization represents users/items via a shared latent space
nodes.description: Matrix factorization models approximate the interaction signal between a user and item as the dot product of a user feature vector and an item feature vector in a shared d-dimensional latent space (Eq. 1), learned by minimizing a loss over observed interactions.

nodes.name: ALS and BPR chosen as well-established, differently-optimized MF baselines
nodes.description: Implicit Alternating Least Squares (ALS) and Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) were selected as embedding models; both leverage historical user-item interactions but differ in optimization objective — ALS uses confidence-weighted feedback while BPR optimizes a ranking-based loss — and both are well-established, efficiently trainable baselines.

nodes.name: Hyperparameters tuned per dataset via validation NDCG@20
nodes.description: For both MF models, hyperparameters (latent factors d, learning rate, regularization strength, training epochs) were tuned on the validation split of warm-up data, selecting per-dataset the configuration yielding the best NDCG@20 (Table 2).

components.description: Method: three state-representation aggregation strategies

nodes.name: User embeddings: static, most personalized but non-adaptive representation
nodes.description: The simplest strategy represents the state solely by the static user embedding p_u; it is the most personalized representation available but remains unchanged throughout online evaluation, yielding stable but non-diversified recommendations and failing to capture behavioral drift in dynamic environments.

nodes.name: Item-averaged embeddings: dynamic but order-agnostic representation
nodes.description: This strategy computes the user state as the average of embeddings of all previously consumed items (Eq. 2), dynamically adapting to behavior changes while maintaining fixed dimensionality, but losing the sequential order of interactions.

nodes.name: Concatenated item embeddings: order-preserving but higher-complexity representation
nodes.description: To preserve sequential information, this strategy concatenates the embeddings of the h most recent consumed items in FIFO order (Eq. 3, zero-padded if fewer than h items exist), explicitly encoding interaction order but increasing computational/memory complexity linearly/quadratically with h, making it the most computationally expensive strategy tested.

components.description: Finding (RQ1): no single embedding model consistently dominates

nodes.name: ALS and BPR performance varies drastically and unpredictably across datasets
nodes.description: Different embedding models lead to significant performance variation with no single algorithm consistently outperforming the other; ALS achieved up to 22x better results than BPR on BestBuy, while BPR outperformed ALS by 47x in specific MovieLens-100k scenarios.

nodes.name: ALS wins the majority of experiments but BPR wins a substantial minority
nodes.description: Holding CMAB algorithm and aggregation function fixed, ALS attained the best overall score in 61% of experiments, with BPR thriving in the remaining 39%, showing alternating dominance across datasets and contexts.

nodes.name: Friedman test shows no statistically significant difference between ALS and BPR overall
nodes.description: A Friedman test comparing ALS and BPR embeddings across all results revealed no statistically significant difference (chi-squared_r=2.67, p=0.102), consistent with the alternating dominance pattern.

components.description: Finding (RQ2): aggregation strategy significantly affects outcomes, defying intuition

nodes.name: Static user embeddings sometimes outperform more sophisticated aggregations
nodes.description: Although expected to generally underperform (and indeed generally the worst among BPR approaches per Table 4), the static user-embedding strategy achieved the best and second-best results on BestBuy and outperformed item concatenation for both BPR and ALS on MovieLens-100k.

nodes.name: Concatenation does not always outperform simpler aggregations despite preserving order
nodes.description: Contrary to the prior assumption that concatenation would be superior due to preserving item-consumption ordering, other (simpler) strategies surpassed concatenation in 41% of experiments.

nodes.name: Friedman/Nemenyi tests confirm item-based aggregations statistically beat user embeddings
nodes.description: A Friedman test comparing the three aggregation strategies found significant differences (chi-squared_r=16.26, p=0.00029, 99% confidence); a post-hoc Nemenyi test (critical difference 0.5522) showed Item-averaged and Concatenated embeddings are statistically superior to User embeddings with 95% confidence, with no significant difference between the two item-based methods.

components.description: Finding (RQ3): state representation quality outweighs bandit algorithm choice

nodes.name: Different CMAB algorithms perform very similarly under a fixed state representation
nodes.description: The performance of LinUCB, LinGreedy, and LinTS using the same state representation is generally very similar, typically differing only in the fourth decimal place, with only a few notable exceptions such as Delicious and MovieLens-100k under item concatenation.

nodes.name: Switching representation/embedding yields far larger gains than switching bandit algorithm
nodes.description: Across all datasets, switching from a lower-quality embedding representation to a more effective aggregation method or embedding model resulted in substantially larger performance gains (up to 47x) than changing the underlying bandit algorithm.

components.description: Overall conclusion: no universal winner, domain-specific evaluation needed

nodes.name: No single embedding model or aggregation method consistently dominates across datasets
nodes.description: Synthesizing the RQ1-RQ3 findings, both the embedding algorithm and the aggregation strategy significantly impact recommendation performance, but no single combination consistently dominates across datasets, underscoring the need for domain-specific, tailored evaluation.

nodes.name: Future CMAB research should prioritize state-representation design alongside algorithmic innovation
nodes.description: Because state-representation quality generally has a stronger effect on results than the specific bandit algorithm, future work should prioritize optimizing embedding-based context representations alongside algorithmic improvements rather than focusing predominantly on new bandit algorithms.

isolated_nodes.name: Foundational CMAB background
isolated_nodes.description: CMABs extend traditional multi-armed bandits by incorporating contextual state representations, exemplified by methods like LinGreedy and LinUCB; the linear bandit is a foundational CMAB variant scoring items via linear regression with an exploration strategy balancing exploration-exploitation.

isolated_nodes.name: Broader CMAB recommender research directions
isolated_nodes.description: The CMAB-based recommender literature has expanded to include pre-filtering items to reduce the action space, clustering users/items to generalize learning, incorporating deep learning or graph-based models, and structured bandits for slate recommendation.

isolated_nodes.name: Datasets and implementation tools used
isolated_nodes.description: Experiments use six public benchmark datasets (Amazon Beauty, Amazon Books, BestBuy, Delicious, MovieLens-100K, MovieLens-25M, RetailRocket) after deduplication/consistency preprocessing, implemented in Python3 using the implicit library for embeddings and the Mab2Rec library for bandit models.

isolated_nodes.name: Related deployment-focused embedding study
isolated_nodes.description: Hejazinia et al. examined deployment aspects and compared different types of embeddings but did not focus specifically on the bandit framework, distinguishing their study's scope from this paper's bandit-centric focus.

isolated_nodes.name: Planned future work directions
isolated_nodes.description: Future work plans include exploring SOTA neural embedding algorithms (RecVAE, Neural Collaborative Filtering), evaluating SOTA deep incremental recommenders (BSARec, GRU4RecCPR, FEARec), analyzing embedding hyperparameter influence, and comparing static versus incrementally learned embeddings.

C1 (motivation: state representation as an overlooked CMAB component) leads to C2 (the paper's three explicit contributions), both grounded further by C3's detailed related-work analysis contrasting content-based versus embedding-based context strategies and noting that state-representation-focused studies achieve more impactful results — directly motivating the paper's design. C4 (experimental protocol) establishes the controlled, static-embedding evaluation methodology that isolates representation effects from confounds like temporal drift, feeding into the two method components: C5 (the ALS/BPR embedding models) and C6 (the three aggregation strategies: user, item-mean, item-concat). The experimental findings are organized directly around the paper's three research questions: C7 answers RQ1 (no embedding model dominates), C8 answers RQ2 (aggregation strategy matters and defies intuition, statistically confirmed), and C9 answers RQ3 (representation quality outweighs bandit algorithm choice) — these three converge in C10, the paper's overall conclusion advocating domain-specific evaluation and prioritizing representation design in future CMAB research, closing the loop back to the literature gap identified in C2. Foundational CMAB background, broader research-direction context, dataset/tooling details, a related deployment-focused study, and planned future work are treated as isolated nodes since they provide supporting context rather than participating in the core causal/argumentative chain.

nodes.name: Robotic datasets lack pretraining scale
nodes.description: Existing vision encoders for robotics face a fundamental bottleneck: robotic datasets lack the scale necessary for large-scale pre-training.

nodes.name: Existing paradigms lack paired vision-action data
nodes.description: Prior work circumvents data scarcity using internet-scale image/language data or egocentric human video, but neither paradigm learns from paired vision and action data that downstream visuomotor control policies require.

nodes.name: Robot trajectories unavailable at scale
nodes.description: Robot trajectories, the most direct source of paired vision-action signal, are not available at pre-training scale.

nodes.name: Motivation to extract actions from human video
nodes.description: The unavailability of robot trajectories at scale motivates extracting action signals from abundant human video instead.

nodes.name: Hand poses as action proxy
nodes.description: CAIP treats human hand poses from large-scale egocentric video as a proxy for end-effector actions, since this representation aligns naturally with downstream robot action spaces.

nodes.name: CAIP proposal
nodes.description: CAIP is introduced as a vision encoder that learns a unified action-image representation through a contrastive objective.

nodes.name: Three-encoder architecture
nodes.description: CAIP's architecture consists of three encoders: vision (ViT-L/16), language (24-layer transformer), and action (lightweight 4-layer transformer), initialized from SigLIP 2 where applicable.

nodes.name: No global pooling of patch features
nodes.description: The vision encoder retains the full patch sequence without global pooling, so text tokens can attend to spatially localized features in the next step.

nodes.name: Two-stage text-conditioned image pooling
nodes.description: Language tokens attend to image patch features to produce text-grounded visual features, then a learnable query token attends over these to produce a single text-conditioned image embedding.

nodes.name: Action encoder trained from scratch
nodes.description: The action encoder is a lightweight 4-layer transformer trained from scratch, processing an action sequence and extracting a CLS token as the action embedding.

nodes.name: SigLIP-style contrastive alignment
nodes.description: A SigLIP-style sigmoid contrastive loss aligns text-conditioned image embeddings with action embeddings, treating each pair independently as binary classification rather than requiring global batch normalization.

nodes.name: Hand pose keypoint representation
nodes.description: Hand poses are represented as 42 keypoints (21 per hand including wrist), each expressed as an SE(3) transform following the MANO hand convention.

nodes.name: Action chunking via relative transforms
nodes.description: Actions are formed by emulating end-effector delta control: the action at offset i is the relative SE(3) transform between the pose at time t and time t+i, for i=1,...,T (T=64).

nodes.name: Large-scale egocentric training data
nodes.description: CAIP trains on 32,041 hours of annotated human egocentric data (lab and in-the-wild) plus ~88 hours of tabletop humanoid manipulation data for embodiment diversity.

nodes.name: CAIP highest average success rate
nodes.description: CAIP achieves the highest average success rate at 76% across six real-world manipulation tasks, outperforming the strongest baseline (SigLIP 2, 43.4%) by over 30 points.

nodes.name: CAIP top on five of six tasks
nodes.description: CAIP attains the top success rate on five of the six manipulation tasks.

nodes.name: Baselines show inconsistent task performance
nodes.description: Baselines do not exhibit consistent behavior: encoders competitive on one task (e.g., MVP on Dispense Soap, DINOv2 on Pour) degrade significantly on others, suggesting non-manipulation-centric representations suit some tasks over others.

nodes.name: CAIP maintains strong performance across all tasks
nodes.description: In contrast to baselines, CAIP maintains strong performance across all tasks, indicating that action-centric contrastive pre-training produces generalizing representations.

nodes.name: CAIP outperforms larger SigLIP 2 SO400M
nodes.description: CAIP outperforms the larger SigLIP 2 SO400M baseline despite being initialized from the smaller SigLIP 2 ViT-L backbone, isolating the performance gain to action-centric pre-training.

nodes.name: CAIP outperforms baselines in zero-shot action classification
nodes.description: CAIP consistently outperforms all baselines, including the strongest (DINOv2), by a substantial margin across the full data-efficiency curve on held-out action classification.

nodes.name: Zero-shot retrieval exceeds baseline linear probes
nodes.description: Zero-shot retrieval with CAIP, despite requiring no in-domain supervision, exceeds the linear-probe performance of every baseline up to 16 samples per class.

nodes.name: CAIP transfers to unseen data
nodes.description: These results suggest CAIP's learned representations transfer effectively to unseen data and capture semantically meaningful structure for action understanding.

nodes.name: CAIP achieves highest success under perturbations
nodes.description: CAIP achieves the highest success rate under every lighting and distractor perturbation, despite all policies being trained only on unperturbed demonstrations.

nodes.name: CAIP most robust in absolute terms
nodes.description: CAIP outperforms Qwen3.5 ViT by roughly 20-30% and degrades far less than MVP under perturbations, making it the most robust encoder in absolute terms despite Qwen3.5 ViT retaining a larger relative fraction of its (much lower) original performance.

nodes.name: Encoder scale ablation
nodes.description: Scaling the vision encoder across ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-SO400M shows increasing scale leads to substantial performance improvements, with ViT-B to ViT-L yielding the largest gain of over 30% on average.

nodes.name: ViT-L selected as primary encoder
nodes.description: Based on the scaling ablation, ViT-L is selected as the primary vision encoder, providing the best trade-off between performance, model size, and inference speed.

isolated_nodes.name: Semantic encoders lack action-centric structure
isolated_nodes.description: Semantic encoders like CLIP and SigLIP provide high-level semantic knowledge, and encoders like DINO capture fine-grained geometric detail, but neither class receives direct action supervision or sees manipulation environments during training.

isolated_nodes.name: Robot trajectory datasets remain small-scale
isolated_nodes.description: While large-scale datasets such as DROID and Open X-Embodiment have led to significant progress, the volume of available robot trajectories remains orders of magnitude smaller than internet-scale video corpora.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior egocentric methods use non-action objectives
isolated_nodes.description: Prior approaches such as R3M and MVP resort to alternative objectives like frame-level contrastive loss or masked autoencoder reconstruction, omitting action-conditioned information critical for downstream control.

isolated_nodes.name: Direct action regression fails as pretraining objective
isolated_nodes.description: Direct action regression pre-training, tested both via MLP head on pooled embeddings and via transformer decoder on full patch sequence, did not produce useful representations.

isolated_nodes.name: Downstream policy architecture
isolated_nodes.description: The downstream policy uses a decoder-only transformer (Qwen3.5-0.8B) trained from scratch on frozen encoder outputs, with an MLP action head predicting flow-matching velocity.

isolated_nodes.name: R3M time-contrastive pretraining
isolated_nodes.description: R3M was among the first frozen backbones pretrained explicitly on human video, using time-contrastive learning and video-language alignment over 3,700 hours of Ego4D, without exposure to ground-truth actions or poses.

isolated_nodes.name: HRP uses affordance-based supervision
isolated_nodes.description: HRP is a step toward explicit action-annotated pre-training, fine-tuning encoders to predict hand-object affordances like contact points and future hand poses, though these signals remain distant from downstream actions.

isolated_nodes.name: Latent action token methods lack explicit action supervision
isolated_nodes.description: A family of methods discretizes inter-frame transitions into latent action tokens via VQ-VAE objectives, relying on ungrounded latent action tokens rather than explicit action supervision.

isolated_nodes.name: Real-world evaluation setup
isolated_nodes.description: Policies are evaluated on a Dexmate Vega bimanual manipulator with 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hands, using three cameras, trained from scratch with only 200 demonstrations per task.

nodes.name: Existing contrastive methods lack clinical knowledge
nodes.description: Existing contrastive learning approaches incorporate subject and signal attributes but do not incorporate clinical knowledge, nor handle missing metadata.

nodes.name: Risk scores as contextual metadata
nodes.description: Clinically validated risk scores translate complex physiological factors into interpretable values that guide clinical actions, and can be leveraged as contextual information for contrastive pretraining.

nodes.name: Clinically-guided contrastive learning proposal
nodes.description: CLEF introduces a novel contrastive learning approach that uses an established clinical risk score to adaptively weight negative pairs.

nodes.name: Explicit missing metadata mechanism
nodes.description: CLEF includes an explicit mechanism to handle missing metadata when computing risk-score-based similarity.

nodes.name: Weighted contrastive loss
nodes.description: Negative pairs contribute unequally to representation learning; a weighting term Wik adjusts the relative importance of negatives according to similarity to the positive.

nodes.name: Risk score dissimilarity Di,k
nodes.description: For a negative pair, dissimilarity Di,k is defined from the squared difference in risk scores, normalized and bounded within [α, 1].

nodes.name: Missing metadata multiplier Mik
nodes.description: A multiplier Mik is assigned to negative pairs based on the number of missing metadata variables, functioning as a reliability adjustment.

nodes.name: Weight matrix W = D ⊙ M
nodes.description: The weight matrix combining dissimilarity and missing-metadata reliability is defined as the Hadamard product of D and M.

nodes.name: Clinically-guided contrastive loss Lw
nodes.description: The clinically-guided contrastive loss Lw uses the weight matrix W to adaptively weight negative pairs in the batch-averaged contrastive objective.

nodes.name: Dissimilarity alignment loss Ld
nodes.description: The dissimilarity alignment loss computes MSE between cosine similarity of embeddings and their corresponding weight, encouraging clinically similar signals to map to nearby embeddings.

nodes.name: Final training objective L = Lw + Ld
nodes.description: The final CLEF objective combines the clinically-guided contrastive loss and the dissimilarity alignment loss with equal weighting.

nodes.name: Missing metadata prevents noisy influence
nodes.description: When many metadata variables are missing, Mik moves the weighting closer to uniform SimCLR-like behavior, preventing uncertain risk differences from unduly influencing the contrastive objective.

nodes.name: Random lead selection during pretraining
nodes.description: During pretraining, one of the 12 leads is randomly selected per sample with stochastic augmentation, so the model is collectively trained across all leads.

nodes.name: CLEF generalizes to any lead
nodes.description: Because CLEF is not restricted to a specific lead during pretraining, it can be fine-tuned to any target lead, supporting cross-device use.

nodes.name: Lead-specific pretraining as upper bound
nodes.description: Pretraining CLEF exclusively on the downstream task's lead yields further AUROC improvements over pretraining on all 12 leads, approaching the performance of supervised ECGFounder.

nodes.name: CLEF outperforms baselines on lead I/II finetuning
nodes.description: CLEF outperforms the best baseline across both leads, achieving average AUROC improvement of 3.1% on lead I and 4.8% on lead II.

nodes.name: CLEF robust across leads
nodes.description: CLEF variants differ by only 0.3%, 0.0%, and 1.4% on average in AUROC across leads I and II, unlike ST-MEM and KED which favor lead I.

nodes.name: CLEF strong on pattern identification tasks
nodes.description: CLEF performs particularly well on form/rhythm/arrhythmia pattern identification tasks, improving AUROC by 5.9% (lead I) and 8.5% (lead II) over strongest baselines.

nodes.name: CLEF vs ECGFounder on lead I vs II
nodes.description: CLEF underperforms supervised ECGFounder on lead I (its trained lead) but outperforms it on lead II, since ECGFounder's performance drops on the untrained lead while CLEF maintains performance across leads.

nodes.name: CLEF outperforms self-supervised baselines
nodes.description: CLEF outperforms SimCLR, BYOL, and MoCo self-supervised pretraining methods, with 100 of 117 instances outperformed by CLEF.

nodes.name: Applying CLEF objective to KED improves performance
nodes.description: Initializing the best-performing baseline (KED) with its pretrained weights and further applying the clinically-guided pretraining objective improves AUROC on nearly all downstream tasks by 3.0% on average.

nodes.name: Missing metadata ablation degrades performance
nodes.description: Without the missing-metadata handling term M, performance of all CLEF models degrades on the majority of tasks, with AUROC decreasing by 1.9% on average.

nodes.name: Wearable datasets more affected by missing metadata ablation
nodes.description: The AUROC decrease from removing missing-metadata handling is larger on wearable datasets (4.0% drop) compared to lead I clinical datasets (1.1% drop).

isolated_nodes.name: AI-assisted ECG diagnosis improvement
isolated_nodes.description: Clinicians using AI were 30% more accurate in diagnosing left ventricular dysfunction from ECGs than those without AI support.

isolated_nodes.name: Single-lead ECG challenge
isolated_nodes.description: Accurate analysis of single-lead ECGs remains a challenge due to reduced spatial information and increased noise and motion artifacts.

isolated_nodes.name: SCORE2 risk score definition
isolated_nodes.description: SCORE2 is a clinically validated function estimating 10-year cardiovascular disease risk based on 7 variables: age, gender, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, diabetes status, total cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol.

isolated_nodes.name: MIMIC-IV-ECG limited metadata
isolated_nodes.description: MIMIC-IV-ECG reports only three variables per subject (age, gender, systolic blood pressure) out of the seven needed for full SCORE2 computation, motivating the missing-metadata handling mechanism.

isolated_nodes.name: Three model scales
isolated_nodes.description: CLEF is pretrained at three scales: small (448K parameters), medium (30.7M parameters), and large (296M parameters), using ResNeXt1D architecture.

isolated_nodes.name: Foundation model baselines
isolated_nodes.description: CLEF is benchmarked against Moirai, Moment, ST-MEM, and KED foundation model baselines, plus SimCLR, BYOL, and MoCo self-supervised algorithms, and supervised ECGFounder.

isolated_nodes.name: Linear probing shows larger CLEF models better
isolated_nodes.description: CLEF-M and CLEF-L outperform all baselines in linear probing with 8.5% and 9.9% average AUROC improvement, but CLEF-S does not outperform KED or Moment, indicating larger models produce better representations.

isolated_nodes.name: Moment outperforms CLEF on MUSIC SCD
isolated_nodes.description: Moment, a general time series model, outperformed CLEF on MUSIC sudden cardiac death prediction, likely because SCD risk depends on long-range temporal patterns more akin to forecasting.

isolated_nodes.name: Loss component ablation on CIFAR-100
isolated_nodes.description: A CIFAR-100 study comparing standard contrastive loss, weighted contrastive loss, dissimilarity alignment loss, and their combinations shows the proposed Lw + Ld achieves clearer separation with lower variance.

isolated_nodes.description: Models were trained on ECGs from a single hospital, limiting representativeness for the general population.
