components.description: Motivation: the modality gap in CLIP and limitations of existing remedies

nodes.name: CLIP's multi-modal feature spaces exhibit a modality gap
nodes.description: Although CLIP achieves remarkable zero-shot performance, its image and text alignment is imperfect: CLIP models tend to encode images and texts into different feature clusters even after sufficient training on massive datasets, a phenomenon termed the modality gap.

nodes.name: The modality gap harms downstream task performance
nodes.description: Prior work shows the modality gap largely affects downstream task performance, especially fine-grained classification, and that CLIP models often fail to retrieve localized objects and attributes in images from corresponding captions.

nodes.name: Pre-training modifications reduce the gap but require costly large-scale retraining
nodes.description: Existing pre-training modifications (auxiliary self-supervised losses, shared encoder weights/feature maps) reduce the modality gap but require training from scratch on million-scale datasets like LAION-400M, incurring heavy computational costs across multiple GPUs, and such pre-trained models are often not published.

nodes.name: Fine-tuning methods are cheaper but degrade zero-shot transfer performance
nodes.description: Fine-tuning methods (prompt tuning, adapters) require much smaller datasets and less compute than pre-training, but degrade the general zero-shot transfer performance because their primary goal is improving target-task performance.

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine proposed: lightweight post-pre-training between pre-training and fine-tuning
nodes.description: The paper proposes a post-pre-training phase between pre-training and fine-tuning, aiming to mitigate the modality gap and enhance zero-shot transfer performance of off-the-shelf pre-trained CLIP models using only small datasets and modest compute (e.g., a single GPU and COCO Captions).

components.description: Challenges specific to post-pre-training: uniformity corruption and catastrophic forgetting

nodes.name: Naive feature-gap minimization corrupts hypersphere uniformity
nodes.description: Directly minimizing the gap between image and text features (naive alignment loss) corrupts the feature space's uniformity on the hypersphere, an important property of contrastive representations that indicates how much input information is preserved.

nodes.name: Post-pre-training with contrastive loss causes catastrophic forgetting
nodes.description: Post-pre-training with contrastive loss causes catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge in pre-trained CLIP models, driven by overfitting due to restricted mini-batch sizes far smaller than those used in original pre-training.

nodes.name: Both challenges must be addressed to design an effective post-pre-training method
nodes.description: Because naive alignment destroys uniformity and contrastive post-pre-training induces catastrophic forgetting, an effective post-pre-training method must reduce the modality gap without sacrificing uniformity or retained knowledge.

components.description: Method: Random Feature Alignment (RaFA) design rationale

nodes.name: Naive L2 alignment loss degrades generalization via uniformity loss
nodes.description: A naive loss minimizing the L2 distance between image and text feature vectors (Eq. 2) improves alignment of positive pairs but destroys hypersphere uniformity by forcing changes to the feature distribution, degrading validation performance as shown by prior work on alignment/uniformity trade-offs.

nodes.name: RaFA instead matches feature distributions to a shared prior via random reference vectors
nodes.description: Instead of directly matching paired features, RaFA refines image and text features to follow a shared prior distribution (e.g., standard Gaussian) by minimizing the L2 distance between each feature vector and a random reference vector sampled from the prior, shared across the image-text pair (Eq. 3).

nodes.name: RaFA indirectly minimizes modality gap while preserving uniformity and avoiding overfitting
nodes.description: By using a shared random reference vector per pair, RaFA indirectly minimizes the modality gap, gradually aligns features to the shared prior, and the randomness helps avoid overfitting to the small post-pre-training dataset and reforms model capacity.

components.description: Method: Hybrid Contrastive-Distillation (HyCD) design rationale

nodes.name: Standard self-distillation from the frozen pre-trained model retains knowledge
nodes.description: To retain past knowledge, a baseline strategy penalizes the post-pre-training model with a knowledge distillation loss where the frozen pre-trained CLIP model acts as teacher, minimizing a batch-wise KL-divergence between teacher and student softmax outputs over image-text similarity matrices (Eqs. 4-7).

nodes.name: Pure self-distillation interferes with RaFA by over-anchoring to pre-trained parameters
nodes.description: Although minimizing the standard self-distillation loss retains past knowledge, it strongly enchains the model's parameters to the pre-trained ones, which was found to interfere with RaFA's feature-alignment objective.

nodes.name: HyCD blends ground-truth pair labels with teacher outputs via alpha-blending
nodes.description: To reconcile RaFA with knowledge retention, HyCD modifies the teacher output by alpha-blending an indicator function for correct image-text pairs with the teacher's similarity output (Eq. 8), letting the model learn the correct pairing directly while referencing the teacher's relative knowledge on other pairs.

nodes.name: HyCD loss computed bidirectionally over image-to-text and text-to-image directions
nodes.description: Using the blended hybrid targets, the HyCD loss is computed as the average of image-to-text and text-to-image KL-divergence losses (Eqs. 9-10), enabling the model to both retain past knowledge and learn new alignment knowledge.

components.description: Method: combined CLIP-Refine objective and training procedure

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine jointly optimizes RaFA and HyCD with equal weighting
nodes.description: CLIP-Refine optimizes model parameters by jointly minimizing the sum of RaFA loss and HyCD loss (Eq. 1); equal contribution of both losses was empirically found to achieve the best performance, avoiding the need for additional balancing hyperparameters.

nodes.name: Combining RaFA and HyCD yields larger gains than either alone
nodes.description: While HyCD alone improves generalization performance of pre-trained CLIP models, combining it with RaFA achieves larger improvements by minimizing the modality gap without losing past knowledge, per the algorithmic procedure in Algorithm 1.

components.description: Related work positioning: distinguishing post-pre-training from prior pre-training and fine-tuning approaches

nodes.name: Prior pre-training modifications require large-scale datasets and multi-GPU compute
nodes.description: Methods adding auxiliary losses (cyclic consistency, fine-grained token similarity, self-supervised augmentation, supervised contrastive, LLM-augmented text) or sharing encoder weights/discrete token spaces require large-scale datasets like CC12M and LAION-400M, incurring high computational costs on multiple GPUs.

nodes.name: Prior fine-tuning methods reduce target-task modality gap but don't target zero-shot transfer
nodes.description: Prompt tuning (CoOp/CoCoOp), visual prompt tuning, unified visual-textual prompt tuning, shared low-rank adapters, and mixup-based feature-space refinement (m2-mix) succeed in reducing the gap on target datasets, but do not intend to improve zero-shot transfer performance, unlike CLIP-Refine's objective.

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine is lightweight, cooperative with pre-training, and targets zero-shot transfer
nodes.description: In contrast to both prior lines, CLIP-Refine improves generalization performance of off-the-shelf pre-trained models using only small datasets (Flickr8/30K, COCO Caption) with a single GPU, is cooperative with any pre-trained model, and can still be followed by fine-tuning to further boost target performance.

components.description: Finding: post-pre-training with plain contrastive loss degrades zero-shot classification

nodes.name: Contrastive and m2-mix post-pre-training degrade zero-shot classification accuracy
nodes.description: On 12 zero-shot classification datasets, post-pre-training with plain contrastive loss (Contrastive, m2-mix) largely degrades top-1 accuracy for all datasets compared to the pre-trained baseline (Table 1).

nodes.name: Small post-pre-training batch size drives catastrophic forgetting
nodes.description: Since Self-KD does not show degradation, the contrastive loss's degradation is attributed to catastrophic forgetting caused by a much smaller mini-batch size (512, single GPU) than at original pre-training (32,768, hundreds of GPUs), limiting negative samples and causing overfitting.

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine improves zero-shot classification across all 12 datasets
nodes.description: In contrast to contrastive-loss baselines, CLIP-Refine impressively improves zero-shot classification performance for all datasets, with ablations showing the gain comes from combining HyCD with RaFA (Table 1).

nodes.name: HyCD+Lalign (naive alignment) performs worst among baselines
nodes.description: HyCD combined with the naive alignment loss (HyCD+Lalign) resulted in the worst performance among baselines, confirming that naively minimizing the image-text feature gap leads to generalization degradation (Table 1).

components.description: Finding: zero-shot retrieval results reveal asymmetric image/text overfitting

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine achieves the best zero-shot retrieval performance with a larger margin than classification
nodes.description: On COCO2017-Val and Flickr8K/30K retrieval, CLIP-Refine achieves the best performance with an even larger margin over baselines than observed in classification tasks (Table 2).

nodes.name: Contrastive and m2-mix improve T→I retrieval but degrade I→T retrieval
nodes.description: Unlike in classification, Contrastive and m2-mix baselines improve text-to-image (T→I) retrieval over the pre-trained model while degrading image-to-text (I→T) retrieval, indicating asymmetric overfitting between modalities.

nodes.name: Image encoders are more prone to overfitting than text encoders due to representation continuity
nodes.description: This asymmetry is explained by images having continuous-valued pixel representations with high degrees of freedom (prone to overfitting on limited negative samples in small batches), while discrete-token text representations have limited degrees of freedom and can learn new knowledge while retaining the past; since zero-shot classification is itself an I→T task, this also explains the classification degradation in P21.

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine prevents I→T overfitting and improves both retrieval directions
nodes.description: CLIP-Refine successfully prevents the overfitting in I→T retrieval and greatly improves performance in both I→T and T→I directions, unlike the contrastive-loss baselines.

components.description: Finding: quantitative feature-space analysis (modality gap, alignment, uniformity)

nodes.name: HyCD+Lalign achieves the best gap/alignment scores but destroys uniformity
nodes.description: Among all methods, HyCD+Lalign achieves the best modality gap and alignment scores, but significantly degrades the uniformity score, indicating that directly minimizing the naive alignment loss destroys the feature space well-constructed by CLIP pre-training (Table 3).

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine consistently improves modality gap, alignment, and uniformity together
nodes.description: In contrast to HyCD+Lalign, CLIP-Refine consistently improves all three scores (modality gap, alignment, uniformity), suggesting that minimizing both the image-text gap and preserving uniformity is important for generalization performance, consistent with prior alignment-uniformity theory (Table 3).

nodes.name: The Gaussian prior naturally balances alignment and uniformity
nodes.description: Because CLIP-Refine penalizes features to follow the shared reference distribution N(0,I), whose samples tend to be uniformly distributed on the hypersphere, it naturally achieves a good balance of alignment and uniformity while reducing the modality gap.

nodes.name: PCA visualization confirms CLIP-Refine reduces the gap while preserving per-modality feature shape
nodes.description: PCA visualization shows the contrastive model enlarges the modality gap, HyCD+Lalign gathers image/text features into the same cluster but distorts each modality's feature distribution, while CLIP-Refine reduces the modality gap while keeping the shape of the pre-trained per-modality feature distributions (Fig. 3).

components.description: Ablation: choice of prior distribution in RaFA

nodes.name: Uniform prior U(0,1) yields weak improvements versus Gaussian priors
nodes.description: Using the uniform distribution U(0,1) as the RaFA prior does not show large improvements in zero-shot performance or uniformity score, likely because samples from U(0,1) do not concentrate on the hypersphere the way N(0,I) samples do, possibly collapsing uniformity gains (Table 4).

nodes.name: Text-feature-statistics Gaussian prior notably improves zero-shot classification
nodes.description: Among Gaussian priors using pre-trained feature statistics, the prior based on text feature statistics N(mu_txt, sigma_txt^2) yields the largest zero-shot classification improvement, indicating that aligning image features toward text-feature statistics is particularly effective, consistent with the I→T retrieval gains observed in Sec 4.2 (Table 4).

nodes.name: Standard Gaussian N(0,I) with sufficient variance performs best overall
nodes.description: Varying variance magnitude beta in zero-mean Gaussian priors shows performance depends on sufficient randomness; N(0,I) (beta=1) achieves the best overall balance of zero-shot accuracy, alignment, and uniformity, emphasizing the importance of randomness in RaFA (Table 4).

components.description: Finding: effect of post-pre-training dataset choice

nodes.name: Most CLIP-Refine variants outperform the pre-trained baseline regardless of dataset
nodes.description: Testing Flickr8K/30K, COCO Caption, CC3M, and CC12M as post-pre-training datasets, most CLIP-Refine models outperform the pre-trained baseline on zero-shot classification and retrieval (Table 5).

nodes.name: Larger datasets (CC3M/CC12M) underperform smaller, higher-quality COCO Caption
nodes.description: CC3M and CC12M, despite being larger, are inferior to COCO Caption, likely because they contain mismatched and noisy image-text pairs, whereas COCO Caption's higher-quality captions better support modality alignment.

nodes.name: Filtering low-quality pairs significantly improves performance, confirming data quality matters
nodes.description: Filtering out low-quality image-text pairs via CLIP-Score-based filtering (DataComp) on CC3M/CC12M yields significant performance improvements, indicating caption quality is crucial and that CLIP-Refine is scalable given high-quality data (Table 5).

components.description: Finding: generalizability across pre-trained model architectures

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine stably improves across six diverse pre-trained CLIP models
nodes.description: Evaluated on ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, OpenCLIP ViT-H/14, OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14, SigLIP ViT-SO400M/14, and DFN ViT-H/14, CLIP-Refine stably improves the pre-trained baseline's zero-shot classification and retrieval performance across all models (Table 6).

nodes.name: Bigger, stronger pre-trained models still retain a modality gap that CLIP-Refine can address
nodes.description: The consistent improvement across model scales suggests that even bigger and stronger pre-trained models still suffer from the modality gap, and modifying it with CLIP-Refine helps improve generalization performance regardless of scale.

components.description: Finding: robustness to mini-batch size in post-pre-training

nodes.name: Plain contrastive loss underperforms pre-trained baseline at feasible batch sizes
nodes.description: Across varying mini-batch sizes in post-pre-training, plain contrastive-loss post-pre-training underperforms the pre-trained baseline at feasible (small) batch sizes, likely due to large discrepancy from the pre-training batch size (32,768) causing forgetting in negative-pair predictions (Fig. 4).

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine consistently outperforms both baselines across all tested batch sizes
nodes.description: CLIP-Refine always outperforms the contrastive-loss baseline and successfully improves over the pre-trained baseline across all feasible mini-batch sizes, showing that HyCD prevents knowledge forgetting even with small mini-batches and few negative pairs (Fig. 4).

components.description: Finding: transferability of CLIP-Refine to downstream fine-tuning

nodes.name: CLIP-Refine improves linear-probe fine-tuning accuracy on ImageNet
nodes.description: Fine-tuning only a linear classification head on ImageNet while freezing post-pre-trained backbones, CLIP-Refine outperforms both the pre-trained and contrastive-loss baselines, showing the method generates useful representations even for downstream fine-tuning (Table 7).

isolated_nodes.name: Modality gap theoretical background
isolated_nodes.description: Liang et al. revealed that pre-trained CLIP models encode image and text into different clusters (modality gap), attributable empirically to the small temperature parameter in CLIP's contrastive loss; Qian et al. theoretically showed contrastive loss cannot reduce the modality gap perfectly.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal definitions of modality gap, alignment, and uniformity metrics
isolated_nodes.description: Modality gap is defined as the squared L2 distance between mean image and text feature vectors (Eq. 11); alignment is the mean squared distance between positive image-text pairs (Eq. 12); uniformity is defined via an RBF-kernel-based measure of how uniformly features are distributed on the hypersphere (Eq. 13); lower values are better for all three.

isolated_nodes.name: Experimental setup details
isolated_nodes.description: Models are trained with AdamW at learning rate 1e-6 for one epoch, mini-batch size 512 by default, α=0.5 for CLIP-Refine, using default image preprocessing per pre-trained model, implemented in PyTorch-1.13 on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80GB VRAM); evaluation spans 12 classification datasets and COCO2017-Val/Flickr8K/30K retrieval tasks.

structural_reasoning: The graph follows a problem-to-method-to-validation structure typical of a representation-learning paper. C1 (modality gap motivation and limitations of pre-training/fine-tuning remedies) leads to C2 (the two specific challenges — uniformity corruption and catastrophic forgetting — that any post-pre-training method must solve), which directly motivates the two core method components: C3 (RaFA, solving the uniformity-corruption challenge via prior-distribution matching) and C4 (HyCD, solving the catastrophic-forgetting challenge via hybrid distillation), unified in C5 (the combined CLIP-Refine objective). C6 positions the method against related pre-training/fine-tuning literature, reinforcing why post-pre-training as a distinct phase is necessary. The experimental components C7-C14 fan out from the completed method: C7 and C8 report the flagship zero-shot classification and retrieval results (including the diagnostic finding about asymmetric image/text overfitting that explains why HyCD+RaFA specifically helps); C9 provides the quantitative alignment/uniformity/modality-gap analysis explaining why CLIP-Refine's Gaussian-prior design works; C10 ablates the prior-distribution choice within RaFA, directly building on and confirming the asymmetry finding from C8; C11-C14 test robustness and generality across post-pre-training datasets, pre-trained model architectures, mini-batch sizes, and downstream fine-tuning transfer, respectively. Modality-gap theoretical background, formal metric definitions, and experimental setup details are treated as isolated nodes since they provide supporting context referenced throughout rather than links in the causal/argumentative chain.

components.description: Motivation: escalating VFM family pre-training costs and the family-size dilemma

nodes.name: CLIP-style VFM pre-training is extremely costly
nodes.description: Contrastive language-image pre-training enables ViTs to achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance and become de facto vision encoders for MLLMs, but pre-training a single ViT-L/14 on LAION-2B requires 1.2x10^5 A100 GPU hours, exceeding $500,000.

nodes.name: Existing acceleration techniques all optimize individual models
nodes.description: Mixed-precision training, system-level optimizations, mask image modeling, input token reduction, loss optimization, and data-efficient designs all share the common underlying viewpoint of optimizing the training of individual models, despite belonging to different research lines.

nodes.name: VFMs are pre-trained as model families with ever-growing family size
nodes.description: VFMs are typically pre-trained as a family of architecturally similar models with varying sizes, and family size shows an ever-growing trend driven by demand for specialized model sizes and broadening parameter ranges from larger models.

nodes.name: Growing family size creates a cost-vs-flexibility dilemma
nodes.description: The ever-growing family size trend creates a dilemma for pre-training model families: affording escalating pre-training costs from ever-growing family size, or compromising deployment flexibility by limiting the number of model sizes offered.

nodes.name: Key question: how to achieve acceleration that scales with family size
nodes.description: Faced with this dilemma, the paper poses the central question of how to achieve pre-training acceleration that scales efficiently with family size, motivating a reexamination of the standard pre-training pipeline.

components.description: Analysis: two bottlenecks in standard pre-training pipelines

nodes.name: Micro-level bottleneck: large models dominate pre-training cost
nodes.description: From the micro view, main pre-training costs stem from large models in the family; computational complexity expands around 4x when selecting a larger ViT variant, and training ViT-H/14 costs over 80x more than training ViT-B/32.

nodes.name: Macro-level bottleneck: individual training is redundant across the family
nodes.description: From the macro view, inefficiency stems from individual training: models are trained using the same objectives, datasets, and protocols, yielding common knowledge within the family, but this is ignored, making traditional individual training highly repetitive and redundant.

nodes.name: Hypothesis: knowledge reuse from small to large models addresses both bottlenecks
nodes.description: The paper hypothesizes that both the micro (large-model cost) and macro (redundant training) bottlenecks can be simultaneously addressed by redefining the training pipeline to enable knowledge reuse from small to large models within the family.

components.description: Method: the model chain concept and CoM-PT pipeline

nodes.name: Models organized in ascending size order into a model chain
nodes.description: Models within a family are organized in ascending order of size to form a model chain, a pre-training sequence starting with the smallest model pre-trained individually in the standard manner, then each subsequent model leverages inverse knowledge transfer from its predecessor (Fig. 2).

nodes.name: Chain design eliminates isolation and reduces cost of larger models
nodes.description: The model chain eliminates the isolation of individual training by ensuring each model inherits knowledge from its strongest predecessor, drastically reducing the prohibitive pre-training costs of larger models while maintaining performance comparable to individual training.

nodes.name: Efficiency scales favorably with family size, sometimes counterintuitively
nodes.description: Beyond per-model efficiency gains, the chain design unlocks training efficiency that scales favorably with family size; e.g., the ViT-T->ViT-S->ViT-B->ViT-L chain reduces training costs by an additional 20% versus ViT-B->ViT-L, since the extended chain's smaller models converge in far fewer epochs, making the total overhead of the first three models smaller than training ViT-B from scratch.

components.description: Method: inverse knowledge transfer concept — dual knowledge representations

nodes.name: Inverse knowledge transfer inverts the teacher-student size relationship
nodes.description: Inverse knowledge transfer enables a knowledge relay along the model chain where each intermediate model first serves as a student learning from its predecessor, then as a teacher guiding its larger successor, differing from traditional KD in that the teacher-student size relation is inverted and intermediate models serve dual roles.

nodes.name: Knowledge exists statically in parameters and dynamically in features
nodes.description: Effective relay requires addressing different forms of knowledge representation: a model's knowledge is statically encoded in the parameter space, while exhibited dynamically in the feature space across different samples.

nodes.name: Weight initialization and feature distillation tailored for the two spaces
nodes.description: Weight initialization and feature distillation are tailored for knowledge reuse in the parameter space and feature space respectively, and their synergy ensures efficient knowledge transfer relay with speedups increasing progressively along the chain (Fig. 1).

components.description: Related work positioning: distinguishing CoM-PT from prior weight-reuse, KD, and CLIP acceleration work

nodes.name: Prior weight-reuse methods (Net2Net, NetExpand) initialize larger models from smaller ones
nodes.description: Net2Net first proposed reusing small model weights to initialize larger models via function-preserving transformations, and NetExpand advanced this using SVD-based width expansion and EMA depth scaling; similar LLM-pretraining approaches were found generally less effective.

nodes.name: Standard knowledge distillation and collaborative learning use large-to-small or same-size transfer
nodes.description: Vanilla KD and FitNet use large teacher logits/features to supervise smaller students, with further techniques on feature transform/selection/ensemble; collaborative learning approaches (ONE, DML) instead perform online ensemble or bidirectional distillation between same- or similar-sized networks.

nodes.name: Prior CLIP acceleration methods (FLIP, DeCLIP, ALIP, LaCLIP, DreamLIP) optimize single models
nodes.description: FLIP accelerates CLIP via random patch masking; data-efficient CLIP methods (DeCLIP, ALIP, LaCLIP, MLLM-A, DreamLIP) reduce required data scale via improved supervision/captioning, but all target single-model training efficiency.

nodes.name: CoM-PT instead targets family-level acceleration that scales with family size
nodes.description: In contrast to weight-reuse, KD/collaborative-learning, and single-model CLIP acceleration lines, CoM-PT focuses on accelerating the training pipeline at the model family level, with the novel objective of scaling efficiently with family size.

components.description: Method detail: inverse weight initialization and inverse feature distillation implementation

nodes.name: Inverse weight initialization handles width and depth differences via insertion and duplication
nodes.description: For block-block width differences, parameters of the smaller teacher are directly inserted into the larger student with remaining parameters randomly initialized; for layer-layer depth differences, weights of each layer are duplicated and indexed as the succeeding layer (Fig. 3, Step 1).

nodes.name: Vanilla implementations are prioritized since the model chain drives primary gains
nodes.description: Since empirical results (Table 4a) reveal the model chain itself drives primary efficiency gains, simplicity is prioritized and both inverse weight initialization and feature distillation are implemented using vanilla approaches rather than sophisticated designs.

nodes.name: Inverse feature distillation mirrors standard feature distillation formulation
nodes.description: Inverse feature distillation applies a feature transform to project student features into the teacher's feature space, minimizing an L2 loss between transformed student features and teacher features (Eq. 1), balanced against the task loss via coefficient α to ensure the distillation loss remains smaller than the task loss.

components.description: Method: three principled rules for model chain design

nodes.name: Two structural operations can further improve chain efficiency
nodes.description: Given a model chain, adding a smaller model before the first model, or inserting a medium-sized model between two chain members, can further accelerate convergence of subsequent models, provided the benefit outweighs the additional training cost.

nodes.name: Rule 1: optimal smallest model selection based on data scale
nodes.description: The smallest model size should be selected based on pre-training data scale — compact enough to maximize efficiency, yet with proper capacity to fit the data distribution, guaranteeing lossless training acceleration and a robust foundation for the chain.

nodes.name: Rule 2: intermediate model variants chosen via expansion ratio trade-off
nodes.description: Intermediate model variants are obtained by expanding their teacher's size; expansion ratios of 2x-4x yield considerable efficiency gains, with larger factors (4x) minimizing overall training cost and smaller factors (2x) maximizing acceleration ratio.

nodes.name: Rule 3: training epochs decrease linearly as model size grows exponentially
nodes.description: Training epoch allocation along the chain decreases linearly as model size increases exponentially under the premise of achieving lossless training acceleration; a linearly decreasing schedule is initialized and validated/relaxed based on the first network pair's outcome.

components.description: Test case: applying CoM-PT to CLIP with LaCLIP baseline and text augmentation

nodes.name: LaCLIP with stronger text augmentation chosen as the baseline
nodes.description: LaCLIP, a strong data-efficient CLIP variant with a neat formulation, is selected as the baseline and boosted using stronger text augmentation, expanding each image-text pair to 16x more text variations with 4 subcaptions randomly selected per iteration.

nodes.name: Standard CLIP contrastive task loss defined over augmented text-image pairs
nodes.description: The text-to-image contrastive loss is computed over M augmented positive text pairs per image (Eq. 2), and combined by duality with the image-to-text loss to form the overall task loss (Eq. 3).

nodes.name: Overall CoM-PT training loss combines task loss and bidirectional inverse feature distillation
nodes.description: The overall training loss sums the task loss and the averaged inverse feature distillation loss over visual and text teacher-student feature pairs (Eq. 4), applied alongside inverse weight initialization, requiring no modification to the baseline method due to CoM-PT's simplicity.

components.description: Finding: pilot study establishes fair baseline convergence and comparison

nodes.name: Standard 32-epoch CLIP schedules are insufficient on smaller datasets
nodes.description: Early CLIP studies standardized 32 epochs on large-scale datasets, and follow-up data-efficient methods adopted the same setting, but the paper empirically reveals models remain far from convergence with only 32 epochs on smaller datasets like CC3M.

nodes.name: 128 epochs established as converged baseline on CC3M; 64 for Merged-15M
nodes.description: Evaluation across 32-256 epochs on CC3M shows performance steadily improves up to 128 epochs, establishing 128 epochs as the standard baseline; for Merged-15M, 64 epochs is set to account for its 5x larger data scale (Fig. 4).

nodes.name: Boosted LaCLIP baseline outperforms leading data-efficient counterparts
nodes.description: Compared against original LaCLIP and MLLM-A (leading contrastive-loss-only approaches), the paper's baseline outperforms both (Table 1), establishing a solid foundation for validating the performance-lossless property of CoM-PT.

components.description: Finding: zero-shot classification and retrieval results demonstrate lossless acceleration

nodes.name: CoM-PT models generally exceed baseline on ImageNet-1K, VTAB+, and COCO
nodes.description: Models pre-trained with CoM-PT generally exceed the baseline on three zero-shot benchmarks, especially for the largest model; e.g., Swin-L on CC3M surpasses baseline by 0.29%/0.88%/1.72% on ImageNet-1K/VTAB+/COCO (Table 2).

nodes.name: Rare underperformance stays within the 0.5% lossless threshold
nodes.description: In the rare cases where performance slightly falls below baseline, differences remain within the defined 0.5% lossless threshold, ensuring family-level lossless acceleration is maintained.

nodes.name: Acceleration ratio increases with model size, up to ~7.5x at ViT-L
nodes.description: The individual acceleration ratio (in MACs and GPU hours) increases with model size, reaching around 7.5x at ViT-L, meaning the total family training cost is lower than training the largest model alone (Fig. 5, Table 2).

nodes.name: GPU-hour acceleration is slightly lower than MACs acceleration due to smaller-model GPU underutilization
nodes.description: The accumulated acceleration ratio in GPU hours is slightly lower than in MACs because smaller models have lower GPU utilization, causing disproportionately longer training time; still, CoM-PT achieves 4.10x/3.80x acceleration for ViT/Swin on CC3M and 2.37x for ViT on Merged-15M.

components.description: Finding: fine-tuning transferability on downstream tasks

nodes.name: CoM-PT-pretrained backbones outperform baseline across segmentation and VL tasks
nodes.description: Models trained with CoM-PT outperform baselines across all five open-vocabulary segmentation datasets (average improvements of 5.64%/6.14% for ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16) and across vision-language benchmarks after LoRA-based fine-tuning (Table 3).

nodes.name: Fine-grained segmentation datasets show especially large gains, suggesting better representations
nodes.description: For fine-grained datasets ADE-847 and PC-459, the gain from CoM-PT exceeds 3x over baseline, suggesting the acceleration stems from both faster convergence and genuinely better representation capability, not just faster training.

components.description: Ablation: the model chain drives primary efficiency gain over inverse weight initialization alone

nodes.name: Inverse weight initialization alone loses efficacy as model size increases
nodes.description: With inverse weight initialization alone (no chain relay), independently trained ViT-S/ViT-B need 1.3x/5.1x more epochs to approach CoM-PT performance, showing IWI alone loses acceleration efficacy as model size increases (Table 4a).

nodes.name: The knowledge transfer relay along the chain is the pivotal mechanism
nodes.description: Because IWI alone degrades with scale, the knowledge transfer relay provided by the model chain plays the pivotal role in accelerating the training pipeline, assisted by both components of inverse knowledge transfer applied at each step.

components.description: Ablation: complementarity of inverse weight initialization and inverse feature distillation

nodes.name: Both IWI and IFD individually improve zero-shot performance, peaking when combined
nodes.description: Table 4(b) shows both inverse weight initialization and inverse feature distillation individually improve zero-shot IN-1K/COCO performance over the baseline, with the combination of both components yielding the best performance.

nodes.name: IWI accelerates early training while IFD sustains benefits throughout
nodes.description: Further analysis reveals IWI primarily accelerates early training, whereas IFD provides sustained benefits throughout training, explaining why combining both components in inverse knowledge transfer yields synergistic gains.

components.description: Finding: training epoch allocation follows the third principled rule

nodes.name: Required training epochs decrease roughly uniformly as model size grows
nodes.description: By interpolating performance curves across epochs, required training epochs for ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-L to match baseline decrease in a roughly uniform manner (23.45, 18.28, 12.34 epochs respectively), even as model size grows exponentially along the chain (Fig. 8).

components.description: Finding: robustness of acceleration across training epochs and data scales

nodes.name: Acceleration ratio remains above 4x even with fewer baseline epochs
nodes.description: Reducing default training epochs on CC3M from 128 to 64 and 32, the overall acceleration ratio stably sustains above 4x, validating that CoM-PT's efficacy does not rely on longer training epochs (Fig. 9a).

nodes.name: Acceleration stabilizes around 2.8x-2.3x as data scale grows toward 2B
nodes.description: Across pre-training data scales from 22.0M to 206.8M image-text pairs, acceleration ratio first sharply decreases then stabilizes around 2.8x from 103.4M to 206.8M pairs, with extrapolation to 2B scale maintaining above 2.3x acceleration (Fig. 9b).

isolated_nodes.name: VFM scalability and system-level pre-training infrastructure
isolated_nodes.description: VFMs demonstrate extraordinary scalability up to 18B parameters and 2B pre-training data scale, relying on system-level optimizations such as distributed data parallel modules, mixed-precision training, and memory management.

isolated_nodes.name: Evaluation protocol overview
isolated_nodes.description: Evaluation spans 45 datasets: zero-shot performance on ImageNet-1K, COCO, and the 35-dataset VTAB+ benchmark; fine-tuning performance on ADE-847/150, PC-459/59, VOC-20 for segmentation (via SAN), and TextVQA, ScienceQA, POPE, VQAv2 for vision-language tasks (via LLaVA-1.5-7B).

isolated_nodes.name: Lossless acceleration definition
isolated_nodes.description: Lossless acceleration is defined as achieving performance with less than 0.5% accuracy loss compared to baseline under the same training protocol while requiring reduced training time and computational complexity; when all models in a family satisfy this, family-level lossless acceleration is considered verified.

isolated_nodes.name: Model families and frameworks used for generalization testing
isolated_nodes.description: Generalization is verified on two model families (ViT and Swin) and datasets CC3M/CC12M (merged into Merged-15M), following hyperparameter settings from prior work.

structural_reasoning: The graph follows a problem-diagnosis-then-solution structure typical of a systems/efficiency paper. C1 (motivation: VFM family cost dilemma) leads into C2 (diagnosis of micro/macro bottlenecks), which motivates the core method components C3 (the model chain concept) and C4 (inverse knowledge transfer's dual parameter/feature-space treatment) — these two form the heart of CoM-PT. C5 positions the method against three related-work lines (weight reuse, KD/collaborative learning, single-model CLIP acceleration), clarifying its family-level novelty. C6 details the concrete vanilla implementations of inverse weight initialization and feature distillation, while C7 supplies three design rules for constructing/extending a model chain in practice; C8 instantiates the full method on CLIP/LaCLIP as the paper's test case. From there, the experimental components fan out: C9 establishes fair baseline convergence prerequisites; C10 and C11 report the flagship zero-shot and fine-tuning transfer results validating lossless acceleration; C12 and C13 are ablations isolating the chain's primacy and the complementarity of the two inverse-transfer components; C14 and C15 examine robustness of the epoch-allocation rule and of acceleration ratios across training budgets and data scales. Background on VFM scalability/infrastructure, the evaluation protocol, the lossless-acceleration definition, and model-family/framework choices are treated as isolated nodes since they are supporting context referenced throughout rather than links in the causal/argumentative chain.

components.description: Motivation: KD training cost and the two obstacles to data pruning for KD

nodes.name: KD achieves efficient inference but not efficient training
nodes.description: Knowledge Distillation lets compact students inherit teacher knowledge for efficient inference, but does not alleviate training burden since students are usually distilled on the entire dataset under teacher guidance, incurring significant training cost.

nodes.name: Data pruning proposed to reduce KD training cost
nodes.description: An emerging line of research points to reducing the number of samples participating in distillation (data pruning) as a way to retain competitive performance while cutting training cost, with Baruch et al. re-evaluating classical pruning methods and Chen et al. introducing a KD-specific pruning method using teacher cross-entropy loss within a medium-difficulty window.

nodes.name: Obstacle 1: Efficiency-Effectiveness trade-off in score estimation
nodes.description: High-fidelity trajectory-based difficulty metrics (EL2N, Forgetting, AUM) are computationally prohibitive for KD because they need training-time statistics not available from pretrained teachers, while cheap CE-loss scoring is an unreliable difficulty indicator since over-parameterized networks can overfit even hard/mislabeled samples, producing weakly discriminative losses.

nodes.name: Obstacle 2: Rigid and suboptimal sampling heuristics
nodes.description: Even with reliable scores, conventional sampling strategies (top-k, fixed-cutoff stratified sampling, window-based selection) impose a fixed selection region that cannot adapt to varying data distributions and teacher-student dynamics across KD settings, limiting performance.

nodes.name: IF-Beta proposed to unify IF scoring with a learnable Beta sampling policy
nodes.description: To overcome both obstacles, the paper proposes IF-Beta (Influence Function based Beta Policy), which unifies influence-function scoring with a learnable probabilistic pruning policy parameterized by a Beta distribution.

components.description: Preliminaries: KD loss and influence function formulation

nodes.name: Standard KD loss combines CE and KL terms
nodes.description: The student is trained by minimizing a weighted combination of standard cross-entropy loss and a KL-divergence distillation term between teacher and student predictive distributions (Eq. 3).

nodes.name: Data pruning is a two-stage pipeline: score then select
nodes.description: Most existing pruning methods follow a two-stage pipeline of estimating a per-sample score (difficulty or uncertainty, typically requiring training dynamics) and then selecting a subset via heuristic rules (top-k, stratified cutoff, sliding window) under a given pruning ratio.

nodes.name: Classical influence functions quantify per-sample impact
nodes.description: Influence functions estimate how a model's predictions would change if a training point were removed, expressed via the gradient and inverse Hessian of the loss at the optimal parameters (Eqs. 4-6), but were historically considered impractical due to high computational cost and unreliable estimation quality in deep networks.

components.description: Finding/Method 1: IF-FVM as an efficient, reliable score estimator

nodes.name: SAM-based fine-tuning toward a flat validation minimum (FVM) stabilizes IF
nodes.description: Building on recent advances showing that optimizing toward a flat validation minimum stabilizes influence estimation, the teacher model is fine-tuned on the validation set using Sharpness-Aware Minimization (Eq. 8), enforcing local flatness of the loss landscape.

nodes.name: IF-FVM score derived from the SAM-tuned teacher
nodes.description: Under the FVM condition, the influence of a training sample on the validation set is computed using gradients and the Hessian of the SAM-tuned teacher (Eq. 9), approximated via a diagonal Fisher Information matrix in place of the full inverse Hessian for practicality at scale.

nodes.name: IF-FVM correlates strongly with trajectory-based difficulty metrics
nodes.description: Spearman rank correlation experiments (Fig. 1) show IF-FVM consistently aligns more strongly with established difficulty metrics (EL2N, AUM) than CE-loss or IF-LiSSA baselines, validating it as a computationally efficient yet robust score estimator for KD pruning.

components.description: Finding/Method 2: limitations of existing sampling strategies motivate the Beta Policy

nodes.name: CCS exhibits a threshold shift between KD and non-KD settings
nodes.description: CCS's optimal cutoff ratio varies significantly between KD and non-KD settings, making pre-defined hyperparameters non-transferable (Figs. 2a-2b).

nodes.name: BWS is hindered by a suboptimal fixed-window design
nodes.description: Replacement experiments show that introducing randomness into BWS's selection window actually improves performance, revealing that its fixed-window design is suboptimal (Fig. 2c).

nodes.name: These findings motivate an adaptive, learnable sampling strategy
nodes.description: The threshold-shift and fixed-window limitations of CCS and BWS underscore the need for an adaptive, learnable sampling strategy beyond rigid heuristic-based selection.

components.description: Method: Beta Policy formulation for adaptive sampling

nodes.name: Scores normalized to percentiles for Beta parameterization
nodes.description: Precomputed IF-FVM difficulty scores are mapped via rank-to-percentile normalization onto [0,1], with smaller normalized values corresponding to more difficult samples.

nodes.name: Selection probability parameterized by a Beta distribution
nodes.description: Each sample's selection probability is parameterized using a Beta distribution over the normalized score (Eq. 10), with learnable parameters ϕ jointly controlling the shape parameters α and β.

nodes.name: Beta Policy defines a fixed-ratio sampling distribution over masks
nodes.description: The Beta Policy is a Beta-distribution-based categorical distribution over binary mask vectors conditioned on ϕ and pruning ratio r, constrained to a fixed number of selected samples (Eqs. 11-12), yielding the pruned subset.

nodes.name: Beta Policy is more flexible than CCS/BWS's fixed supports
nodes.description: The continuous, flexible Beta density over the sample space (Fig. 3) contrasts with the rigid, uniform sampling over predefined support sets used by CCS and BWS, enabling more adaptive selection.

components.description: Method: bilevel optimization of the Beta Policy via policy gradients

nodes.name: Beta Policy search posed as bilevel optimization
nodes.description: Finding the optimal Beta Policy is formulated as a bilevel problem: the outer objective minimizes expected validation loss over policy-sampled masks, while the inner objective trains the student on the sampled subset via the KD loss (Eqs. 13-15).

nodes.name: Direct bilevel gradient requires costly implicit differentiation
nodes.description: Naively differentiating the bilevel objective yields a gradient requiring implicit differentiation through the inner optimum, which is computationally prohibitive for deep networks.

nodes.name: Policy gradient estimator avoids implicit differentiation
nodes.description: By exploiting the Beta Policy's probabilistic formulation, an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (Theorem 1, Eqs. 17-18) is used instead, eliminating the need for implicit differentiation and enabling SGD updates of ϕ (Eq. 19).

components.description: Method: efficient inner-loop optimization via frozen teacher feature space

nodes.name: Inner-loop retraining to convergence per policy update is expensive
nodes.description: Although the outer loop is efficiently optimized via policy gradients, the inner-loop optimization remains costly since it would require retraining the full student network to convergence for every policy update.

nodes.name: Surrogate student: linear classifier on frozen teacher features
nodes.description: The KD structure is leveraged by replacing the full student with a surrogate: a trainable linear classification head attached to frozen teacher features, reformulating the student model as a linear map over frozen features (Eq. 20).

nodes.name: Inner objective reduces to a fast single-linear-layer optimization
nodes.description: The inner-loop objective becomes optimizing only a single linear classifier on the subset (Eq. 21), which is efficient and keeps overall bilevel optimization computationally negligible in overhead.

nodes.name: Formulation generalizes to standard supervised pruning
nodes.description: The general bilevel formulation applies to both KD and standard supervised classification by swapping the inner KD loss for a standard CE loss, enabling IF-Beta to serve as a general-purpose data pruning framework.

components.description: Finding: IF-Beta outperforms baselines across datasets/pruning ratios and surpasses full-data distillation

nodes.name: IF-Beta consistently outperforms retraining and retraining-free baselines
nodes.description: Across CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet under KD, IF-Beta consistently outperforms all baselines including DUAL (which needs partial retraining) and Medium-Difficulty (retraining-free) across all pruning ratios (Fig. 4).

nodes.name: IF-Beta surpasses full-data distillation with less data
nodes.description: IF-Beta enables students trained on a pruned subset to surpass full-data distillation performance, e.g., 70% retained on CIFAR-10 (95.69% vs 95.50%), 90% on CIFAR-100 (79.53% vs 79.38%), and 50% on ImageNet (74.02% vs 73.54%).

nodes.name: Not all training samples are equally beneficial for KD
nodes.description: The ability to surpass full-data performance with fewer samples suggests some samples actively impede student generalization, and pruning them yields a cleaner, more informative training signal.

nodes.name: IF-Beta generalizes across heterogeneous teacher architectures
nodes.description: IF-Beta is further validated with ResNet-50/101, WideResNet, and ViT-Base teachers, consistently outperforming all retraining-free baselines across settings.

components.description: Finding: sample efficiency under constrained training budgets

nodes.name: IF-Beta outperforms full-data and random pruning under tight budgets
nodes.description: Under severely constrained iteration budgets, IF-Beta with 50% data pruned achieves 90.80% (CIFAR-10), 67.31% (CIFAR-100), and 60.70% (ImageNet), all exceeding full-data baselines and consistently beating random pruning (Table 1).

nodes.name: Gains stem from selection quality, not just fewer samples
nodes.description: The consistent margin over random pruning demonstrates that IF-Beta's gains are not solely from a favorable training regime induced by fewer samples but stem from effective sample selection itself.

components.description: Finding: end-to-end compute savings and comparison with efficient KD methods

nodes.name: IF-Beta surpasses full-data performance faster and cheaper
nodes.description: Including the pruning process cost, IF-Beta reaches or surpasses full-data students' final performance using less time across CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet (relative costs 0.806x-0.915x) (Table 2).

nodes.name: IF-Beta beats prior efficient KD methods in accuracy and training time
nodes.description: Distilling ResNet-34 into MobileNet on ImageNet, IF-Beta achieves the best accuracy (71.20%) while requiring only 19.24 hours, less than half the cost of the full-data Baseline (39.86h) and Medium-Difficulty* (36.98h) (Table 3).

nodes.name: Efficiency gains stem from reduced data, fewer teacher queries, and subset quality
nodes.description: The efficiency gains stem from three factors: reduced data volume (70% subset), no repeated teacher queries per epoch, and a higher-quality subset preserving distillation effectiveness even under one-shot teacher logits.

components.description: Finding: generality across distillation objectives

nodes.name: IF-Beta is not tied to a specific KD loss
nodes.description: Evaluated under Relational KD, FitNets, and Attention Transfer objectives on CIFAR-10/100, IF-Beta consistently outperforms both Random pruning and Medium-Difficulty across all losses, pruning ratios, and datasets (Table 4).

nodes.name: Data quality may matter more than the distillation algorithm
nodes.description: Consistent benefits across diverse training budgets, distillation objectives, and teacher-student pairs suggest that careful data curation is a universally effective and complementary strategy for improving efficiency and effectiveness of KD, potentially mattering more than algorithmic specifics.

components.description: Ablation: advantage of the learnable Beta Policy over IF-CCS/IF-BWS

nodes.name: IF-CCS and IF-BWS combine IF scores with fixed selection rules
nodes.description: To isolate the contribution of the sampling policy, CCS and BWS are combined with the paper's IF-based scores (IF-CCS, IF-BWS), which do not require retraining.

nodes.name: IF-Beta outperforms IF-CCS and IF-BWS across ratios and datasets
nodes.description: Across CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet at multiple pruning ratios, IF-Beta consistently outperforms both IF-CCS and IF-BWS (Table 5), demonstrating that the learnable Beta Policy provides clear advantages over fixed-threshold and fixed-window selection even when using the same underlying scores.

components.description: Finding: generality to standard (non-KD) data pruning

nodes.name: IF-Beta remains competitive without KD by swapping in CE loss
nodes.description: With the inner objective replaced by standard CE loss (per P25), IF-Beta remains competitive and consistently outperforms other baselines across all pruning ratios on CIFAR-10/100 in the standard supervised pruning setting (Fig. 5).

nodes.name: Off-the-shelf pretrained models can replace in-domain models for IF scoring
nodes.description: Thanks to the FVM property, a generic ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 can replace an in-domain pretrained model to compute IF scores when no in-domain pretrained model is available, avoiding retraining costs while still yielding competitive pruning performance (Table 6).

nodes.name: IF-Beta can fully avoid retraining cost for standard data pruning
nodes.description: Using a generic pretrained model for scoring means IF-Beta can completely avoid any retraining cost while still providing strong pruning quality in the standard (non-KD) data pruning setting.

isolated_nodes.name: Prior KD acceleration methods trade off student performance
isolated_nodes.description: Several prior methods explored accelerating KD training, but their speedups typically come at the cost of degrading student performance.

isolated_nodes.name: Formal KD notation and loss definitions
isolated_nodes.description: Formal notation for the training dataset, teacher/student networks, and the weighted CE+KL loss combination underlying the KD framework (Eq. 3, Sec 2).

isolated_nodes.name: Baseline method taxonomy
isolated_nodes.description: Baselines are grouped into methods requiring partial/full retraining (EL2N, GraNd, Forgetting, DUAL) and retraining-free methods (Random, Medium-Difficulty), with CCS and BWS re-implemented using the paper's IF-based scores for fair comparison.

isolated_nodes.name: Training and dataset details
isolated_nodes.description: CIFAR-10/100 models are trained with batch size 128 for 40K iterations (~200 epochs); ImageNet students are trained with batch size 128 for 300K iterations (~30 epochs); results are averaged over three random seeds (0,1,2).

structural_reasoning: The graph follows a linear methodological build-up typical of a proposed-method paper. C1 (motivation: KD training cost and the two pruning obstacles) and C2 (KD/IF preliminaries) establish the problem and formal background feeding into C3 (the IF-FVM score estimator, solving obstacle 1) and C4 (empirical critique of CCS/BWS, motivating obstacle 2's fix). C5 (Beta Policy formulation) builds directly on both C3's scores and C4's motivation, feeding into C6 (bilevel optimization via policy gradients) and C7 (efficient feature-space inner loop), which together constitute the full IF-Beta method and also enable generalization to non-KD pruning (P25). The experimental components C8-C13 form a fan-out from the completed method: C8 establishes the flagship result (outperforming baselines, surpassing full-data distillation), which C9 (constrained budgets), C10 (compute savings vs. efficient KD methods), and C11 (generality across KD losses) each extend along a different axis, converging on the paper's central takeaway (P36) that data quality may matter more than the distillation algorithm. C12 isolates the sampling-policy's own contribution via controlled ablation (IF-CCS/IF-BWS), while C13 closes the loop by showing the bilevel framework generalizes beyond KD to standard data pruning, even without any in-domain pretrained model. Baseline taxonomy, formal notation, and training/dataset configuration details are treated as isolated nodes since they provide supporting context rather than participating in the causal/argumentative chains.
